title: IDSPACE: A Novel Document Generator for Reliable Evaluation of Digital Identity Verification Systems [Extended Technical Report]
summary: As services move online, trust institutions such as banks, lenders, and governments must verify the identity of remote users. Fraud detection tools are widely available, but evaluating and fine-tuning them remains difficult because identity documents are sensitive and therefore scarce. Synthetic data generation offers a path forward, and demand is clear: our prior work in this area has been downloaded over $11{,}000$ times (aggregated from eight parts). We introduce IDSpace, extending this line of research in three directions. First, we propose model-guided Bayesian optimization, which tunes generation parameters to maximize both visual similarity and prediction consistency with target-domain models given only a few samples from a target domain. Second, we decouple user-specified metadata (demographics, fraud patterns, capture device) from automatically tuned control parameters (font styles, noise levels, image quality), allowing users to configure evaluations without low-level expertise. Third, we expand beyond template images to support scanned and mobile-captured documents. Experiments show IDSpace improves evaluation consistency by $15-45\%$ over baselines including CycleGAN, diffusion inpainting, and non-guided optimization, using only a few real samples, while improving training accuracy by up to $9\%$ and SSIM similarity with the target domain by $10\%$. We also released a new dataset consisting of $359{,}240$ high-quality synthetic documents across ten European ID types.

AI.tldr: IDSpace is a synthetic identity document generation framework that uses model-guided Bayesian optimization to tune generation parameters, decoupling user metadata from control parameters. It supports scanned and mobile-captured documents, improving evaluation consistency by 15-45% over baselines and releasing a dataset of 359,240 synthetic ID documents across ten European ID types.
AI.motivation: As services move online, trust institutions need to verify remote user identities, but evaluating and fine-tuning fraud detection tools is difficult because identity documents are sensitive and scarce. Synthetic data generation offers a solution, with prior work having been downloaded over 11,000 times.
AI.method: IDSpace proposes three main contributions: 1) Model-guided Bayesian optimization to tune generation parameters for visual similarity and prediction consistency with target-domain models using only a few samples; 2) Decoupling user-specified metadata (demographics, fraud patterns, capture device) from automatically tuned control parameters (font styles, noise levels, image quality); 3) Expanding beyond template images to support scanned and mobile-captured documents.
AI.result: IDSpace improves evaluation consistency by 15-45% over baselines (CycleGAN, diffusion inpainting, non-guided optimization) using only a few real samples, while improving training accuracy by up to 9% and SSIM similarity with the target domain by 10%. A new dataset of 359,240 high-quality synthetic documents across ten European ID types was released.
AI.conclusion: IDSpace provides an effective solution for generating synthetic identity documents for evaluation and training of fraud detection tools, with significant improvements in consistency, accuracy, and visual similarity, while addressing the scarcity of real identity documents.

title: Position: Unlabeled IS NOT Equal to No Human Supervision in Visual Learning
summary: This position paper argues that the absence of labels does not imply the absence of human supervision in visual learning, and urges the research community to identify sources of supervision more explicitly. Many recent methods in computer vision build upon representations learned from large-scale unlabeled data, and are therefore grouped under the same umbrella term ``unsupervised.'' However, different data curation schemes and training objectives embed substantially different human priors on which models rely, and we argue that one ``unsupervised'' umbrella term is no longer capturing these distinctions. This ambiguity makes it harder to compare unsupervised learning research conducted under different assumptions, coinciding with a sharp decline in papers titled with ``unsupervised'' in flagship computer vision conferences since 2021, despite continued growth of the field. While we fully embrace pre-training as a strong foundation for modern computer vision, we advocate for a community-level effort toward greater conceptual clarity: authors are encouraged to disclose priors in data selection and learning objectives, and to specify which components of a learning pipeline depend on which assumptions. Standardized disclosure practices can improve academic communication, ensure fairer comparisons, and preserve methodological diversity in unsupervised learning.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the term "unsupervised learning" in computer vision is too broad and misleading, as many methods that claim to be unsupervised actually rely on human supervision through data curation and training objectives. The authors urge the community to be more explicit about the sources of supervision in their methods.
AI.motivation: The ambiguity in the term "unsupervised" makes it difficult to compare research conducted under different assumptions. The authors note a decline in papers using "unsupervised" in titles at top CV conferences since 2021, despite continued growth in the field.
AI.method: This is a position paper that analyzes the conceptual issues with the term "unsupervised" in visual learning, examining different data curation schemes and training objectives that embed human priors.
AI.result: The paper identifies that various "unsupervised" methods embed substantially different human priors through data selection and learning objectives, making the umbrella term misleading for comparison and communication.
AI.conclusion: The authors advocate for standardized disclosure practices where authors explicitly disclose priors in data selection and learning objectives, and specify which components depend on which assumptions. This will improve academic communication, ensure fairer comparisons, and preserve methodological diversity.

title: Exemplar: Classical Priors Complement Frozen Features for Few-Shot Microscopy Segmentation at Native Resolution
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Code, configurations, and the per-image score records behind every reported number: https://github.com/michalprusek/Exemplar
summary: Segmenting a new biomedical dataset usually means a domain-specific model trained on substantial annotation, or a foundation model steered at inference time. We present Exemplar, a few-shot segmenter that fuses a frozen DINOv3 backbone with a fixed bank of classical native-resolution filter responses in one lightweight head, fitted from the support masks alone. In the few-mask, native-resolution regime, classical priors and frozen self-supervised features are complementary: fused in one head, a single fixed configuration spans eleven biomedical imaging datasets. Under the same head, the classical bank alone reaches 0.693 on the eleven-dataset panel, scored by foreground intersection-over-union or centreline Dice, and the frozen features alone 0.672; the bank leads on seven of the eleven and the features on the rest, and fused they reach 0.782. Against five forward-pass few-shot methods, Exemplar leads in 54 of 55 method-dataset comparisons, 52 of them significant after Holm correction. From a single annotated mask it reaches 0.703 on the same panel, against 0.682 for a from-scratch nnU-Net trained on that same mask. At eight masks nnU-Net overtakes it on the panel mean, chiefly on centreline agreement, but takes 16-77x longer to fit.

AI.tldr: Exemplar is a few-shot biomedical image segmenter that combines frozen DINOv3 self-supervised features with classical filter bank priors in a single lightweight head. It achieves 0.782 mean IoU across 11 diverse biomedical datasets, significantly outperforming 5 competing methods in 54/55 comparisons, while being trained from just 1-8 support masks.
AI.motivation: Biomedical image segmentation typically requires either domain-specific models with extensive annotations or foundation models at inference time. This paper addresses the need for a lightweight few-shot segmenter that can work across diverse biomedical datasets without extensive training, leveraging the complementary strengths of classical image priors and modern self-supervised features.
AI.method: Exemplar fuses a frozen DINOv3 backbone with a fixed bank of classical native-resolution filter responses in one lightweight head. The method is fitted from support masks alone without any task-specific training. Classical filter responses capture low-level image structure while DINOv3 features provide high-level semantic information.
AI.result: On an 11-dataset biomedical imaging panel: classical bank alone achieves 0.693 IoU, frozen features alone achieve 0.672, and fused together reach 0.782. The classical bank leads on 7 datasets while features lead on 4. Against 5 forward-pass few-shot methods, Exemplar wins 54/55 comparisons (52 significant after Holm correction). With a single annotated mask, Exemplar achieves 0.703 vs 0.682 for from-scratch nnU-Net. At 8 masks, nnU-Net overtakes on panel mean but requires 16-77x longer fitting time.
AI.conclusion: Exemplar demonstrates that classical priors and frozen self-supervised features are complementary in few-shot biomedical segmentation. Their fusion in a single lightweight head achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse datasets with minimal annotation requirements, offering an efficient alternative to traditional fully-trained models like nnU-Net.

title: Solving the Needle-in-a-Haystack Problem in Mammography Vision-Language Model with Differentiable Subset Sampling
summary: There is growing interest in adopting CLIP-style vision--language model (VLM) pretraining for mammography. However, models that directly employ the standard CLIP architecture and training objective exhibit limited zero-shot performance in clinically important tasks such as cancer, finding-type, and BI-RADS predictions. We argue that this underwhelming performance is due to neglecting two characteristics of mammography data: (1) its high-res nature, and (2) homogeneity of radiology reports, largely driven by a predominance of negative/benign findings on examinations. We propose TopKSigLIP, a VLM designed to address these two limitations through a novel architecture and learning objectives. Instead of downscaling high-res mammography images to satisfy GPU memory constraints, TopKSigLIP introduces TopK-Patch module that learns to sample a sparse set of high-res patches likely to contain lesions, sidestepping the resolution--batch size tradeoff of VLM training. The sampled patch locations additionally serve as a built-in localization tool. To address report homogeneity, we replace the contrastive loss, which falsely repels semantically similar pairs, with a Sup-sigmoid loss. Sup-sigmoid loss extends the sigmoid loss from SigLIP with soft labels derived from structured data. TopKSigLIP outperforms existing open-source mammography and general medical VLMs on both internal and external benchmarks on density assessment, BI-RADS classification, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction under zero-shot evaluation. TopKSigLIP remains competitive under linear probing despite using a significantly smaller vision encoder and smaller training batches than baselines. The TopK-Patch module additionally achieves superior lesion localization over post-hoc Grad-CAM. Code and weights are made public:https://github.com/Youngseok0001/TopKSigLIP.

AI.tldr: TopKSigLIP is a vision-language model for mammography that addresses two key limitations of standard CLIP: (1) high-resolution image requirements and (2) homogeneity of radiology reports. It introduces a TopK-Patch module for sparse high-res patch sampling and a Sup-sigmoid loss to handle report homogeneity, outperforming existing VLMs on zero-shot mammography tasks.
AI.motivation: Standard CLIP-style VLM pretraining underperforms on mammography tasks due to ignoring two critical characteristics: (1) the high-resolution nature of mammography images, and (2) the homogeneity of radiology reports dominated by negative/benign findings. These limitations affect zero-shot performance in clinically important tasks like cancer detection, finding-type classification, and BI-RADS predictions.
AI.method: TopKSigLIP addresses these limitations through two novel components: (1) TopK-Patch module - learns to sample sparse high-res patches likely to contain lesions, avoiding the resolution-batch size tradeoff; (2) Sup-sigmoid loss - replaces contrastive loss with sigmoid loss extended with soft labels derived from structured data to handle report homogeneity. The model uses a smaller vision encoder and smaller training batches compared to baselines.
AI.result: TopKSigLIP outperforms existing open-source mammography and general medical VLMs on internal and external benchmarks for: density assessment, BI-RADS classification, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction under zero-shot evaluation. It remains competitive under linear probing despite using a significantly smaller vision encoder and smaller training batches. The TopK-Patch module also achieves superior lesion localization over post-hoc Grad-CAM.
AI.conclusion: TopKSigLIP successfully addresses the unique challenges of mammography VLM pretraining through innovative architecture (TopK-Patch) and loss function (Sup-sigmoid). It demonstrates strong zero-shot performance across multiple clinical tasks while being computationally efficient, with the added benefit of built-in lesion localization capabilities.

title: SISER: Speaker-Invariant Speech Emotion Recognition with Entropy-Based Adversarial Training
summary: Speech emotion recognition (SER) faces two fundamental challenges: scarcity of labeled data and inter-speaker variability, both of which hinder generalization of emotion recognition systems. While prior adversarial approaches address speaker variability, they fall short in leveraging powerful pre-trained representations. We propose SISER (Speaker-Invariant Speech Emotion Recognition), integrating wav2vec 2.0 as a feature encoder and ECAPA-TDNN as a speaker discriminator within an entropy-based adversarial training scheme. wav2vec 2.0 provides rich self-supervised representations that alleviate dependency on large labeled datasets, while ECAPA-TDNN enables suppression of speaker identity via a stronger adversarial signal than shallow classifiers. Evaluated on IEMOCAP, SISER achieves a UA of 60.63%, outperforming the baseline (51.15%) and wav2vec 2.0 without speaker suppression (56.46%), with ablation emphasizing that the choice of speaker classifier architecture is a key factor.

AI.tldr: SISER proposes a speaker-invariant speech emotion recognition method that combines wav2vec 2.0 pre-trained representations with ECAPA-TDNN-based adversarial training to address data scarcity and inter-speaker variability challenges. The system achieves 60.63% UA on IEMOCAP, outperforming baseline and wav2vec 2.0 without speaker suppression.
AI.motivation: Speech emotion recognition suffers from two fundamental challenges: (1) scarcity of labeled data and (2) inter-speaker variability, both of which hinder generalization of emotion recognition systems. Prior adversarial approaches address speaker variability but fail to leverage powerful pre-trained representations.
AI.method: SISER integrates wav2vec 2.0 as a feature encoder and ECAPA-TDNN as a speaker discriminator within an entropy-based adversarial training scheme. wav2vec 2.0 provides rich self-supervised representations to alleviate dependency on large labeled datasets, while ECAPA-TDNN enables stronger adversarial signal for suppressing speaker identity compared to shallow classifiers.
AI.result: On IEMOCAP, SISER achieves UA of 60.63%, outperforming the baseline (51.15%) and wav2vec 2.0 without speaker suppression (56.46%). Ablation study confirms that the choice of speaker classifier architecture is a key factor.
AI.conclusion: The combination of self-supervised pre-trained representations (wav2vec 2.0) with a strong speaker discriminator (ECAPA-TDNN) in an adversarial training framework effectively addresses both data scarcity and inter-speaker variability, with the speaker classifier architecture being a critical design choice.

title: The Geometry of Ignorance: LLMs Know When to Temper Bayesian Priors
summary: What does a language model predict when it has few clues? The answer lurks in its unembedding geometry: a single direction of the unembedding matrix encodes the unigram distribution of the training corpus, which serves as the Bayesian prior the model falls back on when uncertain. This structure --- which we term the \emph{direction of ignorance} --- appears in all four model families examined (\texttt{Llama}, \texttt{Qwen}, \texttt{Gemma}, and \texttt{Pythia}), ranging from 0.4B to 405B parameters. Projecting the final prediction state onto this direction yields a per-token \emph{prior loading factor} $λ$, which, empirically, declines steadily as the context becomes more informative. Formally, the same projection decomposes the prediction state into two orthogonal vectors that correspond exactly to the two factors of a tempered Bayesian update: a unigram prior raised to the exponent $λ$ and a context-driven likelihood. This geometric-probabilistic interpretation calibrates $λ$, making it meaningfully comparable across model sizes and families, with larger models generally exhibiting lower prior reliance in the high-context limit. Finally, we show that the direction of ignorance is causally active: raising or lowering $λ$ at the final prediction state steers the prediction toward or away from the unigram prior in KL divergence.

AI.tldr: This paper discovers that language models have a geometric structure in their unembedding matrix that encodes a "unigram prior" - essentially the word frequency distribution of the training data. This direction, called the "direction of ignorance," represents what the model defaults to when uncertain. The projection onto this direction yields a "prior loading factor" λ that decreases as context becomes more informative, and can be interpreted as a tempered Bayesian update.
AI.motivation: To understand what language models predict when they have few clues about the context - i.e., how they handle uncertainty by falling back on prior knowledge.
AI.method: The authors analyzed the unembedding geometry across four model families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Pythia) spanning 0.4B to 405B parameters. They projected the final prediction state onto a specific direction to compute a per-token prior loading factor λ, and demonstrated causal manipulation of predictions by adjusting λ.
AI.result: The direction of ignorance appears consistently across all model families. The prior loading factor λ declines steadily as context becomes more informative. Larger models generally exhibit lower prior reliance in the high-context limit. The geometric-probabilistic interpretation makes λ meaningfully comparable across model sizes and families.
AI.conclusion: The direction of ignorance is causally active - raising or lowering λ at the final prediction state can steer predictions toward or away from the unigram prior in KL divergence. This provides a geometric interpretation of how language models combine prior knowledge with contextual information through a tempered Bayesian update mechanism.

title: Structure and Implementation of New Practical English Textbooks Driven by Artificial Intelligence
summary: Artificial intelligence is changing the form of applied English materials from fixed paper sequences to adaptive learning systems that can diagnose learners, recommend tasks, and provide formative feedback. This paper studies the structure and application of a new practical English textbook driven by artificial intelligence. A five-layer architecture is proposed: knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, and teacher-side governance. A prototype was tested on 186 non-English-major undergraduates for eight weeks of teaching. Compared with a static digital textbook, the proposed system increased the unit completion accuracy from 72.4% to 84.9%, raised the average score for speaking tasks by 10.8 points, and reduced the teacher's correction time by 31.6%. Therefore, an AI-driven textbook can maintain the stability of the curriculum while providing personalised learning paths, rich practice materials and traceable classroom data.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an AI-driven adaptive English learning textbook with a five-layer architecture (knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, teacher-side governance). Tested on 186 undergraduates over 8 weeks, the system improved unit completion accuracy from 72.4% to 84.9%, increased speaking scores by 10.8 points, and reduced teacher correction time by 31.6% compared to static digital textbooks.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to transform applied English materials from fixed, static content into adaptive learning systems capable of diagnosing learner needs, recommending personalized tasks, and providing formative feedback. Traditional textbooks cannot accommodate individual learner differences, while AI enables personalized learning paths while maintaining curriculum stability.
AI.method: The study employed a five-layer AI architecture: (1) knowledge mapping for content organization, (2) learner profiling for diagnosing learner profiles, (3) task generation for creating personalized assignments, (4) feedback orchestration for providing formative feedback, and (5) teacher-side governance for instructor oversight. A prototype was tested on 186 non-English-major undergraduates over an 8-week teaching period and compared against a static digital textbook.
AI.result: The AI-driven system demonstrated significant improvements across three metrics: (1) unit completion accuracy increased from 72.4% to 84.9%, (2) average speaking task scores improved by 10.8 points, and (3) teacher correction time was reduced by 31.6%.
AI.conclusion: AI-driven textbooks can maintain curriculum stability while providing personalized learning paths, rich practice materials, and traceable classroom data. The system successfully balances personalization with standardized learning objectives.

title: CAPQ-FAST: Content-Adaptive Perceived Quality Assessment for Faster Audiovisual Playback
comment: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology, doi: 10.1109/TCSVT.2026.3716481
summary: Faster playback has become a common feature in modern online audiovisual services, allowing users to consume content in less time while still maintaining a coherent viewing experience. However, different modalities of media content, such as video, audio (including speech and music), and audiovisual, exhibit varying requirements for understandability and information integrity under faster playback. These differences lead to noticeable variations in perceived quality depending on the content type. Nevertheless, users' perceived quality at different playback speeds remains insufficiently investigated. To address this gap, this paper conducts a series of subjective experiments to analyze the relationship between playback speed and perceived quality for video, audio, and audiovisual content. Content-specific intrinsic features are extracted to capture temporal dynamics, including temporal information (TI) for video, words per minute (WPM) for speech, and beats per minute (BPM) for music. Predictive models of perceived quality under faster playback are then developed separately for video, speech, and music. By integrating these models, a unified content-adaptive perceived quality assessment model (CAPQ-FAST) is proposed for faster audiovisual playback. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model effectively predicts perceived quality under different playback speeds. This model can help service providers better understand users' viewing intentions and perceptual experiences under faster playback, thereby enabling more adaptive personalized recommendations and playback control to enhance user experience adaptability.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the under-investigated area of users' perceived quality when consuming video, audio, and audiovisual content at faster playback speeds. The study proposes a unified content-adaptive perceived quality assessment model (CAPQ-FAST) that integrates modality-specific predictive models.
AI.motivation: Faster playback is a common feature in modern streaming services, but different content modalities (video, speech, music) have varying requirements for understandability under accelerated playback. Users' perceived quality at different speeds remains insufficiently studied, necessitating systematic investigation.
AI.method: The researchers conducted subjective experiments to analyze the relationship between playback speed and perceived quality across video, audio, and audiovisual content. Content-specific intrinsic features were extracted: Temporal Information (TI) for video, Words Per Minute (WPM) for speech, and Beats Per Minute (BPM) for music. Separate predictive models were developed for each modality, then integrated into a unified CAPQ-FAST model.
AI.result: The proposed CAPQ-FAST model effectively predicts perceived quality under different playback speeds across various content types.
AI.conclusion: The model enables service providers to better understand users' viewing intentions and perceptual experiences under faster playback, facilitating more adaptive personalized recommendations and playback control to enhance user experience.

title: ReRoom: Blending Virtual and Physical Contexts for In Situ Room Planning in Mixed Reality
summary: Planning a real domestic space is an in situ authoring process: users evaluate candidate layouts at true scale, refine their intent, and carry accepted decisions into later iterations. Existing approaches either separate layout editing from the physical room or provide limited support for evaluating and refining whole-room proposals in situ. We present ReRoom, a mixed-reality system for in situ room-layout authoring. ReRoom presents a shared layout state through a virtual room proxy spatially registered to the target room, allowing interaction and layout generation to remain grounded in the physical context. Users refine the current proposal through direct manipulation or language and preserve accepted placements, allowing each generated update to continue the same evolving design. To balance layout quality with generation efficiency, ReRoom uses a skill-guided layout agent whose room-layout design skill operationalizes three principles that we formulate by synthesizing established interior-design guidance for real-room layout generation. The skill grounds these principles in a normalized representation of the scanned room and reusable geometric checks. Evaluations show that ReRoom produces high-quality layouts for non-rectangular rooms, while its in situ workflow improves the room-planning experience over an otherwise equivalent off-site VR workflow. Code will be released upon acceptance of the paper.

AI.tldr: ReRoom is a mixed-reality system for in situ room-layout authoring that allows users to evaluate, refine, and generate room layouts at true scale within the physical space. It uses a skill-guided layout agent based on interior design principles and shows improved layout quality and user experience compared to off-site VR workflows.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches for room layout planning either separate layout editing from the physical room or provide limited support for evaluating and refining whole-room proposals in situ. There was a need for a system that allows users to interact with layout proposals directly in the physical space at true scale.
AI.method: ReRoom presents a shared layout state through a virtual room proxy spatially registered to the target room. Users refine proposals through direct manipulation or language and preserve accepted placements. The system uses a skill-guided layout agent that operationalizes three principles synthesized from interior-design guidance, grounded in a normalized representation of the scanned room and reusable geometric checks.
AI.result: ReRoom produces high-quality layouts for non-rectangular rooms, and its in situ workflow improves the room-planning experience over an otherwise equivalent off-site VR workflow.
AI.conclusion: The research demonstrates that mixed-reality systems for in situ room-layout authoring can produce high-quality layouts and improve user experience compared to traditional off-site VR approaches. The skill-guided layout agent based on design principles is effective for layout generation.

title: Requirements After the First Edit: Mining Late Requirement Emergence and Rework in Real-World Coding-Agent Sessions
summary: Coding agents often implement changes before users have fully articulated their requirements, echoing a pattern from requirements engineering: stakeholders cannot express a constraint until part of the system exists to react to. This volatility is associated with schedule and budget overruns in traditional projects, but only at release-cycle granularity. Existing work on coding agents narrows this gap only partway: curated benchmarks fix requirements before implementation by design, and observational studies report pushback frequency without linking arrivals to the code invalidation they cause. We address this using 3,553 eligible SWE-chat sessions, coding post-implementation requirement arrivals along three dimensions and, where repository state can be replayed, linking each arrival to a proxy: deletion or replacement of prior agent-authored lines. A requirement's arrival is followed by roughly twice as much invalidation as matched non-requirement edits, robust to user-turn and net-deletion checks, though not demonstrated as causal. This burden shows no detectable decline over a session and no detected association with operation type once multiplicity is accounted for; several intervals remain wide. A controlled experiment shows delayed disclosure relocates implementation post-reveal, while advance warning produces no detected effect on overwriting. These results establish late requirement emergence as a measurable source of code invalidation.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes that late requirement arrivals in coding agent sessions cause approximately twice as much code invalidation (deletion/replacement of agent-authored lines) compared to non-requirement edits, using analysis of 3,553 SWE-chat sessions and a controlled experiment.
AI.motivation: Coding agents often implement changes before users fully articulate requirements, creating a "chicken and egg" problem where stakeholders cannot express constraints until part of the system exists. This volatility traditionally causes schedule/budget overruns at release-cycle granularity, but coding agents operate at much finer timescales. Existing work only partially addresses this: benchmarks fix requirements before implementation by design, and observational studies report pushback frequency without quantifying the resulting code invalidation.
AI.method: Analyzed 3,553 eligible SWE-chat sessions, coding post-implementation requirement arrivals along three dimensions. Where repository state could be replayed, linked each requirement arrival to a proxy metric: deletion or replacement of prior agent-authored lines. Conducted a controlled experiment testing delayed disclosure and advance warning effects. Applied robustness checks including user-turn analysis and net-deletion verification.
AI.result: Requirement arrivals are followed by roughly twice as much code invalidation as matched non-requirement edits (robust to user-turn and net-deletion checks, though not demonstrated as causal). This burden shows no detectable decline over a session and no detected association with operation type once multiplicity is accounted for. The controlled experiment shows delayed disclosure relocates implementation post-reveal, while advance warning produces no detected effect on overwriting.
AI.conclusion: Late requirement emergence is a measurable and significant source of code invalidation in coding agent workflows. This establishes a quantitative link between requirement volatility and actual code changes, distinguishing this work from prior studies that only measured pushback frequency. Several intervals remain wide, suggesting areas for future research.

title: WireSeg-32K: A Physics-Grounded Synthetic Dataset for Wire Instance Segmentation
comment: Synthetic Data for Computer Vision @ CVPR 2026 Workshop
summary: Deformable linear objects such as wires and cables are difficult to segment because they are thin, highly deformable, and frequently self-occluded, while large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing or semantic segmentation under constrained settings, or generate visually plausible images without physically grounded wire deformation. We present WireSeg-32k, a synthetic dataset for wire instance segmentation with 32,000 RGB images, instance masks, depth maps, and a complementary real-world test set with annotations. To generate this dataset, we develop DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering, enabling physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse visually grounded scenes. As a simple baseline, LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, showing that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.

AI.tldr: WireSeg-32k is a synthetic dataset of 32,000 RGB images with instance masks and depth maps for wire instance segmentation, generated using DeformX (a Cosserat-rod dynamics coupled with Isaac Sim rendering pipeline). LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on this dataset improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the baseline.
AI.motivation: Deformable linear objects (wires/cables) are difficult to segment due to being thin, highly deformable, and self-occluded. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing under constrained settings or generate visually plausible but physically unrealistic wire deformations. Additionally, large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes.
AI.method: 1) Developed DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline coupling Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering for physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes. 2) Created WireSeg-32k with 32,000 RGB images, instance masks, depth maps, and CAD-based wire assets in diverse visually grounded scenes. 3) Provided a complementary real-world test set with annotations. 4) Applied LoRA fine-tuning to SAM3 (Segment Anything Model 3) on WireSeg-32k.
AI.result: LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, demonstrating that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.
AI.conclusion: Physically grounded synthetic data (via DeformX simulation) can effectively transfer to real-world wire perception tasks, providing a viable solution for training data scarcity in deformable object segmentation.

title: CRAW: Codec Robust Audio Watermarking
summary: Recent advances in generative speech models have made it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic from synthetic audio, enabling new forms of fraud and misinformation. Audio watermarking offers a promising defense by embedding an imperceptible signal into generated speech that can later be detected to verify its provenance. However, recent studies have shown that existing post-hoc watermarking methods fail under neural codecs and denoisers, transformations routinely applied during real-world storage, transmission, and processing, severely limiting their practical utility. Here we introduce CRAW, a codec-robust audio watermarking framework that jointly improves robustness against neural re-synthesis while maintaining high perceptual quality. CRAW combines distortion-aware training with an attention-based pooling mechanism, inference-time perceptual mask- ing, and an error-correcting code to recover the fidelity lost during robust training. Experiments demonstrate that CRAW achieves state-of-the-art robustness against neural codecs, denoisers, and vocoders while maintaining perceptual quality comparable to existing post-hoc watermarking methods. The code is available at https://github.com/DavidC1212/craw.

AI.tldr: CRAW is a codec-robust audio watermarking framework that embeds imperceptible signals into synthetic speech to verify provenance, addressing the vulnerability of existing methods to neural codecs and denoisers.
AI.motivation: Recent advances in generative speech models enable fraud and misinformation, but existing post-hoc audio watermarking methods fail when audio is processed through neural codecs and denoisers—transformations common in real-world storage, transmission, and processing—limiting practical utility.
AI.method: CRAW combines four key techniques: (1) distortion-aware training to learn robustness against neural re-synthesis, (2) attention-based pooling mechanism for feature aggregation, (3) inference-time perceptual masking to preserve quality, and (4) an error-correcting code to recover fidelity lost during robust training.
AI.result: CRAW achieves state-of-the-art robustness against neural codecs, denoisers, and vocoders while maintaining perceptual quality comparable to existing post-hoc watermarking methods.
AI.conclusion: CRAW successfully balances robustness and perceptual quality, making audio watermarking more practical for verifying synthetic speech provenance in real-world applications.

title: Equation Recast for Canonical Operator Learning Across Parametric PDEs
summary: Learning solution operators across broad parameter ranges can require substantial coverage of both input functions and physical parameters, particularly for purely data-driven parametric models. In addition, the resulting models may fail silently outside the training distribution. We introduce equation recast, which reformulates parametric operator learning as the learning of a single canonical operator. Parameter-induced operator variations are derived analytically from the governing equation and absorbed into effective sources, enabling zero-shot prediction across new parameter regimes. Across multi-parameter, nonlinear, and singular PDE settings, equation recast supports extrapolation, integrates sparse heterogeneous datasets in a shared canonical representation, and uses loss of convergence as an internal warning signal for failure of the recast iteration. In high-fidelity tokamak simulations for nuclear fusion, the framework unifies electron-temperature data across four device geometries through canonical-domain mapping within one jointly trained operator. Equation recast provides a route toward reusable neural PDE solvers combining equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference.

AI.tldr: Equation recast reformulates parametric operator learning as learning a single canonical operator, deriving parameter-induced operator variations analytically from governing equations and absorbing them into effective sources. This enables zero-shot prediction across new parameter regimes, integration of sparse heterogeneous datasets, and uses loss of convergence as an internal warning signal for failure.
AI.motivation: Current parametric operator learning requires substantial coverage of input functions and physical parameters, and models fail silently outside the training distribution without warning.
AI.method: The method analytically derives parameter-induced operator variations from governing equations and absorbs them into effective sources, enabling learning of a single canonical operator instead of separate operators for each parameter regime.
AI.result: The framework enables extrapolation, integrates sparse heterogeneous datasets in a shared canonical representation, and uses loss of convergence as an internal warning signal for failure. In tokamak simulations, it unifies electron-temperature data across four device geometries through canonical-domain mapping within one jointly trained operator.
AI.conclusion: Equation recast provides a route toward reusable neural PDE solvers combining equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference.

title: MasterControl Seventeen Every Time
summary: We study a governed approach to enterprise analytics: a language model interprets the question, while deterministic policy selects and runs a pre-approved analytical program that returns both results and evidence. We show that this restriction can remain expressive within a defined analytical class, using relational operations plus aggregation, comparison, windows, ranking, and similarity. Fixed meaning, policy, data, and execution rules also make results replayable. Across 440 runs, three 8B models generated SQL and selected tools at runtime, while Qwen3-8B interpreted intent only and policy executed the approved program. None of 330 runtime-planning episodes matched the full answer-and-evidence contract across all test datasets; the policy-executed analyzer matched 110 of 110. This is a configuration-specific result, not evidence that runtime agents cannot succeed under other designs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a governed approach to enterprise analytics where a language model interprets user questions while a deterministic policy selects and executes pre-approved analytical programs. The approach uses relational operations (aggregation, comparison, windows, ranking, similarity) within a defined analytical class. Experiments across 440 runs show that runtime planning agents (0/330) failed to match a full answer-and-evidence contract, while the policy-executed analyzer achieved 110/110 matches. This is presented as a configuration-specific result rather than general evidence against runtime agents.
AI.motivation: The motivation appears to address reliability and governance in enterprise analytics by constraining AI systems to use deterministic, pre-approved programs rather than allowing runtime planning that might produce inconsistent or unreplayable results. The authors seek to ensure that analytical outputs are trustworthy, replayable, and compliant with defined policies.
AI.method: The method involves a two-component architecture: (1) a language model for question interpretation and intent understanding, and (2) a deterministic policy that selects and executes pre-approved analytical programs from a defined set. The analytical class is bounded to relational operations plus aggregation, comparison, windows, ranking, and similarity. Experiments tested three 8B parameter models for runtime SQL generation and tool selection, compared against a policy-executed approach where Qwen3-8B only interpreted intent.
AI.result: The key results show a stark contrast: none of the 330 runtime-planning episodes (across three 8B models and test datasets) achieved the full answer-and-evidence contract, while the policy-executed analyzer matched 110 out of 110 cases. This suggests that constrained, deterministic execution may be more reliable for governance-critical analytics.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that their governed approach can be expressive within a defined analytical class while providing replayability and reliability through fixed meaning, policy, data, and execution rules. They emphasize that their negative result for runtime planning is configuration-specific and should not be interpreted as general evidence that runtime agents cannot succeed under different designs.

title: Mudragen: Geometrically Supervised Generation of Interacting Two-Hand Mudras for Preserving Indian Classical Dance Heritage
comment: Accepted for publication in ACM Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage (JOCCH) Special Issue on Visual Heritage
summary: Automatic generation of hand gestures is essential for the transmission of Indian classical dance and critical for its preservation. Indian classical dance gesture datasets are inherently low-resource, and the canonical Sanskrit definitions of many mudras lack precise textual descriptions, limiting the effectiveness of conventional text-conditioned image generation models. We present \textbf{MudraGen}, a conditional diffusion framework that synthesizes realistic RGB images of \textit{Samyukta Hasta Mudras} -- interactive two-hand gestures from Bharatanatyam (an Indian classical dance form). Unlike prior work on simple hand signs or single-hand gestures, MudraGen introduces geometry-aware supervision to capture the precise coordination, anatomical validity, and cultural nuance of interacting hands. We formulate three geometry-aware objectives: Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and Shape Consistency, which serves as an anatomical regularizer by encouraging consistent hand morphology while allowing independent hand poses. Together, these objectives guide the diffusion model toward anatomically plausible and well-coordinated hand configurations, enabling the synthesis of photorealistic and pose-accurate gesture images. Experimental results show that MudraGen surpasses existing state-of-the-art generative approaches in visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure, enabling faithful reproduction of complex Samyukta Hasta mudras. Beyond quantitative gains, its ability to generate culturally grounded and structurally consistent gestures highlights practical applications in cultural preservation and dance education.

AI.tldr: MudraGen is a conditional diffusion framework that generates realistic RGB images of Samyukta Hasta Mudras (two-hand interactive gestures from Bharatanatyam Indian classical dance). It addresses the challenge of low-resource datasets and lack of precise textual descriptions by introducing geometry-aware supervision with three objectives: Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and Shape Consistency as an anatomical regularizer.
AI.motivation: The preservation of Indian classical dance requires automatic generation of hand gestures, but existing datasets are low-resource and lack precise Sanskrit textual descriptions of mudras, limiting conventional text-conditioned image generation models.
AI.method: MudraGen uses a conditional diffusion framework with three geometry-aware objectives: (1) Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, (2) Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and (3) Shape Consistency as an anatomical regularizer encouraging consistent hand morphology while allowing independent hand poses.
AI.result: MudraGen surpasses existing state-of-the-art generative approaches in visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure, enabling faithful reproduction of complex Samyukta Hasta mudras.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables synthesis of photorealistic and pose-accurate gesture images with culturally grounded and structurally consistent gestures, demonstrating practical applications in cultural preservation and dance education.

title: TileGS: Tile-Local Depth Binning for Gaussian Splatting Rasterization
summary: Real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high rendering quality, but standard rasterization still traverses a globally sorted tile stream that creates long per-tile ranges and heavy geometry-attribute traffic. We present TileGS, a tile-local reorganization of Gaussian splatting. TileGS turns each long tile range into a sequence of shorter depth-local ranges, rasterizes those ranges in front-to-back order, and applies selective repair where coarse ordering is insufficient to match baseline compositing. Across a 9-scene benchmark on desktop and laptop Ada GPUs, our default No-GW (No Geometry-Write) variant delivers a mean 1.44x raster-kernel speedup on RTX 4090 and mean end-to-end frame speedups of 1.069x on RTX 4090 and 1.094x on RTX 1000 Ada over gsplat--a widely used optimized open-source 3DGS implementation--while matching the gsplat output up to numerical noise (|Delta PSNR| < 0.001 dB, |Delta SSIM| < 0.001, |Delta LPIPS| < 0.001). Full-suite RTX 4090 Nsight Compute profiling reveals TileGS is faster despite lower SM throughput, lower active-warp occupancy, and higher DRAM traffic, while total SASS thread instructions fall by 1.26x. Source-attributed profiling confirms that geometry attributes dominate the remaining memory pressure (85.8% of total raster traffic and 88.6% of excess sectors). Together, these counters support the interpretation that TileGS improves raster performance by reducing effective raster traversal work, rather than by reducing byte volume, improving coalescing, increasing occupancy, or directly reducing measured warp divergence.

AI.tldr: TileGS optimizes 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering by reorganizing tile-based rasterization into shorter depth-local ranges, achieving 1.44x raster-kernel speedup and ~1.07x frame speedup while matching baseline quality metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) within numerical noise.
AI.motivation: Standard 3DGS rasterization traverses a globally sorted tile stream creating long per-tile ranges and heavy geometry-attribute traffic, causing performance bottlenecks despite high rendering quality.
AI.method: TileGS reorganizes Gaussian splatting tile-locally: (1) transforms long tile ranges into shorter depth-local ranges, (2) rasterizes in front-to-back order, (3) applies selective repair where coarse ordering fails to match baseline compositing.
AI.result: On 9-scene benchmark (RTX 4090/RTX 1000 Ada): 1.44x raster-kernel speedup, 1.069x end-to-end frame speedup (RTX 4090), 1.094x (RTX 1000). Quality matches gsplat within |ΔPSNR| < 0.001 dB, |ΔSSIM| < 0.001, |ΔLPIPS| < 0.001. Profiling shows geometry attributes dominate memory pressure (85.8% raster traffic, 88.6% excess sectors).
AI.conclusion: TileGS improves performance by reducing effective raster traversal work rather than reducing byte volume or improving occupancy. The speedup comes from lowering total SASS thread instructions (1.26x reduction) despite lower SM throughput and higher DRAM traffic.

title: Large Language Models and Language Server Protocol: a match made in context
summary: This article introduces Eiffel-tools, a language server protocol (LSP) implementation for the Eiffel programming language that uses Large Language Models (LLMs) to aid the development of statically verified software. The tool provides various interactive and non-interactive commands to produce code and specifications. It uses language and project specific knowledge to precisely direct the LLM and verifies the output using a static verifier. It crafts rich programmatic prompts for the input and corrects or rejects the output. Furthermore, it handles the retries until the program passes verification. The tool's bug fixing capability is evaluated on 2 public datasets using 3 models. The tool can fix 76% to 95% of bugs by combining LLMs and a formal verifier depending on the model and prompts used. The results show the trade-off between the number of fixing attempts and the success rate.

AI.tldr: Eiffel-tools is a Language Server Protocol (LSP) implementation for the Eiffel programming language that leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to assist in developing statically verified software. It uses language and project-specific knowledge to direct LLMs, verifies outputs with a static verifier, and retries until verification passes.
AI.motivation: To improve software development by combining LLMs with formal verification, allowing developers to produce code and specifications that are automatically verified for correctness.
AI.method: Eiffel-tools provides interactive and non-interactive commands for code/specification generation. It crafts rich programmatic prompts tailored to the language and project, verifies LLM output using a static verifier, and iteratively corrects or rejects outputs until they pass verification.
AI.result: The tool achieves 76% to 95% bug-fixing success rates on 2 public datasets using 3 different LLMs, with the exact rate depending on the model and prompts used.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs with formal verifiers is effective for bug fixing, though there is a trade-off between the number of fixing attempts and the success rate.

title: SLIDEFORGE: An LLM Agent for Controllable Editing of Slides as Structured Artifacts
comment: EMNLP 2026 Main Conference. Haozhen and Fulin contributed equally
summary: Current AI agents compellingly describe slides. However, AI-assisted slide editing requires more than understanding: the output must retain layout, style, component structure, and native editability. Towards, AI-assisted slide editing, existing agents operate on screenshots or weak document representations and often fragment coherent visual units, rasterize editable content, or break layout. In contrast, for controllable slide editing, we introduce an agentic framework, SLIDEFORGE, which builds a Deck State Graph, an executable slide state that links visual decomposition, native pptx object structure, and perceptual organization. By recovering human-referable components while retaining fine-grained editable structure, SLIDEFORGE supports theme-preserving reconstruction through slide-native operations and rendered-state verification. We further introduce an evaluation paradigm for controllable slide transformation that jointly measures component recovery, preservation, restyling consistency, visual quality, and native editability. Experiments show that SLIDEFORGE outperforms direct prompting, screenshot-based agents, and generic code-agent baselines across these dimensions. Code is available at https://github.com/UIUC-MONET/SLIDEFORGE.

AI.tldr: SLIDEFORGE is an agentic AI framework for controllable slide editing that preserves layout, style, component structure, and native editability by building a Deck State Graph that links visual decomposition, native pptx object structure, and perceptual organization.
AI.motivation: Current AI agents for slide editing operate on screenshots or weak document representations, which fragment coherent visual units, rasterize editable content, and break layout. AI-assisted slide editing requires more than just understanding - the output must retain layout, style, component structure, and native editability.
AI.method: SLIDEFORGE builds a Deck State Graph - an executable slide state that links visual decomposition, native pptx object structure, and perceptual organization. It recovers human-referable components while retaining fine-grained editable structure, supporting theme-preserving reconstruction through slide-native operations and rendered-state verification.
AI.result: SLIDEFORGE outperforms direct prompting, screenshot-based agents, and generic code-agent baselines across multiple dimensions including component recovery, preservation, restyling consistency, visual quality, and native editability.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully enables controllable slide editing while preserving native editability and visual quality. The introduced evaluation paradigm provides comprehensive assessment of slide transformation capabilities across multiple dimensions.

title: VoxReason: Listener-Free Evaluation of Source-Grounded Speech Planning Before Synthesis
summary: Expressive speech systems make a decision before any waveform is rendered: how an utterance is delivered. In dialogue agents, narration, and role-conditioned TTS, that hidden planning step sets affect, pitch, energy, rate, pause, emphasis, and stance, yet downstream audio scores rarely reveal whether those choices were licensed by the source record, a source-use failure that occurs before any waveform exists. VoxReason makes that pre-synthesis decision measurable as a listener-free task for source-grounded speech planning. Before synthesis, VoxReason measures whether delivery choices are grounded in cited source records. Systems output a source-cited speaking-plan with evidence citations, and a deterministic verifier checks citation legality, slot agreement, unsupported state, schema validity, and one-cue counterfactual locality. On 1,440 checked source-label cases, shortcut controls show why slot accuracy alone is unsafe: a key-lookup oracle reaches 1.000 plan-slot accuracy on seen keys, while an emotion prior still reaches 0.958 slot accuracy on source-key-disjoint cases without citing intensity or identity. In a separate 100-case learned source-key-disjoint comparison, a 7B locality SFT+CF repair improves plan-slot accuracy/locality from 0.684/0.141 to 0.919/1.000, and removing source records lowers citation-required grounded score by 0.488. Rendered waveform quality remains outside the present evaluation.

AI.tldr: VoxReason introduces a listener-free evaluation task to measure whether speech delivery planning decisions (affect, pitch, energy, rate, pause, emphasis, stance) are grounded in cited source records before synthesis. The system outputs source-cited speaking plans with evidence citations, checked by a deterministic verifier for citation legality, slot agreement, schema validity, and counterfactual locality. Experiments show that slot accuracy alone is insufficient (key-lookup oracle achieves 1.000 accuracy; emotion prior achieves 0.958 without proper citation), while a 7B SFT+CF repair approach significantly improves performance on source-key-disjoint cases.
AI.motivation: Current expressive speech systems make hidden planning decisions about delivery before waveform rendering, yet downstream audio evaluation doesn't verify whether these choices are licensed by the source record. This source-use failure occurs before any waveform exists, creating an unmeasurable gap in evaluating whether TTS systems properly ground their expressive choices in source material.
AI.method: VoxReason proposes a pre-synthesis evaluation framework where systems output a source-cited speaking-plan with evidence citations. A deterministic verifier checks: (1) citation legality, (2) slot agreement, (3) unsupported state detection, (4) schema validity, and (5) one-cue counterfactual locality. Experiments include shortcut controls (key-lookup oracle, emotion prior) and a 7B locality SFT+CF repair model trained on source-key-disjoint cases.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Key-lookup oracle achieves 1.000 plan-slot accuracy on seen keys but fails on unseen keys; (2) Emotion prior reaches 0.958 slot accuracy on source-key-disjoint cases without citing intensity or identity; (3) 7B SFT+CF repair improves plan-slot accuracy/locality from 0.684/0.141 to 0.919/1.000; (4) Removing source records lowers citation-required grounded score by 0.488, demonstrating source grounding is essential.
AI.conclusion: Slot accuracy alone is an unsafe metric for evaluating source-grounded speech planning. The study demonstrates that proper citation of source records is critical—removing them significantly degrades performance. The proposed 7B locality repair approach substantially improves both accuracy and locality. However, rendered waveform quality remains outside the present evaluation scope, indicating a limitation in the current framework.

title: From Euclidean to Graph-Structured Data: A Survey of Collaborative Learning
comment: 96 pages. Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), March 2026, with Survey Certification
summary: The conventional approach to machine learning, that is, collecting data, training models, and performing inference in a single location, faces fundamental limitations, including scalability and privacy, that restrict its applicability. To address these challenges, recent research has explored collaborative learning approaches, including federated learning and decentralized learning, where individual agents perform training and inference locally, with limited collaboration. Most collaborative learning research focuses on Euclidean data with regular, grid-like structure (e.g., images, text). However, these approaches fail to capture the relational patterns in many real-world applications, best represented by graphs. Learning on graphs relies on message-passing mechanisms to propagate information between connected nodes, making it conceptually well-suited for collaborative environments where agents must exchange information. Yet, the opportunities and challenges of learning on graph-structured data in collaborative settings remain largely underexplored. This survey provides a comprehensive investigation of collaborative learning from Euclidean to graph-structured data, aiming to consolidate this emerging field. We begin by reviewing its foundational principles for Euclidean data, organizing them along three core dimensions: learning effectiveness, efficiency, and privacy preservation. We then extend the discussion to graph-structured data, introducing a taxonomy of graph distribution scenarios, characterizing associated statistical heterogeneities, and developing standardized problem formulations and algorithmic frameworks. Finally, we systematically identify open challenges and promising research directions.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey investigating collaborative learning from Euclidean to graph-structured data, consolidating this emerging field by reviewing foundational principles for Euclidean data across effectiveness, efficiency, and privacy dimensions, then extending to graph data with taxonomies, problem formulations, and algorithmic frameworks.
AI.motivation: Conventional machine learning approaches face fundamental limitations in scalability and privacy. While collaborative learning approaches (federated/decentralized learning) have been explored for Euclidean data (images, text), the opportunities and challenges of learning on graph-structured data in collaborative settings remain largely underexplored, despite graphs being common in real-world applications.
AI.method: Survey methodology: 1) Review foundational principles for Euclidean data organized along three core dimensions (learning effectiveness, efficiency, and privacy preservation); 2) Introduce taxonomy of graph distribution scenarios; 3) Characterize statistical heterogeneities; 4) Develop standardized problem formulations and algorithmic frameworks; 5) Identify open challenges and research directions.
AI.result: This is a survey paper that consolidates an emerging field rather than presenting experimental results. It provides a comprehensive investigation of collaborative learning on both Euclidean and graph-structured data, establishing taxonomies, problem formulations, and identifying future research directions.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a foundation for the relatively underexplored area of collaborative learning on graph-structured data, identifying key challenges including graph distribution scenarios, statistical heterogeneities, and the need for standardized algorithmic frameworks. Several open challenges and promising research directions are systematically identified.

title: Speculative Macro Commit for Faster Tool-Using Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents spend wall-clock time not only on model inference but also in serial action--observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition, and observation can delay subsequent decisions. We introduce \textbf{Speculative Macro Commit} (SMC), a runtime mechanism for a two-tier agent system: a large authoritative actor model produces the official trajectory, while a faster speculative drafter model continuously predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. SMC mines recurring multi-action skeletons from training traces and stores them in a macro library used to match against action chains predicted by the drafter at runtime. When the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining pre-executed draft steps, together with their observations, to the official trajectory. Using Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as the authoritative actor model and Qwen3.5-4B as the speculative drafter model, SMC matches the sequential agent's overall accuracy while reducing latency by 10.23\% over the Speculative Actions (SA) baseline and 18.59\% over sequential execution on the $τ^2$-Bench Telecom subset. On AppWorld, SMC reduces wall time by 7.7\% over SA baseline and 44.9\% over sequential execution, with a small reduction in task completion. Overall, SMC provides a practical way to reuse multi-step speculative execution and reduce agent latency beyond single-step speculative actions. Our code is publicly available \href{https://github.com/zeyuliu1037/speculative-macro-commit}{\textcolor{magenta}{here}}.

AI.tldr: Speculative Macro Commit (SMC) is a runtime mechanism for tool-using LLM agents that uses a two-tier system: a large authoritative actor model and a faster speculative drafter model. The drafter predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot, and when the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the pre-executed draft steps to the official trajectory. This reduces latency by 10-19% on τ²-Bench and 8-45% on AppWorld while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Tool-using LLM agents spend significant wall-clock time not only on model inference but also in serial action-observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition, and observation delays subsequent decisions. Existing speculative action methods only handle single-step speculation, and there is a need to reuse multi-step speculative execution to reduce agent latency.
AI.method: SMC uses a two-tier agent system: (1) A large authoritative actor model (Qwen3.5-27B INT4) produces the official trajectory; (2) A faster speculative drafter model (Qwen3.5-4B) continuously predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. SMC mines recurring multi-action skeletons from training traces and stores them in a macro library for matching against action chains predicted by the drafter at runtime. When the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining pre-executed draft steps together with their observations to the official trajectory.
AI.result: On τ²-Bench Telecom subset, SMC matches the sequential agent's overall accuracy while reducing latency by 10.23% over the Speculative Actions (SA) baseline and 18.59% over sequential execution. On AppWorld, SMC reduces wall time by 7.7% over SA baseline and 44.9% over sequential execution, with a small reduction in task completion.
AI.conclusion: SMC provides a practical way to reuse multi-step speculative execution and reduce agent latency beyond single-step speculative actions. The approach successfully balances latency reduction with accuracy maintenance, though there is a small trade-off in task completion on some benchmarks.

title: Local Chord Corruption Is Not Recognizer Replay: Chord-Condition Propagation in MIDI-SAG
summary: Synthetic chord corruption provides a controlled stress test for singing accompaniment generation (SAG), whereas complete automatic chord recognition (ACR) replay measures the condition delivered to a deployed system. We compare them by replaying CNN-CRF and DeepChroma+CRF predictions through one fixed MIDI-SAG generator, holding track, seed, context, and scoring window constant. Across 30 paired tracks and three seeds, a central four-second tritone produced larger changed-target and inside-output effects than CNN-CRF replay in STFT, CQT, and CENS; the CENS target gap was positive on 29/30 tracks (mean 0.462). Matching replay support and relation composition reduced this mismatch, with joint matching giving the lowest replay distance in the full-30 analysis. Relative-root substitutions produced 2.88-fold larger CENS full-window output change than same-root quality flips at near-equal dose. The matched surrogate was closer to replay for both recognizer paths. We conclude that localized corruption tests mechanisms, whereas complete replay evaluates deployed chord-condition propagation.

AI.tldr: This paper compares two evaluation methods for Singing Accompaniment Generation (SAG) systems: synthetic chord corruption (controlled stress testing) and complete Automatic Chord Recognition (ACR) replay (real-world evaluation). Using CNN-CRF and DeepChroma+CRF predictors through a fixed MIDI-SAG generator across 30 tracks, they find that synthetic tritone corruption produces larger output changes than CNN-CRF replay, while matched surrogate approaches better approximate replay conditions.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a fundamental question in evaluating SAG systems: how do different testing methodologies compare? Synthetic chord corruption provides controlled stress testing, while ACR replay measures real-world condition propagation in deployed systems. Understanding the differences between these approaches is crucial for proper system evaluation.
AI.method: The authors compared CNN-CRF and DeepChroma+CRF predictions replayed through one fixed MIDI-SAG generator, holding track, seed, context, and scoring window constant. They tested across 30 paired tracks with three seeds, using STFT, CQT, and CENS representations. They analyzed the effects of localized tritone corruption versus complete ACR replay, and compared relative-root substitutions with same-root quality flips at equivalent dose levels.
AI.result: The central four-second tritone produced larger changed-target and inside-output effects than CNN-CRF replay across STFT, CQT, and CENS representations. The CENS target gap was positive on 29/30 tracks (mean 0.462). Matching replay support and relation composition reduced mismatch, with joint matching achieving the lowest replay distance. Relative-root substitutions produced 2.88-fold larger CENS full-window output change than same-root quality flips at near-equal dose. The matched surrogate was consistently closer to replay for both recognizer paths.
AI.conclusion: Localized synthetic corruption (like tritone intervals) is suitable for testing specific mechanisms, while complete ACR replay provides a more realistic evaluation of deployed chord-condition propagation. The choice of evaluation method depends on whether the goal is targeted stress testing or comprehensive deployment readiness assessment.

title: Reparametrizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Palette-based Color and Luminance Editing
summary: Professional color editing requires precise control over both color (hue and saturation) and lightness, ideally through separate, independent controls. We present a real-time interactive color editing framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that supports palette-based recoloring, per-palette tone curves for color-aware luminance adjustment, and pixel-level color constraints. Rather than training a new representation from scratch, we reparameterize the spherical harmonics of a pretrained vanilla 3DGS to encode view-dependent palette weights. We simultaneously solve for weights and palette colors via a loss based on image-space sparsity. Luminance editing is realized as a per-pixel weight shift along the achromatic axis, which we show is equivalent to a per-pixel palette-aware luminance edit. This view-space formulation addresses a core limitation of prior primitive-space methods, where alpha-blending breaks per-Gaussian sparsity and causes edits to bleed into unintended regions. Our edits run in tens of milliseconds via an iteratively reweighted least squares and damped block-coordinate descent that couples tone curves and palette shifts under view-space sparsity. Our representation can be efficiently baked back into a vanilla 3DGS, preserving compatibility with standard viewers. We demonstrate sparser, more localized edits than prior palette-based 3DGS methods, while enabling independent luminance control per palette color and view-consistent pixel-level constraints, capabilities previously unavailable for 3DGS.

AI.tldr: Real-time interactive color editing framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) supporting palette-based recoloring, per-palette tone curves, and pixel-level constraints through view-space reparameterization of spherical harmonics.
AI.motivation: Professional color editing requires precise, independent control over color (hue and saturation) and lightness. Prior primitive-space methods suffer from alpha-blending issues that break per-Gaussian sparsity, causing edits to bleed into unintended regions.
AI.method: Reparameterize spherical harmonics of pretrained vanilla 3DGS to encode view-dependent palette weights. Solve for weights and palette colors simultaneously via image-space sparsity loss. Luminance editing is achieved through per-pixel weight shift along achromatic axis (equivalent to palette-aware luminance edit). Uses iteratively reweighted least squares and damped block-coordinate descent coupling tone curves and palette shifts under view-space sparsity. Representation can be baked back to vanilla 3DGS.
AI.result: Achieves sparser, more localized edits than prior palette-based 3DGS methods. Enables independent luminance control per palette color and view-consistent pixel-level constraints—capabilities previously unavailable for 3DGS. Runs in tens of milliseconds.
AI.conclusion: The proposed view-space formulation successfully addresses the core limitation of primitive-space methods by maintaining sparsity through alpha-blending, enabling professional-grade color editing with independent hue/saturation and lightness controls while preserving compatibility with standard viewers through baking.

title: Compound Prompt Constraints in LLM Code Generation: A Factorial Study of Format, Persona, and Urgency
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in software engineering pipelines for code generation, where production prompts often combine multiple constraints. This paper presents a full-factorial empirical study of how output formatting, persona assignment, and urgency framing jointly affect LLM code-generation reliability. We evaluate all 27 combinations in a controlled 3x3x3 design and decompose each compound condition into an additive prediction and a residual interaction term that captures super-additive degradation. The study uses all 164 HumanEval+ problems across five OpenAI models from the GPT-4o family, GPT-4.1 family, and o3-mini, yielding 22,140 greedy-decoding evaluations. A format-aware extraction pipeline separates formatting failures from reasoning failures, and significance is assessed with McNemar's test, odds ratios, and 95% confidence intervals.
  Results show that compound constraints can produce architecture-dependent degradation not predictable from single-factor experiments. The GPT-4o family exhibits consistent super-additive effects, with pass@1 reductions 3-12 percentage points beyond additive predictions; the largest interaction is -12.2 pp on GPT-4o-mini for JSON + expert persona + moderate urgency. JSON combinations generally produce larger interactions than XML. In contrast, the GPT-4.1 family is largely resistant, while o3-mini shows a qualitatively different pattern in which structured output constraints can improve performance. These findings show that vulnerability is architecture-dependent rather than size-dependent, that individually neutral or beneficial constraints can combine to cause substantial degradation, and that compound-prompt testing should be standard in reliability assessment for LLM-assisted engineering pipelines.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a full-factorial empirical study examining how three prompt constraints (output formatting, persona assignment, and urgency framing) jointly affect LLM code generation reliability across 5 OpenAI models, revealing architecture-dependent super-additive degradation effects.
AI.motivation: Production software engineering pipelines often combine multiple constraints in LLM prompts, but prior research only examines single factors in isolation. This study addresses the gap by investigating compound constraint effects on code generation reliability.
AI.method: Full-factorial 3×3×3 design evaluating all 27 combinations of formatting (JSON/XML/plain), persona (expert/standard/novice), and urgency (high/moderate/none) on 164 HumanEval+ problems across 5 models (GPT-4o family, GPT-4.1 family, o3-mini), totaling 22,140 evaluations. Used McNemar's test, odds ratios, and 95% CIs for significance testing.
AI.result: Compound constraints produce architecture-dependent degradation not predictable from single-factor experiments. GPT-4o family shows consistent super-additive effects (3-12 pp beyond additive predictions), with largest interaction of -12.2 pp on GPT-4o-mini for JSON+expert+moderate urgency. GPT-4.1 family is largely resistant. o3-mini shows qualitatively different pattern where structured output constraints can improve performance.
AI.conclusion: Vulnerability is architecture-dependent rather than size-dependent. Individually neutral or beneficial constraints can combine to cause substantial degradation. Compound-prompt testing should be standard in LLM-assisted engineering reliability assessment.

title: Beyond Small Patches: Black-Box Detection and Purification of Diverse Backdoor Triggers
summary: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly deployed in real-world vision systems, yet their predictions can be covertly manipulated by backdoor attacks, in which malicious triggers cause targeted misclassification while preserving high clean accuracy. Existing defenses often rely on model internals, training data, or clean validation samples, making them difficult to deploy when only black-box access to a trained model is available. We propose TRIM (Trigger Removal by Identifying Manipulated Regions), a deployment-oriented black-box defense that detects and selectively removes backdoor triggers at inference time without requiring model internals, training data, or clean samples. The key insight behind TRIM is to identify image regions that are responsible for anomalous model behavior and purify only those regions while preserving benign content. TRIM innovates via three key components: (i) region-based segmentation with deep feature representations, (ii) adaptive trigger discovery through inpainting and diffusion-based reconstruction to isolate regions responsible for misclassification---without assumptions about trigger type, shape, or location, and (iii) selective region purification that cleans poisoned regions while retaining benign content. To support practical deployment, TRIM further caches feature embeddings of previously identified triggers, enabling efficient recognition and avoiding redundant detection and purification. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and backdoor types, including blended, sparse, varying-size, and multiple triggers, show that TRIM consistently outperforms existing black-box defenses, reducing attack success rates (ASR) to as low as 1.16% while preserving clean accuracy of up to 87.87%.
