These results demonstrate that effective backdoor mitigation is possible at inference time even when the defender has no access to any auxiliary data.

AI.tldr: TRIM is a black-box defense against backdoor attacks that works at inference time by identifying and purifying malicious trigger regions in images without requiring model internals, training data, or clean samples. It uses deep feature-based segmentation, inpainting/diffusion-based trigger discovery, and selective region purification to mitigate backdoor effects while preserving benign content.
AI.motivation: Existing backdoor defenses often require access to model internals, training data, or clean validation samples, making them impractical for deployed vision systems where only black-box access is available. There is a need for a deployment-oriented defense that can detect and remove backdoor triggers at inference time without any auxiliary data.
AI.method: TRIM employs three key components: (1) Region-based segmentation using deep feature representations to identify potential trigger locations, (2) Adaptive trigger discovery through inpainting and diffusion-based reconstruction to isolate regions responsible for misclassification without assumptions about trigger type/shape/location, and (3) Selective region purification that cleans poisoned regions while retaining benign content. Additionally, it caches feature embeddings of previously identified triggers for efficient recognition.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and backdoor types (blended, sparse, varying-size, and multiple triggers) show that TRIM consistently outperforms existing black-box defenses, reducing attack success rates to as low as 1.16% while preserving clean accuracy of up to 87.87%.
AI.conclusion: Effective backdoor mitigation is possible at inference time even when the defender has no access to any auxiliary data. TRIM demonstrates that deployment-oriented black-box defenses can achieve strong performance against various backdoor attacks without requiring model internals, training data, or clean samples.

title: Is Semantics Enough for Speech Mean Opinion Score Prediction?
summary: Mean Opinion Score (MOS) is the gold standard for evaluating synthesized speech naturalness. However, current automatic MOS predictors are dominated by self-supervised learning (SSL) models that prioritize high-level semantics, potentially compromising their ability to capture critical acoustic details. In this paper, we systematically investigate representations from three paradigms: SSLs, acoustic-only neural audio codecs (NACs), and unified NACs that integrate semantics into reconstruction-based architectures. Extensive benchmarking on the standard BVCC and multiple out-of-domain (OOD) datasets demonstrates that features synergizing semantic understanding with fine-grained acoustic modeling achieve a higher performance upper bound in speech quality assessment. Ultimately, our findings highlight that semantics alone are not enough; a dual focus on semantic content and acoustic fidelity is essential for robust MOS prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates different representation learning approaches for predicting Mean Opinion Score (MOS) in synthesized speech, comparing self-supervised learning (SSL), acoustic-only neural audio codecs (NACs), and unified NACs. The study finds that representations combining semantic understanding with fine-grained acoustic modeling achieve superior performance in speech quality assessment.
AI.motivation: Current automatic MOS predictors rely heavily on SSL models that prioritize high-level semantics but may compromise their ability to capture critical acoustic details necessary for accurate quality assessment.
AI.method: The authors systematically benchmark representations from three paradigms: SSLs, acoustic-only NACs, and unified NACs that integrate semantics into reconstruction-based architectures. Evaluation is conducted on the standard BVCC dataset and multiple out-of-domain (OOD) datasets.
AI.result: Features that synergize semantic understanding with fine-grained acoustic modeling achieve a higher performance upper bound in speech quality assessment across both standard and OOD datasets.
AI.conclusion: Semantics alone are insufficient for robust MOS prediction; a dual focus on both semantic content and acoustic fidelity is essential for building effective speech quality assessment models.

title: Modern Transformers Are Implicit Hybrids: From Functional Differentiation to Principled Hybrid Architecture Design
summary: Hybrid architectures combining Full Attention (FA) and Linear Attention (LA) are increasingly prominent, yet their allocation remains heuristic. We seek an evidence-grounded basis in head-level functional organization learned by RoPE-based Transformers. Behavioral probes do not yield a complete taxonomy, so we propose two intervention metrics: RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS), measuring how each frequency affects a head's attention distribution, and RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD), isolating dependence on rotary positional modulation. On Qwen3-series models and Llama3.1, RFIS suggests and RPD verifies a complete taxonomy of retrieval and positional heads separated by a salient mid-low-frequency band. Controlled Transformers show that this boundary follows the training-length positional scale; we term it the Global Positional Band (GPBand). The analysis suggests a potential cause of zero-shot length-extrapolation failure and yields two principles: positional modeling should operate only locally, with global access through position-independent retrieval; and both functions should be assigned at head granularity with layer-specific allocation. We instantiate them in Head-wise Hybrid Architecture (HwH), using NoPE FA for global retrieval and LA for local positional modeling. With an FA-to-LA ratio below 1:3, HwH retains strong language modeling and commonsense reasoning while improving retrieval and substantially strengthening zero-shot long-context extrapolation over Transformer, LA, and a layer-wise hybrid baseline. Ablations validate both principles and component roles, highlighting principled hybrid architecture design as a promising route toward future foundation models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes evidence-based principles for designing hybrid attention architectures that combine Full Attention (FA) and Linear Attention (LA) in RoPE-based Transformers. Through two novel metrics (RFIS and RPD), the authors discover a taxonomy of retrieval vs positional heads separated by a "Global Positional Band" (GPBand), leading to two design principles and a new Head-wise Hybrid Architecture (HwH) that achieves strong performance with improved retrieval and zero-shot length extrapolation.
AI.motivation: Hybrid FA+LA architectures are increasingly used but their allocation remains heuristic. The authors seek an evidence-grounded basis for head-level functional organization in RoPE-based Transformers, as behavioral probes don't yield a complete taxonomy.
AI.method: The authors propose two intervention metrics: (1) RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS) - measuring how each frequency affects a head's attention distribution, and (2) RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD) - isolating dependence on rotary positional modulation. They analyze Qwen3-series and Llama3.1 models, use controlled Transformers to verify the GPBand follows training-length positional scale, and instantiate their findings in Head-wise Hybrid Architecture (HwH) using NoPE FA for global retrieval and LA for local positional modeling.
AI.result: RFIS suggests and RPD verifies a complete taxonomy of retrieval and positional heads separated by a salient mid-low-frequency band (GPBand). HwH with FA:LA ratio below 1:3 retains strong language modeling and commonsense reasoning while improving retrieval and substantially strengthening zero-shot long-context extrapolation over Transformer, LA, and layer-wise hybrid baseline.
AI.conclusion: The paper yields two principles: (1) positional modeling should operate only locally, with global access through position-independent retrieval; and (2) both functions should be assigned at head granularity with layer-specific allocation. Principled hybrid architecture design is a promising route toward future foundation models.

title: Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory
summary: Distributed LLM-agent teams can read the latest shared facts and still act on an obsolete plan. A planner may derive an action from requirement $r_3$, another agent may commit $r_4$, and an executor may receive $r_4$ without replacing the plan derived from $r_3$. We call this \emph{stale-plan execution}: state freshness does not establish that the plan authorizing an action remains valid. We introduce PlanFence, a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol. Plans cite the exact public records they used, and an executor validates only the records that can affect the pending external action, replanning once or blocking when validation is incomplete. In 30 controlled live workflows with a post-plan revision, a freshness-only executor acts on the obsolete plan in every task, whereas PlanFence completes all tasks without an invalid action. Controlled replay reveals two conditional boundaries: proactive synchronization yields lower coordination stall at low churn, while PlanFence avoids repeated update-path coordination as churn grows and avoids validating unrelated state as the shared keyspace grows. These are controlled safety and systems-cost results, not general task-accuracy gains.

AI.tldr: PlanFence is a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol for distributed LLM-agent teams that prevents stale-plan execution by having plans cite exact public records used and executors validate only relevant records before acting.
AI.motivation: Distributed LLM-agent teams can read updated facts but still execute obsolete plans. A planner may derive an action from requirement r3, another agent commits r4, and an executor receives r4 without replacing the plan derived from r3. This stale-plan execution occurs because state freshness doesn't guarantee plan validity.
AI.method: PlanFence protocol: (1) Plans cite exact public records they used, (2) Executors validate only records that can affect the pending external action, (3) Replan once or block when validation is incomplete. Evaluated in 30 controlled live workflows with post-plan revision.
AI.result: Freshness-only executor acts on obsolete plan in every task (30/30 failures). PlanFence completes all tasks without invalid action (30/30 success). Two conditional boundaries: proactive synchronization yields lower coordination stall at low churn; PlanFence avoids repeated update-path coordination as churn grows and avoids validating unrelated state as shared keyspace grows.
AI.conclusion: PlanFence provides a practical solution to stale-plan execution in distributed LLM-agent systems through dependency-scoped validation. The protocol is particularly effective under high churn and large shared keyspace conditions. Results are limited to safety and systems-cost improvements, not general task-accuracy gains.

title: PointGT: Simultaneous Geometry and Texture Editing for Point-Based Representations
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://zvict.github.io/pointgt/
summary: We present PointGT, a point-based 3D representation that enables simultaneous editing of object geometry and appearance. Existing reconstruction and view synthesis techniques produce volumetric 3D representations that are high-quality and photorealistic, but are difficult to edit. In particular, recent efforts to enable texture editing for 3D Gaussian Splatting representations are not compatible with geometry edits and deformations. Our method combines a point-based representation that is well-suited for geometry deformations with a learned UV mapping technique that enables high-resolution texture editing. We show that PointGT enables fine-grained editing of both geometry and texture in point-based neural representations with high rendering quality.

AI.tldr: PointGT is a point-based 3D representation that enables simultaneous editing of object geometry and appearance, combining a point-based representation suited for geometry deformations with a learned UV mapping technique for high-resolution texture editing.
AI.motivation: Existing volumetric 3D representations (like 3D Gaussian Splatting) produce high-quality photorealistic results but are difficult to edit. Specifically, texture editing methods for 3D Gaussian Splatting are incompatible with geometry edits and deformations, limiting the flexibility of 3D content creation.
AI.method: The method combines a point-based representation (well-suited for geometry deformations) with a learned UV mapping technique that enables high-resolution texture editing. This hybrid approach allows simultaneous manipulation of both geometry and appearance.
AI.result: PointGT enables fine-grained editing of both geometry and texture in point-based neural representations while maintaining high rendering quality.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully bridges the gap between high-quality 3D reconstruction/view synthesis and editable representations, providing a versatile tool for 3D content editing.

title: Two Truths and A Lie? Benchmarking Off-the-Shelf LLMs for Requirements Quality Assessment: Performance, False Alarms, and Misses
summary: Requirements engineering (RE) governs the quality of everything downstream in systems engineering (SE); defective requirements that survive review cycles propagate into design rework, schedule delays, and cost overruns. Because requirements are often written in natural language, recent advances in generative AI have raised expectations that large language models (LLMs) can absorb requirement quality assessment, a task otherwise slow and human expertise-intensive. Yet empirical evidence on whether LLMs can be trusted to do so remains scarce. This study presents the first benchmarking analysis of off-the-shelf LLM performance for requirement quality evaluation. Against an expert-derived ground truth built on INCOSE quality criteria, we evaluate ten models spanning two families (OpenAI and Anthropic) and five generations each, across one hundred independent runs, two requirement sets, and five sampling temperatures. Four contributions follow. First, we quantify a strongly asymmetric error profile: across all models and runs, the best-performing Anthropic model detects a median of only 47% of expert-identified issues while false-flagging 11%. Second, performance degrades significantly where SE judgment is required, as necessity and correctness issues are almost always missed. Third, generational progress is non-monotonic, so newer models cannot be assumed better. Fourth, this error behavior shifts only modestly and non-monotonically across sampling temperatures, indicating characteristic model deficiencies rather than inherent stochasticity. Off-the-shelf LLMs are therefore not yet trustworthy autonomous evaluators. Findings also warrant caution for Agentic AI developers: orchestrating these LLM modules in specialized architectures risks compounding these deficiencies rather than correcting them. Their defensible near-term role is human-in-the-loop decision support.

AI.tldr: First benchmarking study evaluating 10 LLMs (OpenAI and Anthropic families, 5 generations each) for requirements quality assessment against expert-derived ground truth. Results show best model detects only 47% of issues with 11% false positives, indicating off-the-shelf LLMs are not yet trustworthy autonomous evaluators.
AI.motivation: Requirements engineering governs downstream system engineering quality, but defective requirements often survive review cycles. LLMs have raised expectations for automating this human expertise-intensive task, yet empirical evidence on LLM trustworthiness for requirement quality evaluation remains absent.
AI.method: Benchmarking analysis of ten models spanning OpenAI and Anthropic families across five generations. Evaluation used expert-derived ground truth based on INCOSE quality criteria, with 100 independent runs, two requirement sets, and five sampling temperatures tested.
AI.result: Four key findings: (1) Strongly asymmetric error profile - best Anthropic model detects only 47% of expert-identified issues while false-flagging 11%; (2) Performance degrades significantly for SE judgment tasks (necessity and correctness issues almost always missed); (3) Generational progress is non-monotonic - newer models not always better; (4) Temperature effects are modest and non-monotonic, indicating characteristic deficiencies rather than stochasticity.
AI.conclusion: Off-the-shelf LLMs are not yet trustworthy autonomous evaluators for requirement quality. Findings caution against Agentic AI architectures that orchestrate these LLM modules, as deficiencies may compound rather than correct. Near-term role should be limited to human-in-the-loop decision support.

title: VeriPhy: Agentic Physical Reasoning for World Model Evaluation and Refinement
summary: Visual fluency in generated video does not imply physical reliability, and a scalar quality score alone is incapable of indicating the obligation a clip violates or the moment it fails. We present VeriPhy, an auditable physical-verification system in which a text-only planner compiles the prompt into typed physical obligations and a statically validated execution plan before any frame is observed. During execution, observations gate and scope only declared calls to frozen low-level experts (e.g., segmentation and tracking, counting, eleven typed physical measurements over the resulting tracks, depth, OCR, and audio-event detection). Each action returns a provenance-carrying evidence record whose payload, when usable, is either a typed measurement or an explicitly tagged learned state. Typed resolvers and fixed composition map usable records to a three-valued state (supported, contradicted, or unknown, surfaced as plausible, implausible, or abstain) with full provenance, so that every verdict is traceable to the evidence that produced it. We anchor evaluation in a 1,500-clip corpus of human-annotated flaw records that localize real generation failures in prompt reference, space, and time. On a 149-clip core carrying 304 such records, VeriPhy accounts for 228, against 164 for a published question-decomposition evaluator given the same clips and the same claims. Recall alone does not separate it from prompting the same backbone monolithically, which reaches 222; what separates them is that each decision retains its evidence record and provenance, making the traces auditable one verdict at a time and usable as the interface through which a critic verdict could be written back into generation.

AI.tldr: VeriPhy is an auditable physical-verification system for generated videos that uses a text-only planner to compile prompts into typed physical obligations, then executes validated plans using frozen low-level experts. It maps evidence to three-valued states (supported/contradicted/unknown) with full provenance, making verdicts traceable and auditable.
AI.motivation: Visual fluency in generated video does not imply physical reliability. A scalar quality score alone cannot indicate what obligation a clip violates or when it fails. Existing evaluation methods lack accountability and provenance tracking.
AI.method: VeriPhy uses a text-only planner to compile prompts into typed physical obligations with a statically validated execution plan before observing any frame. During execution, observations gate and scope only declared calls to frozen low-level experts (segmentation, tracking, counting, 11 typed physical measurements, depth, OCR, audio-event detection). Each action returns a provenance-carrying evidence record. Typed resolvers and fixed composition map usable records to three-valued state (supported, contradicted, or unknown) with full provenance.
AI.result: On a 149-clip core carrying 304 flaw records, VeriPhy accounts for 228, compared to 164 for a published question-decomposition evaluator and 222 for prompting the same backbone monolithically. While recall alone doesn't separate VeriPhy from monolithic prompting, VeriPhy retains evidence records and provenance for each decision, making traces auditable and usable as an interface for critic verdicts to be written back into generation.
AI.conclusion: VeriPhy provides auditable physical verification for generated videos through provenance tracking. The key advantage is not just recall but the ability to trace every verdict to its evidence, enabling auditability at the verdict level and serving as an interface for feedback into generation systems.

title: Beyond .WAV: Design and Software Verification of VocalCap, a Traceable Browser-Based Audio Capture System for Vocal Biomarker Research
summary: Remote voice studies often retain a final audio file with limited evidence about how it was captured, transferred, processed, and accepted. This paper presents VocalCap, an institution-controlled, browser-based system for self-guided capture of voice and related acoustic signals by participants without technical training. A versioned protocol drives the workflow. Each accepted recording retains a browser-native object, a client-lossless Float32 WAV derived from the same MediaStream, and a server-canonical mono PCM16 WAV, linked to evidence of capture execution, technical quality, byte-level integrity, recovery, and transformation provenance. IndexedDB preserves accepted browser artifacts until server confirmation, while session completion requires successful verification of every task and artifact. Software tests challenged the acquisition contracts with malformed or altered objects, exact-zero interruptions, channel-topology variants, and interrupted or repeated operations. A post hoc technical audit of 39 consented pilot recordings found 25 sample-identical stereo files and 14 files with signal confined to the left channel. Topology-aware active-channel selection limited the canonical root-mean-square level difference to less than 0.001 dB in all 14 affected files; equal-weight stereo averaging would have introduced approximately 6.02 dB of attenuation. Production end-to-end verification completed two five-task profiles in Chromium and WebKit, yielding 10 accepted recordings and 30 retained artifacts that passed server-side integrity and format checks. The results verify VocalCap's software behavior under the tested browser-engine conditions. Device-level acoustic agreement, target-population usability, clinical validity, and biomarker performance remain subjects for separate studies.

AI.tldr: VocalCap is a browser-based system for self-guided voice capture in remote studies, ensuring comprehensive provenance and integrity of audio recordings through versioned protocols, dual-format storage, and automated verification.
AI.motivation: Remote voice studies often retain final audio files with limited evidence about how they were captured, transferred, processed, and accepted, lacking transparency in the data pipeline.
AI.method: VocalCap uses a versioned protocol workflow with IndexedDB for browser artifact preservation, dual-format storage (client-lossless Float32 WAV and server-canonical mono PCM16 WAV), and automated verification requiring successful completion of every task and artifact. Testing included malformed objects, channel-topology variants, and interrupted operations.
AI.result: Post hoc audit of 39 recordings found 25 sample-identical stereo files and 14 left-channel-only files. Topology-aware active-channel selection limited RMS level difference to < 0.001 dB (vs. 6.02 dB attenuation from stereo averaging). End-to-end verification yielded 10 accepted recordings and 30 retained artifacts passing integrity checks across Chromium and WebKit.
AI.conclusion: VocalCap successfully verifies software behavior under tested browser conditions. Device-level acoustic agreement, target-population usability, clinical validity, and biomarker performance require separate studies.

title: Tail-Likelihood Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning typically optimizes average reward. For generative policies, the average can hide an important distinction: two policies can achieve the same mean reward while having very different chances of producing a rare but high-reward rollout. This matters as sampling increases during training and inference, since its benefit depends on retaining probability mass on high-reward outcomes. We propose to optimize this coverage directly. Rather than considering only expected reward, we consider all of its upper tails: for each reward threshold, how likely is the policy to exceed it? This turns a continuous reward into a family of binary success events. We introduce Tail-Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (TailRL), which maximizes the log-probability of exceeding a randomly chosen reward threshold. Its gradient gives more weight to rare, high-reward rollouts and can be interpreted as a mixture of Best-of-(k) gradients. TailRL requires only a simple modification to the advantage function, making it compatible with existing reinforcement learning pipelines. Across object localization, maze navigation, GUI grounding, and code optimization, TailRL leverages rare high-reward training samples to avoid suboptimal solutions and yields models that benefit more from additional samples at inference time.

AI.tldr: TailRL is a new reinforcement learning approach that optimizes the upper tails of the reward distribution rather than just average reward. It maximizes the log-probability of exceeding randomly chosen reward thresholds, giving more weight to rare high-reward rollouts. This simple modification to the advantage function is compatible with existing RL pipelines and helps models benefit more from additional sampling.
AI.motivation: Standard RL optimizes average reward, which can hide important differences between policies - two policies can have the same mean reward but very different probabilities of achieving rare high-reward outcomes. This matters because the benefit of sampling during training and inference depends on retaining probability mass on high-reward outcomes.
AI.method: TailRL transforms the continuous reward optimization problem into a family of binary success events by considering all upper tails of the reward distribution. It maximizes the log-probability of exceeding a randomly chosen reward threshold. The gradient gives more weight to rare, high-reward rollouts and can be interpreted as a mixture of Best-of-(k) gradients. It requires only a simple modification to the advantage function.
AI.result: Across four domains (object localization, maze navigation, GUI grounding, and code optimization), TailRL leverages rare high-reward training samples to avoid suboptimal solutions and yields models that benefit more from additional samples at inference time.
AI.conclusion: TailRL provides a simple yet effective way to optimize for tail performance in reinforcement learning. By focusing on the probability of exceeding reward thresholds rather than just expected reward, it better leverages rare high-reward rollouts and improves performance when additional sampling is available at inference time.

title: A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) teaching assistants powered by large language models (LLMs) offer scalable educational support but often provide limited personalization. This study presents a prompt-engineering-based framework for personalizing general-purpose LLM/RAG-based AI teaching assistants such as Jill Watson across academic disciplines and courses. The framework adapts responses using six learner-specific dimensions: self-assessment, abstraction preference, verbosity preference, perceptual orientation, information processing style, and level of understanding, yielding 96 distinct learner profiles. Student queries are additionally analyzed using Bloom's Taxonomy to estimate cognitive complexity at the interaction level. Learner attributes and cognitive assessments are encoded in structured prompts that condition the LLM without requiring model retraining. The framework is evaluated through experiments using NLP metrics and a human study with five participants. Results show perceived differences in response style and structure across personalization conditions, with statistical analyses identifying learner attributes associated with measurable response changes. These findings provide preliminary evidence that prompt-based personalization can support adaptive behavior in LLM-powered educational agents.

title: P-CORE: Self-Supervised Surface Consistency for Point-Based Neural Editing
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project Page: https://zvict.github.io/p-core/
summary: Advances in neural rendering have enabled high-fidelity multi-view reconstruction of 3D scenes. However, free-form non-rigid shape editing remains a significant challenge. Point-based neural representations are highly desirable for multi-view reconstruction because they lack fixed connectivity, which does not constrain the learned surface topology to that of the initialization. Yet this same property causes point-based representations to struggle with holes and surface discontinuities under large deformations. To address this, we propose a novel self-supervised method to enable point-based representations to adapt to large deformations without requiring ground truth multi-view images of deformed geometry. The key idea is to generate random deformations and to ensure consistency in the predicted surface before and after deformation. In particular, the surface prediction from the deformed point cloud should be the same as the deformation applied to the surface prediction from the original point cloud. We incorporate our approach into attention-based point representations, which differ from splatting-based point representations in their use of a learned interpolation kernel between points as opposed to a Gaussian kernel around each point. This learned interpolation kernel can learn to adapt to large deformations, without requiring addition or removal of points. We show that our framework significantly enhances its robustness to large deformations. Experiments on synthetic geometry editing benchmarks (Neural Editor, Objaverse) demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing point-based methods in zero-shot editing and significantly reduces artifacts. Furthermore, qualitative results on the DTU and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets demonstrate our method's effectiveness on real-world scenes.

AI.tldr: A self-supervised method enabling point-based neural rendering to handle large deformations in 3D scene editing by enforcing consistency between deformed and original surface predictions, using attention-based learned interpolation kernels.
AI.motivation: Point-based neural representations are desirable for multi-view reconstruction due to their lack of fixed connectivity, but they struggle with holes and surface discontinuities under large deformations. Current methods require ground truth multi-view images of deformed geometry, which is impractical.
AI.method: The method generates random deformations and ensures consistency: the surface prediction from the deformed point cloud should equal the deformation applied to the surface prediction from the original point cloud. This is incorporated into attention-based point representations using a learned interpolation kernel (instead of Gaussian kernel) that can adapt to large deformations without adding/removing points.
AI.result: The framework significantly enhances robustness to large deformations. On synthetic benchmarks (Neural Editor, Objaverse), it outperforms existing point-based methods in zero-shot editing and substantially reduces artifacts. Qualitative results on real-world datasets (DTU, Mip-NeRF 360) demonstrate effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed self-supervised approach successfully enables point-based neural representations to handle large deformations without requiring ground truth deformed geometry, achieving superior editing quality and robustness compared to existing methods.

title: Refusing the Impossible: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Code Hallucination in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) often produce code that looks plausible but is not grounded in reality. The code may import packages that do not exist or claim to implement algorithms that violate proven theorems, while still compiling and running. We study \emph{code hallucination} as \emph{ungrounded generation} and separate it from ordinary \emph{code error} (bugs in otherwise grounded programs). We propose a taxonomy with three dimensions: \textbf{groundedness} (absolute violations of universal truths vs.\ relative fabrications of contingent or ecosystem-specific facts), \textbf{manifestation level} (syntactic, semantic, or factual), and \textbf{behavior} (from confident fabrication to degenerate output), organized into a severity ordering. We build an \textbf{adversarial} suite of deliberately unsatisfiable tasks where the correct response is to refuse and categorize the responses under our taxonomy. The suite contains \textbf{270 prompts} across six languages and 24 subcategories, paired with \textbf{91 matched solvable controls}, and responses are judged by a two-tier protocol validated against human labels (82\% agreement, $κ{=}0.73$). Across twelve open-weight code and reasoning models (4{,}332 judged responses), models produce ungrounded code on about 60\% of unsatisfiable prompts and refuse only 27\%, while wrongly refusing 0\% of the solvable controls.

AI.tldr: This paper studies "code hallucination" in LLMs - code that looks plausible but is ungrounded in reality (e.g., importing non-existent packages or implementing algorithms that violate proven theorems). The authors propose a three-dimensional taxonomy (groundedness, manifestation level, behavior) and evaluate 12 models on 270 unsatisfiable prompts and 91 solvable controls.
AI.motivation: Large language models often produce code that compiles and runs but contains false claims - such as importing non-existent packages or implementing algorithms that violate proven theorems. This "code hallucination" is distinct from ordinary bugs and represents a growing concern for developers relying on LLMs for code generation.
AI.method: The authors proposed a taxonomy with three dimensions: (1) groundedness - absolute violations of universal truths vs. relative fabrications of contingent facts, (2) manifestation level - syntactic, semantic, or factual, and (3) behavior - from confident fabrication to degenerate output. They built an adversarial suite of 270 unsatisfiable prompts across six languages and 24 subcategories, paired with 91 matched solvable controls. Responses were judged by a two-tier protocol validated against human labels (82% agreement, κ=0.73). Twelve open-weight code and reasoning models were evaluated (4,332 judged responses).
AI.result: Models produce ungrounded code on approximately 60% of unsatisfiable prompts and refuse only 27% of them, while wrongly refusing 0% of the solvable controls. This indicates that LLMs frequently generate plausible but ungrounded code when asked to solve impossible tasks.
AI.conclusion: Code hallucination is a significant problem in LLMs, with models generating ungrounded code in the majority of cases when faced with unsatisfiable prompts. The proposed taxonomy provides a useful framework for understanding and categorizing different types of code hallucination. The low refusal rate (27%) suggests that current models struggle to recognize when tasks are impossible, highlighting the need for improved calibration in code generation models.

title: Who Speaks for the Pruned? Visual Token Pruning as Coverage Optimization
summary: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of vision-language models (VLMs), but most methods only ask which tokens to keep. This retained-token view can keep redundant high-scoring tokens while leaving discarded evidence without a close representative. We propose CoverPruner, a training-free pruner that asks the complementary demand-side question: after a token is removed, which surviving original token represents it for the target VLM? CoverPruner formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM), covering the full projected visual-token set with query-weighted demand. It instantiates RCM with projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe. Across multiple VLM architectures and compression rates, CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods, with the largest gains usually appearing under aggressive compression.

AI.tldr: CoverPruner is a training-free visual token pruning method for vision-language models (VLMs) that asks "which surviving token represents a removed token?" rather than just "which tokens to keep." It formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM) using projector-space coverage and a lightweight attention probe, achieving superior accuracy across multiple VLM architectures, especially under aggressive compression.
AI.motivation: Existing visual token pruning methods only ask which tokens to keep (retained-token view), which can result in redundant high-scoring tokens being retained while discarded evidence lacks close representatives. This limitation becomes particularly problematic under aggressive compression.
AI.method: CoverPruner formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM), which covers the full projected visual-token set with query-weighted demand. It instantiates RCM using projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe. The method is training-free.
AI.result: CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods across multiple VLM architectures and compression rates. The largest gains appear under aggressive compression settings.
AI.conclusion: By addressing the complementary demand-side question of token representation after removal, CoverPruner provides a more effective token pruning approach for VLMs, particularly beneficial for aggressive compression scenarios.

title: Neural Music Enhancement with Dual Time-Frequency Spectral Representations for Prediction and Discrimination
summary: Non-professional music recordings shared online often suffer from background noise and reverberation, degrading perceived quality and limiting reuse. This paper proposes DSME, a music enhancement model based on dual time-frequency spectral representations. Within a generative adversarial framework, DSME uses short-time Fourier transform (STFT) spectra for generation and constant-Q transform (CQT) spectra for discrimination. Leveraging STFT's fixed window, invertibility, and predictability, the generator estimates clean amplitude-phase spectra from degraded inputs and reconstructs waveforms via inverse STFT. Exploiting CQT's log-frequency, variable-window structure aligned with musical octaves, we design an octave-segmented CQT discriminator. We also introduce a chroma-spectrum loss to emphasize pitch and harmonic consistency. Experiments show DSME outperforms baselines in objective and subjective tests, validating the effectiveness of the dual-spectrum approach.

AI.tldr: DSME is a music enhancement model using dual time-frequency spectral representations (STFT and CQT) within a generative adversarial framework to remove background noise and reverberation from non-professional music recordings.
AI.motivation: Non-professional music recordings shared online often suffer from background noise and reverberation, which degrades perceived quality and limits reuse potential.
AI.method: The model uses a GAN framework where the generator employs short-time Fourier transform (STFT) spectra for clean amplitude-phase estimation and waveform reconstruction via inverse STFT, while the discriminator uses octave-segmented constant-Q transform (CQT) spectra leveraging CQT's log-frequency structure aligned with musical octaves. A chroma-spectrum loss is introduced to emphasize pitch and harmonic consistency.
AI.result: DSME outperforms baseline methods in both objective and subjective evaluation tests, validating the effectiveness of the dual-spectrum approach.
AI.conclusion: The dual time-frequency spectral representation approach successfully enhances music quality by combining STFT's invertibility and predictability with CQT's musical octave alignment, offering a promising solution for improving non-professional music recordings.

title: Mesh-Native Physics-Informed Graph Surrogates for TCAD-in-the-Loop Design Space Exploration
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)
summary: High-fidelity TCAD simulation of drift-diffusion transport remains the workhorse of emerging FinFET device design, but it is computationally expensive, especially for 3D structures where runtime escalates steeply with mesh complexity. This sharply limits multi-objective design space exploration. Existing machine-learning surrogates map a fixed set of design parameters to a few scalar device metrics, discarding the underlying physics and losing transferability across device geometries and families. A physics-informed graph attention network (GAT) surrogate is proposed. It operates directly on the tetrahedral TCAD mesh and predicts, at every mesh node, the electrostatic potential together with the electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels, the fundamental unknowns of the drift-diffusion system. Training combines a data loss with finite-volume current-continuity residuals, embedding carrier-transport physics into the objective. Operating on the mesh as a graph, the surrogate inherits size generalization: a model trained on few-fin meshes applies unchanged to substantially larger arrays, bounded at inference only by GPU memory. Per-node uncertainty from a deep ensemble drives an active-learning loop that screens large candidate pools in seconds and forwards only the most informative designs for full simulation. Benchmarked against Sentaurus Device on multi-fin tri-gate FinFETs, the surrogate reproduces the three drift-diffusion fields with sub-volt per-field RMSE and reaches a per-design throughput orders of magnitude higher than the full simulator. The advantage grows with device size: on large multi-fin arrays that are prohibitively slow to simulate directly, inference still completes in under a second per device, enabling Pareto-front exploration across device scales infeasible for direct TCAD sweeps.

AI.tldr: A physics-informed graph attention network (GAT) surrogate model for TCAD drift-diffusion simulation of FinFET devices. It operates on tetrahedral meshes, predicts fundamental unknowns (potential, quasi-Fermi levels), and achieves size generalization while enabling active learning through uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: High-fidelity TCAD drift-diffusion simulation is computationally expensive for 3D structures, limiting multi-objective design space exploration. Existing ML surrogates discard physics and lose transferability across device geometries.
AI.method: Physics-informed GAT operating on tetrahedral TCAD mesh as a graph. Predicts node-level electrostatic potential and electron/hole quasi-Fermi levels. Training combines data loss with finite-volume current-continuity residuals. Uses deep ensemble for per-node uncertainty quantification driving active learning.
AI.result: Sub-volt RMSE for all three drift-diffusion fields. Per-design throughput orders of magnitude higher than full simulator. Inference under 1 second per device for large multi-fin arrays. Enables Pareto-front exploration across device scales infeasible for direct TCAD.
AI.conclusion: The physics-informed GAT surrogate achieves accurate, fast inference with size generalization, enabling efficient design space exploration for FinFET devices that would be prohibitively slow with traditional TCAD simulation.

title: Caught in the Story: Narrative Captivity in Multi-turn LLMs Conversation
summary: People increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for everyday advice, making ethically charged interpersonal problems a practical moral-advisory context. Most prior work has studied this context through single-turn judgments or pressure-laden rebuttals, assumptions that poorly match how guidance is sought in real-world contexts. These assumptions leave unclear whether narration alone, without an explicit opposing position, can shift model judgments during multi-turn moral consultation. Yet real-world moral-conflict conversation often elicits one party's self-justifying account, which can unfold over multiple turns and create information asymmetry. We introduce \textbf{narrative captivity}, a failure mode in which a model treats an unopposed one-sided account as complete and aligns with the narrator's interpretation without seeking missing perspectives. To measure this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of $5{,}078$ interpersonal-conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions. Across 17 LLMs, narrative captivity is widespread: end-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by 25 percentage points on average beyond the matched single-turn baseline. Stage-level analysis identifies preference optimization as a major contributor, while four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation. We hope our project fosters LLM advisors that preserve independent judgment in real-world consultation.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "narrative captivity," a failure mode where LLMs align with a one-sided account in multi-turn moral consultation without seeking missing perspectives. The authors built a benchmark of 5,078 interpersonal conflict scenarios across six moral dimensions and tested 17 LLMs, finding that multi-turn narration shifts judgments by 25 percentage points on average beyond single-turn baselines.
AI.motivation: Real-world moral guidance seeking involves multi-turn conversations with one party's self-justifying account, which creates information asymmetry. Prior work studied single-turn judgments or pressure-laden rebuttals, which poorly match how advice is actually sought. This leaves unclear whether narration alone can shift model judgments without an explicit opposing position.
AI.method: The authors built a benchmark of 5,078 interpersonal-conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions. They tested 17 LLMs across these scenarios, comparing multi-turn narration conditions against matched single-turn baselines. They also performed stage-level analysis and tested four inference-time mitigation strategies.
AI.result: Narrative captivity is widespread across 17 LLMs. End-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by 25 percentage points on average beyond the matched single-turn baseline. Preference optimization is identified as a major contributor. Four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals that current LLM advisors may fail to preserve independent judgment in real-world consultation when faced with one-sided narratives. The authors hope this work fosters LLM advisors that maintain independent judgment and seek missing perspectives rather than simply aligning with the narrator's interpretation.

title: TruncGradGS: Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting via Truncated Gradient Updates
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has become a de facto scene representation for novel view synthesis, yet robustly learning 3D Gaussian primitives from visual input remains challenging. Standard optimization relies on gradient-based updates, but a common issue is the gradient vanishing phenomenon: a pixel far from a Gaussian primitive often has diminishing gradient magnitudes to influence primitive attributes, resulting in suboptimal scene reconstruction. In this paper, we propose a method to address gradient vanishing with a piecewise truncated gradient formulation that improves the optimization stability and robustness to initializations. We show that our method consistently improves 3D Gaussian Splatting with random and COLMAP initializations while being generalizable across static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting. As a by-product, we also examine the limitations of current benchmarks for dynamic scenes, and introduce a novel dataset for benchmarking dynamic Gaussian Splatting using synthetic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in both static and dynamic settings for the public benchmarks and our proposed dataset.

AI.tldr: A method to address gradient vanishing in 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization using piecewise truncated gradient formulation, which improves reconstruction quality and robustness to initializations. Includes a new dataset for benchmarking dynamic Gaussian Splatting.
AI.motivation: Standard gradient-based optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting suffers from gradient vanishing: pixels far from Gaussian primitives have diminishing gradient magnitudes, leading to suboptimal scene reconstruction.
AI.method: Proposed a piecewise truncated gradient formulation that improves optimization stability and robustness to initializations. Also introduced a novel dataset for benchmarking dynamic Gaussian Splatting using synthetic 3D scenes.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in 3D Gaussian Splatting with both random and COLMAP initializations, demonstrated effectiveness across static and dynamic settings on public benchmarks and the proposed dataset.
AI.conclusion: The piecewise truncated gradient formulation effectively addresses gradient vanishing in 3D Gaussian Splatting, providing more stable and robust optimization across various scenarios.

title: TIPCODER: Reinforcement Learning Boosted Test-time Instruction Proposer for Code Generation
comment: 15 pages, accepted by findings of EMNLP 2026
summary: Test-time scaling for code generation typically explores the solution space by sampling multiple programs from a fixed instruction. We study a complementary direction: instance-level instruction-space exploration. Our observation is that many coding failures stem from missing constraints, overlooked edge cases, or misleading reasoning paths induced by the original prompt. To address this, we propose TipCoder, a test-time instruction proposer that generates problem-specific auxiliary tips before code synthesis. TipCoder distills multi-turn debugging trajectories into proactive guidance and further optimizes the Proposer with reinforcement learning using a marginal-utility reward. At inference time, it generates both a base solution and a tip-guided solution, and applies a Reward Model for post-hoc selection. This exploration-selection design allows tips to expose additional candidate potential while reducing regressions from unnecessary guidance. Across the evaluated code-generation benchmarks and target Code LLMs, TipCoder provides a consistent instruction-level test-time scaling strategy, comparing favorably with stochastic sampling and generic prompt optimization baselines under a shared reward-model-based selection protocol.

AI.tldr: TipCoder proposes a test-time instruction-space exploration method for code generation that generates problem-specific auxiliary tips before code synthesis, using a dual-solution generation and reward-model-based selection approach to improve code generation quality.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to address the limitation of existing test-time scaling methods for code generation, which focus on solution-space exploration (sampling multiple programs). The authors observe that many coding failures stem from missing constraints, overlooked edge cases, or misleading reasoning paths in the original prompt, suggesting a complementary direction: instance-level instruction-space exploration.
AI.method: TipCoder consists of three key components: (1) A tip generation module that distills multi-turn debugging trajectories into proactive guidance; (2) Reinforcement learning optimization using marginal-utility reward to improve the Proposer; (3) An exploration-selection design that generates both base and tip-guided solutions, then applies a Reward Model for post-hoc selection.
AI.result: TipCoder provides a consistent instruction-level test-time scaling strategy across evaluated code-generation benchmarks and target Code LLMs. It compares favorably with stochastic sampling and generic prompt optimization baselines under a shared reward-model-based selection protocol.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that exploring instruction-space (generating problem-specific tips) is a complementary and effective approach to solution-space scaling for code generation. The exploration-selection design allows tips to expose additional candidate solutions while reducing regressions from unnecessary guidance.

title: RoboTok: An Internet-Scale Data Engine for Human Demonstration Retrieval and Dexterous Manipulation Learning
summary: Robot learning increasingly depends on broad and diverse demonstrations, yet collecting robot data remains expensive and poorly suited to covering the long tail of real-world tasks. To address this bottleneck, we introduce RoboTok, an internet-scale data engine that, given a query human manipulation video, retrieves manipulation-relevant human demonstrations from web videos for training dexterous robot policies. Specifically, we learn a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories expressed in estimated actor-centered reference frames. This representation enables manipulation behaviors to be compared across variations in camera viewpoint, scene appearance, and actor occlusions, while remaining compact enough for efficient search and continual indexing over internet-scale video collections. We evaluate RoboTok against existing robot-data retrieval approaches on retrieval benchmarks and downstream robot policy performance. Our results show that RoboTok retrieves more relevant manipulation demonstrations and improves downstream task success, establishing hand-pose trajectory-aware retrieval as a way to make web video a scalable and continuously growing source of supervision for robot learning.

AI.tldr: RoboTok is an internet-scale data engine that retrieves manipulation-relevant human demonstration videos from the web for training dexterous robot policies. It learns a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories in actor-centered reference frames, enabling comparison across viewpoint, appearance, and occlusion variations.
AI.motivation: Robot learning requires broad and diverse demonstrations, but collecting robot data is expensive and cannot cover the long tail of real-world tasks. There is a need to leverage internet-scale video data as a scalable source of supervision.
AI.method: RoboTok learns a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories expressed in estimated actor-centered reference frames. This representation enables manipulation behaviors to be compared across variations in camera viewpoint, scene appearance, and actor occlusions while remaining compact for efficient search and continual indexing over internet-scale video collections.
AI.result: RoboTok retrieves more relevant manipulation demonstrations compared to existing robot-data retrieval approaches and improves downstream robot policy performance and task success.
AI.conclusion: Hand-pose trajectory-aware retrieval establishes web video as a scalable and continuously growing source of supervision for robot learning, addressing the data bottleneck in robot policy training.

title: PACodec: A Low-bitrate Neural Speech Codec with Parallel Additive Vector Quantization
summary: This paper proposes PACodec, a novel low-bitrate neural speech codec based on parallel additive vector quantization (PAVQ). Unlike the mainstream residual vector quantization (RVQ) used in most neural speech codecs, where vector quantizers (VQs) are sequentially dependent, the PAVQ strategy adopted in PACodec aggregates parallel quantization results to optimize bitrate usage. Specifically, the PAVQ adopts a "global-local-global" (GLG) design: the global encoded features are quantized in parallel by multiple independent VQs, each attending to a local component of the representation, and their outputs are aggregated through addition to yield the final global quantization result for decoding. Experimental results show that PACodec, as each VQ focuses only on local information, supports smaller codebooks and reduces bitrate by 30% compared with baselines at the same decoding quality, with only minor model complexity. Further analysis shows that, owing to the GLG framework of PAVQ, the proposed PACodec is disentanglement-friendly, and each independent VQ captures different aspects of speech, e.g., content, timbre, and acoustic details, suggesting potential for application to downstream tasks such as voice conversion.

AI.tldr: PACodec is a low-bitrate neural speech codec using parallel additive vector quantization (PAVQ) with a "global-local-global" design, where multiple independent VQs quantize local components of global features and aggregate outputs through addition. It achieves 30% bitrate reduction compared to baselines while maintaining decoding quality.
AI.motivation: Mainstream neural speech codecs use residual vector quantization (RVQ) with sequentially dependent VQs, which is inefficient in bitrate usage. There was a need for a more efficient quantization approach that reduces bitrate while maintaining quality.
AI.method: PACodec uses PAVQ with a "global-local-global" (GLG) design: global encoded features are quantized in parallel by multiple independent VQs, each attending to a local component of the representation. Their outputs are aggregated through addition to yield the final global quantization result for decoding.
AI.result: PACodec achieves 30% bitrate reduction compared to baselines at the same decoding quality, with only minor model complexity. Each independent VQ captures different aspects of speech (content, timbre, acoustic details), demonstrating disentanglement-friendly properties.
AI.conclusion: The GLG framework of PAVQ enables efficient bitrate usage through parallel quantization. PACodec's disentanglement properties suggest potential for downstream applications such as voice conversion.

title: TRACE: Spatiotemporal Contact Memory Graph Network Simulator for Granular Dynamics
summary: Learned graph simulators provide an efficient alternative to high-fidelity solvers for granular dynamics. However, granular motion depends strongly on inter-granular contact history, which is difficult to preserve when particle contacts form, break, and rearrange. Existing simulators mainly store temporal information in node features or node-level memory. Here we introduce TRACE, a graph-network simulator that stores interaction history directly on contact edges. Each edge maintains a persistent memory updated by attention-based message passing and a gated recurrent unit, while an edge-identity dictionary preserves this memory as the contact graph changes. A physics-structured decoder predicts inter-granular normal and tangential contact forces, enforces the Coulomb friction limit, and applies equal-and-opposite internal forces. The model is trained with single-step pretraining followed by autoregressive rollout fine-tuning. We evaluate TRACE on 2D and 3D granular column-collapse benchmarks. In both cases, TRACE produces stable, physically consistent long-horizon rollouts, closely reproducing the final deposit geometry and the kinetic energy released during collapse. Compared with graph network simulator (GNS) and node-memory graph neural simulator (NMGNS), TRACE reduces long-rollout position error by 31-62% and final-deposit error by 58-89% across the two benchmarks, while using fewer parameters and maintaining near-zero particle interpenetration. TRACE also achieves 12.2$\times$ and 8.9$\times$ speedups over the material point method (MPM) reference solver in 2D and 3D, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/Data-Driven-Computational-Geotechnics/TRACE.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a learned graph simulator for granular dynamics that stores interaction history directly on contact edges using attention-based message passing and GRU, achieving 31-62% lower position error and 58-89% lower deposit error than existing methods while being 8.9-12.2x faster than traditional MPM solvers.
AI.motivation: Granular dynamics simulations are computationally expensive using traditional solvers. Existing learned simulators struggle to preserve inter-granular contact history when particle contacts form, break, and rearrange, as they mainly store temporal information in node features or node-level memory.
AI.method: TRACE uses a graph-network architecture with persistent edge memory updated by attention-based message passing and gated recurrent units (GRU). An edge-identity dictionary preserves memory as the contact graph changes. A physics-structured decoder predicts normal and tangential contact forces, enforces Coulomb friction limit and equal-and-opposite internal forces. Training involves single-step pretraining followed by autoregressive rollout fine-tuning.
AI.result: On 2D and 3D granular column-collapse benchmarks, TRACE reduces long-rollout position error by 31-62% and final-deposit error by 58-89% compared to GNS and NMGNS, while using fewer parameters and maintaining near-zero particle interpenetration. Achieves 12.2x and 8.9x speedups over MPM reference solver in 2D and 3D respectively.
AI.conclusion: Storing interaction history directly on contact edges with edge-identity preservation is more effective than node-level memory for granular dynamics simulation. TRACE achieves superior accuracy and efficiency compared to existing learned simulators and traditional solvers.

title: Dude: A Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for Paper-Code Discrepancy Detection
summary: LLM-empowered paper-code discrepancy detection has received growing concern since the scaling of research submissions exceeds the manual review capability. However, the limited context capacity and one-sided discrepancy detection of existing single-agent LLM paradigms lead to an inferior recall performance in detecting discrepancies. In this paper, we propose Dude, the first Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for paper-code discrepancy detection. We discover that the granularity asymmetry of the paper-language and code-language introduces over-interpretation and over-reporting challenges in a multi-agent system design for discrepancy detection, resulting in increasing false positives. To address this, we propose a granularity-aligned negotiation and a two-stage salience-filtering mechanism in Dude, which effectively prevents agents from falsely reporting discrepancies. Experimental results in real-world paper-code discrepancy datasets showcase Dude's significant recall and precision improvement by up to 22.8%, increasing F1 score by up to 18.7% compared to baseline methods.

title: Building Pretraining Data for World Models: An Unreal Engine-Based Pipeline for Action-Conditioned Video Generation
summary: Action-conditioned video models require large-scale visual data paired with control signals that are temporally aligned with the resulting scene transitions. Such supervision is difficult to obtain from ordinary real-world video because the actions that caused each visual change are typically unknown. We present a large-scale synthetic data production pipeline built on Unreal Engine for generating action-conditioned, multi-view video. To accommodate the different execution requirements of real-time physics and high-quality offline rendering, the pipeline executes trajectory generation and final rendering in two stages: Stage I runs real physics in PIE and records per-frame character states, control inputs, and camera states into an intermediate trajectory representation; Stage II replays those trajectories in a new engine process and renders them offline with Movie Render Queue (MRQ). Around this core, we develop a distributed production system with cache-aware task partitioning, node-local slot scheduling, automated scene screening, aesthetic and luminance filtering, partial-output recovery, asynchronous upload, and continuous cluster health monitoring. The production cluster contains 25 servers with eight NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs per server. From 2,384 asset packs, 429 levels were retained for production together with a pool of 40 humanoid characters. The pipeline has produced 2,691 hours of 1080p video and 6,076 hours of 720p video. We describe the system architecture, the implementation decisions that emerged from production failures, and the limitations of using perceptual quality proxies for world-model data curation. The pipeline described in this report constitutes the Unreal Engine synthetic-data production component used in EchoWM.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a large-scale synthetic data production pipeline built on Unreal Engine for generating action-conditioned, multi-view video for training world models. The pipeline uses a two-stage architecture: Stage I runs real-time physics to capture character states, control inputs, and camera states; Stage II replays trajectories for high-quality offline rendering. The system includes distributed production features like cache-aware task partitioning, automated screening, and cluster health monitoring. The production cluster consists of 25 servers with 8 NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs each, and has produced 2,691 hours of 1080p video and 6,076 hours of 720p video from 429 levels and 40 humanoid characters.
AI.motivation: Action-conditioned video models require large-scale visual data paired with temporally aligned control signals. However, obtaining such supervision from real-world video is challenging because the actions causing visual changes are typically unknown. This creates a data bottleneck for training world models that understand action-to-outcome relationships.
AI.method: The pipeline employs a two-stage architecture: (1) Stage I executes real-time physics in PIE (Play In Editor) mode, recording per-frame character states, control inputs, and camera states into an intermediate trajectory representation; (2) Stage II replays trajectories in a separate engine process for offline rendering using Movie Render Queue (MRQ). Around this core, they developed a distributed production system with cache-aware task partitioning, node-local slot scheduling, automated scene screening, aesthetic/luminance filtering, partial-output recovery, asynchronous upload, and continuous cluster health monitoring. The cluster contains 25 servers with 8 NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs each, using 429 retained levels from 2,384 asset packs and 40 humanoid characters.
AI.result: The pipeline produced 2,691 hours of 1080p video and 6,076 hours of 720p video. The system successfully handled the challenge of reconciling real-time physics requirements with high-quality offline rendering through the two-stage trajectory approach.
AI.conclusion: The paper describes the system architecture and implementation decisions that emerged from production failures, highlighting limitations of using perceptual quality proxies for world-model data curation. This pipeline constitutes the Unreal Engine synthetic-data production component used in EchoWM, demonstrating a viable approach for generating large-scale action-conditioned video data when real-world supervision is unavailable.

title: The Psychological Costs of Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Software Engineering
summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to augment software engineering (SE) workflows. While code generation remains the main use case, organizations are actively seeking AI integration in other practices such as test cases generation and code reviews. Organizational AI adoption strategies seem to focus on tangible outcomes such as productivity. However, AI is a disruptive force, introduced into settings where role identity, team norms, and the sources of job satisfaction were well established before the recent advances in generative AI. Historically, technological disruptions have caused psychological and social strains in workplaces, ranging from anxiety and eroded meaning to deskilling and disrupted professional identities. The assumption that AI for SE is cost-free may not be accurate. Therefore, in this study we sought to understand the psychological costs software professionals experience during organizational AI adoption. We carried out a case study in a large software development services company, one year after the company launched its AI adoption. We collected qualitative data through meetings and semi-structured interviews (N = 21). We found that software professionals experience accountability anxiety, craft identity disruption, meaning and satisfaction erosion, cognitive and workload intensification, and uncertainty distress. Practitioners manage these costs through practices that restore control, mitigate them through protective and identity-preserving adaptations, or absorb them, carrying what neither can resolve. We contribute to AI-human collaboration in SE by repositioning AI adoption as a human transition, not only a technological and organizational one.

AI.tldr: This study investigates the psychological costs that software professionals experience when organizations adopt AI tools in software engineering workflows. Through a case study conducted one year after AI adoption in a large software development services company, the researchers identified five key psychological costs: accountability anxiety, craft identity disruption, meaning and satisfaction erosion, cognitive and workload intensification, and uncertainty distress. The study contributes by reframing AI adoption as a human transition rather than merely a technological or organizational change.
AI.motivation: While AI adoption in software engineering focuses on tangible outcomes like productivity, the psychological and social impacts on software professionals have been overlooked. Historical technological disruptions have caused workplace anxiety, eroded meaning, deskilling, and disrupted professional identities. The researchers question whether AI adoption is truly cost-free and seek to understand the psychological costs experienced by software professionals during organizational AI adoption.
AI.method: Case study conducted in a large software development services company, one year after the company launched its AI adoption initiative. Qualitative data was collected through meetings and semi-structured interviews with 21 participants (N = 21).
AI.result: The study identified five psychological costs experienced by software professionals: (1) accountability anxiety, (2) craft identity disruption, (3) meaning and satisfaction erosion, (4) cognitive and workload intensification, and (5) uncertainty distress. Practitioners manage these costs through: practices that restore control, protective and identity-preserving adaptations, or absorbing what cannot be resolved.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes to AI-human collaboration in software engineering by repositioning AI adoption as a human transition, not only a technological and organizational one. Organizations should consider the psychological impacts on employees when implementing AI tools.

title: Learning to Zoom Efficiently with a Contrastive Curriculum
summary: Using a zoom-in tool is an important foundational part of modern visual agents, because it allows to efficiently handle tasks involving high-resolution images. Most previous methods need an extensive warm-start supervised fine-tuning phase for teaching models zoom-in. We show that this is not necessary by proposing a new intrinsic reward for learning tool use in MLLMs without the need for additional labels or warm-start SFT. Our InfoNCE-style reward uses a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as a contrastive training signal. Empirical experiments on $V^*$, HRBench and MME-RealWorld show that our approach is competitive while being more efficient. When used as a drop-in replacement for SFT, we even outperform all baselines. To directly measure the zoom-in ability of models, we further introduce the scalable synthetic Muffin&Chihuahua (M&C) dataset. Each image consists of a grid with every cell either showing a muffin or chihuahua. Leveraging the M&C dataset's unique region of interest labels, we find that recall is the metric that most strongly correlates the zoom-in region with final task performance. Our model and code for reproduction is publicly available under https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2026-zoom-in

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an intrinsic reward-based approach for teaching multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) to use zoom-in tools without requiring warm-start supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The method uses an InfoNCE-style reward with a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as contrastive training signal.
AI.motivation: Current methods for teaching visual agents to use zoom-in tools require extensive warm-start supervised fine-tuning, which is inefficient and demands additional labels. The authors argue this is unnecessary and propose learning tool use through intrinsic rewards instead.
AI.method: The proposed approach uses an InfoNCE-style intrinsic reward that employs a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as a contrastive training signal. This eliminates the need for additional labels or warm-start SFT. The authors also introduce the synthetic Muffin&Chihuahua (M&C) dataset - a scalable dataset where each image contains a grid of muffins or chihuahuas with region of interest labels, designed to directly measure zoom-in ability.
AI.result: Empirical experiments on V*, HRBench, and MME-RealWorld show that the approach is competitive while being more efficient. When used as a drop-in replacement for SFT, it outperforms all baselines. Analysis on the M&C dataset reveals that recall is the metric that most strongly correlates zoom-in region selection with final task performance.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that intrinsic rewards can effectively teach MLLMs zoom-in tool usage without warm-start SFT, achieving superior performance with better efficiency. The introduced M&C dataset provides a scalable way to evaluate zoom-in capabilities, with recall being the most predictive metric for task success.

title: StrixAE: An Intelligent Agent for Audio Enhancement under Complex Distortion Coupling in Real-World Scenarios
summary: Audio enhancement in real-world scenarios involves complex distortion couplings and requires personalized enhancement. Existing solutions struggle to address both simultaneously. To improve robustness and enable autonomous operation in such scenarios, we propose StrixAE, an agent based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). StrixAE leverages the MLLM as a controller to coordinate multiple audio enhancement and personalization models. To further enhance system robustness, reduce artifacts, and improve generalization across diverse real-world scenarios, StrixAE is trained through a two-stage process: first, CoT supervised fine-tuning on AcoustBench to ground basic reasoning and tool invocation; second, Audio Perception Reinforcement Learning (APRL), a reward design specifically tailored for audio restoration pipelines that jointly optimizes format validity, structural coherence, and perceptual quality. Unlike generic RL fine-tuning, APRL introduces structured rewards that enforce executable pipelines and logical section ordering, enabling the agent to produce reliable, interpretable enhancement plans without hallucinated tools. Based on real-world test datasets, our proposed method outperforms most existing open-source and proprietary solutions, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple perceptual metrics and demonstrating strong generalization robustness.

AI.tldr: StrixAE is an MLLM-based agent for real-world audio enhancement that coordinates multiple enhancement models through a two-stage training process: CoT supervised fine-tuning on AcoustBench and Audio Perception Reinforcement Learning (APRL). It achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple perceptual metrics with strong generalization.
AI.motivation: Real-world audio enhancement involves complex distortion couplings and requires personalized enhancement. Existing solutions struggle to address both simultaneously. There is a need for a robust, autonomous system that can handle diverse real-world scenarios.
AI.method: StrixAE uses an MLLM as a controller to coordinate multiple audio enhancement and personalization models. Training involves two stages: (1) CoT supervised fine-tuning on AcoustBench for basic reasoning and tool invocation, and (2) Audio Perception Reinforcement Learning (APRL) with structured rewards that optimize format validity, structural coherence, and perceptual quality while enforcing executable pipelines and logical section ordering.
AI.result: Outperforms most existing open-source and proprietary solutions on real-world test datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple perceptual metrics and demonstrating strong generalization robustness.
AI.conclusion: The proposed StrixAE with APRL training effectively addresses complex audio enhancement challenges by combining MLLM-based orchestration with structured reinforcement learning, enabling reliable and interpretable enhancement plans without hallucinated tools.

title: No-Regret Bayesian Optimization with Finite-Library Input-Warped Kernels
summary: Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO) excels at black-box optimization of costly functions, e.g., hyperparameter optimization (HPO) and multi-agent system (MAS) design. Convergence-rate guarantees exist for select methods, notably GP upper confidence bound (GP-UCB), but require a fixed kernel. Critically, the kernel encodes how input proximity affects objective value similarity. When raw coordinates poorly match this geometry - as with log-scaled hyperparameters or localized peaks - input warping can greatly improve sample efficiency, yet known GP-UCB proofs require a fixed kernel. We propose Finite-Library Input-Warped Bayesian Optimization (FLIWBO), which selects warps from a finite library of smooth input maps by any history-dependent rule. It adapts the input geometry to accelerate learning while retaining high-probability convergence guarantees under mild hypotheses, with an explicit $\sqrt(N_\varepsilon)$ library-size cost. Controlled diagnostics show that finite-library warping repairs planted geometry mismatches and identify FLIWBO failure cases. Across four repeated benchmarks - warped synthetic objectives, a confidence-fence trap, and Fashion-MNIST HPO - FLIWBO-UCB beats raw-coordinate GP-UCB under misspecified geometry, escapes traps that defeat even oracle-warp expected improvement, and recovers much of the gain from manual log scaling, while leading the tested methods that admit a matching regret guarantee. A 20-dimensional MAS design study further shows feasibility under costly noisy evaluations. Code for experiments is available: https://github.com/edvin-ketabati/bogp-paper-experiments.
