AI.tldr: FLIWBO addresses the limitation that GP-UCB requires a fixed kernel, which fails when raw coordinates poorly match the underlying geometry (e.g., log-scaled hyperparameters). The method selects input warps from a finite library while retaining high-probability convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: When raw coordinates poorly match the geometry (log-scaled hyperparameters, localized peaks), input warping can improve sample efficiency, but existing GP-UCB proofs require a fixed kernel, breaking convergence guarantees.
AI.method: Finite-Library Input-Warped Bayesian Optimization (FLIWBO) selects warps from a finite library of smooth input maps using any history-dependent rule, retaining convergence guarantees with an explicit √(N_ε) library-size cost.
AI.result: FLIWBO-UCB outperforms raw-coordinate GP-UCB under misspecified geometry, escapes traps that defeat oracle-warp expected improvement, and recovers gains from manual log scaling. Tested on warped synthetic objectives, confidence-fence trap, Fashion-MNIST HPO, and 20-dimensional MAS design.
AI.conclusion: FLIWBO provides a principled way to adapt input geometry while maintaining theoretical guarantees, achieving superior sample efficiency across diverse benchmarks including hyperparameter optimization and multi-agent system design.

title: DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval: Evaluating Implicit Instruction Following in Full-Duplex Voice Agents
summary: Full-duplex voice agents must continuously decide when to listen, backchannel, interrupt, handle speech overlaps, take the floor, and yield. Existing benchmarks largely test these behaviors through explicit turn-management instructions, while deployed agents are often configured through roles or personas from which the appropriate conversational behavior must be inferred. We introduce DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval (DSB-IFEval) for evaluating implicit instruction-following in real-time spoken interaction. (DSB-IFEval) comprises 1,038 test cases spanning eight diverse assistant roles and evaluates five conditioning protocols for instruction-following: default behavior, explicit behavioral instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona--rule conditioning, and instruction conflict. We measure real-time floor management using a deterministic Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) and persona-consistent content using LLM-judged Persona Adherence Score (PAS). Across six real-time speech systems, we find architecture-dependent trade-offs. Full duplex models like F-Actor and PersonaPlex are more sensitive to whether conversational behavior is stated explicitly or must be inferred from a persona, with adherence dropping by 9.7% and 4.5%, respectively, under persona-only conditioning. In contrast, GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat strongly adhere to persona-consistent content, but their floor behavior does not adapt across explicit and persona-only instructions and remains constrained on several proactive actions. We further find that even if systems reliably follow conflicting directives to their prescribed persona, they still struggle to override them under safety conflict. These results show that inferring the behavior implied by a role, executing it at the appropriate conversational moment, and resolving competing instructions remain distinct challenges for full-duplex voice agents.

AI.tldr: DSB-IFEval is a benchmark with 1,038 test cases across 8 assistant roles evaluating how well full-duplex voice agents follow implicit instructions (persona-based) versus explicit behavioral instructions in real-time spoken interaction. The study reveals significant architecture-dependent trade-offs, with some models being sensitive to conditioning type while others struggle with proactive behaviors and safety conflicts.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks test explicit turn-management instructions, but deployed voice agents are typically configured through roles or personas from which conversational behavior must be inferred. This gap between evaluation (explicit instructions) and deployment (persona-based) motivates the need for evaluating implicit instruction-following in real-time spoken interaction.
AI.method: The benchmark evaluates 5 conditioning protocols: default behavior, explicit behavioral instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona-rule conditioning, and instruction conflict. Real-time floor management is measured using Instruction Adherence Score (IAS), while persona-consistent content is judged by LLM (Persona Adherence Score - PAS). Six real-time speech systems were tested: F-Actor, PersonaPlex, GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat.
AI.result: Full duplex models (F-Actor, PersonaPlex) are more sensitive to explicit vs persona-only conditioning, with adherence dropping by 9.7% and 4.5% respectively under persona-only conditioning. GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat strongly adhere to persona-consistent content but their floor behavior does not adapt across conditioning types and remains constrained on proactive actions. Even systems that follow conflicting directives to their persona struggle to override them under safety conflicts.
AI.conclusion: Inferring behavior implied by a role, executing it at the appropriate conversational moment, and resolving competing instructions remain distinct challenges for full-duplex voice agents. The study highlights the need for better implicit instruction-following capabilities in real-time spoken interaction systems.

title: Code Transformation Rule Synthesis using LLMs: Potential and Limits
comment: Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: Due to their black-box nature, LLMs suffer from limited explain- ability and a lack of determinism. Their usage cost can also rise, particularly with repetitive tasks on large codebases. To mitigate this, we conduct a novel empirical study targeting three domain- specific languages for transformation rules, namely Comby, GritQL, and Ast-Grep. We evaluate three LLMs (GPT-5.4, GPT-oss-120B, and Llama3.1-8B) on six diverse datasets covering four software- evolution tasks: API misuse correction, program repair, API migra- tion, and language version migration. Our results provide evidence that transformation rule synthesis moves beyond proof-of-concept with strong frontier models. GPT-5.4 achieves consistently high rule applicability rates and produces transformations closest to the ground truth across most benchmarks. Smaller and open-weight GPT-oss-120B and Llama3.1-8B models remain effective for simpler, localized changes but struggle with complex migration scenarios. We also observe non-negligible generalizability through the usage of meta-variables and through a high reuse score in the first quartile of many datasets. Finally, when compared to the anti-unification algorithm, LLMs outperform it in correctness, but underperform in rule applicability. Overall, our results show great potential for LLMs to generate sound, correct, generalizable, and reusable rules.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates three LLMs (GPT-5.4, GPT-oss-120B, Llama3.1-8B) on transforming code using three domain-specific languages (Comby, GritQL, Ast-Grep) across six datasets covering four software evolution tasks (API misuse correction, program repair, API migration, language version migration).
AI.motivation: LLMs face challenges of limited explainability, lack of determinism, and high usage costs, especially for repetitive tasks on large codebases. The study investigates whether transformation rule synthesis using LLMs can move beyond proof-of-concept to practical application.
AI.method: Empirical study comparing three LLMs on three DSLs across six datasets covering four software evolution tasks. Evaluated rule applicability, correctness compared to ground truth, generalizability through meta-variables, and reuse scores. Also compared LLM performance against anti-unification algorithm.
AI.result: GPT-5.4 achieves highest rule applicability and produces transformations closest to ground truth. Smaller models (GPT-oss-120B, Llama3.1-8B) work well for simpler, localized changes but struggle with complex migrations. Meta-variables show good generalizability with high reuse scores. LLMs outperform anti-unification in correctness but underperform in rule applicability.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show great potential for generating sound, correct, generalizable, and reusable transformation rules for code, with strong frontier models like GPT-5.4 being most effective, though smaller models remain useful for simpler tasks.

title: ProgResViT: Progressive Resolution and Width for Adaptive Vision Transformers
summary: Vision Transformers (ViTs) typically process every image using a fixed input resolution and model width, even though many images can be classified with substantially less computation. We introduce ProgResViT, an input-adaptive ViT that performs inference progressively across multiple rounds. The first round processes a low-resolution image with a narrow subnetwork. Inference terminates when the prediction is sufficiently confident; otherwise, the model reuses the representations produced in the current round and proceeds with a higher-resolution input and a wider subnetwork to refine its prediction. As all rounds share a single backbone, we propose Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG), which conditions token fusion and layer outputs on the current round, block, and input resolution. On image classification, applying ProgResViT to DeiT yields better accuracy-compute trade-offs than adaptive-width, adaptive-depth, and dynamic-token baselines. With knowledge distillation, a DeiT-based ProgResViT achieves 84.9% top-1 accuracy, slightly exceeding the reported DeiT-III-S accuracy under a comparable evaluation setting. We show that the same design also provides favorable accuracy-compute trade-offs for self-supervised DINO representations and downstream semantic segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/ds-kiel/ProgResViT.

AI.tldr: ProgResViT is an input-adaptive Vision Transformer that performs inference progressively across multiple rounds, starting with low-resolution/narrow subnetwork and refining predictions with higher resolution/wider subnetwork only when needed. It uses Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG) to condition token fusion and layer outputs on current round, block, and input resolution.
AI.motivation: Vision Transformers (ViTs) typically process every image using a fixed input resolution and model width, even though many images can be classified with substantially less computation. This inefficiency motivates the development of adaptive inference methods.
AI.method: ProgResViT performs inference progressively across multiple rounds. The first round processes a low-resolution image with a narrow subnetwork. Inference terminates when prediction is sufficiently confident; otherwise, the model reuses representations from the current round and proceeds with higher-resolution input and wider subnetwork to refine prediction. All rounds share a single backbone, and Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG) conditions token fusion and layer outputs on the current round, block, and input resolution.
AI.result: ProgResViT applied to DeiT yields better accuracy-compute trade-offs than adaptive-width, adaptive-depth, and dynamic-token baselines. With knowledge distillation, a DeiT-based ProgResViT achieves 84.9% top-1 accuracy, slightly exceeding the reported DeiT-III-S accuracy under comparable evaluation settings. The same design also provides favorable accuracy-compute trade-offs for self-supervised DINO representations and downstream semantic segmentation.
AI.conclusion: ProgResViT demonstrates that progressive, input-adaptive inference can achieve superior accuracy-compute trade-offs across multiple vision tasks including image classification, self-supervised representation learning (DINO), and semantic segmentation, outperforming existing adaptive methods.

title: Evaluating Graph Neural Networks for Change-Criticality Classification in Maritime Navigation Charts
comment: Accepted at IEEE International Geoscience and Remote Sensing Symposium (IGARSS) 2026
summary: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a class of neural networks suitable for learning on graph-structured data. Their application to spatial data is a natural extension, however its relatively unclear which message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representation is best suited for classifying changes to objects in electronic navigational charts (ENCs)--geospatial vector datasets used for marine navigation. Maintaining these datasets is a challenge, and categorizing changes to objects in the ENC based on their significance to navigational safety is of particular importance. Here, we propose to represent these vector navigation datasets as a graph structure where the spatial objects serve as nodes and their spatial and semantic relationships form edges. We encode both the old ENC dataset and new ENC dataset into a pair of graphs and frame the task as a graph-pair classification problem. Building on this representation, we investigate the use of GNN architectures to classify whether the encoded graphs constitutes a critical or non-critical risk to navigational safety. We train and evaluate several GNN architectures and model configurations on ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts. Our results demonstrate that graph-based representations improve the classification of ENC updates, providing a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to classify changes in Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs) as critical or non-critical risks to navigational safety. The approach represents spatial objects as nodes and their relationships as edges, encoding old and new ENC datasets as graph pairs for classification.
AI.motivation: Maintaining ENC datasets is challenging, and categorizing changes based on navigational safety significance is important but unclear which GNN message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representations are best suited for this task.
AI.method: Represent ENC vector navigation datasets as graph structures where spatial objects serve as nodes and their spatial/semantic relationships form edges. Encode both old and new ENC datasets as a pair of graphs and frame the task as graph-pair classification. Train and evaluate several GNN architectures on ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts.
AI.result: Graph-based representations improve classification of ENC updates, providing a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.
AI.conclusion: GNNs are effective for classifying ENC changes by safety significance, offering a scalable solution for ENC maintenance automation.

title: Do GUI Agents Know When Not to Act? Enabling Conflict-Aware Termination for Multimodal GUI Agents
summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are increasingly used to execute natural-language instructions on user interfaces, yet real users may issue infeasible instructions due to benign mistakes. A reliable agent should not only know how to act, but also when not to act. In this work, we introduce CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark covering instruction-internal conflicts and instruction-GUI context conflicts to study conflict-aware termination. Our evaluation reveals severe execution-biased overcompliance: agents that perform well on feasible tasks often continue to execute blindly under conflicting instructions. To mitigate this behavior, we propose CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that aligns an agent's feasibility awareness with its action generation. CONFLICTGUARD contains two coupled components: a feasibility verification protocol that guides the agent to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and a conditional action modulation mechanism that steers agents from over-compliant execution into termination-oriented behavior. Experiments across five widely-used agents demonstrate that CONFLICTGUARD improves average conflict task success rate significantly, while preserving normal GUI-task performance. These results validate that a lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI Agent's competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions.

AI.tldr: CONFLICTGUI is a benchmark for evaluating GUI agents' ability to recognize and terminate execution when faced with conflicting instructions (either internal conflicts or conflicts with GUI context). CONFLICTGUARD is an inference-time framework that improves agents' conflict awareness through feasibility verification and action modulation.
AI.motivation: Real users may issue infeasible instructions due to benign mistakes. Current GUI agents exhibit "execution-biased overcompliance" - they continue executing blindly even under conflicting instructions, which is problematic for reliable agent behavior.
AI.method: CONFLICTGUARD uses two coupled components: (1) a feasibility verification protocol that guides the agent to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and (2) a conditional action modulation mechanism that steers agents from over-compliant execution into termination-oriented behavior.
AI.result: CONFLICTGUARD significantly improves average conflict task success rate while preserving normal GUI-task performance across five widely-used agents.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI agents' competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions.

title: Can LLMs Extract Architectural Design Decisions from Source Code Commits? - A Preliminary Exploratory Study
comment: Accepted at IdeaArch Workshop at ECSA 2026
summary: Context: Architectural Design Decisions (ADDs) capture the rationale behind the structure and evolution of software systems but are rarely documented explicitly, and are often hidden inside source code commits. Recovering them is important for Architectural Knowledge Management (AKM). Problem: Extracting ADDs from commits is challenging due to their implicit and unstructured nature. Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities in understanding code and text, yet their effectiveness for this task remains underexplored. Study: We present a preliminary study using four LLMs (Gemini 3 Pro, DeepSeek R1, Kimi K2, Qwen3) with zeroshot and fewshot prompting on 30 developer-written ADDs from open-source projects. We score outputs with ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore, and one author manually reviews the Gemini outputs. Results: All models reach a BERT-F1 above 0.81, and fewshot prompting improves alignment (Gemini BERT-F1: 0.828 to 0.847). However, the generated ADDs are often too long, implementation-focused, and miss the rationale behind the decision. This highlights opportunities for architecture-aware LLM systems and automated AKM.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using Large Language Models (LLMs) to extract Architectural Design Decisions (ADDs) from source code commits. Four LLMs were tested with zero-shot and few-shot prompting on 30 developer-written ADDs from open-source projects. While all models achieved BERT-F1 scores above 0.81 and few-shot prompting improved results, the generated ADDs tended to be too long, implementation-focused, and missing key rationale behind decisions.
AI.motivation: Architectural Design Decisions are rarely explicitly documented and are often hidden within source code commits. Recovering these decisions is crucial for Architectural Knowledge Management (AKM), but current extraction methods struggle with the implicit and unstructured nature of commits. While LLMs show strong code understanding capabilities, their effectiveness for this specific task remains underexplored.
AI.method: The study used four LLMs (Gemini 3 Pro, DeepSeek R1, Kimi K2, and Qwen3) with both zero-shot and few-shot prompting strategies. They evaluated outputs on 30 developer-written ADDs from open-source projects using four metrics: ROUGE-L, BLEU, METEOR, and BERTScore. One author manually reviewed the Gemini outputs for qualitative assessment.
AI.result: All models achieved BERT-F1 scores above 0.81. Few-shot prompting improved alignment, with Gemini showing improvement from 0.828 to 0.847 BERT-F1. However, the generated ADDs suffered from being too long, overly implementation-focused, and failing to capture the rationale behind architectural decisions.
AI.conclusion: While LLMs show promise for ADD extraction (demonstrated by high BERT-F1 scores), significant opportunities remain for improvement. The study highlights the need for architecture-aware LLM systems that can better capture decision rationale rather than just implementation details. This work paves the way for automated AKM tools that could help developers document and recover architectural knowledge from code commits.

title: Counting Animals in Camera-Traps Image Sequences without Count Labels: Winning Solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge
summary: Camera traps have become an essential tool for wildlife monitoring, motivating the development of computer vision methods for the automated extraction of information from these data. While most prior work has focused on species identification, many ecological applications also require estimating the number of unique individuals appearing across short image sequences. This task is particularly challenging because camera traps typically acquire bursts of images at approximately one frame per second, creating large temporal discontinuities that may make conventional multi-object tracking methods unreliable, and because manually collecting individual count annotations is prohibitively expensive. In this work, we describe the winning solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge, which introduced a benchmark for counting animals at the sequence level under realistic annotation constraints where count annotations are unavailable for training. Our approach, MaxBoxCount, combines a strong species classification pipeline with a simple yet effective counting heuristic based on MegaDetector detections to estimate the number of unique individuals without requiring count annotations. Code is available at https://github.com/alcunha/iwildcam2021ufam.

AI.tldr: This paper presents MaxBoxCount, the winning solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge, which addresses the problem of counting unique animal individuals in camera trap image sequences without requiring count annotations for training. The approach combines species classification with a detection-based counting heuristic.
AI.motivation: Camera traps are essential for wildlife monitoring, but existing computer vision methods focus mainly on species identification rather than individual counting. The task is challenging due to large temporal discontinuities (burst images at ~1 frame/second) and the high cost of manually annotating individual counts.
AI.method: The proposed MaxBoxCount method combines: (1) a strong species classification pipeline, and (2) a simple counting heuristic based on MegaDetector detections to estimate the number of unique individuals without requiring count annotations.
AI.result: The method won the iWildCam 2021 Challenge, which introduced a benchmark for animal counting at the sequence level under realistic annotation constraints where count annotations are unavailable for training.
AI.conclusion: A simple yet effective approach combining species classification with detection-based counting can successfully estimate individual counts in camera trap sequences without requiring manual count annotations, demonstrating the practical applicability of this method for real-world wildlife monitoring.

title: Test-time adaptation for speech enhancement with an autoregressive speech prior
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a promising direction for improving speech enhancement models under mismatched acoustic conditions, without requiring access to labeled target data. In this work, we propose a single-utterance TTA method that regularizes a pretrained speech enhancement model using an autoregressive prior trained on clean speech latent representations extracted from a neural audio codec. Adaptation is performed by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the enhanced speech distribution and the clean speech prior. Experiments across multiple noisy speech datasets show consistent improvements in speech quality, particularly under training-testing noise mismatch conditions. Code and audio examples are available online.

AI.tldr: A test-time adaptation (TTA) method for speech enhancement that uses an autoregressive prior trained on clean speech latent representations from a neural audio codec. Adaptation is performed via KL divergence minimization between enhanced and clean speech distributions.
AI.motivation: To improve speech enhancement models under mismatched acoustic conditions without requiring labeled target data, addressing the common problem of train-test distribution mismatch in practical deployment scenarios.
AI.method: 1) Extract clean speech latent representations using a neural audio codec; 2) Train an autoregressive prior on these clean speech latents; 3) At test time, adapt a pretrained enhancement model by minimizing KL divergence between enhanced speech distribution and the clean speech prior; 4) Uses single-utterance adaptation requiring no additional labeled data.
AI.result: Consistent improvements in speech quality across multiple noisy speech datasets, with particularly notable gains under training-testing noise mismatch conditions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed TTA approach effectively bridges the domain gap between training and testing conditions by leveraging a learned clean speech prior, demonstrating that autoregressive priors on codec latents can serve as effective regularizers for test-time adaptation of speech enhancement models.

title: Verify Before You Distill: Prompt-Level Teacher Gating for On-Policy Distillation
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) accelerates post-training by providing dense token-level supervision from a frozen teacher on the student's own rollouts. Vanilla OPD applies this supervision uniformly across prompts, without checking whether the teacher is reliable for each prompt. Because reverse KL is mode-seeking, a confidently wrong teacher can induce a strong yet misleading update. Distributional proxies, such as entropy or teacher-student likelihood agreement, measure uncertainty or agreement but do not directly verify outcome correctness. We introduce Teacher-Gated On-Policy Distillation (TGOPD), built on the principle that teacher reliability should be verified at the prompt level before dense supervision is admitted. TGOPD estimates reliability from a small set of verifier-scored teacher probes and routes each prompt exclusively to dense OPD when the reliability check passes or to verifier-grounded GRPO otherwise. Across 4B and 35B students in mathematics, code, and instruction following, TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD in all six single-domain settings and achieves higher seven-benchmark averages at both scales under multi-domain training. By using otherwise-idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation, TGOPD also reduces teacher-side compute waste in asynchronous OPD, increasing teacher-node GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9% in the measured 4B single-domain run.

AI.tldr: TGOPD addresses a key weakness in on-policy distillation where uniformly applying teacher supervision leads to harmful updates when the teacher is confidently wrong. The method uses small verifier-scored probe sets to estimate teacher reliability at the prompt level, routing each prompt to dense OPD only when reliability passes, otherwise using verifier-grounded GRPO. This approach consistently outperforms Vanilla OPD across math, code, and instruction-following tasks at both 4B and 35B scales, while also improving teacher GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9%.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a frozen teacher on student rollouts to accelerate post-training. However, vanilla OPD applies this supervision uniformly without checking teacher reliability for each prompt. Since reverse KL is mode-seeking, a confidently wrong teacher can induce strong yet misleading updates. Existing distributional proxies (entropy, teacher-student agreement) measure uncertainty but don't verify outcome correctness directly.
AI.method: TGOPD introduces a prompt-level routing mechanism based on teacher reliability estimation. The method estimates reliability from a small set of verifier-scored teacher probes. Each prompt is then routed exclusively: (1) to dense OPD when the reliability check passes, or (2) to verifier-grounded GRPO when the reliability check fails. This approach uses otherwise-idle teacher capacity for reliability estimation, improving compute efficiency.
AI.result: Across 4B and 35B student models in mathematics, code, and instruction following domains: (1) TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD in all six single-domain settings; (2) achieves higher seven-benchmark averages at both scales under multi-domain training; (3) increases teacher-node GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9% in the measured 4B single-domain run, reducing teacher-side compute waste.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-level teacher reliability verification is essential for effective on-policy distillation. By routing prompts based on verified reliability rather than applying uniform supervision, TGOPD achieves consistent improvements across diverse domains and model scales while also addressing compute efficiency in asynchronous OPD setups.

title: Beyond "Made with AI": Visualizing Provenance Density to Mitigate the Transparency Penalty
summary: As generative AI makes polished prose cheap to produce, users can no longer rely on fluency as a proxy for truth. We call this failure mode the Fluency Trap: users trust fluent hallucinations while also discounting accurate content once it is disclosed as AI-generated. Binary ``Made with AI'' labels respond with authorship disclosure, but they do not show what supports a claim. We propose Provenance Density, an evidence-visualization interface that shows the density of verified claims in a text. In a user study with 81 participants, an idealized Provenance Density interface produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication ($+4.15$ points, $d=1.82$), whereas participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. A technical audit with 200 samples shows that retrieval density alone is insufficient; unexpectedly, the Consistency Veto carries most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries. As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must move from authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization.

AI.tldr: As AI-generated text becomes indistinguishable from human writing, users fall into a "Fluency Trap" - trusting fluent hallucinations while discounting accurate AI-generated content. This paper proposes "Provenance Density," an evidence-visualization interface showing the density of verified claims in text, which significantly improved users' ability to discern truth from fabrication.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that fluency can no longer serve as a proxy for truth in the age of generative AI. Users paradoxically trust polished AI-generated misinformation while discounting accurate AI-generated content once labeled. Binary "Made with AI" labels fail to provide actionable evidence about claim accuracy.
AI.method: Two-pronged approach: (1) A user study with 81 participants testing an idealized Provenance Density interface against a no-signal control; (2) A technical audit with 200 samples evaluating retrieval density alone and the Consistency Veto mechanism.
AI.result: Provenance Density produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication (+4.15 points on a discernmenet metric, Cohen's d=1.82), while participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. Unexpectedly, retrieval density alone was insufficient; the Consistency Veto mechanism carried most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries.
AI.conclusion: Effective transparency in the AI era must evolve from simple authorship disclosure (binary "Made with AI" labels) toward evidence visualization that shows what supports claims. The Consistency Veto mechanism is particularly important for discriminating between true and fabricated content on dynamic queries.

title: No One Left Behind: Cross-Level Analysis for Sustainable Software Engineering
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME)
summary: Software engineers expect a software system to be efficient, maintainable, economically viable, and socially responsible throughout its lifecycle. Unfortunately, decisions made at the organizational, process, or product levels of software development - even when they improve one of these goals - often have unintended long-term consequences at other levels. In response, software-engineering research has explored different ways to achieve software sustainability, including energy efficiency, resource optimization, and code maintainability. However, existing research offers limited explanations for how sustainability problems emerge and reinforce one another across the socio-technical levels of software engineering. Moreover, we argue that sustainability challenges are not isolated but rather systemic: They stem from interactions among organizational priorities, development practices, and technical conditions. In this vision paper, we introduce the concept of sustainability antipatterns to capture conditions that systematically produce unsustainable outcomes. We demonstrate how this concept can help expose cross-level misalignments between socio-technical levels and sustainability dimensions that remain difficult to recognize through artifact-centric or dimension-specific analyses. To guide future research, we outline concrete directions for identifying, formalizing, detecting, and mitigating sustainability anti-patterns. We envision sustainability anti-patterns as a foundation for an integrated and actionable research agenda on sustainable software engineering.

AI.tldr: A vision paper introducing "sustainability antipatterns" as a conceptual framework to identify and address systemic sustainability challenges in software engineering that arise from interactions across organizational, process, and technical levels.
AI.motivation: Software engineering decisions at organizational, process, or product levels often create unintended long-term consequences across other levels. Existing sustainability research (energy efficiency, resource optimization, code maintainability) is dimension-specific and fails to explain how sustainability problems emerge and reinforce each other across socio-technical levels. The authors argue sustainability challenges are systemic rather than isolated.
AI.method: The paper introduces the concept of "sustainability antipatterns" - conditions that systematically produce unsustainable outcomes. This conceptual framework is designed to expose cross-level misalignments between socio-technical levels and sustainability dimensions that are difficult to recognize through artifact-centric or dimension-specific analyses.
AI.result: The authors demonstrate how sustainability antipatterns can help identify cross-level misalignments that remain hidden in traditional analyses. They outline concrete directions for future research: identifying, formalizing, detecting, and mitigating sustainability anti-patterns.
AI.conclusion: The authors envision sustainability antipatterns as a foundation for an integrated and actionable research agenda on sustainable software engineering, providing a holistic framework to address systemic sustainability challenges.

title: An Ensemble-Based Self-Taught Learning Approach for Parking Space Classification Under Limited Data
summary: Parking spot classification is a fundamental task in intelligent transportation systems, yet most deep learning approaches rely on large amounts of annotated data and exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous environments. To address these limitations, we investigate a self-taught learning framework based on unsupervised representation learning with convolutional autoencoders. The proposed approach learns transferable visual representations from unlabeled data and reuses the learned encoders as fixed feature extractors for supervised classification with limited annotated samples in the target domain. To further enhance robustness and mitigate architectural bias, an ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders is employed, with independent classifier heads and prediction fusion at inference time. Experiments conducted on the PKLot and CNRPark benchmarks under cross-dataset evaluation protocols show that the proposed ensemble-based strategy substantially reduces annotation requirements while improving robustness under significant domain shifts, achieving accuracies between 93\% and 96\% in data-constrained scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a self-taught learning framework for parking spot classification that uses unsupervised representation learning with convolutional autoencoders to reduce annotation requirements and improve cross-domain generalization. An ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders with prediction fusion achieves 93-96% accuracy on PKLot and CNRPark benchmarks under data-constrained scenarios.
AI.motivation: Most deep learning approaches for parking spot classification rely on large amounts of annotated data and exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous environments. This limits practical deployment in real-world intelligent transportation systems.
AI.method: The proposed approach uses a self-taught learning framework with: (1) unsupervised representation learning via convolutional autoencoders on unlabeled data, (2) fixed feature extractors reusing learned encoders, (3) supervised classification with limited annotated samples in target domain, (4) ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders with independent classifier heads, and (5) prediction fusion at inference time for robustness.
AI.result: The ensemble-based strategy substantially reduces annotation requirements while improving robustness under significant domain shifts, achieving accuracies between 93% and 96% in data-constrained scenarios on PKLot and CNRPark benchmarks under cross-dataset evaluation protocols.
AI.conclusion: Self-taught learning with ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders is an effective approach for parking spot classification that addresses data scarcity and domain shift challenges, achieving strong performance with limited annotations while maintaining robustness across heterogeneous environments.

title: Masked Autoregressive Speech Enhancement with Continuous Neural Audio Codec Representations
comment: Presented at the 19th International Workshop on Acoustic Signal Enhancement (IWAENC), Sep 2026, Cremona, Italy
summary: Most previous work on speech enhancement (SE) based on masked generative modeling relied on discrete token representations of audio signals, obtained using neural audio codecs (NACs). However, a recent study has shown that continuous latent representations of NACs can be advantageous for SE in terms of speech quality and intelligibility. In this work, we propose masked autoregressive SE (MARSE), a method for SE based on iterative decoding of masked clean speech frames using continuous NAC representations of speech. In particular, we investigate a set of different decoding policies, ceteris paribus, that is, using the same DNN (a Conformer model), the same NAC (the DAC codec) and the same training setup. The results show that MARSE enables a flexible trade-off between SE performance and computational cost. Audio examples and code are available online.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes MARSE (masked autoregressive speech enhancement), a method that uses continuous latent representations from neural audio codecs (NAC) for speech enhancement through iterative decoding of masked clean speech frames. The study investigates different decoding policies while controlling for the same Conformer model, DAC codec, and training setup, demonstrating a flexible trade-off between performance and computational cost.
AI.motivation: Previous speech enhancement work relied on discrete token representations from neural audio codecs, but recent research shows continuous latent representations can improve speech quality and intelligibility. This work aims to explore this advantage systematically by investigating different decoding policies.
AI.method: The proposed MARSE method uses iterative decoding of masked clean speech frames with continuous NAC representations. The study controls variables strictly: using the same Conformer DNN, the same DAC codec, and the same training setup to isolate the effect of different decoding policies.
AI.result: MARSE enables a flexible trade-off between speech enhancement performance and computational cost, allowing practitioners to balance quality and efficiency based on their needs.
AI.conclusion: The research demonstrates that continuous latent representations from NACs are advantageous for speech enhancement, and the proposed MARSE framework provides a practical approach to achieving customizable performance-computational trade-offs through various decoding policies.

title: Causal Foundation Models
summary: Causal inference is the practice of estimating the effect of a treatment or intervention from data. It traditionally requires a bespoke pipeline for every new problem: first proposing a causal mechanism, selecting a compatible estimator, and finally training it. Meanwhile, across diverse settings and modalities, much of machine learning has shifted to the paradigm of foundation models: networks pretrained once at scale and applied to new tasks without fine-tuning. Causal foundation models (CFMs) bring this paradigm to causal inference. CFMs are pretrained neural networks that estimate causal quantities, such as the average treatment effect, on entirely new datasets using in-context learning without requiring model updates. This work provides a practical introduction to this emerging area. We summarize the necessary background in causal inference and machine learning before discussing CFMs. Throughout, we include example code and Jupyter notebooks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Causal Foundation Models (CFMs), a novel paradigm that applies the foundation model approach from machine learning to causal inference. CFMs are pretrained neural networks capable of estimating causal quantities like average treatment effects on new datasets using in-context learning without requiring fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Traditional causal inference requires building a custom pipeline for each new problem—proposing causal mechanisms, selecting compatible estimators, and training models from scratch. This is inefficient. Meanwhile, machine learning has embraced foundation models (pretraining once at scale, then applying to new tasks). The authors aim to bring this paradigm to causal inference, enabling reusable pretrained models for causal estimation.
AI.method: The paper provides a practical introduction combining: (1) background on causal inference concepts, (2) background on machine learning/foundation models, (3) discussion of CFMs specifically, with example code and Jupyter notebooks for implementation.
AI.result: A tutorial-style introduction to CFMs that bridges causal inference and foundation model research, enabling practitioners to apply pretrained causal models to new datasets without model updates via in-context learning.
AI.conclusion: CFMs represent an emerging paradigm that could democratize causal inference by reducing the need for bespoke pipelines. The work provides accessible entry point for researchers and practitioners interested in applying foundation model techniques to causal estimation problems.

title: AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery
comment: 17 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to ITAT 2026 (Information Technologies -- Applications and Theory), CEUR Workshop Proceedings. Code: https://github.com/JanPastorek/AutoGraphForge
summary: We report on our ongoing project to develop a computational pipeline, AutoGraphForge, for an automated graph-theoretic conjecturing-refuting-formalizing-proving system. Conjecture generation is counterexample-guided and runs in rounds: a Graffiti3 generator proposes conjectures over a small, evolving snapshot table $T$ (initially a few hundred graphs with their computed invariants) that grows only by counterexamples to its own conjectures. A novelty filter of $559$ classical and folklore relations, closed under transitive composition and linear identity substitution, decides via a linear program whether a candidate is already implied by known results. Surviving candidates are tested against a dataset of about $348,000$ graphs, unioning the complete House of Graphs invariant export, the exhaustive census of all connected graphs on at most nine vertices, several extremal families (strongly regular, minimal Ramsey, Cayley, cages, barbells, lollipops, spiders), and random models. Counterexample-search algorithms then attack the remainder. Run for several rounds on an HPC cluster, the loop yields $6,522$ conjectures that survived the refutation dataset, the novelty filter and every active-search run -- among them nontrivial relations between the annihilation number and the edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which we prove by hand. A subsequent formalization and proving stage deterministically translates each surviving conjecture into a Lean 4 statement skeleton; every candidate proof is kernel-verified against a pinned mathlib4 and our custom invariant preamble. This stage integrates two neural provers -- DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B (served with vLLM) and the Lean-specialised OProver-32B -- behind the independent kernel check. It is implemented end-to-end and passes initial sanity checks, with the full pipeline currently running on the cluster.

AI.tldr: AutoGraphForge is an automated pipeline for graph-theoretic conjecture generation, refutation, formalization, and proof. It uses Graffiti3 for conjecture generation, filters novelty against 559 relations, tests against ~348,000 graphs, and formalizes survivors in Lean 4 with neural prover assistance. The system produced 6,522 surviving conjectures, including nontrivial relations between annihilation number and edge-cover number.
AI.motivation: To automate the discovery and verification of graph theory conjectures, combining counterexample-guided conjecture generation, large-scale refutation testing, and formal proof assistance using modern AI provers.
AI.method: The pipeline uses Graffiti3 generators over an evolving snapshot table, a novelty filter with 559 classical relations tested via linear programming, a refutation dataset of ~348,000 graphs (including House of Graphs, exhaustive census up to 9 vertices, and various extremal families), counterexample-search algorithms, and Lean 4 formalization with neural provers (DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B and OProver-32B).
AI.result: After several rounds on an HPC cluster, the system yielded 6,522 conjectures that survived refutation, novelty filtering, and all active searches. Examples include nontrivial relations between annihilation number and edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which were proven by hand.
AI.conclusion: The full end-to-end pipeline is implemented and running, with initial sanity checks passed. It demonstrates the feasibility of fully automated conjecture generation, refutation, formalization, and AI-assisted proving in graph theory.

title: LabelMate: An LLM-Driven Framework for Refined Issue Report Labeling
summary: Software users often submit issue reports to a product's issue tracking system to report defects, suggest enhancements, or raise other product-related concerns. Labeling these issue reports supports effective planning and improves community engagement. However, many issue reports remain unlabeled due to the substantial manual effort required to design an appropriate label taxonomy, then assign suitable labels from this taxonomy to new issue reports. Existing automated labeling approaches attempt to mitigate these challenges. However, they suffer from key limitations, such as extensive manual intervention, the assignment of generic labels, and a dependence on existing labeled datasets. To address these limitations, we propose LabelMate, a novel Large Language Model (LLM)-driven framework that (1) derives a comprehensive, project-specific label set from historical issue reports and (2) automatically assigns relevant labels to new issue reports without requiring any pre-labeled training data. We evaluate LabelMate on 16,500 issue reports from 30 popular and diverse GitHub repositories. Based on this dataset, our approach generates a coherent list of 275 labels and achieves an average labeling accuracy of 89.84%, a statistically significant improvement over existing generic label assigning approaches. These results demonstrate that LabelMate offers an efficient, domain-adaptive solution to streamline the issue labeling process.

AI.tldr: LabelMate is an LLM-driven framework that automatically derives project-specific label sets from historical issue reports and assigns labels to new issues without requiring pre-labeled training data, achieving 89.84% accuracy on 16,500 reports from 30 GitHub repositories.
AI.motivation: Software issue reports need labels for planning and community engagement, but manual labeling is time-consuming. Existing automated approaches have significant limitations: they require extensive manual intervention, assign generic labels, and depend on pre-labeled datasets.
AI.method: LabelMate uses a Large Language Model to (1) derive a comprehensive, project-specific label set from historical issue reports and (2) automatically assign relevant labels to new issue reports without any pre-labeled training data. Evaluation was performed on 16,500 issue reports from 30 popular GitHub repositories.
AI.result: The approach generated 275 coherent labels and achieved an average labeling accuracy of 89.84%, representing a statistically significant improvement over existing generic label assigning approaches.
AI.conclusion: LabelMate offers an efficient, domain-adaptive solution to streamline the issue labeling process, eliminating the need for extensive manual effort and pre-labeled training data while maintaining high accuracy.

title: MedQA-MM: Shortcuts Behind Medical Visual Reasoning
summary: A benchmark score credits final answers, but not the route by which an item can be answered. In medical multimodal multiple-choice questions (MCQs), this distinction matters because a correct answer can be supported by the intended image finding or by benchmark-preserved cues in the wording of answers, non-visual clinical text, visible image text, artificial annotations, or device/context artifacts. We call the resulting score-level overinterpretation reasoning inflation. Here, a route is an observable input path that can support answer selection, not a claim about the model's hidden cognition. Across six medical multimodal MCQ datasets, we separate candidate cues from behavioral evidence through prompt- and image-side audits, modality ablations, and matched repairs that preserve the medical target and answer key. In a 13-configuration open-model panel, full-input accuracy is 62.63%, while text-only and options-only settings achieve 53.96% and 29.71%, respectively. Removing length-gap, absolute/conspicuous, and spatial/prepositional cues lowers accuracy by 6.58, 3.50, and 4.77 percentage points. We also construct MedQA-MM, a 1,000-item shortcut-mitigated subset, where text-only and options-only accuracy fall to 5.21% and 12.33%. This does not imply that models never use images; it shows that medical image-reasoning claims require route-level evidence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "reasoning inflation" in medical multimodal multiple-choice questions (MCQs), where benchmark scores credit final answers without distinguishing whether the correct answer was derived from the intended image-based reasoning or from shortcut cues (e.g., text in answers, non-visual clinical context, visible image text, artificial annotations, or device artifacts). The authors propose a "route" framework to audit input paths that support answer selection, and across six datasets and 13 model configurations, they find that text-only and options-only settings achieve significant accuracy (53.96% and 29.71%), demonstrating that models often rely on non-visual cues. They also introduce MedQA-MM, a 1,000-item shortcut-mitigated subset where text-only accuracy drops to 5.21%, reinforcing that medical image-reasoning claims require route-level evidence.
AI.motivation: Current medical multimodal benchmarks reward correct answers without verifying whether the model actually used the intended image-based reasoning. This creates "reasoning inflation" where high scores may reflect shortcut exploitation rather than genuine visual understanding. The authors aim to expose this gap and demonstrate that medical image-reasoning claims are often unsubstantiated at the route level.
AI.method: The authors conduct prompt- and image-side audits, modality ablations, and matched repairs across six medical multimodal MCQ datasets using a 13-configuration open-model panel. They identify and remove specific shortcut cues (length-gap, absolute/conspicuous, and spatial/prepositional cues) to measure their impact on accuracy. They also construct MedQA-MM, a 1,000-item subset designed to mitigate shortcut cues while preserving the medical target and answer key.
AI.result: Full-input accuracy is 62.63%, while text-only and options-only settings achieve 53.96% and 29.71%, respectively. Removing length-gap, absolute/conspicuous, and spatial/prepositional cues lowers accuracy by 6.58, 3.50, and 4.77 percentage points. In MedQA-MM, text-only accuracy falls to 5.21% and options-only to 12.33%.
AI.conclusion: High benchmark scores in medical multimodal MCQs do not necessarily reflect genuine image-based reasoning. The authors argue that medical image-reasoning claims require route-level evidence—behavioral audits that separate genuine visual reasoning from shortcut-based answer selection. The MedQA-MM subset provides a more rigorous benchmark for evaluating true multimodal medical reasoning.

title: Compressing Streaming Neural Audio Encoders via Latent-Space Distillation
summary: System-wide Dictation on Apple devices runs entirely on-device, and the speech it transcribes reaches the foundation model through a tokenizer: an encoder that maps short windows of waveform onto the representation the language model reads. Because that model is sparsely activated under Instruction-Following Pruning, only a small subset of its experts occupies DRAM at any time, so the always-on tokenizer competes for the same memory, and its parameter count bears directly on power and latency. In this work we study how to compress such a tokenizer by distillation, taking as the supervision target neither the discrete token nor the output distribution but the pre-quantizer latent the model actually consumes - the last representation the two token interfaces share. We train only the student encoder to regress the teacher's per-frame latent under a squared-error objective, with a single affine layer absorbing the teacher-student width mismatch. Because the target precedes both the quantizer and the language-model bridge, one recipe covers both token interfaces we support, and applies both to a tokenizer pretrained alone and to one jointly trained with a language model. At 2.8x compression the distilled student stays within 1.9% relative WER of its teacher on five of six teacher-student pairs without any fine-tuning, and improves on an independently trained tokenizer of identical capacity by 3.9% relative.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a distillation method to compress speech tokenizers for on-device dictation on Apple devices. By training a student encoder to regress the teacher's pre-quantizer latent representations, the method achieves 2.8x compression while maintaining near-teacher accuracy (within 1.9% relative WER).
AI.motivation: On Apple devices, System-wide Dictation runs entirely on-device with a sparsely activated language model. The always-on tokenizer competes for the same DRAM memory, and reducing its parameter count directly impacts power and latency. Existing compression methods target discrete tokens or output distributions, but this work proposes using the pre-quantizer latent as the supervision target.
AI.method: The approach uses knowledge distillation with the pre-quantizer latent (the last representation before quantization and language model interface) as the supervision target. A student encoder is trained to regress the teacher's per-frame latent under a squared-error objective, with a single affine layer to handle teacher-student width mismatch. This single recipe applies to both token interfaces and works for both standalone pretrained tokenizers and jointly trained tokenizer-language model pairs.
AI.result: At 2.8x compression, the distilled student stays within 1.9% relative Word Error Rate (WER) of its teacher on five of six teacher-student pairs without any fine-tuning. It also improves on an independently trained tokenizer of identical capacity by 3.9% relative.
AI.conclusion: The proposed latent-based distillation method effectively compresses speech tokenizers while preserving recognition accuracy. Using pre-quantizer latents as supervision targets provides a unified approach for different token interfaces and training configurations, achieving significant compression with minimal accuracy degradation.

title: ObserverBench: Testing Mechanistic Estimates for Intervention and Control
comment: 28 pages, 4 figures. Code, benchmark, leaderboards, and submission interface: https://kwisatzh.github.io/observerbench/. Frozen artifact release: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22136091
summary:
Mechanistic interpretability is increasingly used to guide interventions such as activation steering, circuit removal, and safety monitoring. Yet an internal estimate that is accurate on average can still choose a poor action.
  We present ObserverBench, a benchmark framework for testing whether an internal estimator---an observer---is adequate for the intervention, control, or safety task it directs. Each task fixes the model, information boundary, allowed actions, decision rule, held-out cases, and loss. The benchmark reports estimation accuracy separately from the loss caused by the chosen action.
  Theory and experiments show why both are needed. In closed-loop control, observer errors matter at the starting point and along directions the allowed intervention can reach. On circuit-intervention tasks in GPT-2-small and Qwen2.5-7B, pairwise observers predict unseen effects more accurately without always choosing better actions; observers trained on action loss choose lower-loss actions. In safety triage, a score that perfectly separates violations can allocate a fixed intervention budget poorly when violations have different costs. Across Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B-it, and prospectively frozen Qwen3.5-9B APPS tasks, AUROC can rank monitors differently from deployment loss, and the best information source changes across models. Sparse SAE readouts also trail their layer-matched dense controls on the reported Qwen panels, under disclosed activation-density or checkpoint mismatches.
  ObserverBench provides fixed task contracts, runnable baselines, and table-based submissions for evaluating interpretability methods through the actions they enable.

AI.tldr: ObserverBench is a benchmark framework for evaluating whether internal estimators (observers) in mechanistic interpretability are adequate for their intended intervention, control, or safety tasks. It separately reports estimation accuracy from action loss, addressing the problem that accurate average estimates can still lead to poor actions.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that an internal estimate accurate on average can still choose a poor action when used for interventions like activation steering, circuit removal, and safety monitoring. Existing benchmarks don't distinguish between estimation accuracy and the actual loss caused by chosen actions.
AI.method: The benchmark fixes for each task: the model, information boundary, allowed actions, decision rule, held-out cases, and loss. It reports estimation accuracy separately from action loss. Experiments include closed-loop control analysis, circuit-intervention tasks on GPT-2-small and Qwen2.5-7B, and safety triage tasks across Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B-it, and Qwen3.5-9B APPS.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) In closed-loop control, observer errors matter at the starting point and along directions the allowed intervention can reach. (2) Pairwise observers predict unseen effects more accurately without always choosing better actions; observers trained on action loss choose lower-loss actions. (3) In safety triage, perfect separation can still lead to poor budget allocation when violations have different costs. (4) AUROC can rank monitors differently from deployment loss, and the best information source changes across models. (5) Sparse SAE readouts trail layer-matched dense controls on disclosed activation-density or checkpoint mismatches.
AI.conclusion: ObserverBench provides fixed task contracts, runnable baselines, and table-based submissions for evaluating interpretability methods through the actions they enable. The key insight is that both estimation accuracy AND action loss must be measured separately, as they can diverge significantly.

title: Making Every Tool Call Count: Necessary Tool-Evidence Path Rewards for Agentic Vision-Language Models
summary: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) can directly answer many image-grounded questions, yet they often struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. To acquire this missing evidence, agentic VLMs invoke tools such as image cropping, image search, and text search. However, existing training paradigms primarily evaluate tool-use based on final answer correctness, leaving evidence acquisition and utilization insufficiently supervised. This leads to two critical shortcomings: (i) models frequently issue redundant or off-target tool calls that fail to gather necessary evidence, and (ii) even when appropriate tools are called, models often fail to extract the necessary information from the resulting observations. To address these limitations, we introduce the NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), a novel annotation scheme that explicitly specifies the essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls for each query. Building upon this, we propose NTEP-R (NTEP Reward), a supervision mechanism ensuring that each tool invocation strictly advances the reasoning process toward the final solution. Specifically, our approach rewards the agent for aligning its pre-call intent with a necessary evidence-seeking goal, and for ensuring the information summarized from the post-call observation aligns with the necessary evidence. Furthermore, we introduce a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant calls that revisit satisfied NTEP goals. Extensive evaluations on seven image-grounded benchmarks demonstrate that our 8B-parameter instantiation, NTEP-8B, significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency within a unified three-tool framework. These results highlight the critical value of fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision for training robust agentic VLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), a novel annotation and supervision scheme for training agentic VLMs to use tools (image cropping, image search, text search) more effectively by explicitly supervising evidence acquisition and utilization throughout the reasoning process.
AI.motivation: Modern VLMs struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. Existing training paradigms only evaluate final answer correctness, failing to supervise evidence acquisition. This leads to two critical issues: (i) redundant or off-target tool calls that fail to gather necessary evidence, and (ii) failure to extract necessary information from tool observations.
AI.method: The authors propose NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), an annotation scheme specifying essential external evidence and tool calls for each query. Building upon this, they introduce NTEP-R (NTEP Reward), a supervision mechanism that rewards agents for aligning pre-call intent with necessary evidence-seeking goals and ensuring post-call observations align with necessary evidence. They also add a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant tool calls.
AI.result: NTEP-8B (8B parameters) significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency within a unified three-tool framework across seven image-grounded benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision is critical for training robust agentic VLMs, enabling more effective evidence acquisition and utilization during complex visual reasoning tasks.

title: When Models Edit Too Much: On the Fidelity of Minimal Code Edits
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to edit existing code, but correctness alone is not enough: useful repairs should also be minimal, reviewable, and faithful to the original implementation. We study over-editing, the tendency of a model to rewrite code beyond what is required to fix a bug. We construct an evaluation framework from 400 BigCodeBench problems by injecting controlled AST-level corruptions into reference solutions, giving each repair task a known minimal patch. Across frontier LLMs, over-editing is widespread even among strong models like GPT-5.5: high Pass@1 can coexist with unnecessarily large edits and added cognitive complexity. A preservation instruction substantially reduces this behavior, lowering average excess Levenshtein distance from 0.195 to 0.131, reducing added cognitive complexity by 26.6%, and increasing Pass@1 by 2.3 points. However, these gains do not simply follow from a larger reasoning budget or larger models. We next ask whether minimal editing can be learned directly during post-training. We observe that supervised fine-tuning overfits to seen corruption patterns, whereas reinforcement learning gives the best out-of-domain edit-fidelity and performance-retention trade-off. These results position edit fidelity as a distinct axis of code-repair quality and show that it can be measured and learned.

AI.tldr: This paper studies "over-editing" in LLMs - the tendency to rewrite more code than necessary when fixing bugs. The authors create an evaluation framework using 400 BigCodeBench problems with injected AST-level corruptions to identify minimal patches. They find over-editing is widespread even in frontier models, and demonstrate that preservation instructions and reinforcement learning can reduce this behavior while maintaining performance.
AI.motivation: Current LLM code editing evaluations focus only on correctness (whether the bug is fixed), but ignore whether the repair is minimal and reviewable. The authors argue that useful repairs should be minimal, reviewable, and faithful to the original implementation. This gap motivates the study of over-editing behavior.
AI.method: The authors construct an evaluation framework from 400 BigCodeBench problems by injecting controlled AST-level corruptions into reference solutions, creating tasks with known minimal patches. They measure over-editing using excess Levenshtein distance and added cognitive complexity. They test frontier LLMs including GPT-5.5, evaluate preservation instructions, and compare supervised fine-tuning vs reinforcement learning for learning minimal editing.
AI.result: Over-editing is widespread across frontier LLMs even among strong models like GPT-5.5 - high Pass@1 can coexist with unnecessarily large edits and added cognitive complexity. Preservation instruction reduces excess Levenshtein distance from 0.195 to 0.131, reduces added cognitive complexity by 26.6%, and increases Pass@1 by 2.3 points. These gains don't simply follow from larger reasoning budget or larger models. Supervised fine-tuning overfits to seen corruption patterns, while reinforcement learning provides the best out-of-domain edit-fidelity and performance-retention trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Edit fidelity (minimal editing) is a distinct and measurable axis of code-repair quality that can be learned. Reinforcement learning is superior to supervised fine-tuning for learning minimal editing behavior that generalizes to unseen corruption patterns. The results position over-editing as an important but solvable problem in LLM code editing.

title: Tensor-based Brain Surface Modeling and Analysis
summary: We present a unified computational approach to tensor-based morphometry in detecting the brain surface shape differences between two clinical groups based on magnetic resonance images. Our approach is novel in a sense that we combined surface modeling, surface data smoothing and statistical analysis in a coherent unified mathematical framework. The cerebral cortex has the topology of a 2D highly convoluted sheet. Between two different clinical groups, the local surface area and curvature of the cortex may differ. It is highly likely that such surface shape differences are not uniform over the whole cortex. By computing how such surface metrics differ, the regions of the most rapid structural differences can be localized. To increase the signal to noise ratio, diffusion smoothing based on the explicit estimation of Laplace-Beltrami operator has been developed and applied to the surface metrics. As an illustration, we demonstrate how this new tensor-based surface morphometry can be applied in localizing the cortical regions of the gray matter tissue growth and loss in the brain images longitudinally collected in the group of children.

AI.tldr: A unified computational approach for tensor-based morphometry (TB-SM) that detects brain surface shape differences between clinical groups by combining surface modeling, smoothing via Laplace-Beltrami operator, and statistical analysis, applied to longitudinal pediatric MRI data to localize cortical gray matter changes.
AI.motivation: The cerebral cortex has a highly convoluted 2D sheet topology, and surface shape differences (local area, curvature) between clinical groups are likely non-uniform across the cortex. Traditional methods may not adequately capture these localized structural changes.
AI.method: Unified framework combining: (1) Surface modeling of cortical topology, (2) Diffusion smoothing using explicit Laplace-Beltrami operator estimation to improve signal-to-noise ratio, (3) Statistical analysis to identify regions of rapid structural difference.
AI.result: The method successfully localizes cortical regions showing gray matter tissue growth and loss in longitudinal pediatric brain images.
AI.conclusion: TB-SM provides an effective tool for detecting and localizing subtle, regional brain surface shape differences in clinical neuroimaging studies.

title: Learnable composition for neural operators
summary: Neural operators are fast, differentiable surrogates for physical simulation, but their accuracy often degrades when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions differ from training. Supervised adaptation can recover accuracy, but even a small target set requires costly high-fidelity simulations. We therefore ask how pretraining and transfer can be designed together to reduce this deployment cost. LatentDDM first pretrains a neural operator to predict fields on small subdomains. For a new setting, it freezes this operator and trains only a lightweight module that composes the local predictions. We evaluate our method on two complementary problems: steady Darcy flow, where long-range pressure coupling must extend across increasingly large porous domains, and unsteady incompressible flow around a pitching airfoil, where rollout errors compound as target pitching frequencies exceed the training range. Compared with the capacity-matched models that process the full domain at once, LatentDDM's error is 36-56% lower on larger Darcy domains after adaptation with 16 target simulations. It also improves 20-step field rollouts in fast-pitching airfoil flow, both zero-shot and after few-shot calibration. These results identify the co-designed local pretraining and composition-level transfer as a promising design principle for physical foundation models.

AI.tldr: LatentDDM is a neural operator adaptation method that pretrains on small subdomains then freezes the operator while training only a lightweight composition module for new settings, reducing deployment costs for physical simulation surrogates.
AI.motivation: Neural operators degrade in accuracy when domain geometry, size, or operating conditions differ from training. Supervised adaptation requires costly high-fidelity simulations, even for small target sets. The paper seeks to reduce deployment costs by co-designing pretraining and transfer learning.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) Pretrain a neural operator to predict fields on small subdomains; (2) For new settings, freeze this operator and train only a lightweight module that composes local predictions. Evaluated on Darcy flow (varying domain size) and pitching airfoil flow (varying frequencies).
AI.result: 36-56% lower error on larger Darcy domains after adaptation with 16 target simulations. Improves 20-step field rollouts for fast-pitching airfoil flow, both zero-shot and after few-shot calibration.
AI.conclusion: Co-designed local pretraining and composition-level transfer is a promising design principle for physical foundation models, enabling efficient adaptation to new domains with minimal high-fidelity simulation data.

title: GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving
summary: Long-output reasoning has made the key--value (KV) cache a critical memory bottleneck for efficient LLM serving. Existing KV compression methods usually rely on a predefined per-request budget and adjust only which KV states are retained, leaving the total capacity fixed throughout decoding. However, reasoning workloads exhibit substantial demand variation: different requests require different KV capacities, and the attention demand of an individual request evolves during generation. We introduce \textbf{GrowPage}, an on-demand KV budgeting framework that treats KV capacity as a runtime resource. GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behaviors, and uses their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At each capacity boundary, GrowPage either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page when broader demand emerges. By integrating with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction, GrowPage preserves continuous batching and prefix caching. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance--throughput trade-off over existing approaches.

AI.tldr: GrowPage is an on-demand KV caching framework that dynamically adjusts KV memory allocation for LLM serving based on real-time attention demand, using dual-timescale query summaries to track and adapt to evolving attention patterns during generation.
AI.motivation: Existing KV compression methods use fixed per-request budgets with static total capacity, but reasoning workloads exhibit substantial demand variation - different requests need different KV capacities, and individual requests' attention demand evolves during generation. This creates a memory bottleneck for efficient LLM serving.
AI.method: GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture both recent and long-term attention behaviors. It uses relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At each capacity boundary, GrowPage either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page when broader demand emerges. It integrates with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction to preserve continuous batching and prefix caching.
AI.result: Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance-throughput trade-off over existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: GrowPage effectively addresses the KV cache memory bottleneck in LLM serving by treating KV capacity as a runtime resource that adapts to actual demand, providing better efficiency for reasoning workloads through dynamic on-demand memory allocation.

title: ATIBA: Grounded Integrity and Quality Checking for Research Papers
comment: Accepted at The First International Workshop on Automated Techniques for Integrity and Quality in Software-Engineering Research (ATIQSER 2026)
summary: Checking a manuscript's reference integrity, its compliance with a target venue's specific submission rules, and its adherence to community reporting standards is manual, repetitive, and different for every venue so in practice it is done inconsistently or skipped. We present ATIBA, a tool that runs five grounded integrity and quality checks on a manuscript: a reference-integrity check that verifies each citation against bibliographic sources and flags retracted or unfindable references; a venue/track compliance check that derives submission criteria directly from a venue's own call-for-papers page and evaluates the manuscript against them, each verdict anchored to a verbatim quote from that page; an empirical-standards compliance check against the ACM SIGSOFT Empirical Standards, with a hallucination defence that discards any evidence quote it cannot locate verbatim in the manuscript; a multi-mode AI review (venue-specific, formal, and page-anchored annotation) powered by GPT-5.4 through Azure OpenAI; and a citation-suggestion feature that proposes candidate references for a manuscript and verifies each against bibliographic sources before it is shown to the user. All five checks are designed around the same principle: an LLM is only trusted to judge, never to invent the evidence it judges against. We evaluated ATIBA through a moderated user study with 13 non-author participants. Agreement across the six survey items ranged from 69% to 92%, with a mean of 85%, providing initial evidence of positive perceived usefulness across the evaluated workflows. These findings establish perceived usefulness; objective accuracy remains to be measured.

AI.tldr: ATIBA is an automated manuscript quality assurance tool that performs five integrity checks: reference integrity verification, venue compliance validation, empirical standards compliance, multi-mode AI review, and citation suggestion.
