The tool uses LLMs for judgment but never for inventing evidence, anchoring all verdicts to verifiable sources. A user study with 13 participants showed 85% mean agreement on perceived usefulness.
AI.motivation: Manual manuscript checking (reference integrity, venue compliance, community standards) is tedious, venue-specific, and often skipped or done inconsistently in practice. There is a need for automated, reliable manuscript quality assurance.
AI.method: ATIBA implements five grounded checks: (1) Reference-integrity check against bibliographic sources; (2) Venue/track compliance check deriving criteria from CFP pages with verbatim quotes; (3) Empirical-standards compliance check against ACM SIGSOFT Empirical Standards with hallucination defence; (4) Multi-mode AI review using GPT-5.4 via Azure OpenAI; (5) Citation-suggestion with verification. Core principle: LLM judges but never invents evidence. Evaluated through moderated user study with 13 non-author participants.
AI.result: Agreement across six survey items ranged from 69% to 92%, with a mean of 85%, providing initial evidence of positive perceived usefulness across evaluated workflows. Objective accuracy remains to be measured.
AI.conclusion: ATIBA demonstrates the feasibility of automated manuscript quality assurance with grounded integrity checks. The user study shows promising perceived usefulness, but objective accuracy evaluation is needed. The tool's core principle of using LLMs for judgment while anchoring to verifiable sources addresses hallucination concerns.

title: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Training
comment: Accepted to Pacific Graphics 2026 (conference track). Project page: https://sorenzhang574.github.io/Laplacian-GS/
summary: A key bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting training is the continual growth of Gaussian primitives, which increases optimization cost and slows convergence, especially at high resolutions. We propose Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies, a simple yet efficient 3DGS scheme that combines Laplacian image decomposition with coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged training. After fitting lower-frequency structure, we archive the corresponding Gaussian field so that subsequent fields can optimize higher-frequency residuals without carrying the full primitive burden, and we compose the rendered components in the image domain via a Laplacian-style reconstruction at inference time. This design reduces the number of active Gaussians during training, thereby lowering optimization overhead and accelerating training. The proposed scheme is plug-and-play and orthogonal to prior 3DGS accelerations: it can be directly combined with strong backbones such as Taming-3DGS and FastGS to improve training speed with competitive reconstruction quality. It achieves average speedups of 1.73x and 1.21x at 1K setting, and 1.74x and 1.33x at 4K setting on Taming-3DGS and FastGS, with larger gains on more challenging scenes and increasingly pronounced benefits at higher resolutions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies, a method to address the computational bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting training caused by continual growth of Gaussian primitives. The approach combines Laplacian image decomposition with coarse-to-fine frequency-staged training, archiving lower-frequency Gaussian fields to allow subsequent fields to optimize higher-frequency residuals without carrying the full primitive burden.
AI.motivation: A key bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting training is the continual growth of Gaussian primitives, which increases optimization cost and slows convergence, especially at high resolutions. The authors aim to reduce the number of active Gaussians during training to lower optimization overhead and accelerate training.
AI.method: The proposed Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies scheme combines Laplacian image decomposition with coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged training. After fitting lower-frequency structure, the corresponding Gaussian field is archived so that subsequent fields can optimize higher-frequency residuals without carrying the full primitive burden. The rendered components are composed in the image domain via Laplacian-style reconstruction at inference time.
AI.result: The method achieves average speedups of 1.73x and 1.21x at 1K resolution, and 1.74x and 1.33x at 4K resolution on Taming-3DGS and FastGS backbones respectively. Larger gains are observed on more challenging scenes, with increasingly pronounced benefits at higher resolutions.
AI.conclusion: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies is plug-and-play and orthogonal to prior 3DGS accelerations. It can be directly combined with strong backbones such as Taming-3DGS and FastGS to improve training speed with competitive reconstruction quality.

title: LeanStream: A Speculate-and-Refine Streaming Framework for Efficient on-Device LLM Inference
comment: 6 pages, 13 figures. To appear in the Proceedings of the 32nd Annual International Conference on Mobile Computing and Networking (MobiCom '26)
summary: On-device LLM inference is attractive for privacy and responsiveness, but remains challenging on mobile and embedded devices because model weights far exceed available DRAM. Prior systems exploit activation sparsity and offload weights to SSD or flash storage, but face a fundamental systems trade-off: accurate sparse execution decisions require the latest context, whereas efficient computation-I/O overlap requires early prediction. As a result, existing designs either serialize execution or incur redundant weight fetches, extra computation, and large cache overheads. We present LeanStream, a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for efficient on-device LLM inference. LeanStream progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O. We implement LeanStream on both mobile and embedded platforms. Compared with prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8$\times$ to 7.5$\times$ at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6$\times$ to 2.1$\times$.

AI.tldr: LeanStream is a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for efficient on-device LLM inference on mobile and embedded devices. It addresses the memory bottleneck by enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O through progressive refinement of computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results.
AI.motivation: On-device LLM inference is attractive for privacy and responsiveness but remains challenging on mobile and embedded devices because model weights far exceed available DRAM. Prior systems exploit activation sparsity and offload weights to SSD or flash storage, but face a fundamental trade-off between accurate sparse execution (requiring latest context) and efficient computation-I/O overlap (requiring early prediction), leading to serialized execution or redundant weight fetches.
AI.method: LeanStream implements a streaming speculate-and-refine framework that progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results. This enables fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O, avoiding the traditional trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.
AI.result: LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8× to 7.5× at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6× to 2.1×.
AI.conclusion: LeanStream successfully addresses the memory and computation-I/O overlap challenges in on-device LLM inference, achieving significant improvements in both memory efficiency and throughput on mobile and embedded platforms.

title: PPO-STGNN: A Proximal Policy Optimization Approach with Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for DAG Task Scheduling in Cloud-Edge-End Computing
summary: With the rapid development of the Internet of Things, computation intensive directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks have become increasingly common in cloud-edge-end collaborative environments. However, cloud, edge, and end nodes are highly heterogeneous in computing capacity, network bandwidth, and energy consumption, which makes the efficient scheduling of tasks with complex dependencies an NP-hard problem. Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement-learning methods often fail to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources. This paper proposes PPO-STGNN, a DAG task-scheduling algorithm that integrates proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs). The method uses an STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph, and then optimizes the scheduling policy through PPO to minimize makespan and schedule length ratio (SLR) while improving CPU and memory load balancing. To accelerate convergence, a multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining. Experimental results show that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining a low completion time, making it suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge- end DAG scheduling scenarios.

AI.tldr: PPO-STGNN is a novel DAG task-scheduling algorithm for cloud-edge-end collaborative environments that combines proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs) to handle complex task dependencies in heterogeneous computing environments.
AI.motivation: Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement-learning methods fail to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources in heterogeneous cloud-edge-end environments, where scheduling DAG tasks with complex dependencies remains an NP-hard problem.
AI.method: The proposed PPO-STGNN uses an STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph, then optimizes the scheduling policy through PPO to minimize makespan and schedule length ratio (SLR) while improving CPU and memory load balancing. A multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining to accelerate convergence.
AI.result: Experimental results show that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining a low completion time.
AI.conclusion: PPO-STGNN is suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge-end DAG scheduling scenarios, offering a promising approach to balance multiple objectives in complex scheduling problems.

title: SWE-Gate: Passing Functional Tests Is Not Enough for Software Engineering Agents
summary: Repository-level software engineering benchmarks have significantly advanced the evaluation of coding agents, but existing benchmarks primarily measure whether generated patches pass functional tests and overlook review-derived acceptance constraints (review constraints) that often influence whether a patch is acceptable in real-world software development. We introduce SWE-Gate, a repository-level benchmark for software engineering agents that explicitly evaluates review constraint compliance alongside functional correctness. SWE-Gate derives review constraints from real pull request review comments and synthesizes repository-level repair instances around these constraints. Each instance provides separate functional and constraint tests, together with non-compliant and gold patches, enabling explicit separation between issue resolution capability and review constraint compliance. We construct SWE-Gate with 303 repository-level repair instances spanning 75 open-source Python repositories across diverse software domains. Experiments with four LLM backends spanning different capability levels under a common coding-agent scaffold reveal a substantial gap between functional success and success under the complete repair specification: among 644 repairs that pass the functional tests, 221 fail to satisfy the provided review constraints. These findings show that functional-only evaluation overestimates agents' ability to satisfy the full requirements of repository-level repair tasks. The replication package including code, data, and experimental results is available at https://github.com/DeepSoftwareAnalytics/SWE-Gate.

AI.tldr: SWE-Gate is a new repository-level benchmark for software engineering agents that evaluates both functional correctness and review constraint compliance. Derived from real pull request review comments, it addresses the limitation of existing benchmarks that only measure functional tests. The benchmark contains 303 repair instances across 75 Python repositories. Experiments reveal that 34% of repairs passing functional tests fail to satisfy review constraints, showing functional-only evaluation significantly overestimates agent capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing repository-level software engineering benchmarks only measure whether generated patches pass functional tests, overlooking "review constraints" - acceptance criteria derived from real pull request review comments that influence patch acceptability in real-world development. This leads to an inflated assessment of agent capabilities.
AI.method: SWE-Gate constructs repository-level repair instances by deriving review constraints from real PR review comments and synthesizing repairs around these constraints. Each instance includes separate functional and constraint tests, along with non-compliant and gold patches. The benchmark was evaluated using four LLM backends under a common coding-agent scaffold.
AI.result: Among 644 repairs that passed functional tests, 221 (34%) failed to satisfy the provided review constraints. This substantial gap demonstrates that functional-only evaluation significantly overestimates agents' ability to meet full repair specifications in repository-level tasks.
AI.conclusion: Functional-only evaluation is insufficient for assessing software engineering agents. Future benchmarks and evaluations should incorporate review constraint compliance to better reflect real-world software development requirements and accurately measure agent capabilities.

title: The Gradient Does Not See Rank: Rank-Indifference in Matrix-CODI on ProsQA
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop, https://openreview.net/forum?id=Spof4PusVI. 9 pages. Corrects a data-entry error in the workshop version: the seed-1337 accuracy in the three-seed replication was reported as 80.47% (a control run); the archived value is 78.91%, so the three-seed mean is 81.0 +/- 2.0pp (was 81.5 +/- 1.2pp). All other results are unchanged
summary: Continuous chain-of-thought models compress reasoning into latent tokens. Matrix-valued variants, which route each latent token through a d x d matrix bottleneck, introduce rank as a single-sample structural observable on the latent matrix Z. If matrix latents carry parallel reasoning paths via superposition, rank should track them, and truncating Z to low rank should hurt accuracy on tasks whose solutions plausibly require multiple components. Across four training regimes of a matrix-CODI model (three on ProsQA, one on GSM8K-Aug below the learning threshold), the rank-k projection ablation curve is flat to within 0.6 percentage points. A three-seed replication yields 81.0 +/- 2.0 percentage points accuracy while the final effective rank of Z spans {4, 12, 13}; the loss does not reward any particular rank. To test whether rank-blindness arises from the flatten-then-project readout alone, we trained four readouts: a bilinear reparametrization, a bilinear-plus-GELU readout nonlinear in Z, an SVD-augmented readout feeding singular values through an MLP, and a quadratic readout in Z Z^T. All four rank-k curves remain flat (Spearman p-values 0.63, 0.14, 0.82, 0.46). The flat curves persist for readouts nonlinear in Z. A linear probe on Z underperforms a raw pretrained hidden state at target prediction (AUC 0.673 vs. 0.846). A negative control on vanilla GPT-2 SFT (no matrix bottleneck, no Z, three seeds, n=500) reproduces a flat rank-k curve under the same intervention paradigm with pooled-mean range 0.20pp, and a random-h sensitivity floor lands at the same accuracy: the rank-k ablation alone conflates rank-blindness with position-irrelevance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether matrix-valued latent tokens in continuous chain-of-thought models actually utilize their full rank capacity for reasoning. Across multiple training regimes and readout architectures, rank-k projection ablation curves remain flat, suggesting models don't leverage the full rank structure despite having a d×d matrix bottleneck.
AI.motivation: The researchers wanted to test whether matrix latents carrying parallel reasoning paths via superposition would show rank-dependent performance, and whether truncating Z to low rank would hurt accuracy on tasks requiring multiple reasoning components.
AI.method: The authors trained a matrix-CODI model across four regimes (three on ProsQA, one on GSM8K-Aug), performed rank-k projection ablations, tested four different readout architectures (bilinear, bilinear+GELU, SVD-augmented, quadratic), used linear probes on Z, and ran a negative control on vanilla GPT-2 SFT.
AI.result: Rank-k projection curves remained flat within 0.6 percentage points across all conditions. Three-seed replication showed 81.0±2.0% accuracy while effective rank of Z spanned {4, 12, 13}. All four readout variants showed flat rank-k curves (Spearman p-values: 0.63, 0.14, 0.82, 0.46). Linear probe on Z underperformed raw pretrained hidden states (AUC 0.673 vs 0.846). The negative control also reproduced a flat rank-k curve.
AI.conclusion: The rank-k ablation alone cannot distinguish between rank-blindness and position-irrelevance. The loss does not reward any particular rank, suggesting the model isn't using the full rank capacity of the matrix bottleneck for multi-component reasoning.

title: What Matters for Aggressive Decoding-Time KV Eviction? Temporal Aggregation and Ranking Preservation
summary: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses heavily on designing better token scoring functions, while the temporal rule that aggregates scores across decode steps is often treated as an implementation detail. Under aggressive KV compression, we find that exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation makes approximately order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level. Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets, whereas KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer alter the ranking and degrade substantially. We associate this stability with the evaluated aggregation, which couples layer weighting and temporal retention. Building on this observation, we introduce InertiaKV, an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method, and InertiaKV-Lazy, its periodic-refresh variant, which yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. We also study Score-Free decoding as a separate empirical operating point: it scores the full context once at the first decode step, freezes that ranking, and incurs an average quality change of +0.03 while removing all subsequent scoring. Across six open-weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks, the results identify temporal aggregation and ranking preservation as distinct, consequential design factors; they do not imply that scoring quality is irrelevant in general.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that under aggressive KV cache compression, exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation makes different token scoring functions largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level, while temporal aggregation and ranking preservation emerge as critical design factors. The study introduces InertiaKV and Score-Free decoding as novel approaches.
AI.motivation: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses heavily on designing better token scoring functions, while treating temporal score aggregation across decode steps as an implementation detail. This work investigates whether scoring function choices matter under aggressive KV compression with different temporal aggregation methods.
AI.method: Evaluated multiple scoring functions (Value-norm, entropy, KeyDiff, key norm, recency, learned scorer) across different temporal aggregation methods (primarily EMA) using six open-weight backbones on LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks.
AI.result: EMA aggregation makes approximately order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable. Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets, while KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and learned scorer alter ranking and degrade substantially. InertiaKV yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput, and Score-Free decoding achieves +0.03 average quality change while removing all subsequent scoring.
AI.conclusion: Temporal aggregation and ranking preservation are distinct, consequential design factors in KV cache compression. This does not imply scoring quality is irrelevant in general, but highlights that under EMA aggregation, the temporal rule coupling layer weighting and retention dominates performance.

title: DRACO: Fine-Grained Credit Assignment with Dynamic Rubrics for Long-Horizon Agent Training
summary: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards works well when a task has a programmatic checker, but most long-horizon agent domains have none. We work in the outcome-blind setting, where ground-truth success signals are not available. Multi-criteria rubrics are a popular way to supply such a reward; they are scored once per trajectory, but a single scalar is a poor signal across tens of steps. We propose DRACO: Distributing Rubric-based Advantage for Credit Optimization. It generates rubrics dynamically during training to track the policy's evolving capability, scores those rubrics once per completed trajectory, and redistributes that judgment over the steps responsible for annotated rubrics to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO. The redistribution is closed-form and does not introduce any trained attribution module. On AppWorld, DRACO gains 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with a sparse ground-truth reward, despite not using any verifiers itself. On out-of-domain Tau-Bench, it gains 5.3 points over the base model even without a frontier judge, beating both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based training settings. The code for DRACO is available at https://github.com/IBM/draco.

AI.tldr: DRACO is a reinforcement learning method that handles outcome-blind settings where ground-truth success signals are unavailable. It dynamically generates rubrics during training, scores them once per trajectory, and redistributes that judgment over the responsible steps to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO, without requiring any trained attribution module.
AI.motivation: Current RLVR methods work well with programmatic checkers, but most long-horizon agent domains lack such verifiers. Multi-criteria rubrics are popular but scored once per trajectory, providing poor signal across tens of steps. The outcome-blind setting lacks ground-truth success signals, making it challenging to train effective agents.
AI.method: DRACO generates rubrics dynamically during training to track the policy's evolving capability, scores those rubrics once per completed trajectory, and redistributes that judgment over the steps responsible for annotated rubrics to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO. The redistribution is closed-form and does not introduce any trained attribution module.
AI.result: On AppWorld, DRACO gains 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with a sparse ground-truth reward, despite not using any verifiers. On out-of-domain Tau-Bench, it gains 5.3 points over the base model even without a frontier judge, beating both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based training settings.
AI.conclusion: DRACO successfully addresses the outcome-blind setting problem by dynamically generating rubrics and redistributing trajectory-level judgments to per-step advantages, achieving superior performance without requiring programmatic checkers or ground-truth rewards.

title: Distilling deep optical flow stereo methods to retrieve dense three-dimensional wind fields
summary: Geostationary atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) provide the dense horizontal wind vectors (u,v) and heights ingested into data assimilation systems. Traditional AMVs track features using window-based cross-correlation and estimate heights via infrared brightness temperatures paired with numerical weather prediction (NWP) background states, creating a circular dependency that yields inaccurate heights, high computational cost, and sparse retrievals. Stereo winds from GEO-GEO and GEO-LEO geometrically resolve heights from parallax shifts across different poses, eliminating NWP dependence and improving accuracy, but they remain computationally heavy with limited coverage. In this work, we replace window-based tracking in stereo matching with deep optical flow for efficient, improved retrieval. Fine-tuning balances a self-supervised geometric residual loss with supervised radiosonde reconstruction. To eliminate multi-satellite overlap requirements, we distill the stereo teacher into a single-satellite student model. Chi-square and height uncertainties from the teacher are emulated by the student for quality assurance. The student generates winds across full-disk GEO imagery globally. Validation compares stereo and student models against radiosondes, operational AMVs, ERA5 reanalysis, and EarthCARE cloud profiles. Results through triple collocation show that stereo winds improve performance beyond operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, and 7.3 μm), wit degradation in the long-wave infrared (11.2 μm) band.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a deep learning approach to improve geostationary atmospheric motion vectors (AMVs) by replacing traditional window-based cross-correlation tracking with deep optical flow, using a teacher-student distillation framework to enable single-satellite stereo wind retrieval without multi-satellite overlap requirements.
AI.motivation: Traditional AMVs suffer from circular dependency (using NWP for height estimation), inaccurate heights, high computational cost, and sparse retrievals. While stereo winds from GEO-GEO and GEO-LEO can geometrically resolve heights without NWP, they remain computationally heavy with limited coverage due to multi-satellite overlap requirements.
AI.method: The approach replaces window-based tracking in stereo matching with deep optical flow. A fine-tuning strategy balances a self-supervised geometric residual loss with supervised radiosonde reconstruction. To eliminate multi-satellite overlap requirements, the stereo teacher model is distilled into a single-satellite student model, which emulates chi-square and height uncertainties from the teacher for quality assurance.
AI.result: Validation through triple collocation shows that stereo winds improve performance beyond operational AMVs for water vapor bands (6.2, 6.9, and 7.3 μm), with degradation observed in the long-wave infrared (11.2 μm) band. The student model generates winds across full-disk GEO imagery globally.
AI.conclusion: Deep optical flow combined with teacher-student distillation successfully enables efficient single-satellite stereo wind retrieval, improving upon operational AMVs for water vapor bands while eliminating the need for multi-satellite overlap. The approach maintains quality assurance through uncertainty emulation from the teacher model.

title: CulturalMenuBench: Probing the Knowledge-Application Gap in Multimodal Culinary Reasoning
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Findings. Code and data: https://github.com/BobTsang-NLP/CulturalMenuBench
summary: Multimodal language models achieve near-ceiling scores on food recognition benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether this success reflects genuine cultural understanding or mere visual matching. To probe this distinction, we introduce CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark of 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions; its 10 tasks pair final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels, spanning basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluating 12 models exposes a substantial knowledge-application gap: models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines, despite an identical four-way format. Diagnostic analyses explain why: error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). The knowledge is thus present but cannot be activated through visual input. An ablation confirms these tasks genuinely require procedural evidence: removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades process-grounded tasks while others remain stable. Overall, CulturalMenuBench shows that near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, motivating training that explicitly connects perception, procedure, and cultural context. Code and data are publicly available.

AI.tldr: CulturalMenuBench is a benchmark testing whether multimodal language models truly understand cultural food contexts or merely perform visual matching. The benchmark contains 4,870 items across 10 languages and 18 regions with 10 tasks pairing dish/cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels.
AI.motivation: Multimodal models achieve high scores on food recognition benchmarks, but it's unclear whether this reflects genuine cultural understanding or just visual matching. The researchers wanted to probe this distinction.
AI.method: The researchers created CulturalMenuBench with 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions, with 10 tasks pairing final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels. They evaluated 12 models and performed diagnostic analyses including error pattern analysis, correlation with visual distinctiveness, comparison of text-only vs image-only classification, and ablation studies removing sequential cooking images.
AI.result: Models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% on Chinese regional cuisine attribution. Error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). Removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades process-grounded tasks.
AI.conclusion: Near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge. The knowledge is present but cannot be activated through visual input. This motivates training that explicitly connects perception, procedure, and cultural context.

title: When Depth Hurts: Reliability-Aware Geometry Distillation for Depth-Free RGB-D Salient Object Detection
summary: Depth can resolve appearance ambiguity in RGB-D salient object detection (SOD), yet sensor depth is not uniformly reliable. Missing regions, blurred boundaries, and structural artifacts can propagate through multimodal fusion and make an RGB-D detector less accurate than its RGB-only counterpart. Existing quality-aware approaches regulate observed depth but remain dependent on the same potentially defective modality. We propose \method, a reliability-aware geometry distillation framework developed for RGB-D SOD benchmarks without using dataset-provided depth during training or inference. A frozen Depth Anything V2 model serves only as a training-time teacher, transferring dense relative geometry, hierarchical spatial attention, and boundary structure to a compact edge-aware geometry branch. Pooled bidirectional interaction aligns geometry with appearance, and a pixel-wise reliability estimator selectively injects geometry that is compatible with the current RGB representation. The teacher is removed after training, leaving an RGB-only inference network. Trained on 2,985 RGB-mask pairs, \method{} achieves the best or tied-best result in 26 of 36 metric-dataset comparisons against ten recent RGB-D SOD methods, including a 13.4\% relative MAE reduction on ReDWeb-S. When retrained on DUTS-TR, it also improves the strongest prior $F$-measure by 4.2\% on PASCAL-S, showing that the distilled geometry transfers beyond a particular sensor or dataset domain. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a reliability-aware geometry distillation framework for RGB-D salient object detection that uses a frozen Depth Anything V2 model as a training-time teacher to transfer geometry knowledge to an RGB-only inference network, eliminating dependence on potentially defective sensor depth.
AI.motivation: RGB-D SOD suffers from unreliable depth data (missing regions, blurred boundaries, artifacts) that can make multimodal detectors less accurate than RGB-only ones. Existing quality-aware approaches remain dependent on defective depth modalities.
AI.method: A geometry distillation framework using a frozen Depth Anything V2 teacher to transfer dense relative geometry, hierarchical spatial attention, and boundary structure to a compact edge-aware geometry branch. Features pooled bidirectional interaction and a pixel-wise reliability estimator for selective geometry injection. The teacher is discarded after training, leaving an RGB-only network.
AI.result: Achieved best or tied-best results in 26/36 metric-dataset comparisons against 10 RGB-D SOD methods. Demonstrated 13.4% relative MAE reduction on ReDWeb-S. When retrained on DUTS-TR, improved F-measure by 4.2% on PASCAL-S, showing cross-domain transferability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully distills geometry knowledge from a depth model into an RGB-only network, achieving superior performance while avoiding sensor depth reliability issues. The approach generalizes beyond the original training domain, validating the effectiveness of geometry distillation.

title: Scaling Laws, Tabular Data and Actuarial Ratemaking Models
summary: Scaling laws in modern deep learning describe how held-out loss improves as model capacity, training data, and compute increase, often following power-law trends. We investigate whether analogous scaling regularities arise in actuarial ratemaking, where data are tabular, heterogeneous, and noisy, and where classical models such as GLMs remain strong baselines. Using a real-world motor insurance portfolio, we train models from different families across increasing fractions of the training data and multiple random seeds, evaluating out-of-sample Poisson deviance, a likelihood-based loss for Poisson count predictions in which lower values indicate better held-out fit. We find that all model families improve with additional data, but scaling exponents differ substantially: TabM exhibits markedly stronger data scaling than purely supervised tabular Transformers and standard MLP baselines. Transformer variants show weak parameter scaling unless augmented with additional inductive biases (TabM-style adaptation or self-supervision). These results provide quantitative guidance on model selection by data regime and suggest that effective scaling on actuarial tabular tasks depends on architecture and loss function objective design, with simple increases in Transformer size providing limited gains.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether scaling laws observed in modern deep learning (where model performance improves predictably with data, compute, and parameters) apply to actuarial ratemaking with tabular insurance data. The study compares multiple model families (GLMs, TabM, Transformers, MLPs) on a motor insurance portfolio, evaluating out-of-sample Poisson deviance across increasing data fractions and random seeds.
AI.motivation: To determine if scaling laws from deep learning generalize to actuarial tasks with tabular, heterogeneous, noisy data where classical GLMs remain strong baselines. The goal is to provide quantitative guidance for model selection based on data regime.
AI.method: Using a real-world motor insurance portfolio, the researchers trained models from different families across increasing fractions of training data with multiple random seeds. Performance was evaluated using out-of-sample Poisson deviance (a likelihood-based loss for Poisson count predictions where lower values indicate better fit).
AI.result: All model families improved with additional data, but scaling exponents differed substantially. TabM exhibited markedly stronger data scaling than purely supervised tabular Transformers and standard MLP baselines. Transformer variants showed weak parameter scaling unless augmented with additional inductive biases (TabM-style adaptation or self-supervision).
AI.conclusion: Effective scaling on actuarial tabular tasks depends on architecture and loss function objective design. Simple increases in Transformer size provide limited gains. The findings provide quantitative guidance on model selection by data regime, suggesting that TabM-style architectures are more suitable for data-scaling in actuarial applications.

title: NeoRed: A Knowledge-Logic-Alignment Multimodal Large Language Model for Neonatal Respiratory Disease Diagnosis
summary: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, posing substantial challenges in clinical practice. Despite recent advances, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face two key limitations in neonatal diagnosis: (1) domain gap arising from predominantly adult training data; (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis. To address these challenges, we collect two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and propose NeoRed, to the best of our knowledge, the first MLLM tailored for neonatal respiratory disease, filling the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation. To enhance joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays, we design a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework which constrains model behavior from three perspectives: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention across modalities; 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) aligns the semantics of generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic reports generation, achieving ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. NeoRed also preserves competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray). Datasets will be available upon application.

AI.tldr: NeoRed is the first Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) specifically designed for neonatal respiratory disease diagnosis, addressing domain gaps and insufficient clinical context integration through a Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework.
AI.motivation: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, but existing MLLMs face two key limitations: (1) domain gap from predominantly adult training data, and (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis.
AI.method: The authors collected two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and proposed NeoRed with a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework that includes three components: (1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) - incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations; (2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) - aligns generated report semantics with multimodal diagnostic logic; (3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) - establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions.
AI.result: NeoRed achieves ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. It also preserves competitive performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray).
AI.conclusion: NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic report generation and fills the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation. The KLA framework effectively enhances joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays.

title: FoRIS: Progressive Foreground Refinement for Training-Free In-Context Segmentation
summary: In-Context Segmentation (ICS) aims to precisely segment arbitrary semantic concepts, such as objects or parts, given one or a few annotated visual exemplars. In this paper, we revisit ICS from a more classical segmentation perspective, viewing it as a coarse-to-fine progressive refinement process. Rather than directly predicting the final mask through reference-query matching, we progressively refine the segmentation from coarse and ambiguous foreground responses to precise and complete foreground structures. Building upon this perspective, we propose a training-free in-context segmentation framework, termed FoRIS. Specifically, FoRIS consists of three key stages: Foreground Purification, Foreground Localization, and Foreground Consolidation, which progressively suppress background distractions, localize discriminative target regions, and recover complete foreground structures through semantic aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate that FoRIS achieves SOTA performance across semantic and part segmentation tasks, with average improvements of 4.5 and 4.8 mIoU points over existing approaches in the 1-shot and 5-shot settings, respectively. Code: https://github.com/Xi-Mu-Yu/FoRIS.

AI.tldr: FoRIS is a training-free in-context segmentation framework that treats ICS as a coarse-to-fine progressive refinement process, achieving SOTA performance with 4.5 and 4.8 mIoU improvements in 1-shot and 5-shot settings respectively.
AI.motivation: Current ICS methods directly predict final masks through reference-query matching, which may be suboptimal. The authors revisit ICS from a classical segmentation perspective, viewing it as a coarse-to-fine progressive refinement process.
AI.method: FoRIS consists of three key stages: (1) Foreground Purification - suppress background distractions, (2) Foreground Localization - localize discriminative target regions, (3) Foreground Consolidation - recover complete foreground structures through semantic aggregation. The approach is training-free.
AI.result: FoRIS achieves SOTA performance across semantic and part segmentation tasks, with average improvements of 4.5 mIoU points in 1-shot setting and 4.8 mIoU points in 5-shot setting over existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: The coarse-to-fine progressive refinement perspective is effective for in-context segmentation, and FoRIS demonstrates the value of this approach through significant performance improvements without requiring training.

title: Kernel Reboot: Breaking the Boundaries of Neural Tangent Kernels for Neural Fields
comment: Published in IEEE TPAMI, vol. 48, no. 9, pp. 10940-10957, Sep. 2026. Author version adds related-work references and biography updates; Figures 12 and 13 were regenerated from the same locked hyperparameter sweep. Tabulated results, reported best points, scientific claims, and conclusions are unchanged
summary: Neural fields (NFs) map continuous coordinates to signals such as color or density, but fast high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations remains difficult. Classical Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regression gives closed-form fits, yet it is fundamentally linear and cannot accumulate reusable task priors. We develop three algorithms that address these gaps. NTK-KIP learns a distilled support set of coordinates (and optional labels) so that a finite NTK can inpaint large missing regions from little observed data, yielding a compact non-linear representation instead of a raw kernel solve. MetaQuill meta-learns a shared initialization for an INR so that new scenes can be adapted by updating only a small task-specific weight offset, which provides true feature learning and a reusable prior. Finally, MetaQuill-KIP fuses both ideas: it seeds the task with a KIP-style non-linear warm start, then refines only that small offset around the meta-learned initialization. MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations, while requiring only lightweight per-instance adaptation, whereas diffusion-style baselines typically depend on large pretrained generative priors and costly per-image tuning. This shows that NTK-driven neural fields can be made both non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction.

AI.tldr: This paper develops three algorithms (NTK-KIP, MetaQuill, and MetaQuill-KIP) to address challenges in fast high-quality neural field reconstruction from sparse observations, combining neural tangent kernel methods with meta-learning to achieve non-linear representations with reusable task priors.
AI.motivation: Neural fields (NFs) map continuous coordinates to signals but face difficulty with fast high-quality reconstruction from sparse observations. Classical NTK regression is fundamentally linear and cannot accumulate reusable task priors, limiting practical few-shot reconstruction capabilities.
AI.method: Three algorithms are developed: (1) NTK-KIP learns a distilled support set of coordinates so finite NTK can inpaint large missing regions from little observed data; (2) MetaQuill meta-learns a shared initialization for INR allowing adaptation via small task-specific weight offsets; (3) MetaQuill-KIP fuses both approaches - seeding with KIP-style non-linear warm start then refining only small offset around meta-learned initialization.
AI.result: MetaQuill-KIP achieves high-PSNR reconstructions and semantically plausible inpainting under very sparse observations while requiring only lightweight per-instance adaptation, outperforming diffusion-style baselines that depend on large pretrained generative priors and costly per-image tuning.
AI.conclusion: NTK-driven neural fields can be made both non-linear and meta-learnable, narrowing the gap between analytic kernels and practical few-shot reconstruction. The approach demonstrates that combining kernel methods with meta-learning enables true feature learning with reusable priors while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Feature Reconfiguration With Visual Prior for Medical Lesion Segmentation
summary: Lesion segmentation in medical images plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. Despite significant advances, lesion segmentation remains challenging due to two major factors: (1) complex background interference; (2) diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder based methods mainly focus on enhancing feature extraction or redesigning decoding strategies. However, they lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during the encoding stage, limiting their effectiveness in handling these challenges. To address these limitations, we propose FreNet, a feature reconfiguration framework with visual priors, which performs pixel-level reconfiguration before encoding and feature-level reconfiguration during encoding for precise medical lesion segmentation. To suppress background responses, we propose an Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN), which models a continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure input image before encoding stage. To better handle diverse lesion morphology, we design a Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module to progressively reconfigure backbone features during encoding stage. Within DFR, the Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) decouples backbone features in frequency domain to enhance foreground-background discriminability, while the Spatial Localization Module (SLM) spatially relocates and improving spatial stability after frequency decoupling. Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities demonstrate that FreNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, our method achieves Dice improvements of 5.0% over SOTA method and 7.2% over SAM.

AI.tldr: FreNet is a feature reconfiguration framework for medical lesion segmentation that uses visual priors from SAM to reconfigure input images before encoding and performs dual-domain feature reconfiguration (frequency and spatial) during encoding to handle complex background interference and diverse lesion morphology.
AI.motivation: Lesion segmentation faces two major challenges: complex background interference and diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder methods lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during encoding, limiting their effectiveness in handling these challenges.
AI.method: FreNet consists of two key components: (1) Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN) - models continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure input images before encoding to suppress background responses; (2) Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module - contains Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) to decouple features in frequency domain for enhanced foreground-background discriminability, and Spatial Localization Module (SLM) to spatially relocate and improve spatial stability after frequency decoupling.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities show FreNet significantly outperforms SOTA methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, FreNet achieves 5.0% Dice improvement over SOTA and 7.2% over SAM.
AI.conclusion: FreNet effectively addresses lesion segmentation challenges through visual prior guidance and dual-domain feature reconfiguration, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple medical imaging datasets.

title: Exploring the Potential of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training for Multi-Source Remote Sensing Data
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Submitted to AAAI 2027
summary: Contrastive language-image learning (CLIP) has become a key paradigm for remote sensing vision-language understanding. However, existing remote sensing contrastive learning methods are mostly built on RGB-oriented CLIP architectures, making it difficult to exploit heterogeneous sensors such as SAR, multi-spectral imaging (MSI), and hyperspectral imaging (HSI). To address this limitation, we propose OmniRSCLIP, an end-to-end contrastive learning framework that supports multi-source sensor inputs for remote sensing vision-language modeling. The key idea is to extend CLIP beyond its fixed RGB input interface without breaking the pretrained visual knowledge. To this end, OmniRSCLIP introduces Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD), which formulates arbitrary-channel adaptation as a basis recomposition problem: pretrained CLIP patch embeddings provide transferable spatial bases, while wavelength-conditioned coefficients span sensor-specific embedding kernels within a constrained visual prior space. This design avoids forcing heterogeneous sensors into a fixed-channel input space, while aligning them in a unified image-text semantic space. We further introduce a spectral-context-aware mask-based contrastive learning scheme to suppress modality-specific redundant features and enhance fine-grained image-text alignment. Finally, to support multi-modal training, we construct OmniRS5M, the first large-scale remote sensing image-text corpus covering RGB, SAR, MSI, and HSI. Experiments on retrieval, zero-shot classification, and semantic localization show that OmniRSCLIP preserves strong RGB-domain performance while effectively extending CLIP to heterogeneous remote sensing modalities.

AI.tldr: OmniRSCLIP extends CLIP to support multi-source remote sensing sensors (SAR, MSI, HSI) beyond RGB through Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD) and spectral-context-aware contrastive learning, with a new dataset OmniRS5M.
AI.motivation: Existing remote sensing contrastive learning methods are built on RGB-oriented CLIP architectures, making it difficult to exploit heterogeneous sensors such as SAR, multi-spectral imaging (MSI), and hyperspectral imaging (HSI).
AI.method: The paper proposes OmniRSCLIP, an end-to-end contrastive learning framework that supports multi-source sensor inputs. It introduces: (1) Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD), which formulates arbitrary-channel adaptation as a basis recomposition problem using pretrained CLIP patch embeddings as transferable spatial bases and wavelength-conditioned coefficients for sensor-specific embedding kernels; (2) A spectral-context-aware mask-based contrastive learning scheme to suppress modality-specific redundant features and enhance fine-grained image-text alignment.
AI.result: OmniRSCLIP preserves strong RGB-domain performance while effectively extending CLIP to heterogeneous remote sensing modalities. Experiments on retrieval, zero-shot classification, and semantic localization demonstrate these capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework successfully enables CLIP to handle heterogeneous remote sensing modalities while maintaining RGB performance, addressing a key limitation in remote sensing vision-language understanding.

title: Routing Is Not Enough: Diagnosing Intra-Adapter Subspace Contention in MoE+LoRA Fine-Tuning
comment: 13 pages, 1 figure, 16 tables. Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
summary: Multi-domain fine-tuning often combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming that token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. We test this assumption in MoE+LoRA using Python code paired with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning. Although these domains show near-disjoint expert routing, adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating that routing separation alone may not prevent negative transfer. To localize the failure, we introduce Jaccard routing overlap and adapter-gradient cosine similarity, which measure expert sharing and update compatibility, respectively. These diagnostics indicate that interference arises mostly from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. We address this issue with SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed. We evaluate SpawnLoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings and find that it effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA. These results demonstrate that structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether token-level routing in MoE+LoRA can separate domain-specific updates, finding that routing separation alone fails to prevent negative transfer. The authors introduce SpawnLoRA, which adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts to address gradient interference.
AI.motivation: Multi-domain fine-tuning combines MoE routing with LoRA, assuming token-level routing separates domain-specific updates. This assumption was untested, and the authors discovered that adding biomedical data substantially increases code perplexity, indicating negative transfer occurs despite routing separation.
AI.method: The authors paired Python code with biomedical text and mathematical reasoning for testing. They introduced two diagnostic metrics: (1) Jaccard routing overlap to measure expert sharing, and (2) adapter-gradient cosine similarity to measure update compatibility. They then proposed SpawnLoRA, which dynamically adds gated sub-adapters inside MoE experts when adapter-level contention is detected, while keeping the router fixed.
AI.result: Diagnostic metrics revealed that interference arises from nearly orthogonal domain gradients competing within the same low-rank adapter subspace. SpawnLoRA effectively reduces negative transfer compared with standard and rank-adaptive LoRA on Phi-tiny-MoE-instruct and OLMoE-1B-7B across multiple mixture settings.
AI.conclusion: Structural separation inside experts provides benefits beyond routing or rank expansion alone. The key insight is that preventing negative transfer requires addressing gradient interference within the adapter subspace, not just relying on routing separation.

title: Dalek: A Constructive Agent Machine
summary:
We present Dalek, a closed machine designed for agents that realizes self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization on any substrate satisfying a general host contract. The machine is built from three primitives---actors, messages, and channels. Four obligations---a host boundary, a construction language, admissible transitions, and rule heredity---give its boundary, identity, and closure a structural basis.
  Von Neumann's 1948 self-reproducing automaton supplies a hereditary constructional core: a self-description together with a constructor, a copier, and a controller. Dalek combines this core with the four obligations and rederives its medium for a text-and-message agent substrate, adding explicit structures for boundary, identity, history, and growth. A large language model and a compiler occupy the payload position and form a general capability producer. New capabilities are authored, compiled, installed into the description, and inherited by descendants. The same path produces the machine's own organs and even its runtime, closing heredity and evolution within the machine.

AI.tldr: Dale k is a closed machine for agents that achieves self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization using three primitives (actors, messages, channels) and four obligations (host boundary, construction language, admissible transitions, rule heredity). It extends Von Neumann's self-reproducing automaton with a large language model and compiler as payload, enabling capabilities to be authored, compiled, installed, and inherited by descendants.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to create a general framework for autonomous agents that can self-reproduce and evolve on any substrate satisfying a host contract, combining Von Neumann's hereditary constructional core with modern AI capabilities.
AI.method: The approach uses three primitives (actors, messages, channels) and four obligations (host boundary, construction language, admissible transitions, rule heredity) to define a closed machine. A large language model and compiler occupy the payload position to produce general capabilities.
AI.result: The machine achieves closed heredity and evolution - new capabilities can be authored, compiled, installed into the description, and inherited by descendants, including the machine's own organs and runtime.
AI.conclusion: Dale k represents a theoretical framework for self-evolving agents that combines classical automata theory with modern LLM capabilities, providing a structural basis for autonomous machine reproduction and evolution.

title: Neural-Collapse-guided Task-Free Continual Anomaly Detection
summary: Recent years have witnessed growing interest in continual anomaly detection for industrial visual inspection. However, real-world manufacturing environments exhibit unpredictable shifts in data distributions, rendering task-dependent continual learning assumptions impractical. To address this limitation, we formulate industrial anomaly detection as a task-free continual learning problem and propose NC-TFAD, a neural-collapse-inspired, geometry-driven framework for learning from non-stationary data streams without task boundaries. NC-TFAD freezes a pretrained backbone and aligns streaming features to a simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) prototype space to stabilize representation geometry under non-stationary streams. To satisfy the NC-inspired geometric construction in the absence of real anomalies, we generate synthetic anomaly samples as auxiliary anchors during training. Building on this geometry, we further introduce inter- and intra-class regularization together with a Focal Neural Collapse Contrastive (FNCC) loss to suppress representation drift and improve normal-anomaly separability. Finally, a normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch constructs calibrated patch-wise deviation maps from normal training samples and fuses them with a weak self-attention prior, producing anomaly heatmaps without pixel-level annotations. Extensive experiments on MVTec AD and VisA show that NC-TFAD consistently outperforms representative task-free continual learning methods adapted from general vision, as well as unified anomaly detection baselines, in both image-level detection and pixel-level localization under the task-free continual learning protocol. These results highlight that geometry-driven modeling offers an effective and robust solution for task-free continual anomaly detection in real-world industrial applications.

AI.tldr: NC-TFAD addresses industrial anomaly detection as a task-free continual learning problem using neural collapse theory. It aligns streaming features to an ETF prototype space, uses synthetic anomalies as anchors, and employs FNCC loss with a normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch for anomaly heatmap generation, outperforming existing methods on MVTec AD and VisA.
AI.motivation: Real-world manufacturing environments have unpredictable data distribution shifts, making task-dependent continual learning assumptions impractical. Existing methods require clear task boundaries, which don't exist in practical industrial settings.
AI.method: 1) Freeze pretrained backbone and align streaming features to simplex ETF prototype space; 2) Generate synthetic anomaly samples as auxiliary anchors for NC-inspired geometric construction; 3) Apply inter/intra-class regularization with Focal Neural Collapse Contrastive (FNCC) loss to suppress representation drift; 4) Use normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch with weak self-attention prior for pixel-level anomaly heatmaps.
AI.result: NC-TFAD consistently outperforms representative task-free continual learning methods and unified anomaly detection baselines on MVTec AD and VisA in both image-level detection and pixel-level localization under task-free continual learning protocol.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-driven modeling via neural collapse theory offers an effective and robust solution for task-free continual anomaly detection in real-world industrial applications.

title: Frontier LLMs are effective batch optimizers: Assessing reasoning models in continuous and discrete settings
summary: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have become attractive priors for optimization due to their large-scale pretraining that enables them to navigate a variety of optimization settings. However, the effectiveness of modern reasoning LLMs in batch optimization settings remains underexplored. Here we investigate the performance of the current generation of frontier LLMs as batch optimizers in both continuous and discrete settings. We find that while LLMs are competitive zero-shot batch optimizers for numerical test functions, their performance is brittle compared to classical non-LLM optimization approaches. However, LLM priors are significantly better in semantically rich settings, indicating that their batch optimization behavior is highly effective when navigating and reasoning over the discrete spaces most similar in structure to their pretraining data.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether modern frontier large language models (LLMs) can serve as effective batch optimizers in both continuous and discrete optimization settings. The study finds that while LLMs perform competitively as zero-shot optimizers for numerical test functions, their performance is inconsistent compared to classical optimization methods. However, LLMs excel in semantically rich, discrete optimization spaces that resemble their pretraining data.
AI.motivation: The motivation stems from the observation that frontier LLMs have become attractive priors for optimization due to their large-scale pretraining, yet their effectiveness in batch optimization settings—particularly for modern reasoning LLMs—remains underexplored.
AI.method: The researchers evaluated the current generation of frontier LLMs as batch optimizers across both continuous and discrete optimization settings, testing their zero-shot performance against classical optimization approaches.
AI.result: LLMs demonstrated competitive zero-shot optimization capabilities for numerical test functions but exhibited brittle performance compared to classical non-LLM methods. Importantly, LLM priors performed significantly better in semantically rich settings, suggesting their effectiveness is highest when navigating discrete spaces with structure similar to their pretraining data.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that LLM-based batch optimization is highly effective in semantically rich, discrete spaces that align with LLM pretraining, but remains inferior to classical approaches in traditional numerical optimization tasks.

title: GPS-Bench: A Governance Policy Benchmark for Automating Policy Analysis
summary: Policy analysis requires more than predicting whether a proposal will pass: it requires identifying who will be affected, how those actors respond, and what follows. LLM-based policy simulations model these processes at scale, but their validity is hard to establish when plausible behaviour is never compared with observed outcomes. We introduce GPS-Bench, an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that links policies to relevant actors, actor actions and downstream impacts using legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, economic data and other public evidence. Actors are reconstructed from the dated record rather than prompted as archetypes, so a persona is an evidence object with provenance; a human-annotated pool forms the Gold evaluation set, while cases labelled by a separate LLM from retrieved evidence are treated as Silver supervision and never as test labels. Because every inference mode reads the same grounded state and emits the same schema, GPS-Bench turns "does multi-agent simulation help?" into a controlled comparison: we contrast joint reasoning, independent and communicating actor agents, graph-based methods and weight-level fine-tuning over one policy state. Fine-tuning on the grounded record gives the strongest actor-level impact prediction, and decomposition does not beat it; what decomposition adds is mechanism. Agents hold private, non-identical evidence, each seeing its own exposure clause, and address named partners with concrete joint proposals, what they offer, what they need in return, and why acting together beats acting alone, so the coalitions that form can be checked against the commitments the record holds. GPS-Bench therefore gives a common empirical setting for studying when evidence, actor modelling and multi-agent interaction improve the prediction and interpretation of policy outcomes.

AI.tldr: GPS-Bench is an evidence-grounded benchmark for evaluating LLM-based governance policy simulations. It links policies to actors, actions, and downstream impacts using real-world records (legislative, lobbying, regulatory, corporate filings). The benchmark enables controlled comparisons between different reasoning approaches (joint reasoning, multi-agent, graph-based, fine-tuning) over the same policy state. Fine-tuning on grounded records outperforms decomposition methods for impact prediction, while decomposition provides mechanistic explanation. The benchmark uses human-annotated Gold labels and LLM-generated Silver supervision, with agents holding private evidence to simulate realistic coalition formation.
AI.motivation: LLM-based policy simulations lack validity because they predict outcomes without comparing against observed results. Policy analysis requires more than pass/fail predictions—it needs to identify affected actors, their responses, and downstream consequences. Existing methods cannot be properly evaluated when "plausible behavior" is never validated against real-world outcomes.
AI.method: GPS-Bench constructs actors from dated legislative records rather than prompting archetypes, creating evidence-backed personas with provenance. It uses Gold evaluation set (human-annotated) and Silver supervision (LLM-labeled from retrieved evidence, never used as test labels). The benchmark compares four inference modes over identical grounded state: (1) joint reasoning, (2) independent agents, (3) communicating actor agents, (4) weight-level fine-tuning. Agents hold private, non-identical evidence with exposure clauses and address partners with concrete joint proposals including offers, needs, and rationale for coalition.
AI.result: Fine-tuning on the grounded record achieves the strongest actor-level impact prediction. Decomposition methods do not outperform fine-tuning in prediction accuracy. The key advantage of decomposition is providing mechanistic explanation of how outcomes emerge. The multi-agent setup with private evidence allows verification of coalition formation against recorded commitments.
AI.conclusion: GPS-Bench establishes a common empirical framework for studying when evidence grounding, actor modeling, and multi-agent interaction improve policy outcome prediction and interpretation. It transforms the question "does multi-agent simulation help?" into a controlled experimental comparison. The benchmark enables rigorous evaluation of different reasoning approaches against observed policy outcomes, advancing the validity of LLM-based policy simulations.

title: Portable Causal Fairness Across Synthetic Data Generator Families
summary: When a statistical agency or regulator releases synthetic data in place of sensitive records, it chooses the generator that produces the table, and can shape that generator so unfair pathways are absent. DECAF made this concrete on one non-private GAN: three fairness definitions become three sets of edge cuts on the generator's causal graph. Whether the mechanism belongs to DECAF, or to causal factorisation itself, was untested. We port all three definitions to nine generators from three unrelated families (marginals-based, GAN, and diffusion, each with differentially private variants), across three levels of formal privacy guarantee, over 2,520 matched-pair runs on Adult and COMPAS datasets. The mechanism transfers everywhere, and our new causal diffusion backbone yields the fairest release of any family we tested, at fidelity close to the marginals tier. Applying the cut barely moves fidelity, only costs a downstream classifier about $0.07$ to $0.15$ AUC on average, and adding privacy guarantees don't make the data less fair.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether DECAF—a fairness mechanism that uses causal graph edge cuts to ensure synthetic data lacks unfair pathways—transfers across nine different generators (marginals-based, GAN, and diffusion models) with differential privacy variants. Testing 2,520 matched-pair runs on Adult and COMPAS datasets, the authors find the mechanism works universally, with a new causal diffusion model achieving the best fairness at near marginal-tier fidelity, while adding privacy guarantees does not reduce fairness.
AI.motivation: Prior work (DECAF) demonstrated that three fairness definitions can be translated into edge cuts on a generator's causal graph for one non-private GAN. However, it remained untested whether this mechanism generalizes to other generators or to causal factorization itself. This work aims to verify the transferability of DECAF across diverse generator families and privacy levels.
AI.method: The study ported three fairness definitions to nine generators from three unrelated families: marginals-based, GAN, and diffusion models (each with differentially private variants). Experiments covered three levels of formal privacy guarantees, running 2,520 matched-pair experiments on Adult and COMPAS datasets. A new causal diffusion backbone was also developed.
AI.result: The DECAF mechanism transfers across all generator families. The new causal diffusion backbone yields the fairest release among all tested families, achieving fidelity close to the marginals tier. Applying fairness cuts minimally impacts fidelity, reducing downstream classifier AUC by only 0.07-0.15 on average. Notably, adding privacy guarantees does not make the data less fair.
AI.conclusion: DECAF's fairness mechanism is universal and transfers across all generator families. The proposed causal diffusion model represents a novel approach for fair synthetic data generation. The findings suggest that fairness and privacy can be simultaneously achieved without significant trade-offs in utility.

title: HalluPeer: A Taxonomy-driven Benchmark for Detecting Hallucinations in Scientific Peer Reviews
summary: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as review assistants, yet LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers. We introduce HalluPeer, a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, providing aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews, annotated for detection, classification, and localization. Our pipeline induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identifies review contexts, and injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments on 12K papers and 38K reviews show that existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique, while evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification. Our project page can be found in https://github.com/Lin-TzuLing/HalluPeer.git

AI.tldr: HalluPeer is a benchmark designed to detect hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, addressing the risk that LLMs used as review assistants may generate fluent but unsupported claims. The benchmark provides aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews with annotations for detection, classification, and localization.
AI.motivation: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as review assistants. However, LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers.
AI.method: The authors introduce HalluPeer with a pipeline that: 1) induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, 2) identifies review contexts, 3) injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments were conducted on 12K papers and 38K reviews.
AI.result: Existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique. Evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification.
AI.conclusion: HalluPeer reveals that current hallucination detection methods are inadequate for peer review contexts, and patterns identified in the benchmark appear in real peer reviews, underscoring the importance of developing source-aware verification systems for LLM-assisted peer review.

title: When Do Frozen VLMs Respond to Image-Free Object-Token Edits? An Answer-Key-Free Protocol and What It Reveals
summary: Answering what-if queries about a scene with a VLM usually means injecting the assumption as text or repainting the scene with a generative model. We instead move the edit to the representation level, before the model input. The image is abstracted into a set of object-level tokens, and the original image never enters the VLM. This design rests on an open question: when do frozen VLMs actually respond to such token edits? We introduce an answer-key-free protocol: no post-edit answer is annotated. It scores edits whose answers are logically determined, and audits itself by reversing each scoreable choice. The protocol reveals three structures. The response is not free: explicit edit teaching, not ordinary VQA training, produces it in dense scenes and multiplies it in sparse ones, on all three operations. Once on, it is governed by token cleanliness and density, with deployable detector+segmenter tokens competitive with the oracle and outperforming it on VRSBench. And reading is a separable axis: the image-free token route preserves 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline's free-text VQA, and the answers measurably depend on the tokens. The response, cleanliness, and reading structures are sign-preserved across two remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) and three frozen LM backbones. We release the probe generator, records, judge logs, and code.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel approach for answering "what-if" queries about scenes by editing at the representation level (token level) rather than the input level. Instead of injecting assumptions as text or repainting the scene, they abstract images into object-level tokens, keeping the original image from entering the VLM. They introduce an answer-key-free protocol for evaluation and reveal three key structures: edit teaching is required for response, token cleanliness/density governs the response, and reading is a separable axis. The method preserves 92-96% of VQA performance and shows consistent results across datasets and backbones.
AI.motivation: Current approaches to answering what-if queries about scenes using VLMs require either injecting assumptions as text or repainting the scene with a generative model. This paper aims to move the edit to the representation level, before the model input, by abstracting the image into object-level tokens. An open question motivates this work: when do frozen VLMs actually respond to such token edits?
AI.method: The authors introduce an answer-key-free protocol that scores edits whose answers are logically determined without requiring post-edit answer annotations. The protocol audits itself by reversing each scoreable choice. They investigate three structures: (1) what produces the response (edit teaching vs ordinary VQA training), (2) what governs the response once produced (token cleanliness and density), and (3) whether reading is a separable axis (image-free token route vs patch-token baseline). They test deployable detector+segmenter tokens and compare against oracle performance.
