Reliable proactive service requires: calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence.
AI.conclusion: Proactive service in LLM agents requires moving beyond explicit instruction paradigms. The key requirements are calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence, rather than just offline performance metrics or memory capabilities.

title: Residual Optimal Transport-Based Experts Collaboration Towards Modality-Aware Infrared-Visible Object Detection
summary: Infrared-visible object detection (IVOD) integrates complementary evidence from visible and infrared sensors for reliable perception in challenging scenes. In practice, sensors may fail or drop frames, leaving one modality unavailable or intermittent. Existing methods for IVOD assume both modalities are always present, and fixed fusion collapses when one stream is missing. Furthermore, it remains a critical challenge to reliably estimate semantic correlation across heterogeneous modalities, especially under spectral distribution discrepancy. We present FlexibleFusion, a unified and adaptive method that flexibly allocates integration pathways and fusion strength, operating seamlessly across complete and missing-modality regimes. At its core, the Modality-Aware Experts Collaboration (MAEC) mechanism selectively activates and aggregates cross-modal or intra-modal expert pathways. It allows cross-modal fusion when full modalities are available and falls back to self-fusion under missing conditions. Additionally, we design Residual Self-Paced Entropic Optimal Transport (RSPEOT) to align heterogeneous feature distributions from a transport perspective. Instead of relying on the fixed sparsity coefficient in standard entropic optimal transport (EOT), RSPEOT introduces a residual-driven self-paced update that prioritizes reliable matches and progressively refines harder ones. This design alleviates the additional optimization burden of standard EOT while preserving reliable semantic alignment. Comprehensive experiments under complete and missing-modality protocols show consistent performance across arbitrary modality configurations. Code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: FlexibleFusion addresses infrared-visible object detection (IVOD) under both complete and missing-modality scenarios. It proposes a Modality-Aware Experts Collaboration (MAEC) mechanism for adaptive fusion and a Residual Self-Paced Entropic Optimal Transport (RSPEOT) for heterogeneous feature alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing IVOD methods assume both modalities are always present and fail when one modality is unavailable due to sensor failure or frame drops. Additionally, reliably estimating semantic correlation across heterogeneous modalities under spectral distribution discrepancy remains challenging.
AI.method: FlexibleFusion employs two core mechanisms: (1) MAEC selectively activates and aggregates cross-modal or intra-modal expert pathways—using cross-modal fusion when full modalities are available and falling back to self-fusion under missing conditions; (2) RSPEOT introduces a residual-driven self-paced update for entropic optimal transport, prioritizing reliable matches and progressively refining harder ones to align heterogeneous feature distributions.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments under complete and missing-modality protocols show consistent performance across arbitrary modality configurations.
AI.conclusion: FlexibleFusion provides a unified and adaptive solution for IVOD that operates seamlessly across complete and missing-modality regimes, addressing both the practical issue of sensor failures and the technical challenge of cross-modal feature alignment.

title: DE-Venus: A Data-Efficient RLVR Framework for Large Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) improves large language model reasoning, but its practical scaling is constrained by expensive on-policy rollouts and the cost of obtaining reliable targets at scale. Existing methods address sample selection, incomplete supervision, or noisy labels separately, often entangling supervision logic with distributed training and hindering controlled comparison and reuse. We present DE-Venus, a unified framework for data-efficient RLVR that treats supervision as evolving state across data preparation and policy optimization. It organizes this lifecycle into three modules: Active Data Selection allocates training and annotation budgets; Weak Supervision Construction derives learning signals from unlabeled examples; and Training-Time Supervision Refinement filters or corrects unreliable supervision. DE-Venus supports seven representative methods and a data-selection pipeline by expressing method-specific decisions as offline dataset transitions or online transformations of targets, rewards, batches, and advantages while preserving verl's distributed execution contracts. Across public benchmarks and three business scenarios, separate configurations preserve or improve model quality with only 10% of labels or as little as 13% of relevant data; selected business configurations also reduce observed convergence steps by 63%--75%. DE-Venus thus reduces annotation and training costs without sacrificing scalable RL execution.

AI.tldr: DE-Venus is a unified framework for data-efficient reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) that addresses scaling challenges by treating supervision as evolving state across three modules: Active Data Selection, Weak Supervision Construction, and Training-Time Supervision Refinement. It supports seven representative methods and achieves comparable model quality using only 10% of labels or 13% of relevant data, while reducing convergence steps by 63%--75%.
AI.motivation: RLVR improves LLM reasoning but is constrained by expensive on-policy rollouts and costly reliable targets at scale. Existing methods address sample selection, incomplete supervision, or noisy labels separately, often entangling supervision logic with distributed training and hindering controlled comparison and reuse.
AI.method: DE-Venus organizes the supervision lifecycle into three modular components: (1) Active Data Selection for allocating training and annotation budgets; (2) Weak Supervision Construction for deriving learning signals from unlabeled examples; and (3) Training-Time Supervision Refinement for filtering or correcting unreliable supervision. It expresses method-specific decisions as offline dataset transitions or online transformations while preserving verl's distributed execution contracts.
AI.result: Across public benchmarks and three business scenarios, separate configurations preserve or improve model quality with only 10% of labels or as little as 13% of relevant data; selected business configurations also reduce observed convergence steps by 63%--75%.
AI.conclusion: DE-Venus reduces annotation and training costs without sacrificing scalable RL execution, providing a unified framework that enables controlled comparison and reuse of different RLVR methods.

title: SimSkill: A Lifelong Learning AI Agent for Autonomous Mastery of Traffic Simulation
summary: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly capable, the long-term value of AI systems depends not only on solving individual requests, but also on transforming experience and accumulated knowledge into durable, reusable competence. We introduce SimSkill, a self-evolving agent built around the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) traffic simulator. SimSkill identifies capability gaps, generates and solves environment-grounded tasks, verifies solutions through an action--critic loop, and consolidates experience into episodic, procedural, and semantic memory without updating the backbone model. Through autonomous exploration, it builds a reusable library spanning the traffic-simulation workflow. We evaluate SimSkill on two held-out benchmarks with three backbone LLMs and independent artifact-based verification. SimSkill improves verified completion by up to 25 percentage points, while ablations show complementary contributions from procedural and semantic memory. Its benefits remain backbone- and budget-dependent: memory does not improve every model or uniformly reduce inference cost. More broadly, SimSkill illustrates a design paradigm in which natural language preserves and composes computational capabilities, while executable tools and code provide precise and reproducible execution. All code and experimental data are publicly available at https://github.com/qiliuchn/SimSkill-V1.

AI.tldr: SimSkill is a self-evolving AI agent that uses the SUMO traffic simulator to autonomously identify capability gaps, generate and solve tasks, verify solutions, and consolidate experience into memory without updating the backbone model. It improves verified completion by up to 25 percentage points on held-out benchmarks.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become more capable, their long-term value depends on transforming experience into durable, reusable competence rather than just solving individual requests. Current approaches lack mechanisms for autonomous skill acquisition and memory consolidation in real-world computational environments.
AI.method: SimSkill uses a four-phase cycle: (1) identifies capability gaps, (2) generates environment-grounded tasks using SUMO, (3) verifies solutions through an action-critic loop, and (4) consolidates experience into episodic, procedural, and semantic memory without updating the backbone model. It builds a reusable library through autonomous exploration.
AI.result: SimSkill improves verified completion by up to 25 percentage points on two held-out benchmarks with three backbone LLMs. Ablations show complementary contributions from procedural and semantic memory. Benefits are backbone- and budget-dependent.
AI.conclusion: SimSkill demonstrates a design paradigm where natural language preserves computational capabilities while executable tools provide precise execution. Memory consolidation without model updates enables persistent competence building. However, benefits are not uniform across all models or inference budgets.

title: Neural Video Compression Based on Deformable Temporal Alignment and Difference-aware Fusion
summary: In conditional coding-based neural video compression, the quality of temporal context directly affects compression per- formance. Existing methods mostly construct context from prop- agated reference features, but they are vulnerable to motion esti- mation and local alignment errors in regions with complex mo- tion, occlusion, and high-frequency textures, resulting in inaccu- rate temporal information. To address this issue, this paper pro- poses a method combining deformable temporal alignment and difference-aware spatial selective fusion. A Context-aware Tem- poral Alignment Module is used to generate complementary tem- poral context, while a Difference-aware Spatial Selective Fusion module adaptively selects reliable temporal information and sup- presses misalignment. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves certain rate-distortion performance improve- ment over DCVC-DC.

title: A Large Open Multi-Energy Corpus of Soil Compaction Tests, with Machine-Learning Baselines
summary: Every engineered fill is specified by a maximum dry density and an optimum moisture content. Each determination needs a full Proctor test. Published correlations rest on one to four hundred specimens, usually from one laboratory at one compactive energy, and are seldom released. This paper releases a corpus without those limits. It holds 2,854 laboratory compaction tests from six public sources, across 162 provenance groups and four Proctor energy levels, with fines from 1.5 to 100%. Every record is audited to the Proctor method its source names, and no energy is inferred. Screening on the zero-air-voids condition removed 11.8% of harmonised records, and 5.7% of those with a measured specific gravity. A material share of published compaction data is physically impossible. The optimum degree of saturation over the corpus is 0.815 at a coefficient of variation of 11%. That is a baseline, not a constant. Both parameters are then estimated from one classification suite and the compaction standard. A tabular foundation model reaches R2 0.824 for density and 0.784 for water content under random folds. It reaches 0.727 and 0.696 with folds drawn around provenance, and 0.520 and 0.614 with a whole source held out. Compactive energy is negligible marginally yet decisive conditionally. Density on the 66 modified-Proctor records is predicted at R2 0.740 with it and -0.651 without. Symbolic regression yields closed forms coupled through a phase relation. No predicted pair can then exceed the zero-air-voids line. The predictions are for screening, not acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper releases a large dataset of 2,854 compaction tests to develop predictive models for maximum dry density and optimum moisture content. It finds that about 8% of published data is physically impossible, establishes baseline values (optimum saturation = 0.815), and develops models that can predict compaction parameters from classification data, though performance degrades significantly when predicting for unknown sources.
AI.motivation: Current compaction correlations are limited by small sample sizes (1-400 specimens), single-laboratory data, and limited release. There was no comprehensive, publicly available dataset to develop robust prediction models for engineered fill specifications.
AI.method: The study compiled 2,854 laboratory compaction tests from six public sources across 162 provenance groups and four Proctor energy levels (fines content 1.5-100%). Each record was audited to its named Proctor method with no energy inference. Data was screened using zero-air-voids condition. Predictive models were developed using tabular foundation models and symbolic regression, tested under various cross-validation schemes (random folds, provenance-based folds, hold-out source).
AI.result: 1) 11.8% of harmonized records and 5.7% with measured specific gravity were physically impossible; 2) Optimum degree of saturation = 0.815 (CV=11%); 3) Tabular model R²: 0.824 (density), 0.784 (water content) with random folds; 4) R² drops to 0.520/0.614 when holding out entire source; 5) Compactive energy negligible marginally but decisive conditionally; 6) Modified-Proctor prediction: R² 0.740 with energy, -0.651 without; 7) Symbolic regression yields phase-coupled closed forms that respect zero-air-voids constraints.
AI.conclusion: A significant portion of published compaction data is physically impossible. While predictive models can achieve good accuracy within known populations (R² > 0.78), they perform poorly for unknown sources (R² ~ 0.52-0.61). Compactive energy is conditionally decisive. The models are suitable for screening purposes only, not for acceptance of engineered fill. The baseline saturation value (0.815) is a statistical parameter, not a constant.

title: Rethinking World Models for Safety-Critical Embodied Systems
summary: World models have progressed from compact latent dynamics to generative, controllable, and interactive simulators of embodied environments. However, high predictive likelihood and visual fidelity do not necessarily ensure that a model preserves the evidence required for safe decision-making. This perspective identifies three structural mismatches in current world modeling: likelihood versus risk, prediction versus intervention, and finite-horizon prediction versus accumulated consequences. We propose the Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) as a decision-centric research direction for safety-critical embodied systems. RIWM organizes world modeling around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability, and integrates four interdependent capabilities: decision-relevant representation, counterfactual reasoning, safety-critical episodic memory, and runtime safety assurance. It distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences while using epistemic uncertainty to qualify the evidence supporting action. We further discuss open challenges in identifying consequential futures, validating counterfactual reasoning, maintaining revisable safety memories, translating learned consequences into executable constraints, and determining when evidence is sufficient to act. This perspective argues that future world models should move beyond predicting likely futures toward identifying which futures matter, revising judgments through experience, and recognizing when to act, revise, sense, defer, or abstain.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper argues that current world models for embodied AI systems focus too much on predictive accuracy (likelihood and visual fidelity) while neglecting safety-critical decision-making requirements. The authors propose a Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) framework that organizes world modeling around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability, with four key capabilities: decision-relevant representation, counterfactual reasoning, safety-critical episodic memory, and runtime safety assurance.
AI.motivation: The authors identify a fundamental gap in current world modeling research: high predictive likelihood and visual fidelity do not necessarily ensure that a model preserves the evidence required for safe decision-making. This is particularly critical for safety-critical embodied systems where errors can have real-world consequences.
AI.method: The paper takes a conceptual/position paper approach, analyzing three structural mismatches in current world modeling (likelihood vs risk, prediction vs intervention, finite-horizon vs accumulated consequences) and proposing a new framework called RIWM that reorganizes world modeling around decision-centric principles.
AI.result: The paper proposes the RIWM framework with four interdependent capabilities: (1) decision-relevant representation, (2) counterfactual reasoning, (3) safety-critical episodic memory, and (4) runtime safety assurance. The framework distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences while using epistemic uncertainty to qualify evidence supporting actions.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that future world models should move beyond predicting likely futures toward identifying which futures matter, revising judgments through experience, and recognizing when to act, revise, sense, defer, or abstain. They also identify five open challenges: identifying consequential futures, validating counterfactual reasoning, maintaining revisable safety memories, translating learned consequences into executable constraints, and determining when evidence is sufficient to act.

title: Gradients Know What Outcomes Don't: Unlocking Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning with Gradient-Aligned Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) drives chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models, yet its binary outcome reward cannot distinguish among correct trajectories. Existing dense reward alternatives, from surface heuristics to process reward models, either ignore the expert solutions already present in training corpora or require expensive offline annotation. We propose Gradient-Aligned Reward (GAR), which operates in the policy's own gradient space: truncated backpropagation through the output projection layer extracts a compact gradient vector for each rollout, and cosine similarity with an expert-anchor gradient yields a dense, reasoning-aware reward with less than 9% wall-clock overhead. We prove that this cosine admits a multiplicative decomposition into prediction-error and activation-pattern factors, providing a concrete characterization of what the alignment signal measures. On Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, GAR consistently improves over GRPO and other baselines on competition-level math benchmarks and transfers to GPQA Diamond and MMLU-Pro without domain-specific data. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LQgdwind/GAR.

AI.tldr: GAR (Gradient-Aligned Reward) is a novel dense reward mechanism for RLVR that operates in the policy's gradient space, using cosine similarity between rollout gradients and expert-anchor gradients to provide reasoning-aware rewards with minimal overhead.
AI.motivation: RLVR uses binary outcome rewards that cannot distinguish among correct trajectories, while existing dense reward alternatives either ignore expert solutions in training data or require expensive offline annotation.
AI.method: GAR uses truncated backpropagation through the output projection layer to extract compact gradient vectors for each rollout, then computes cosine similarity with an expert-anchor gradient to generate dense, reasoning-aware rewards.
AI.result: GAR provides less than 9% wall-clock overhead while achieving better performance on math benchmarks compared to GRPO and other baselines.
AI.conclusion: The cosine similarity can be multiplicatively decomposed into prediction-error and activation-pattern factors, providing a concrete characterization of the alignment signal. GAR offers an efficient way to leverage expert solutions without requiring expensive offline annotation.

title: DNative-Twin: Decision Graphs and Digital Twins for Reconstructable Agentic Decisions
summary: AI agents increasingly gather evidence, invoke tools, apply constraints, and produce decisions that people or software may commit to action. A final output alone cannot show which evidence, tool state, rule, authorization, or action path produced it. We present DNative-Twin, a graph-native digital twin that records a committed agentic decision as a typed trajectory and re-executes its decision mechanism under declared conditions. The graph links the state observed by the agent, the path it followed, and the authority behind the resulting action. The twin synchronizes this information, replays the mechanism in isolation, and compares it under controlled changes. We instantiate the framework in enterprise decision processes using three public process logs and controlled replay suites. The experiments identify a specific failure: graph structure localizes represented changes but cannot determine the consequence of an unobserved tool state. In a three-condition controlled experiment with 300 injected instances, unresolved-divergence recall increased from 0 to 0.667 when replay-contract state was added and to 1.0 when verification results were also available; the held-out set contained no critical-class instance. Across 500--5,000 BPI 2020 cases, median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds on the reported platform. These results separate the roles of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence in reviewing a decision mechanism.

AI.tldr: DNative-Twin is a graph-native digital twin framework that records AI agent decisions as typed trajectories and enables re-execution under controlled conditions to verify decision mechanisms. It links observed state, action paths, and authority to enable transparency in agentic decision-making.
AI.motivation: AI agents increasingly make decisions that humans or software act upon, but the final output alone cannot reveal which evidence, tools, rules, or authorization paths produced it. This lack of transparency creates accountability and verification challenges in enterprise decision processes.
AI.method: The framework instantiates a graph structure that records committed agentic decisions as typed trajectories. It synchronizes decision information, replays the mechanism in isolation, and compares outputs under controlled changes. The approach was evaluated using three public process logs and controlled replay suites, including a three-condition controlled experiment with 300 injected instances and 500-5,000 BPI 2020 cases.
AI.result: In the three-condition experiment, unresolved-divergence recall increased from 0 to 0.667 when replay-contract state was added, and to 1.0 when verification results were also available. The held-out set contained no critical-class instances. Across 500-5,000 BPI 2020 cases, median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate that graph structure can localize represented changes but cannot determine the consequence of an unobserved tool state. The study separates the roles of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence in reviewing decision mechanisms, showing that combining all three achieves perfect recall (1.0).

title: SafeRI: Recognition and Intervention for Token-Level Safety Intervention in Large Vision Language Models
comment: Preprint. 13 pages, 4 figures. Main paper with appendix
summary: Existing safety alignment methods for vision-language models usually modify the model behavior globally: once the safety parameters are trained or loaded, they participate in both unsafe and already-safe generations. This always-on intervention can unnecessarily perturb the model's original reasoning path and degrade general multimodal capabilities. We argue that safety alignment should be an on-demand intervention rather than a permanent modification to every decoding trajectory. To this end, we propose a streaming recognition and gated LoRA framework for intrinsic VLM safety. During autoregressive generation, a lightweight recognizer estimates whether the current pre-token generation state is safe or unsafe. Its output updates the LoRA gate for the following decoding step; otherwise, generation follows the frozen-backbone policy. The LoRA module is trained from unsafe prefixes, transition statements, and safe continuations, so that it learns to redirect unsafe generations back to safe responses after activation. Experiments across multiple safety and general-purpose benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in post-alignment settings.

AI.tldr: A new safety alignment framework for vision-language models (VLMs) that uses a streaming recognition and gated LoRA approach to provide on-demand safety intervention rather than permanently modifying model behavior. A lightweight recognizer estimates safety during autoregressive generation and activates a LoRA module only when needed to redirect unsafe generations to safe responses.
AI.motivation: Existing safety alignment methods globally modify model behavior (always-on intervention), which unnecessarily perturbs the model's original reasoning path and degrades general multimodal capabilities. The authors argue safety alignment should be an on-demand intervention rather than a permanent modification to every decoding trajectory.
AI.method: The framework consists of two components: (1) A lightweight streaming recognizer that estimates whether the current pre-token generation state is safe or unsafe during autoregression; (2) A gated LoRA module whose output is updated based on the recognizer's output for the following decoding step. If unsafe, the LoRA module is activated to redirect to safe responses; if safe, generation follows the frozen-backbone policy. The LoRA module is trained from unsafe prefixes, transition statements, and safe continuations.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple safety and general-purpose benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in post-alignment settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed streaming recognition and gated LoRA framework can effectively provide on-demand safety intervention for VLMs, preserving the model's original reasoning capabilities while redirecting unsafe generations when needed.

title: From Zero to Hero: An Open LLM Ecosystem for Armenian
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures, 13 tables. Data and model: https://huggingface.co/collections/COPA-AI/armenian-llm-ecosystem. Code: https://github.com/COPATeam/armenian_llm_ecosystem
summary: Pretraining data for Armenian, a morphologically rich and low-resource language, is scarce, and no open Armenian LLM has been released with the data and recipe needed to reproduce it. To address this gap, we curate and release two datasets. ArmWeb is an extensively validated corpus of 4.37M Armenian news documents. ArmSTEM is a parallel English-Armenian collection of 373K math and science problems with step-by-step solutions, translated into Armenian and verified through both answer-preserving LLM judgment and human evaluation. Continued pretraining of Gemma-4-E4B on these datasets yields arm-gemma-e4b, which outperforms every existing open Armenian model as well as its unadapted base, and is the first open Armenian LLM with complete training data and recipe. Our ablations show that news-only continued pretraining improves fluency while eroding knowledge, a pattern we also observe in existing Armenian models, and that a small share of verified translated STEM data reverses the loss. We further find that the largest public Armenian corpora overlap web-derived evaluation panels heavily, including a train/test self-overlap inside FineWeb-2. We openly release all data, models, and code.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the lack of open-source Armenian LLMs by creating two datasets (ArmWeb with 4.37M news documents and ArmSTEM with 373K parallel math/science problems) and continuing pretraining of Gemma-4-E4B to create arm-gemma-e4b, which outperforms all existing open Armenian models.
AI.motivation: Armenian is a morphologically rich, low-resource language with scarce pretraining data, and no open Armenian LLM with reproducible data and recipe existed before this work.
AI.method: The authors curated two datasets: ArmWeb (extensively validated 4.37M Armenian news documents) and ArmSTEM (parallel English-Armenian STEM problems with step-by-step solutions, translated and verified via LLM judgment and human evaluation). They then performed continued pretraining on Gemma-4-E4B using these datasets.
AI.result: arm-gemma-e4b outperforms all existing open Armenian models and its unadapted base model. Ablations show news-only pretraining improves fluency but erodes knowledge, while a small share of verified STEM data reverses this loss. The study also reveals significant overlap between public Armenian corpora and evaluation panels, including train/test self-overlap in FineWeb-2.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first open Armenian LLM with complete training data and recipe. The authors recommend using mixed data (news + STEM) for continued pretraining and openly release all data, models, and code.

title: Transfiver: Human-AI Co-Inference through a Shared Editable State
summary:
Long-term human-AI interaction is difficult because the information that guides inference is updated implicitly by the model and is not directly inspectable or controllable by the user. We introduce the TRANSparent Framework for Interactive, Verifiable, Editable Representation (Transfiver), an architecture for human-AI co-inference through a shared editable state. Its central idea is that interaction-specific information is maintained in a single persistent state $(S_t)$ that both the model and the human update.
  Transfiver distinguishes two modes of state evolution. In an implicit stream update, the model interprets ongoing interaction and decides whether new information revises an existing state item or creates a new one. In an explicit directed edit, a human inspects and modifies an addressed item. Both act on the same underlying state, so a human correction changes the state that subsequent computation reads, rather than adding another instruction or separate record.
  The architecture separates shared parameters $(θ)$, learned before ordinary use, from the persistent state $(S_t)$, which evolves during deployment without parameter retraining. Extending Transfiver to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states remains open.

AI.tldr: Transfiver is a novel architecture for human-AI co-inference that uses a shared editable persistent state (S_t) which both the model and human can update, enabling verifiable and controllable AI interaction.
AI.motivation: Long-term human-AI interaction is challenging because the information guiding inference is updated implicitly by the model and is not directly inspectable or controllable by users.
AI.method: Transfiver uses a shared persistent state (S_t) with two update modes: (1) implicit stream update where the model interprets interaction and decides whether to revise existing state or create new entries, and (2) explicit directed edit where humans inspect and modify addressed items. The architecture separates pre-trained shared parameters (θ) from the persistent state that evolves during deployment without retraining.
AI.result: The framework enables human corrections to directly modify the state that subsequent computation reads, rather than adding separate instructions or records. This allows verifiable and controllable human-AI co-inference.
AI.conclusion: Transfiver provides a promising architecture for interactive, verifiable, and editable AI representation. Future work involves extending to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states.

title: WIDE: Wildcard Inference with Dynamic Expansion for Cross-Modal Generative Retrieval
comment: Accepted to the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026). 10 pages, 5 figures
summary: Generative retrieval has demonstrated significant success by unifying representation learning and search into a single sequence-to-sequence generation task. However, extending this paradigm to cross-modal retrieval reveals a critical challenge arising from the inherent information asymmetry across different modalities, such as the gap between concise text queries and dense visual candidates. This structural mismatch causes the autoregressive decoder to suffer from forced hallucination when generating identifiers via standard trie-constrained beam search, where the model is severely penalized for failing to guess fine-grained details absent from the query, allowing irrelevant candidates to hijack top rankings. To address this issue, we propose Wildcard Inference with Dynamic Expansion (WIDE). WIDE employs Adaptive Entropy Thresholding (AET) to calibrate layer-specific uncertainty boundaries offline. During the decoding generation phase, Asymmetry-aware Wildcard Decoding (AWD) detects semantic blind spots and emits wildcards instead of forced deterministic identifiers, dynamically expanding the search space without incurring log-probability penalties. Finally, Blind-Spot Re-ranking (BSR) evaluates the expanded candidate pool using a hybrid scoring mechanism that combines discrete generation confidence with continuous semantic similarity. Extensive experiments on the M-BEIR benchmark demonstrate that WIDE outperforms state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods, effectively suppressing forced hallucination while maintaining compact index structures.

AI.tldr: WIDE addresses forced hallucination in cross-modal generative retrieval by using adaptive entropy thresholding to detect semantic blind spots, emitting wildcards to dynamically expand search space, and leveraging hybrid scoring for re-ranking. It outperforms SOTA methods on M-BEIR.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal retrieval faces a critical challenge from information asymmetry between concise text queries and dense visual candidates. This structural mismatch causes the autoregressive decoder to suffer from forced hallucination when generating identifiers via standard trie-constrained beam search, where the model is penalized for failing to guess fine-grained details absent from the query, allowing irrelevant candidates to hijack top rankings.
AI.method: The proposed WIDE framework consists of three components: (1) Adaptive Entropy Thresholding (AET) calibrates layer-specific uncertainty boundaries offline; (2) Asymmetry-aware Wildcard Decoding (AWD) detects semantic blind spots during decoding and emits wildcards instead of forced deterministic identifiers, dynamically expanding the search space without log-probability penalties; (3) Blind-Spot Re-ranking (BSR) evaluates the expanded candidate pool using a hybrid scoring mechanism combining discrete generation confidence with continuous semantic similarity.
AI.result: WIDE outperforms state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on the M-BEIR benchmark, effectively suppressing forced hallucination while maintaining compact index structures.
AI.conclusion: WIDE successfully addresses the forced hallucination problem in cross-modal generative retrieval by dynamically expanding the search space when semantic blind spots are detected. The method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the M-BEIR benchmark while maintaining compact index structures.

title: Time Without Timesteps: Simulating Coupled Dynamical Systems via Self-Consistency
summary: Numerical simulation of dynamical systems is usually organized as a causal march through time: each state is computed from the previous one. We explore a different formulation for coupled systems. For each subsystem type we train a neural surrogate mapping a full driving trajectory and initial condition directly to a full output trajectory; following classical waveform relaxation, coupled systems are assembled by enforcing self-consistency among these trajectories: simulation becomes a fixed-point problem over complete trajectories rather than a stepwise rollout. On coupled van der Pol oscillators and Hodgkin-Huxley neuron networks, sequential depth becomes the number of solver iterations: 4-10 Newton iterations where the reference integrator takes 1500 steps. The gradient likewise loses its time recursion: it becomes a linear system solved by GMRES at memory independent of solver depth. A single scalar measured from the learned operator, the spectral radius of its Jacobian, predicts in advance where the coupled solve will converge; past that boundary, unrolled backpropagation diverges and a Neumann adjoint fails, while the implicit gradient remains correct to 0.04%. We report where the approach succeeds and where surrogate error degrades it.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a neural surrogate-based approach for simulating coupled dynamical systems, where instead of stepwise time marching, complete trajectories are computed as fixed-point solutions. The method eliminates time recursion in both forward simulation and gradient computation, replacing sequential steps with parallel fixed-point iterations.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical simulation of dynamical systems uses causal time marching (each state computed from previous state). This approach has fundamental limitations: sequential depth grows with simulation time, and backpropagation through time (BPTT) suffers from vanishing gradients and high memory costs. The authors seek a parallel, memory-efficient alternative that reformulates simulation as a fixed-point problem over complete trajectories.
AI.method:
1. Train neural surrogates mapping (full driving trajectory + initial condition) → full output trajectory
2. Apply classical waveform relaxation: coupled systems assembled by enforcing self-consistency among trajectories
3. Simulation becomes a fixed-point problem over complete trajectories rather than stepwise rollout
4. Use Newton iterations (4-10) for the coupled solve instead of 1500 reference integrator steps
5. Gradient computation: implicit gradient via linear system solved by GMRES (memory independent of solver depth)
6. Use spectral radius of Jacobian of learned operator as predictor for convergence
AI.result:
1. Sequential depth reduced to 4-10 Newton iterations vs 1500 steps in reference integrator
2. Gradient loses time recursion - solved by GMRES, memory independent of solver depth
3. Spectral radius of Jacobian predicts convergence in advance
4. Past convergence boundary: unrolled backpropagation diverges, Neumann adjoint fails, but implicit gradient remains accurate (0.04% error)
5. Successfully demonstrated on coupled van der Pol oscillators and Hodgkin-Huxley neuron networks
AI.conclusion: The approach succeeds when the neural surrogate is accurate and the spectral radius indicates convergence will occur. It fails/degrades when surrogate error is high or when operating past the convergence boundary. The key insight is that implicit gradient through the fixed-point solve remains stable even when unrolled backpropagation diverges, providing a robust alternative to BPTT for long-horizon coupled dynamical system simulation.

title: Govern the Model, Not Only the Data: Storage, Circulation, and Learning in Creative AI
summary: Federated learning is increasingly presented as a privacy-preserving advance: personal data remain on the device, and only model updates are shared. It borrows the vocabulary of the federated social web, yet inverts its logic, distributing computation while the resulting model stays with whoever convened the training. We argue that federation is not in itself a remedy for extractive AI, because outcomes depend on who governs the data and the model and who has agency over the practices that shape them. We describe three layers at which a creative community can hold its work: storage, circulation, and learning. Examining artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures, we show that creator governance is established at storage and circulation but stops at learning: contributors can consent to training, yet have little say over the resulting model or its federation. We map the research space this opens, pairing technical open problems with the human questions from which they unfold. We propose four design principles for a creative data commons that governs models and their federation, not only datasets: govern the model, not only the corpus; make the terms legible at the moment of contribution; design for refusal as a first-class state; and decide stewardship in the open and account for it.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques federated learning as a privacy-preserving solution, arguing it inverts the federated social web's logic by distributing computation while keeping the resulting model with the trainer. The authors examine three governance layers (storage, circulation, learning) in creative communities and find that creator governance stops at the learning layer. They propose four design principles for a creative data commons that governs models and their federation.
AI.motivation: The paper challenges the assumption that federated learning inherently protects creator interests. The authors argue that despite federated learning's privacy-preserving narrative, it actually inverts the federated social web logic—distributing computation while centralizing the model with the trainer. This raises concerns about extractive AI practices and creator agency.
AI.method: The authors conduct a conceptual analysis examining artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures across three layers: storage, circulation, and learning. They map technical open problems alongside human governance questions.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that creator governance is established at storage and circulation layers but stops at the learning layer. Contributors can consent to training but have little say over the resulting model or its federation. This governance gap creates an extractive dynamic despite federated learning's distributed computation.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose four design principles for a "creative data commons" that governs models and their federation: (1) govern the model, not only the corpus; (2) make terms legible at the moment of contribution; (3) design for refusal as a first-class state; and (4) decide stewardship in the open and account for it. This opens a new research space pairing technical challenges with human governance questions.

title: SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. https://openreview.net/forum?id=wPfw7GkMns
summary: Proteins are fundamental to biological processes, with their function determined by the complex interplay between the amino acid sequence and the three-dimensional structure. Developing generative models capable of understanding this intrinsically multi-modal relationship is crucial for fields like drug discovery and protein engineering. Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e., generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space. SimpleDesign leverages a single-stage end-to-end objective that combines discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. In order to effectively model the difference in sequence and structure modalities, we develop a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that allows modality-specific processing while keeping global self-attention over both modalities. We train SimpleDesign on over 2M sequence-structure pairs achieving strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.

AI.tldr: SimpleDesign is a multi-modal protein design model that performs co-design of protein sequences and structures in a single-stage end-to-end training process, eliminating the need for multi-stage training with autoencoders. It uses a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture and achieves strong performance on benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Proteins function depends on the relationship between amino acid sequence and 3D structure. Existing models require multi-stage training (autoencoder for latent representations, then generative modeling in latent space). This work hypothesizes that multi-stage training is unnecessary for performant co-design models.
AI.method: SimpleDesign uses a single-stage end-to-end objective combining discrete cross-entropy for sequences and regression objective for structures. It employs a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture enabling modality-specific processing while maintaining global self-attention over both modalities. Trained on over 2 million sequence-structure pairs.
AI.result: Achieves strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-stage training with autoencoders is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models; a single-stage end-to-end approach in data space can achieve excellent results.

title: SVG-Score: Human-Aligned Evaluation of Text-to-SVG Generation
summary: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation is attracting increasing attention as generative models improve in expressiveness and controllability. Progress, however, is held back by the lack of domain-specific evaluation protocols: current practice relies on metrics designed for natural images, most notably CLIPScore, which was never trained on vector graphics and aligns only partially with human judgment. We introduce \textbf{\ours}, a human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation. Through controlled caption and image perturbations, we first show that CLIP-based scores barely react to the errors SVG generators actually make, such as wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations, and that off-the-shelf Vision-Language Model (VLM) judges, while more sensitive, respond unevenly across error types and SVG styles. We then introduce a human-annotated dataset for \textit{Semantic Alignment}, measuring how faithfully a generated SVG reflects its caption. Building on it, we develop two complementary evaluators: CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics and then aligned to human preferences, for fast large-scale evaluation, and a VLM judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning, for more expressive and interpretable assessment. Using both, we benchmark major open-source, commercial, and optimization-based SVG generators on an independent caption set.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the lack of proper evaluation metrics for text-to-SVG generation by creating a human-aligned evaluation framework called (the name appears to be cut off). The authors demonstrate that existing CLIP-based metrics fail to detect SVG-specific errors and that off-the-shelf VLM judges respond unevenly. They introduce a human-annotated dataset and two complementary evaluators: adapted CLIP scorers and a trained VLM judge.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to solve the evaluation gap in text-to-SVG generation. Current practice uses metrics designed for natural images (like CLIPScore), which were never trained on vector graphics and don't align with human judgment for SVG-specific errors such as wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations.
AI.method: The authors first conducted controlled experiments with caption and image perturbations to analyze weaknesses of existing metrics. They then created a human-annotated dataset for Semantic Alignment. Using this dataset, they developed two evaluators: (1) CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics and aligned to human preferences for fast evaluation, and (2) a VLM judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning for more expressive assessment.
AI.result: The study found that CLIP-based scores barely react to SVG-specific errors like wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations. Off-the-shelf VLM judges are more sensitive but respond unevenly across error types and SVG styles. The benchmark evaluated major open-source, commercial, and optimization-based SVG generators.
AI.conclusion: The paper introduces a comprehensive human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation that addresses the limitations of existing metrics. The combination of adapted CLIP scorers and a trained VLM judge provides both fast large-scale evaluation and expressive, interpretable assessment capabilities.

title: FlashRender: Few-Step Generative Rendering via Camera-Controlled Video MeanFlow
summary: We present FlashRender, a few-step generative rendering framework that retakes a source video along a target camera trajectory in seconds. We identify sampling-step-dependent camera control as a prominent manifestation of discretization error in existing multi-step generative rendering models and show that resolving this inconsistency substantially lowers denoising trajectory curvature, facilitating subsequent step distillation. To this end, we introduce Representation Transformation and Alignment (RETA), which aligns hidden source-video representations with target-video features from a frozen visual geometry model. This directly encodes the geometric transformation within the source-video stream, enabling sampling-step-consistent camera control. We then fine-tune the model with the MeanFlow objective on the lower-curvature denoising trajectory induced by RETA, allowing the model to more effectively address discretization error. Finally, we apply on-policy flow map distillation to correct self-rollout errors under fixed few-step sampling. Extensive experiments show that RETA, MeanFlow, and on-policy flow map distillation play complementary roles in few-step generative rendering. Together, they enable our approach to match multi-step baselines in video quality and geometric consistency at 25x lower sampling cost while achieving superior camera controllability, even under out-of-distribution target camera trajectories.

AI.tldr: FlashRender is a few-step generative rendering framework that retakes a source video along a target camera trajectory in seconds. It addresses discretization error in multi-step generative rendering models through three complementary techniques: RETA for sampling-step-consistent camera control, MeanFlow for lower-curvature denoising trajectory, and on-policy flow map distillation for self-rollout error correction.
AI.motivation: The paper identifies sampling-step-dependent camera control as a prominent manifestation of discretization error in existing multi-step generative rendering models. This inconsistency leads to higher denoising trajectory curvature, which hinders subsequent step distillation and reduces rendering quality and geometric consistency.
AI.method: The approach introduces three key techniques: (1) Representation Transformation and Alignment (RETA) - aligns hidden source-video representations with target-video features from a frozen visual geometry model to encode geometric transformation within the source-video stream; (2) MeanFlow objective - fine-tunes the model on the lower-curvature denoising trajectory induced by RETA to address discretization error; (3) On-policy flow map distillation - corrects self-rollout errors under fixed few-step sampling.
AI.result: The approach achieves comparable video quality and geometric consistency to multi-step baselines at 25x lower sampling cost. It also demonstrates superior camera controllability, even under out-of-distribution target camera trajectories.
AI.conclusion: RETA, MeanFlow, and on-policy flow map distillation play complementary roles in few-step generative rendering. Together, they enable efficient high-quality video rendering with strong camera control capabilities, significantly reducing computational cost while maintaining quality.

title: RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory
summary: Repeating a small block of middle layers increases a language model's effective inference depth without adding parameters or generating extra tokens, and recent work shows that this latent recurrence improves reasoning. However, two design choices limit these gains. Each iteration sees only the previous output and cannot directly access earlier computations. Moreover, a fixed loop count wastes depth on easy inputs while leaving hard ones with too little computation. We introduce RecurTrace, which addresses both limitations using the loop's own trajectory. Specifically, Loop Memory Attention lets each looped layer attend to its own states from previous iterations along the loop-time axis, so the model can revisit earlier computations instead of relying on the latest state alone. A halting head then reads the loop state and predicts whether to continue, with supervision from an oracle that identifies when additional depth still reduces loss. In a controlled MathQA comparison on the same looped backbone, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. By comparison, ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop, and CALM reaches only 54.1% with 5.6 loops, while the stronger LoopUS-Conf and TaH-Mismatch baselines reach 55.3% at 3.2 loops and 55.7% at 2.1 loops. Finally, RecurTrace improves generation accuracy over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, with the gain growing with model size from 0.6 to 3.4 points.

AI.tldr: RecurTrace is a method that improves language model reasoning by enabling recurrent layers to attend to their own states from previous iterations (Loop Memory Attention) and adaptively deciding when to halt computation (halting head). This addresses two key limitations in prior approaches: inability to access earlier computations and fixed loop counts that waste computation on easy inputs.
AI.motivation: The research addresses two limitations in existing latent recurrence approaches for language models: 1) Each iteration only sees the previous output without direct access to earlier computations, and 2) Fixed loop counts waste depth on easy inputs while providing insufficient computation for hard inputs. The goal is to improve reasoning performance while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.method: RecurTrace introduces two key components: 1) Loop Memory Attention - allows each looped layer to attend to its own states from previous iterations along the loop-time axis, enabling the model to revisit earlier computations rather than relying solely on the latest state; 2) A halting head that reads the loop state and predicts whether to continue, trained with supervision from an oracle that identifies when additional depth still reduces loss.
AI.result: On MathQA, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. Compared to baselines: ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop; CALM reaches 54.1% with 5.6 loops; LoopUS-Conf achieves 55.3% at 3.2 loops; TaH-Mismatch achieves 55.7% at 2.1 loops. RecurTrace also improves generation accuracy over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B scales, with gains growing from 0.6 to 3.4 points as model size increases.
AI.conclusion: RecurTrace successfully addresses the limitations of prior latent recurrence approaches by enabling models to access earlier computations and adaptively determining loop counts. The method outperforms existing approaches including ACT, PonderNet, CALM, LoopUS-Conf, and TaH-Mismatch on MathQA, with gains that scale with model size, demonstrating the effectiveness of combining memory attention with adaptive halting for improved reasoning in language models.

title: CauseCollab: Causal Unified and Modality-Agnostic Network for Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception
summary: Collaborative perception enhances environment understanding through multi-agent information sharing, but its performance in real-world scenarios is constrained by heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures. Recent protocol-based two-stage methods alleviate this problem by mapping heterogeneous features into a shared protocol space; however, independently trained modality-specific converters often generate modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, leading to semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, which is particularly pronounced in scenarios with large modality discrepancies. To address this issue, we propose CauseCollab, a causal unified and modality-agnostic network. CauseCollab formulates representation learning in the protocol space from a causal perspective, explicitly disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders via causal metric learning. Meanwhile, CauseCollab adopts context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. In addition, integrating new modalities only requires training adapters with minimal parameters. Extensive experiments on the OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets demonstrate that CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.

AI.tldr: CauseCollab addresses heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architecture disparities in collaborative perception by proposing a causal unified and modality-agnostic network that disentangles semantic factors from modality-specific confounders via causal metric learning, achieving state-of-the-art performance on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets.
AI.motivation: Current protocol-based two-stage methods for collaborative perception map heterogeneous features into a shared protocol space, but independently trained modality-specific converters generate pseudo-protocol distributions causing semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, especially in scenarios with large modality discrepancies.
AI.method: CauseCollab uses (1) causal metric learning to explicitly disentangle semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders in the protocol space, (2) a context-guided Unified Converter to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency for heterogeneous modalities, and (3) adapter-based architecture allowing new modalities to be integrated with minimal parameter training.
AI.result: CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.
AI.conclusion: The causal perspective approach effectively addresses semantic inconsistency in heterogeneous collaborative perception, and the modular adapter design enables flexible integration of new modalities with minimal computational overhead.

title: Occlusion-Robust Multimodal Emotion Recognition in VR via Fusion of Facial Images and EMG
comment: Joint Proceedings of the ACM Intelligent User Interfaces (IUI) Workshops 2026
summary: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) fundamentally limit emotion recognition in virtual reality (VR): by occluding the upper face, they render conventional image-based facial expression analysis incomplete, particularly for applications requiring real-time affective assessment. We address this challenge by fusing lower-face video with facial electromyography (EMG) from the occluded upper face to classify seven emotional categories (six basic emotions plus neutral). We introduce a synchronized multimodal dataset from 20 participants, pairing lower-face video with seven-channel upper-face EMG elicited by validated emotion stimuli. Under subject-independent test, our proposed late-fusion architecture merging convolutional visual embeddings with RBF-kernel EMG representations achieves 51% macro-F1, outperforming both image-only (41%) and EMG-only (43%) baselines. These results demonstrate that upper-face EMG provides robust complementary information under HMD-induced visual occlusion and establish a foundation for multimodal emotion recognition in naturalistic VR environments. This approach facilitates affect-adaptive applications, including communication training and therapeutic interventions. The dataset will be shared upon request under an ethical-use agreement.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses emotion recognition in VR environments where head-mounted displays (HMDs) occlude the upper face, making conventional facial expression analysis incomplete. The authors propose fusing lower-face video with facial electromyography (EMG) from the occluded upper face to classify seven emotional categories. Their late-fusion architecture achieves 51% macro-F1, outperforming both image-only (41%) and EMG-only (43%) baselines.
AI.motivation: Head-mounted displays in VR fundamentally limit emotion recognition by occluding the upper face, rendering conventional image-based facial expression analysis incomplete. This is particularly problematic for applications requiring real-time affective assessment, such as communication training and therapeutic interventions.
AI.method: The authors introduced a synchronized multimodal dataset from 20 participants, pairing lower-face video with seven-channel upper-face EMG elicited by validated emotion stimuli. They proposed a late-fusion architecture that merges convolutional visual embeddings (from lower-face video) with RBF-kernel EMG representations (from upper face). Subject-independent testing was used for evaluation.
AI.result: The proposed late-fusion architecture achieved 51% macro-F1, outperforming both image-only (41%) and EMG-only (43%) baselines. This demonstrates that upper-face EMG provides robust complementary information under HMD-induced visual occlusion.
AI.conclusion: Upper-face EMG provides robust complementary information under HMD-induced visual occlusion. This approach establishes a foundation for multimodal emotion recognition in naturalistic VR environments and facilitates affect-adaptive applications including communication training and therapeutic interventions. The dataset will be shared upon request under an ethical-use agreement.

title: TIGPO: Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
summary: Graph-based policy optimization improves credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents by organizing rollout trajectories into state-transition graphs. However, existing methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, discarding transitions discovered by earlier policies and limiting advantage estimation to small, batch-local rollout groups. We propose \emph{Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization} (TIGPO), which extends graph-based credit assignment across policy updates. TIGPO maintains a persistent transition graph for each task, allowing valid transitions discovered by different policy versions to jointly determine credit for current rollouts. To actively reconnect current exploration with historical experience, TIGPO allocates a fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots for ordinary task sampling and Revisit slots for delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks. For each revisit, TIGPO pairs the current rollout group with its corresponding earlier Exploration group to construct a cross-temporal reference. The enlarged reference is designed to stabilize relative advantage estimation under small rollout groups, while comparison on the same task directly captures policy improvement across training stages. Historical transitions and scores serve only as structural and detached statistical references and are never replayed in the policy loss. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.

AI.tldr: TIGPO extends graph-based credit assignment for LLM agents across policy updates by maintaining a persistent transition graph for each task, allocating rollout budget between Exploration and Revisit slots to reconnect current exploration with historical experience.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based policy optimization methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, discarding transitions discovered by earlier policies and limiting advantage estimation to small, batch-local rollout groups. This limits the effectiveness of credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents.
AI.method: TIGPO maintains a persistent transition graph for each task across policy updates, allowing transitions discovered by different policy versions to jointly determine credit. It allocates a fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots (ordinary task sampling) and Revisit slots (delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks). For each revisit, TIGPO pairs current rollout groups with earlier Exploration groups to construct cross-temporal references, stabilizing advantage estimation while directly capturing policy improvement across training stages.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.
AI.conclusion: TIGPO successfully extends graph-based credit assignment across policy updates by using persistent transition graphs and cross-temporal references, effectively addressing the limitations of batch-local advantage estimation in existing methods.

title: Semantic Bayesian World Models
summary: Knowledge graphs describe reality in crisp assertions, while the systems now consuming them, foundation models and autonomous agents, reason natively in probabilities. We argue that this mismatch is why the integration of language models and knowledge graphs remains a data-feeding pipeline rather than a unified reasoning architecture. We envision Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs): a Web that describes the world not as a database of facts but as a shared, evolving fabric of beliefs over knowledge graphs, where ontological axioms constrain priors, observations update beliefs by Bayesian conditioning, and actions intervene upon the world. We work through what an agent gains from such a model: a home-security agent deciding whether the figure at the gate is a courier or a burglar, an actuarial estimate aggregated by entailment rather than by string frequency, a planning task that language models reliably fail, and the estimation of quantities that no document has ever stated. We then set out what the community must build to make them possible: belief annotation over RDF~1.2, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols by which agents that have never met can exchange, and disagree over, calibrated beliefs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs) as a solution to the fundamental mismatch between knowledge graphs (crisp facts) and modern AI systems (probabilistic reasoning). The vision is to transform the Web from a database of facts into a fabric of beliefs over knowledge graphs, where ontological axioms constrain priors, observations update beliefs via Bayesian conditioning, and actions can intervene on the world.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that knowledge graphs represent reality as crisp, deterministic assertions, while foundation models and autonomous agents reason natively in probabilities. This mismatch prevents true integration—currently, language models and KGs only interact through data-feeding pipelines rather than unified reasoning architectures.
AI.method: The paper is a conceptual/position paper that proposes a new framework rather than presenting experimental results. It envisions SBWMs where: (1) ontological axioms constrain prior beliefs, (2) observations update beliefs through Bayesian conditioning, and (3) actions can intervene upon the world. The authors illustrate the concept through four scenarios: home security (courier vs. burglar), actuarial estimation via entailment, planning tasks, and estimating unstated quantities.
AI.result: This is a visionary paper without empirical results. The "results" are conceptual demonstrations showing what agents could achieve with SBWMs: calibrated probabilistic reasoning over structured knowledge, aggregation via logical entailment rather than string frequency, and the ability to estimate quantities never explicitly stated in any document.
AI.conclusion: The paper outlines a research agenda for the community, identifying four technical requirements: (1) belief annotation over RDF, (2) probabilistic entailment regimes, (3) semantic calibration layers, and (4) protocols for agents to exchange and disagree over calibrated beliefs. This represents a long-term vision for probabilistic semantic Web infrastructure.

title: Drive-HWM: Hierarchical World Models for Dynamic-Latent Guided Autonomous Driving
summary: World models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by predicting how traffic scenes may evolve and using such predictions to support action generation. However, existing approaches either separate future prediction from action generation or jointly predict them at the same temporal scale, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve long-horizon anticipation and responsive, observation-grounded decision making. We present Drive-HWM, a hierarchical slow--fast world modeling framework that organizes future representation prediction and action generation at complementary temporal scales. The slow world model predicts multi-step future representations to capture extended scene evolution. To explicitly model the abundant motion dynamics in driving environments, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Latents learned through optical-flow prediction. Guided by these future representations, the fast model uses a lightweight multimodal backbone and an autoregressive expert to jointly predict the next frame and the immediate action from the latest observation. Next-frame prediction encourages the fast model to capture imminent scene evolution, while one-step action generation allows decisions to be continuously updated as new observations arrive. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 demonstrate the strong driving performance of Drive-HWM. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the hierarchical slow--fast design, dynamics-aware future representations, and joint next-frame and action prediction.

AI.tldr: Drive-HWM is a hierarchical slow-fast world modeling framework for autonomous driving that organizes future representation prediction and action generation at complementary temporal scales, using Dynamic-Aware Latents learned through optical-flow prediction to model motion dynamics.
AI.motivation: Existing world model approaches for autonomous driving either separate future prediction from action generation or jointly predict them at the same temporal scale, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve long-horizon anticipation and responsive, observation-grounded decision making.
AI.method: Drive-HWM uses a hierarchical slow-fast architecture: (1) Slow world model predicts multi-step future representations to capture extended scene evolution; (2) Dynamic-Aware Latents learned through optical-flow prediction explicitly model motion dynamics; (3) Fast model uses a lightweight multimodal backbone and autoregressive expert to jointly predict next frame and immediate action from latest observation, guided by future representations from the slow model.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 demonstrate strong driving performance. Comprehensive ablation studies validate the effectiveness of: hierarchical slow-fast design, dynamics-aware future representations, and joint next-frame and action prediction.
AI.conclusion: Drive-HWM successfully achieves both long-horizon anticipation and responsive decision making through its hierarchical slow-fast world modeling approach, with the Dynamic-Aware Latents effectively capturing motion dynamics in driving environments.

title: Inferred Generative-Process Diversity Predicts Correlated Failure Across Language Models
summary: Diversity is a widely observed factor in the resilient function of collective systems, yet the type of diversity that matters depends on the properties and failure modes of the system. This distinction is important for systems composed of multiple language models. Different models may be treated as independent components even when their behaviour and failures remain strongly correlated. Assessments of language-model populations using semantic similarity demonstrate limited semantic diversity, but this captures only differences in the meaning of observed outputs. We argue that a more fundamental notion of model diversity is generative-process diversity, the differences between processes capable of generating the observed outputs. Drawing from Algorithmic Information Theory, we use Normalised Compression Distance between raw model outputs, residualised against a permutation control, as a measure of inferred generative-process diversity. Across 38 language models, this measure identifies population structure missed by semantic similarity and predicts cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated failure among model pairs across ten disjoint benchmark families, beyond semantic similarity and model-pair capability. The cross-benchmark partial rank association is $-0.216$ with a 95% interval of $[-0.309,-0.122]$, and the estimate is negative on all ten benchmarks. These results indicate that increased generative-process diversity is associated with reduced correlated failure in model pairs that is not attributable to semantic similarity or capability. Inferred generative-process diversity offers a novel and practical approach for investigating diversity of multi-model systems in safety-relevant contexts.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "generative-process diversity" as a fundamental measure of diversity among language models, distinct from semantic similarity. Using Normalised Compression Distance on raw model outputs, the authors find that this measure captures population structure missed by semantic approaches and predicts reduced correlated failure across 38 models tested on ten benchmark families (partial rank association = -0.216, 95% CI [-0.309, -0.122]).
AI.motivation: Current assessments of language model populations rely on semantic similarity, which only captures differences in output meaning. However, this fails to capture "generative-process diversity" - fundamental differences in how models generate outputs. This distinction matters for system resilience, as models may appear independent but share correlated failure modes.
AI.method: The authors use Normalised Compression Distance (NCD) between raw model outputs, residualised against a permutation control, as a measure of inferred generative-process diversity. They tested 38 language models across ten disjoint benchmark families and assessed how this measure predicts cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated failure among model pairs.
AI.result: The measure identifies population structure missed by semantic similarity and predicts cross-task variation in correlated failure beyond semantic similarity and model-pair capability. The cross-benchmark partial rank association is -0.216 with 95% CI [-0.309, -0.122], and the estimate is negative on all ten benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Increased generative-process diversity is associated with reduced correlated failure in model pairs, beyond what can be explained by semantic similarity or capability differences. This provides a novel and practical approach for investigating diversity of multi-model systems in safety-relevant contexts.

title: Adapting to Evolving Requirements: Agentic AI for Retail Supply Chain Operations
summary: Retail supply chain operations rely on coupled decision modules that must adapt as requirements evolve. LLMs offer a natural-language interface for this task, but existing methods primarily focus on individual optimization models. Extending them to heterogeneous decision pipelines is challenging because a requirement may admit multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects. We formulate requirement-driven adaptation as the joint selection of an intervention route and an admissible module-level change, and propose a graph-constrained agentic framework in which domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces and a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs. In collaboration with a large retail partner, we evaluate 100 warehouse requirements elicited from practitioner interviews, with GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek as base LLMs. Relative to direct LLM reformulation, our framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models, raising end-to-end success from 72--76% to 79--83%.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the challenge of adapting retail supply chain operations, which involve coupled decision modules, using LLMs. The authors propose a graph-constrained agentic framework that jointly selects intervention routes and module-level changes, validated through downstream KPIs. Evaluation on 100 warehouse requirements shows improvements in end-to-end success rates from 72-76% to 79-83% across three LLM models.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM methods for supply chain optimization focus on individual models but struggle with heterogeneous decision pipelines where requirements admit multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects. There's a need for a framework that can handle coupled decision modules and select appropriate interventions.
AI.method: The paper proposes a graph-constrained agentic framework with: (1) Domain agents that expose admissible reformulation interfaces, (2) A central processor that searches over bounded intervention paths, (3) Joint selection of intervention route and admissible module-level change. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs.
