The sharp worst-case complexity depends on threshold VC dimension d, with a separation factor of Θ(√p) between Gaussian and heavy-tailed designs under isotropy. A distribution-free fallback provides a weaker guarantee.

title: Towards Numerical TOHTN Planning with SMT-based HTN-SAT Encoding
summary: While HTN planning has received significant attention in recent years, support for numerical reasoning remains very limited. In this paper, we investigate numerical Totally-Ordered HTN (TOHTN) planning and show how standard SAT-based encodings can be naturally extended with SMT to handle numeric fluents. In addition, we introduce a benchmark suite for numerical TOHTN planning, providing a first common basis for evaluation in this setting. Experimental results show that this simple encoding already constitutes a competitive baseline. This work opens the way to more expressive approaches to HTN planning.

AI.tldr: This paper extends SAT-based HTN planning encodings with SMT to handle numerical fluents in Totally-Ordered HTN planning, and introduces a benchmark suite for evaluation. The approach serves as a competitive baseline for numerical HTN planning.
AI.motivation: HTN planning has received significant attention in recent years, but support for numerical reasoning remains very limited. This gap restricts the ability to handle real-world problems involving quantities, resources, and continuous change.
AI.method: The paper extends standard SAT-based encodings with SMT (Satisfiability Modulo Theories) to handle numeric fluents. This involves combining propositional logic (SAT) with theories of arithmetic and other decidable theories (SMT) to represent and reason about numerical constraints in TOHTN planning.
AI.result: Experimental results show that this simple encoding already constitutes a competitive baseline. The benchmark suite provides a first common basis for evaluation in numerical TOHTN planning.
AI.conclusion: This work opens the way to more expressive approaches to HTN planning by demonstrating that SMT-based extensions are viable for numerical reasoning in TOHTN planning.

title: Cross-Dataset Transfer and Reliability of Explainable Artificial Intelligence for RhythmFormer Remote Photoplethysmography
summary: Background. Remote photoplethysmography estimates the cardiovascular pulse from facial video, and its explanations have rested on inspecting heatmaps rather than on quantitative evidence about where a model reads it. We quantified the explanations and asked whether such explanations transfer between datasets and track model performance. Method. We trained eight condition-specific RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG, recorded under three illumination levels, speaking, rotation, and cycling, estimated one heart rate per 5.12-second clip, and set them beside a UBFC-rPPG reproduction. Raw attention, rollout, attention flow, and Beyond Intuition were assessed by skin coverage and the Salience-guided Faithfulness Coefficient (SaCo). Results. Beyond Intuition ranked highest on both datasets, at median coverage 0.789 and SaCo 0.837 on Static level 3 against 0.826 and 0.917 on UBFC-rPPG; lower ranks differed. Within one participant of one condition, neither measure was related to a clip's heart-rate error, waveform correlation, or signal-to-noise ratio on either dataset: 186 of the 252 coefficients fell below $|ρ|=0.10$ and 28 reached $p<0.05$ against the 13 expected by chance. Across the eight scenarios only Beyond Intuition's coverage followed the three performance measures, at $ρ=-0.43$, $+0.57$, and $+0.43$, while the attention-only methods' SaCo ran opposite to each. It failed at 40 lux alone, its median coverage falling to 0.180 and its median SaCo to $-0.178$, whereas motion degraded the estimates far more without such a drop. Conclusions. Skin coverage and SaCo carry information complementary to the performance measures rather than a proxy for them: attributing to the skin does not guarantee an accurate estimate. What an attribution reveals about a condition is where the model looks rather than how faithfully its map is ordered.

AI.tldr: This study quantifies the explanations of remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) models by evaluating where RhythmFormer models actually read pulse signals from facial video. Using attention visualization methods (Raw attention, Rollout, Attention flow, Beyond Intuition), the researchers assessed whether explanation quality transfers between datasets and correlates with model performance. Results show Beyond Intuition performs best but explanation quality doesn't reliably predict heart rate estimation accuracy, revealing a gap between where models look and how accurately they measure.
AI.motivation: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) estimates cardiovascular pulse from facial video, but explanations of these models have relied on heatmap inspection rather than quantitative evidence. The researchers wanted to determine whether explanation methods transfer between datasets and whether they can predict model performance—essentially asking "where does the model actually read the pulse?"
AI.method: Trained eight condition-specific RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG dataset under various conditions (three illumination levels, speaking, rotation, cycling). Evaluated explanation methods (Raw attention, Rollout, Attention flow, Beyond Intuition) using skin coverage and Salience-guided Faithfulness Coefficient (SaCo). Compared results across datasets (NCKU-rPPG and UBFC-rPPG) and correlated explanation metrics with heart-rate error, waveform correlation, and signal-to-noise ratio.
AI.result: Beyond Intuition achieved highest rankings on both datasets (median coverage 0.789, SaCo 0.837 on Static level 3; 0.826, 0.917 on UBFC-rPPG). Most correlation coefficients (186/252) were below |ρ|=0.10, indicating no relationship between explanation metrics and performance measures. Only Beyond Intuition's coverage showed moderate correlation with performance metrics (ρ = -0.43 to +0.57). The method failed at 40 lux (coverage 0.180, SaCo -0.178), while motion degraded estimates more severely without such explanation breakdown.
AI.conclusion: Skin coverage and SaCo provide information complementary to performance metrics rather than serving as proxies for accuracy. Attributing to skin does not guarantee accurate heart rate estimation. Attribution methods reveal where models look, not how faithfully their attention maps correspond to actual pulse signal quality. This highlights a fundamental limitation in using explanation methods to validate or predict rPPG model performance.

title: An Adversarial Zero-Shot Learning Approach for Anomaly Detection in Multivariate IoT Traffic Data
summary: Anomaly detection in Internet of Things (IoT) networks presents unique challenges due to the diversity of devices, lack of labeled data, and domain variability across environments. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection that leverages adversarial learning and contrastive loss within a sequence-based Variational Autoencoder (VAE) architecture. Our method enables zero-shot domain adaptation by jointly optimizing domain-invariant latent representations and semantically structured embedding spaces, without requiring labeled data or raw feature transfer. To address the heterogeneity of IoT deployments, we introduce encoder and decoder adaptor layers that align feature distributions across domains while preserving contextual semantics. Additionally, we propose a destination-based segmentation strategy to better model real-world communication structures in IoT traffic. Our framework is comprehensively evaluated on six distinct datasets spanning industrial, enterprise, general-purpose, smart home, and military automation domains across 44 transfer scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization in several cross-domain settings and competitive performance against a contrastive domain-adaptation baseline under realistic, heterogeneous, and privacy-constrained IoT conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel zero-shot domain adaptation framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection in IoT networks, using a sequence-based VAE with adversarial learning and contrastive loss. The method includes encoder/decoder adaptor layers for cross-domain feature alignment and a destination-based segmentation strategy, evaluated across 44 transfer scenarios in 6 diverse IoT domains.
AI.motivation: IoT anomaly detection faces challenges from device diversity, lack of labeled data, and domain variability across different environments. Existing methods struggle with zero-shot generalization to new domains without requiring labeled data or raw feature transfer.
AI.method: The framework combines: (1) Sequence-based VAE architecture with adversarial learning and contrastive loss, (2) Encoder and decoder adaptor layers for domain-invariant latent representations while preserving contextual semantics, (3) Destination-based segmentation strategy to model real-world IoT communication structures. Joint optimization enables domain adaptation without labeled data or raw feature transfer.
AI.result: Evaluated on 6 datasets spanning industrial, enterprise, general-purpose, smart home, and military automation domains across 44 transfer scenarios. The method demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization in several cross-domain settings and competitive performance against a contrastive domain-adaptation baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses zero-shot domain adaptation for IoT anomaly detection under realistic, heterogeneous, and privacy-constrained conditions, achieving strong generalization across diverse IoT environments without requiring labeled data or raw feature transfer.

title: More Criticism Does Not Make a Better Review: EquiReview-R
summary: AI reviewers can now produce many specific criticisms, but more criticism is not necessarily a better review. A review may miss a consequential weakness or retain an allegation that available evidence does not support. These failures require opposite corrections, yet generation-oriented systems and aggregate measures obscure the distinction. We therefore recast AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set, with omission and overcritique treated as separate risks. Building on this formulation, we introduce EquiReview-R, which resolves existing concerns against localized evidence, searches for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives, and returns stop, continue, or defer. To expose the failure mode that motivates this design, we construct an evidence-linked trajectory corpus. Its retrospective analysis shows why revision must precede further search: nearly all concerns in a high-recall review lack a definitive evidential disposition, while an earlier refinement mechanism cannot revise them. On a frozen cohort of previously unseen papers, EquiReview-R satisfies the prespecified non-inferiority criterion for major omission, reduces major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, and attains a one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9% while stopping on 52.4% of papers. Computation-matched controls, controlled pairs, and ablations show that the gain comes from revision rather than extra inference or shorter output. We release the corpus as ReviewTrace, an evidence-linked resource for studying review revision, disagreement, and provenance.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a critical limitation in AI-assisted peer review systems: the inability to distinguish between missing critical weaknesses (omission) and unsupported allegations (overcritique). The authors propose EquiReview-R, which treats these as separate risks and uses evidence-guided refinement before searching for additional concerns. The system achieves significant improvements: reducing major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, attaining a 9.9% omission upper bound, and stopping on 52.4% of papers while maintaining non-inferiority for omission detection.
AI.motivation: Current AI review systems produce many criticisms but fail to distinguish between two opposite failure modes: missing consequential weaknesses (omission) and retaining unsupported allegations (overcritique). Generation-oriented systems and aggregate measures obscure this distinction, making it impossible to apply appropriate corrections.
AI.method: The authors recast AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set. EquiReview-R operates in two phases: (1) Resolve existing concerns against localized evidence, and (2) Search for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives. The system returns stop, continue, or defer decisions. They construct an evidence-linked trajectory corpus (ReviewTrace) to study why revision must precede further search.
AI.result: On a frozen cohort of previously unseen papers, EquiReview-R: (1) satisfies the prespecified non-inferiority criterion for major omission, (2) reduces major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, (3) attains a one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9%, and (4) stops on 52.4% of papers. Controlled experiments show the gains come specifically from revision, not extra inference or shorter output.
AI.conclusion: The key insight is that revision must precede further search—nearly all concerns in a high-recall review lack definitive evidential disposition, and earlier refinement mechanisms cannot revise them. The released ReviewTrace corpus enables further research on review revision, disagreement, and provenance in AI peer review systems.

title: ARCOS: Zero-shot Boundary Localization for Corneal Layer Segmentation Across Optical Coherence Tomography Devices
summary: Accurate segmentation of corneal layers in optical coherence tomography (OCT) is essential for quantitative assessment of corneal morphology, including layer thickness and structural changes associated with disease or surgery. However, automatic segmentation remains challenging because corneal interfaces are thin, affected by speckle noise, and variable across acquisition devices. In this work, we propose ARCOS, a patch-based zero-shot boundary localization framework for corneal layer segmentation in clinical anterior-segment OCT images. Rather than performing conventional region classification, the method predicts boundary heatmaps for the main corneal interfaces from overlapping native-resolution patches. Patch-level predictions are stitched across the full B-scan and converted into boundary locations to obtain continuous, anatomically ordered layer segmentations. The network combines multi-scale feature fusion with a self-conditioned refinement module that uses intermediate boundary information to improve local heatmap predictions while preserving spatial detail. The method was evaluated on clinical OCT images acquired from multiple devices and compared with representative segmentation baselines using boundary localization and derived thickness metrics. The proposed method achieved an off-by-one boundary localization accuracy of 95.1% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.514 pixels on the matched-device test set. In zero-shot cross-device evaluation, it maintained an average off-by-one accuracy of 84.3% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.855 pixels across unseen acquisition devices, outperforming the baseline models. Thickness estimates derived from the predicted boundaries showed low error across corneal regions, supporting the method's use for quantitative corneal OCT analysis.

AI.tldr: ARCOS is a patch-based zero-shot framework for segmenting corneal layers in anterior-segment OCT images. It predicts boundary heatmaps from overlapping patches and uses multi-scale feature fusion with self-conditioned refinement to achieve high accuracy across different acquisition devices without requiring retraining.
AI.motivation: Automatic corneal layer segmentation in OCT is challenging due to thin interfaces, speckle noise, and device variability. Existing methods struggle with cross-device generalization, limiting clinical applicability.
AI.method: The method uses a patch-based approach that predicts boundary heatmaps for corneal interfaces from overlapping native-resolution patches. It combines multi-scale feature fusion with a self-conditioned refinement module that leverages intermediate boundary information to improve local predictions while preserving spatial detail. Patch-level predictions are stitched across the full B-scan and converted into continuous, anatomically ordered layer segmentations.
AI.result: On the matched-device test set: 95.1% off-by-one boundary localization accuracy, 0.514 pixels mean absolute error. In zero-shot cross-device evaluation: 84.3% off-by-one accuracy, 0.855 pixels mean absolute error, outperforming baseline models. Thickness estimates showed low error across corneal regions.
AI.conclusion: ARCOS achieves robust boundary localization performance across multiple acquisition devices in a zero-shot setting, demonstrating strong generalization capability. The method supports quantitative corneal OCT analysis with clinically acceptable accuracy for thickness measurements.

title: LongCounsel-8: A Benchmark Suite for Longitudinal Depression Tracking from Multi-Session Counseling Dialogues
summary: Tracking depression from multi-session counseling dialogues requires estimating both current symptom severity and how it changes across sessions. Yet progress on this task is constrained by the scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized session-level depression labels. Existing resources typically provide either multi-session conversations without depression labels or labeled interviews in a single session. Building such a benchmark poses three challenges: maintaining longitudinal consistency and diversity, grounding symptom progression in empirical patterns, and expressing controlled depression states naturally without exposing target labels. To address these challenges, we introduce LongCounsel-8, a benchmark suite of three independently generated datasets totaling 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories, grounded in real-world client profiles, depression trajectories, symptom compositions, and counseling patterns. We combine profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization to address these challenges. Across the benchmark, simulated self-reports closely recover the controlled states, supporting label fidelity. Experiments on existing depression tracking methods reveal three key findings: (1) lower single-session score error does not guarantee accurate identification of trend, i.e., improvement or worsening; (2) existing methods are consistently less reliable on worsening trajectories; and (3) additional session history may reduce the accuracy of trend prediction. Together, these findings establish LongCounsel-8 as a foundation for advancing depression assessment from static, single-session prediction toward reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change.

AI.tldr: LongCounsel-8 is a benchmark suite for tracking depression from multi-session counseling dialogues, comprising 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories across three datasets. It addresses the scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized session-level depression labels by using profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization.
AI.motivation: The scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized session-level depression labels constrains progress on tracking depression across sessions. Existing resources provide either multi-session conversations without labels or labeled interviews in a single session, making it difficult to estimate both current symptom severity and how it changes across sessions.
AI.method: The benchmark combines three independently generated datasets totaling 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories. It uses profile-grounded simulation (grounded in real-world client profiles), empirically informed state construction (based on depression trajectories and symptom compositions), and indirect behavioral realization (to express controlled depression states naturally without exposing target labels).
AI.result: Simulated self-reports closely recover the controlled states across the benchmark, supporting label fidelity. Experiments reveal: (1) lower single-session score error does not guarantee accurate trend identification; (2) existing methods are consistently less reliable on worsening trajectories; (3) additional session history may reduce trend prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LongCounsel-8 establishes a foundation for advancing depression assessment from static, single-session prediction toward reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change. The key findings highlight the need for methods that better handle trend prediction, especially for worsening trajectories, and suggest that simply adding more session history may not improve accuracy.

title: FiMI Banking: A Sovereign Model for Indian Retail Banking
summary: Banks need conversational systems that can answer product questions, assist customers with account-related requests, and operate safely within strict operational and regulatory constraints. General-purpose language models do not reliably meet these requirements. They fall short when a task requires grounded information, correct tool use, or cautious handling of bank-specific sensitive situations. We introduce FiMI Banking, a controlled Indian retail-banking setting. We build it from vetted banking documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer backgrounds, and banking tools. We evaluate two post-training approaches: preference optimization for response-level behavior, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks. Preference optimization improves safe behavior substantially: out-of-scope refusal rises from 52% to 80%. Reinforcement learning improves edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while using 29% fewer generated tokens. These results show that preference optimization and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents.

AI.tldr: FiMI Banking is a controlled Indian retail-banking setting for evaluating language models in banking tasks. Two post-training approaches are compared: preference optimization (improving safe behavior from 52% to 80% refusal rate) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (improving edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive tasks from 0.590 to 0.679, while using 29% fewer tokens).
AI.motivation: General-purpose language models fail to meet banking requirements for grounded information, correct tool use, and cautious handling of sensitive situations. Banks need conversational systems that can answer product questions, assist with account requests, and operate safely within strict operational and regulatory constraints.
AI.method: FiMI Banking was built from vetted banking documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer backgrounds, and banking tools. Two post-training approaches were evaluated: (1) preference optimization for response-level behavior, and (2) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks.
AI.result: Preference optimization substantially improved safe behavior, with out-of-scope refusal rising from 52% to 80%. Reinforcement learning improved edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while using 29% fewer generated tokens.
AI.conclusion: Preference optimization and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents, with each approach targeting different aspects of banking task performance.

title: Do Video Generators Track the World Across Segments? A Benchmark and Method for World-State Reasoning in Video Continuation
summary: Video generators build long videos by composing shorter parts, either by generating segments one after another or by autoregressively extending chunks. Each new part usually depends on memories of historical observations, such as recent frames, selected key frames, memory banks, or cached features. These memories preserve visible evidence from the past, but current generators do not reliably turn such evidence into a world-state interface: what holds in the video world after previous actions and how it should change under the next prompt. A past frame remains valid history, but it may not describe the state needed by the next segment; some states must instead be inferred from occluded or implicit changes rather than copied from a directly observed frame. This creates a simple but overlooked question for video continuation: given a previous video, its prompt, and a new prompt, can a model generate a continuation that reflects the state determined by both the historical video and the new prompt? To answer this question, we introduce Statebench, a benchmark that targets this gap by testing continuations over three state categories: past-visible states, occluded-process states, and complex-transition states. We further propose Stateagent, which explicitly maintains an entity-state representation, updates it under the new prompt, grounds the predicted post-action state as a future end frame, and renders the next video. Experiments show that our method improves controlled video continuation by raising the all-case state score (SCS-All) from 45.2 to 69.3, and also benefits story generation at the one-minute scale. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/StateAgent.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses a gap in video generation: current models fail to properly maintain world state when continuing videos. The authors introduce Statebench, a benchmark testing video continuations across three state categories (past-visible, occluded-process, and complex-transition states), and Stateagent, a method that explicitly maintains entity-state representation to generate accurate continuations.
AI.motivation: Current video generators rely on historical observations (frames, key frames, memory banks) but fail to properly track world state - what holds in the video world after previous actions and how it should change under the next prompt. The key insight is that some states must be inferred rather than directly observed (e.g., occluded changes), creating a need for models that can track state determined by both historical video and new prompts.
AI.method: Stateagent explicitly maintains an entity-state representation, updates it under the new prompt, grounds the predicted post-action state as a future end frame, and renders the next video segment. The method was evaluated on Statebench, a new benchmark targeting three state categories: (1) past-visible states, (2) occluded-process states, and (3) complex-transition states.
AI.result: The method improves controlled video continuation significantly, raising the all-case state score (SCS-All) from 45.2 to 69.3. It also benefits story generation at the one-minute scale.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Stateagent approach demonstrates that explicitly maintaining entity-state representations significantly improves video continuation quality. The Statebench benchmark provides a valuable testbed for evaluating state tracking in video generation, addressing a previously overlooked but important aspect of long-form video generation.

title: LeanGRPO: Eliminating Redundant Recomputation in Diffusion RL
summary: Diffusion reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved significant success in post-training image and video generative models. However, most diffusion RL methods, including DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO, recompute selected timesteps with gradient tracking after rollout. Under on-policy training with the same backend for rollout and update, this recomputation is mathematically redundant. Intuitively, the rollout and policy update steps can reuse the same feed-forward backbone to avoid redundant computation, but doing so can incur a large memory overhead during rollout. To address the issue, we present LeanGRPO by restructuring the data-parallel layout and introducing two recompute-free training schedules for trajectory-logprob diffusion RL: (1) LeanGRPO-Retain enables gradient tracking during rollout and directly reuses the resulting computation graphs and saved activations for backward during update, requiring no recomputation; and (2) LeanGRPO-Reweight also enables gradients during rollout, but immediately backpropagates each selected step using a provisional advantage and delays gradient synchronization, then corrects the provisional gradients with the true advantage after the trajectory is completed. These schedules target different model scales and input sizes. Across FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan, LeanGRPO achieves up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup while preserving the original optimization objective.

AI.tldr: LeanGRPO addresses computational redundancy in diffusion reinforcement learning by eliminating timestep recomputation during policy updates. It introduces two recompute-free training schedules that enable gradient tracking during rollout, achieving up to 1.83x speedup while preserving the original optimization objective.
AI.motivation: Diffusion RL methods like DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO recompute selected timesteps with gradient tracking after rollout. This recomputation is mathematically redundant in on-policy training with the same backend for rollout and update. While reusing the same feed-forward backbone could avoid redundant computation, it would incur large memory overhead during rollout. The authors aim to eliminate this redundancy efficiently.
AI.method: LeanGRPO restructures the data-parallel layout and introduces two recompute-free training schedules: (1) LeanGRPO-Retain enables gradient tracking during rollout and directly reuses the resulting computation graphs and saved activations for backward during update, requiring no recomputation; (2) LeanGRPO-Reweight enables gradients during rollout, backpropagates each selected step using a provisional advantage, delays gradient synchronization, then corrects the provisional gradients with the true advantage after trajectory completion.
AI.result: Across FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan models, LeanGRPO achieves up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup while preserving the original optimization objective.
AI.conclusion: LeanGRPO successfully eliminates the mathematically redundant recomputation in diffusion RL by enabling gradient tracking during rollout. The two proposed schedules target different model scales and input sizes, providing flexible trade-offs between memory usage and computational efficiency. This work demonstrates that significant speedups are achievable without sacrificing optimization quality in diffusion reinforcement learning.

title: Interface-Induced Trajectory Censoring
comment: 39 pages, 14 pages main text. Code, data, and pre-registrations: https://github.com/nebula-1999/Interface-Induced-Trajectory-Censoring
summary:
Agent evaluations report a tool-call rate read off the serving stack. That number can be zero while the model is emitting well-formed calls: the interface censors the trajectory before anything downstream sees it.
  On BFCL v4's own data, executor and scorer, holding weights, cases, decoding and seeds fixed and changing only the serving adapter, the same model scores 0.00 or 0.96 / 0.19. A 2x2 over chat template and parser locates the effect exactly: both main effects are exactly zero and all of it sits in the interaction -- no component is defective, and repairing one side of the contract buys precisely nothing. On tau-bench's 115 interactive retail tasks the same swap moves server-parsed calls from 0 to 636 and tasks reaching any tool execution from 0 to 103. Our probe reproduces the funnel across a 21x scale range of Qwen2.5-Coder: the server parses 0/100 at every size while well-formed emitted calls rise to 80/100 at 32B (~72 after calibration against an adjudicated gold standard). Under a matched envelope, across a comparable scale span, the silent fraction stays at 0-2, a prediction committed to the repository before the run. Llama-3.1-8B's 23% rate of calling the task function itself as a tool falls to 0 under one strict:true flag.
  The mismatch reaches inside the training loop, and its consequence is scale-dependent: in verl's AgentLoop at 7B, 45 of 115 generations carry a complete call; 0 are accepted, 0 execute, 0 return an observation. At 1.5B the same zero is over-determined, so we report the two scales separately. At evaluation time, repairing the adapter restores the mechanism but not a significant outcome gain: parsing 0->84, rescues 0->9, pass rate 53->62 (n.s.). We release a 98-line preflight check that catches every silent failure here. The observed tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone; it is a property of the model-interface stack that measures it.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a critical measurement artifact in agent evaluations: the reported tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone but of the model-interface stack. The serving stack can censor well-formed tool calls, causing reported rates to be zero while the model actually emits valid calls. Experiments across multiple benchmarks (BFCL v4, tau-bench), models (Qwen2.5-Coder at 21x scale, Llama-3.1-8B), and training loops (verl's AgentLoop) demonstrate this issue, with the same model scoring 0.00 or 0.96 depending on the serving adapter used.
AI.motivation: The research aims to expose a fundamental flaw in how agent evaluations measure tool-call rates. The authors noticed that reported tool-call rates can be zero even when models emit well-formed calls, suggesting the measurement apparatus itself (the serving stack/interface) is censoring trajectories before downstream components can process them.
AI.method: The authors conducted controlled experiments by varying only the serving adapter while keeping weights, cases, decoding, and seeds fixed. They performed a 2x2 factorial experiment over chat template and parser, probed across a 21x scale range of Qwen2.5-Coder, tested Llama-3.1-8B with different strict flags, and examined verl's AgentLoop at two scales (7B and 1.5B). They also released a 98-line preflight check to detect silent failures.
AI.result: The same model scores 0.00 or 0.96/0.19 on BFCL v4 depending on the adapter. On tau-bench retail tasks, server-parsed calls increase from 0 to 636 and tasks reaching tool execution from 0 to 103. For Qwen2.5-Coder, server parses 0/100 at all sizes while well-formed calls rise to 80/100 at 32B. Llama-3.1-8B's 23% self-call rate drops to 0 with strict:true. In verl's AgentLoop at 7B, 45/115 generations have complete calls but 0 execute. Repairing the adapter at evaluation time improves parsing (0→84) and rescues (0→9) but pass rate only increases from 53% to 62% (not significant).
AI.conclusion: The observed tool-call rate is a property of the model-interface stack, not the model alone. No single component is defective—the entire effect sits in the interaction between model output and interface parsing. This has implications for training loops (where the mismatch causes scale-dependent consequences) and evaluation (where repairing the adapter restores the mechanism but yields minimal outcome gains). A preflight check can catch these silent failures.

title: CoFiE: Coarse-to-Fine Evidence Selection for Efficient Streaming Video Understanding
summary: Streaming video understanding requires Vision Language Models (VLLMs) to process growing video streams and answer user questions under tight latency constraints. Existing methods improve efficiency through token pruning and memory-bank schemes, but mainly reduce visual tokens after visual encoding. Consequently, downstream token pruning alone cannot substantially reduce end-to-end latency because the expensive frame encoding cost has already been incurred. We propose CoFiE, a Coarse-to-Fine Evidence Selection framework that decouples evidence selection into a coarse, query-agnostic filtering stage before the vision encoder and a fine, query-specific refinement stage during LLM prefill. CoFiE introduces Novelty-Guided Frame Filtering to retain visually distinctive candidate frames and Query-Specific Evidence Refinement to select the frames most relevant to the user query. This design removes substantial redundancy before frame encoding while preserving query-specific refinement once semantic information becomes available. Experiments show that CoFiE establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off across multiple video understanding benchmarks, reaching 78.86% accuracy on StreamingBench and 68.72% on OvO-Bench, with improvements of up to 3.15% over prior methods. Even with up to 80% evidence-frame filtering, CoFiE outperforms strong open-source multimodal models while improving end-to-end inference latency by up to 2.54 times.

AI.tldr: CoFiE proposes a coarse-to-fine evidence selection framework for streaming video understanding that filters frames before expensive vision encoding (coarse, query-agnostic) and refines them during LLM prefill (fine, query-specific), achieving state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off with 78.86% on StreamingBench and 68.72% on OvO-Bench while improving inference latency by up to 2.54x.
AI.motivation: Existing VLLM methods for streaming video understanding reduce visual tokens after encoding, but the expensive frame encoding cost has already been incurred, limiting end-to-end latency improvements. There is a need to reduce redundancy before frame encoding while preserving query-specific refinement capabilities.
AI.method: CoFiE introduces a two-stage evidence selection: (1) Novelty-Guided Frame Filtering - a coarse, query-agnostic filtering stage before the vision encoder to retain visually distinctive candidate frames; (2) Query-Specific Evidence Refinement - a fine, query-specific refinement stage during LLM prefill to select frames most relevant to the user query.
AI.result: CoFiE achieves 78.86% accuracy on StreamingBench and 68.72% on OvO-Bench, with improvements of up to 3.15% over prior methods. Even with up to 80% evidence-frame filtering, CoFiE outperforms strong open-source multimodal models.
AI.conclusion: CoFiE establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off for streaming video understanding by decoupling evidence selection into coarse pre-encoding and fine post-encoding stages, reducing substantial redundancy before frame encoding while preserving query-specific refinement capabilities.

title: Coupled Scaling: A Representational Accessibility Framework for Neural Scaling Laws
comment: 35 pages, 2 figures. Code and reproducibility artifacts: https://github.com/quintonvina/coupled-scaling/tree/v1.0-reanalysis
summary: Existing theories derive neural scaling from data geometry or a specified data-model spectrum, but systems trained on the same data can scale differently when architecture or optimization changes the representations they can efficiently reach. We introduce Coupled Scaling, a task-conditioned framework in which finite-budget scaling depends on the relation between task structure and the geometry accessible to an architecture-optimization system. In a solvable mode-truncation model, loss separates into target energy outside architectural support and an unresolved supported tail. For an arbitrary priority order, the residual lies between the best-N supported tail and the tail beyond the largest completed high-value prefix. If the cumulative-tail and coverage log-rates are $γ_{A,T}$ and $ρ_{A,O,T}$, the residual exponent lies in $[ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T},γ_{A,T}]$. Under bounded off-prefix gain, the completed prefix is rate-determining and $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T}$; for $a_{A,T,j}\asymp j^{-b_{A,T}}$, this gives $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T}-1)$. A fixed-kernel specialization derives the training-time exponent from the near-zero tail of a task-weighted spectral measure defined independently of the loss fit. The framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and motivates two tests: static task-relevant geometry should track loss at a common budget, while multiscale geometry should track coupling-specific exponent ordering, including reversal across contrasting tasks. An audit of released emergence trajectories identifies the controls needed for a direct factorial test that measures geometry separately from the scaling fit.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "Coupled Scaling," a framework that explains how neural network scaling depends on the relationship between task structure and the geometry accessible to a given architecture-optimization system. The framework derives scaling exponents from the interplay between architectural support and finite-budget data acquisition, with applications to understanding emergence in large models.
AI.motivation: Existing neural scaling theories derive from data geometry or data-model spectrum, but fail to account for how different architectures and optimizations can lead to different scaling behaviors when trained on identical data. The authors seek to develop a framework that captures how task structure interacts with the geometric representations an architecture-optimization system can efficiently reach.
AI.method: The authors introduce a solvable mode-truncation model where loss separates into target energy outside architectural support and an unresolved supported tail. They analyze residual between best-N supported tail and tail beyond largest completed high-value prefix. Using cumulative-tail log-rate γ and coverage log-rate ρ, they derive residual exponent bounds. They also specialize to fixed-kernel case to derive training-time exponent from near-zero tail of task-weighted spectral measure.
AI.result: The residual exponent lies in [ργ, γ]. Under bounded off-prefix gain, the completed prefix is rate-determining giving exponent α = ργ. For power-law tail distributions a ∼ j^(-b), this yields α = ρ(b-1). The framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and enables two tests: static task-relevant geometry tracking loss at common budget, and multiscale geometry tracking coupling-specific exponent ordering including reversal across contrasting tasks.
AI.conclusion: The Coupled Scaling framework provides a principled way to understand how architecture-optimization systems interact with task structure to determine scaling behavior. It motivates empirical tests including an audit of released emergence trajectories to identify controls needed for factorial tests measuring geometry separately from scaling fit. The framework bridges the gap between theoretical scaling laws and practical observations of architecture-dependent scaling differences.

title: Common-Witness Certificates and Sharp Feature Bounds for Counterfactual Image Auditing
summary: An image editor may satisfy every regional plausibility constraint separately even when no single latent explanation fits the complete output. We formalize this local-to-global failure using a common witness grade and witness nerve. The framework separates auditing from causal identification: shared exogeneity alone allows every coupling of the regime marginals, whereas an externally justified witness relation yields sharp partial-identification bounds for prespecified image features. Helly-type arguments provide short incompatibility certificates for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases; a blocker-hypergraph formula gives exact repair counts. Simultaneous confidence regions for the regime marginals give finite-sample outer coverage of the complete identified interval. Controlled MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB studies demonstrate the predicted local-global separation, while synthetic experiments test sharp bounds, certificate recovery, and structured computation. The method audits a declared feature relation and does not identify unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a formal framework for detecting and quantifying local-to-global inconsistencies in image editing, where regional plausibility constraints can be satisfied individually but no single latent explanation fits the complete output. The method uses witness grades and witness nerves to audit feature relations without identifying unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that image editors may satisfy every regional plausibility constraint separately, yet no single latent explanation exists that fits the entire output. This local-to-global failure is a fundamental identification issue in causal inference for image analysis, requiring formal tools to detect and measure such incompatibilities.
AI.method: The framework employs: (1) witness grade and witness nerve for formalizing local-to-global failures; (2) separation of auditing from causal identification, where shared exogeneity allows coupling of regime marginals; (3) externally justified witness relations for sharp partial-identification bounds; (4) Helly-type arguments for incompatibility certificates with quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases; (5) blocker-hypergraph formula for exact repair counts; (6) simultaneous confidence regions with finite-sample outer coverage.
AI.result: The method provides: (1) sharp partial-identification bounds for prespecified image features; (2) incompatibility certificates for various loss structures; (3) exact repair counts via blocker-hypergraph; (4) finite-sample confidence regions for regime marginals. Empirical validation on Controlled MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB demonstrates local-global separation, sharp bounds, certificate recovery, and structured computation.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method successfully audits declared feature relations without identifying unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals. It provides a principled framework for detecting local-to-global inconsistencies in image editing, with theoretical guarantees (sharp bounds, incompatibility certificates) and empirical validation across multiple image datasets.

title: Understanding Autonomous Driving Datasets by Describing Differences between Image Subsets in Natural Language
comment: 9 pages, 5 figures, submitted to the IEEE Open Journal of Intelligent Transportation Systems (OJ-ITS), our implementation and benchmark dataset are available at https://github.com/KIT-MRT/AD-Diff
summary: Understanding the composition of large-scale autonomous driving datasets is essential for safety, robustness, and reliable operation across domains. For example, domain shift between locations could lead to the operating environment being misaligned with the training data, resulting in potentially dangerous performance degradation. Yet, existing data analysis pipelines largely rely on metadata, predefined labels, or manual inspection, which provide limited semantic insight or do not scale. This paper studies set difference captioning: given two subsets of images, the goal is to produce a natural-language hypothesis describing differences between the target and reference set. Building on a two-stage formulation, we adapt the method to autonomous driving by focusing on object-centric patches derived from object detection, which simplifies aggregation and enables attribution of differences to specific object instances or categories. To evaluate this setting in-domain, we introduce a new benchmark, AD-Diff Bench. Low-concentration experiments assess the suitability of set-difference-captioning approaches to sparse, real-world differences. We restrict our experiments to open-weight models to support reproducibility and ease of deployment. The proposed benchmark and analysis provide a step towards practical, human-interpretable dataset introspection for autonomous driving datasets. Our implementation and benchmark dataset are available at https://github.com/KIT-MRT/AD-Diff

AI.tldr: This paper proposes set difference captioning for autonomous driving dataset introspection, using object-centric patches from object detection to describe differences between image subsets. They introduce AD-Diff Bench for evaluation and use open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Understanding large-scale autonomous driving datasets is critical for safety and robustness. Domain shift between locations can cause performance degradation. Existing data analysis methods rely on metadata, predefined labels, or manual inspection, which provide limited semantic insight or don't scale.
AI.method: The paper studies set difference captioning: given two subsets of images, generate natural-language hypotheses describing differences between target and reference sets. They adapt a two-stage formulation to autonomous driving by focusing on object-centric patches derived from object detection, which simplifies aggregation and enables attribution of differences to specific object instances or categories. Experiments use open-weight models for reproducibility.
AI.result: The paper introduces AD-Diff Bench, a new benchmark for evaluating set-difference-captioning in autonomous driving. Low-concentration experiments assess suitability for sparse, real-world differences. The implementation and benchmark are publicly available.
AI.conclusion: The proposed benchmark and analysis provide a step towards practical, human-interpretable dataset introspection for autonomous driving datasets, enabling better understanding of dataset composition and domain shifts.

title: WeatherNext 3: Increasing resolution and performance of global weather models with raw observations
summary: State-of-the-art AI weather models have shown impressive medium-range forecast skill and computational efficiency, but suffer two key shortcomings: their forecasts have lower spatial and temporal resolution than the best physics-based models and they are exclusively initialized with and trained on analysis data. As a result, they cannot directly make use of observations, and any biases in the analysis are inherited by the forecast. WeatherNext 3 addresses these shortcomings and establishes a new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting skill. First, WeatherNext 3 generates new forecasts every hour (rather than every 6 hours like traditional global models) by ingesting low-latency geostationary satellite data. Second, WeatherNext 3's temporal and spatial resolution are on par with physics-based global models, with hourly time steps and 0.1 degree resolution for single-level variables, including solar radiation and cloud cover. Third, WeatherNext 3 moves beyond traditional analysis variables by learning to predict satellite-derived precipitation estimates, as well as tropical cyclone and station observations. Modelling sparse station data allows WeatherNext 3 to make 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions at any location and time, conditioned on local geographical features, with substantially lower error than competing global models, even when evaluated against unseen stations. Together, WeatherNext 3's capabilities move operational AI-based weather forecasting beyond emulating the traditionally distinct stages of data assimilation, forecasting and post-processing, which helps to further push the frontier of performance and granularity for global weather prediction.

AI.tldr: WeatherNext 3 is a new AI-based weather forecasting model that addresses key limitations of existing AI weather models by generating hourly forecasts at 0.1-degree resolution, ingesting low-latency geostationary satellite data, and learning to predict satellite-derived precipitation and station observations. It achieves superior probabilistic medium-range forecasting skill and can make temperature/dewpoint predictions at any location, even at unseen stations.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art AI weather models suffer from two key shortcomings: (1) lower spatial and temporal resolution compared to the best physics-based models, and (2) being exclusively initialized with and trained on analysis data, meaning they cannot directly use observations and inherit any biases in the analysis. This limits their operational utility and accuracy.
AI.method: WeatherNext 3 implements three key innovations: (1) Hourly forecast generation by ingesting low-latency geostationary satellite data (vs. traditional 6-hour intervals); (2) Temporal and spatial resolution matching physics-based models - hourly time steps at 0.1-degree resolution for single-level variables including solar radiation and cloud cover; (3) Learning to predict satellite-derived precipitation estimates, tropical cyclone positions, and station observations, enabling 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions at any location conditioned on local geographical features.
AI.result: WeatherNext 3 establishes a new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting skill. It achieves substantially lower error than competing global models for 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions, even when evaluated against unseen stations. The model integrates data assimilation, forecasting, and post-processing into a unified system.
AI.conclusion: WeatherNext 3 demonstrates that operational AI-based weather forecasting can move beyond emulating the traditionally distinct stages of data assimilation, forecasting, and post-processing. This unified approach pushes the frontier of performance and granularity for global weather prediction, offering higher resolution and more accurate probabilistic forecasts than previous AI models.

title: The Dually Flat Geometry of Planning as Inference
summary: We present an alternative characterization of the occupancy measure of reinforcement learning, obtained by embedding the planning criterion into the dynamics through a resetting planning process. Its stationary measure, which we term visitation measure, is the object on which the information geometry of decision making is most naturally expressed. The achievable visitation measures form a dually flat statistical manifold whose two affine charts are the visitation probabilities and the log-policies, dual under the conditional entropy. This structure makes planning-as-inference generalize from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of the visitation, each iterate solved by one natural-gradient step, and gives the temporal-difference error the interpretation of a marginal-utility estimate. We develop the geometry and its consequences for reinforcement learning and theoretical neuroscience.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an alternative characterization of reinforcement learning's occupancy measure by embedding planning criteria into dynamics through a resetting planning process. The resulting visitation measure forms a dually flat statistical manifold, enabling planning-as-inference to generalize to nonlinear functionals via natural-gradient steps, with temporal-difference errors interpreted as marginal-utility estimates.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to bridge reinforcement learning and information geometry by providing a natural geometric framework for decision making. They seek to generalize planning-as-inference beyond linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of the visitation measure.
AI.method: The paper embeds the planning criterion into the environment dynamics through a resetting planning process. The stationary measure (visitation measure) is analyzed as a dually flat statistical manifold with two affine charts: visitation probabilities and log-policies, dual under conditional entropy.
AI.result: The achievable visitation measures form a dually flat statistical manifold. Each planning iteration can be solved by one natural-gradient step, and the temporal-difference error obtains the interpretation of a marginal-utility estimate.
AI.conclusion: This geometric framework connects reinforcement learning and theoretical neuroscience, providing a unified perspective on decision making through information geometry and enabling generalization from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of visitation.

title: DropClick: Semi-Automated One-Click Segmentation for Agricultural Robotic Data
summary: Labelling vision datasets, especially for segmentation tasks, is a laborious and costly process that stymies novel developments in agricultural robotics. In this paper, we present DropClick, a click-guided segmentation tool that simplifies the annotation process. Our system utilises single-click inputs on objects to generate pseudo-labels, which can replace manual annotations. DropClick stands out as it is a semi-automated approach and does not require a click for every object in the scene. It can therefore further reduce the required amount of user input drastically. We evaluate our method on two challenging agricultural robotic datasets, SB20 and BUP20 for plant and fruit segmentation, respectively. DropClick is first trained on a small subset of just 5 images from the original training data. This DropClick model can then be deployed as a one-click segmentation system and achieves comparable or higher performance than other one-click methods achieving an mIoU of 70.0 and 72.6 points, for SB20 and BUP20 respectively. DropClick then excels at maintaining high performance when clicks are not given (e.g. dropped); when 50% of the clicks are missing it still maintains an mIoU of 68.9 and 71.3 points, for SB20 and BUP20 respectively. We validate DropClick as a pseudo-labelling approach by taking its outputs to train a Mask2Former instance-based segmentation model in a semi-supervised manner. In this process, partially removing user input from DropClick yields similar high performance when compared to providing all clicks, at 70.1 vs 70.7 points AP50 for SB20 and no difference for BUP20 at 77.0 for both models; at the same time saving 46.3% of total input for SB20 and 31.9% for BUP20.

AI.tldr: DropClick is a click-guided segmentation tool for agricultural robotics that generates pseudo-labels from single-click inputs, reducing annotation effort. Trained on only 5 images, it achieves mIoU of 70.0/72.6 on SB20/BUP20 datasets and maintains performance even with 50% missing clicks. When used for semi-supervised training of Mask2Former, it saves 46.3% and 31.9% of user input while maintaining comparable performance.
AI.motivation: Labelling vision datasets for segmentation tasks is laborious and costly, hindering developments in agricultural robotics. There is a need for a simplified annotation tool that reduces manual effort while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: DropClick uses single-click inputs on objects to generate pseudo-labels. It is a semi-automated approach that does not require a click for every object in the scene. The method was trained on a small subset of just 5 images and evaluated for both one-click segmentation and pseudo-labelling with Mask2Former.
AI.result: One-click segmentation achieves mIoU of 70.0 (SB20) and 72.6 (BUP20). With 50% clicks missing, it maintains mIoU of 68.9 and 71.3 respectively. For pseudo-labelling, partially removing user input yields AP50 of 70.1 vs 70.7 (SB20) and 77.0 for both (BUP20), while saving 46.3% input for SB20 and 31.9% for BUP20.
AI.conclusion: DropClick effectively reduces annotation effort in agricultural robotics datasets. It can be trained on minimal data (5 images), maintains robustness when clicks are missing, and successfully enables semi-supervised training of Mask2Former with significantly reduced user input while achieving comparable performance to full annotation.

title: Neural-Network Maxent: a general extension with learned nonlinearity, applied to time-series for Desert Locust distribution modelling
summary: Species Distribution Modelling (SDM) is essential for understanding how environmental conditions shape biodiversity, particularly for destructive pests such as the Desert Locust (Schistocerca gregaria), whose breeding dynamics are tightly coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions. Maxent has become the dominant method for presence-only data, but its reliance on a linear combination of hand chosen feature transforms limits its ability to capture the nonlinear, temporal relationships common in ecological monitoring, where covariates such as precipitation, soil moisture, and vegetation indices evolve meaningfully over time. Standard implementations flatten time-series covariates into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal. We introduce RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent framework that replaces the fixed feature dictionary with a neural network, specifically a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), trained end to end via backpropagation. The approach preserves Maxent's presence only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, differing only in that the nonlinearity is learned from data rather than fixed in advance. We apply RNN Maxent to map suitable habitat for the Desert Locust using 50 day environmental time series derived from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, maintaining a 7 day gap between covariates and presence records to yield forecasting behavior. Compared against standard Maxent, RNN Maxent improves performance across metrics (ROC AUC 0.862 std 0.036 vs. 0.792; F1 0.671 std 0.056 vs. 0.590).

AI.tldr: RNN Maxent is a novel extension of Maxent that uses Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) to capture temporal relationships in environmental time series for species distribution modeling, applied to Desert Locust habitat prediction.
AI.motivation: Standard Maxent relies on linear combinations of hand-chosen feature transforms, limiting its ability to capture nonlinear, temporal relationships in ecological monitoring. Time-series covariates are flattened into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal for forecasting pest breeding dynamics.
AI.method: RNN Maxent replaces the fixed feature dictionary in Maxent with a GRU neural network trained end-to-end via backpropagation. It preserves Maxent's presence-only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, learning nonlinearities from data rather than fixing them in advance. The model uses 50-day environmental time series from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, with a 7-day gap between covariates and presence records to yield forecasting behavior.
AI.result: RNN Maxent significantly outperforms standard Maxent: ROC AUC 0.862 (std 0.036) vs 0.792; F1 0.671 (std 0.056) vs 0.590.
AI.conclusion: RNN Maxent successfully integrates deep learning temporal modeling with Maxent's presence-only framework, achieving substantial performance improvements for Desert Locust habitat suitability mapping and demonstrating the value of preserving sequential structure in environmental time series for species distribution modeling.

title: LLM4CKD: Large Language Models for Early Stage Chronic Kidney Disease Screening
summary: Early screening of chronic kidney disease (CKD) is critical for timely intervention, yet most machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches require labeled data and model training, limiting their use in real-world screening settings. This study evaluates the effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) for CKD screening under zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning settings and compares them with traditional ML and DL methods. We propose a framework that uses clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates to enable LLM-based inference without task-specific training. LLM performance is evaluated across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings, and compared with standard ML, DL, and tabular foundation model (TFM) baselines, and existing CKD screening tools. The results show that LLMs can achieve competitive performance using only a small number of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. However, their performance remains model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases. In contrast, ML, DL, and TFM models show more consistent improvement with larger training data. Overall, the findings highlight a trade-off between data efficiency and stability, suggesting that LLMs may serve as a flexible complementary approach for CKD screening when labeled data are limited.

AI.tldr: The study evaluates large language models (LLMs) for chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening using zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning, without requiring task-specific training. It compares LLM performance with traditional ML, DL, and tabular foundation models across various data settings.
AI.motivation: Early CKD screening is critical for timely intervention, but traditional ML/DL approaches require labeled data and model training, limiting their real-world applicability. There needs to be a method that can work with limited labeled data.
AI.method: The study proposes a framework using clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates to enable LLM-based inference without task-specific training. LLM performance is evaluated across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings, and compared with standard ML, DL, TFM baselines, and existing CKD screening tools.
AI.result: LLMs can achieve competitive performance using only a small number of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. However, their performance remains model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases. In contrast, ML, DL, and TFM models show more consistent improvement with larger training data.
AI.conclusion: There is a trade-off between data efficiency and stability. LLMs may serve as a flexible complementary approach for CKD screening when labeled data are limited, but traditional ML/DL models offer more consistent performance with larger datasets.

title: ToPO: Token-Conditioned Preference Routing for Attention-Based Latent Diffusion Models
summary: Pairwise preference labels rank complete images, yet Diffusion-DPO applies their effect over many spatial and denoising-time coordinates. For attention-based, noise-prediction latent diffusion, ToPO (Token-Oriented Preference Optimization) constructs a per-minibatch, detached, separable spatial-temporal route from branchwise squared-residual contrast in a frozen reference denoiser. Preferred-branch cross-attention uses content tokens to modulate the spatial factor, and an auxiliary pixel-midpoint ordering term is added without local labels or a learned reward model. In matched three-seed retrainings with a shared update schedule, ToPO has higher endpoint estimates than Diffusion-DPO on all five reported SD-1.5 metrics and on HPSv2, ImageReward, and CLIP for SDXL. It also receives larger raw win shares in an aggregate blind SDXL A/B study. These findings are scoped to the reported equal-update U-Net protocols rather than an equal-compute comparison.

AI.tldr: ToPO (Token-Oriented Preference Optimization) is a new method for optimizing latent diffusion models using pairwise preference labels. It constructs a per-minibatch spatial-temporal route from branchwise squared-residual contrast in a frozen reference denoiser, using preferred-branch cross-attention with content tokens to modulate the spatial factor. It outperforms Diffusion-DPO on multiple metrics across SD-1.5 and SDXL models.
AI.motivation: The existing Diffusion-DPO method applies preference labels over many spatial and denoising-time coordinates, which may be inefficient. ToPO aims to address this by focusing on token-level preference optimization rather than applying effects across all coordinates.
AI.method: ToPO constructs a per-minibatch, detached, separable spatial-temporal route from branchwise squared-residual contrast in a frozen reference denoiser. It uses preferred-branch cross-attention where content tokens modulate the spatial factor. An auxiliary pixel-midpoint ordering term is added without requiring local labels or a learned reward model. The method was tested with matched three-seed retrainings using a shared update schedule.
AI.result: ToPO has higher endpoint estimates than Diffusion-DPO on all five reported SD-1.5 metrics and on HPSv2, ImageReward, and CLIP for SDXL. It also receives larger raw win shares in an aggregate blind SDXL A/B study.
AI.conclusion: ToPO demonstrates superior performance over Diffusion-DPO in preference optimization for diffusion models. However, findings are scoped to equal-update U-Net protocols rather than equal-compute comparisons, limiting generalizability to scenarios with different computational constraints.

title: On the Interaction Between Model Compression and Test-Time Adaptation
summary: Deep neural networks deployed in the wild must be both efficient and adaptable, requiring model compression and test-time adaptation (TTA). While both are well studied in isolation, their interaction remains poorly understood. We systematically analyze how structured compression affects a model's ability to adapt under distribution shift. Using ResNet-18 and ViT-Base on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C, we evaluate multiple compression methods combined with standard TTA techniques. We introduce a diagnostic framework that examines representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility. Our results reveal a consistent gap: although compressed models retain high accuracy under supervised adaptation, their TTA performance degrades significantly with increasing compression. We show that this stems from reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability. These effects strongly depend on the compression method, highlighting the need to design compression strategies that preserve adaptability.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the interaction between model compression and test-time adaptation (TTA), revealing that while compressed models maintain supervised accuracy, their TTA performance degrades significantly with increased compression due to reduced representational diversity and structural constraints.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks need both efficiency (via compression) and adaptability (via test-time adaptation), but how these two techniques interact in practice remains poorly understood. This gap in knowledge is critical for deploying models in real-world scenarios with distribution shifts.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyze how structured compression affects adaptation under distribution shift using ResNet-18 and ViT-Base on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C benchmarks. They combine multiple compression methods with standard TTA techniques and introduce a diagnostic framework examining representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility.
AI.result: Compressed models retain high accuracy under supervised adaptation but exhibit significantly degraded TTA performance with increasing compression. This performance gap stems from reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability. The effect varies depending on the compression method used.
AI.conclusion: There exists a consistent trade-off between compression and TTA performance. The findings highlight the need to design compression strategies that specifically preserve adaptability, rather than focusing solely on accuracy or efficiency. Future compression methods should consider maintaining representational diversity and adaptation subspace compatibility.

title: InSituMeasure: Probing Situated Measurement Grounding in Industrial Scenes with Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: For trained operators, gauge reading requires little specialized knowledge, low cognitive effort, and high repeatability. Yet Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) remain unreliable in continuous-valued measurement despite strong results on general multimodal benchmarks. Existing benchmarks expose this weakness but isolate measurement from realistic, knowledge-grounded settings, with limited situated context, specialized instruments, real-world noise, and matched diagnostic annotations, reducing realism and constraining root-cause analysis. We introduce InSituMeasure to evaluate situated measurement grounding. It contains 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes across eight functional categories of professional engineering instruments, with dense gauge-attribute annotations and noise tags for failure diagnosis. We define metrics for numerical accuracy under predefined tolerances and unit consistency, rejection of fake or unanswerable tasks, and alignment between model failures and annotated error factors. Across 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs, the best model reaches only 25.7\% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8\% confidence-diagnosis F1, revealing a substantial gap between general multimodal competence and reliable situated measurement. Further analysis identifies failures from text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and authentic industrial noise, including mixed disturbances, viewpoint deviation, occlusion, and environmental interference.

AI.tldr: InSituMeasure is a new benchmark evaluating MLLMs on situated measurement grounding in real industrial monitoring scenes. It contains 2,922 gauge images across 8 engineering instrument categories with dense annotations and noise tags. The best model achieves only 25.7% value-unit accuracy and 51.8% confidence-diagnosis F1, revealing a substantial gap between general multimodal capabilities and reliable industrial measurement.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks fail to capture realistic gauge reading challenges: they isolate measurement from knowledge-grounded settings, lack situated context, specialized instruments, real-world noise, and diagnostic annotations. This reduces realism and constrains root-cause analysis. The core problem is that MLLMs perform well on general multimodal benchmarks but remain unreliable for continuous-valued measurement tasks essential in industrial settings.
AI.method: The authors created InSituMeasure with 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes across eight functional categories of professional engineering instruments. They developed dense gauge-attribute annotations and noise tags for failure diagnosis. They defined metrics for: (1) numerical accuracy under predefined tolerances, (2) unit consistency, (3) rejection of fake or unanswerable tasks, and (4) alignment between model failures and annotated error factors. They evaluated 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs on this benchmark.
AI.result: The best model achieved only 25.7% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8% confidence-diagnosis F1. Analysis identified three main failure sources: text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and authentic industrial noise (mixed disturbances, viewpoint deviation, occlusion, and environmental interference).
AI.conclusion: There is a substantial gap between general multimodal competence and reliable situated measurement in industrial settings. Current MLLMs cannot be trusted for precise gauge reading in professional engineering contexts. Future work should address the identified failure modes to improve MLLM reliability in real-world industrial measurement tasks.

title: Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model for WSI Classification in Histopathology
summary: Histopathological subtyping relies on the recognition of characteristic histological patterns. These patterns may be expressed by individual tissue structures or by the spatial distribution and co-occurrence of multiple structures, and they often span irregularly shaped tissue regions, termed semantic units in this work. However, conventional patch-based representations may fragment such units and fail to explicitly preserve their internal spatial organization, while efficiently modeling relationships among numerous spatially separated units remains challenging. To address these limitations, we propose the Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model (SASG-SSM), a flexible and efficient framework for whole slide image (WSI) classification. Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) first approximate irregularly shaped semantic units by adaptively grouping spatially connected patches guided by class-agnostic visual-semantic priors. By representing patches as graph nodes with adjacency edges, SASGs preserve their internal spatial organization rather than treating them as an unordered set. A Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) subsequently combines a graph neural network encoder for intra-subgraph topology encoding with a Mamba-based state space encoder for efficient contextualization across large numbers of subgraphs. This module integrates local structural information within semantic units with global contextual information arising from their distribution and co-occurrence across the WSI, while efficiently modeling a large number of spatially distributed regions. Extensive experiments across four WSI subtyping datasets demonstrate consistent advantages over representative state-of-the-art methods. Further evaluations under small-cohort and few-shot settings demonstrate robustness and data efficiency under limited training data. Code will be released at https://github.com/HLSvois/SASG-SSM.

AI.tldr: SASG-SSM is a novel framework for whole slide image (WSI) classification that uses semantic-aware subgraphs to capture irregular tissue regions and combines graph neural networks with Mamba-based state space models for efficient contextualization across spatially distributed regions.
AI.motivation: Conventional patch-based methods fragment semantic units (irregular tissue regions) and fail to preserve their internal spatial organization, while efficiently modeling relationships among numerous spatially separated units remains challenging.
AI.method: The framework uses Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) to group spatially connected patches guided by class-agnostic visual-semantic priors, representing patches as graph nodes with adjacency edges. A Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) combines a graph neural network encoder for intra-subgraph topology with a Mamba-based state space encoder for efficient cross-subgraph contextualization.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across four WSI subtyping datasets demonstrate consistent advantages over state-of-the-art methods. The method also shows robustness and data efficiency under small-cohort and few-shot settings.
AI.conclusion: SASG-SSM effectively integrates local structural information within semantic units with global contextual information across the WSI, while efficiently handling large numbers of spatially distributed regions. The approach addresses key limitations of patch-based representations in histopathology image analysis.

title: Local Updates, Global Learning (LUGL): Playing Games with non-incremental Learners
summary: The dominance of Neural Networks (NNs) in RL is partially due to their incremental learning capability, which naturally suits the online, non-stationary nature of self-play training. However, gradient-boosted trees like LightGBM are widely recognised as the state of the art for tabular data in supervised learning, often outperforming NNs in accuracy and efficiency. Game states are inherently tabular---discrete actions, categorical card identities, structured board positions---which makes them an ideal candidate for tree-based methods.
