Nine frontier large models were evaluated on a 1,770-task slice (1,745 Part tasks + 25 Assembly tasks).
AI.result: Among nine standalone models, no single model leads all four metrics. Executability ranges from 0.565 to 0.812, Solid IoU from 0.2841 to 0.5379, and Surface IoU from 0.112 to 0.217 across four Part regimes. For assembly tasks, Codex with GPT-5.5 improves executability and IoU metrics over standalone GPT-5.5 but lowers Judge score by 6.98 percentage points. Key failure modes include missing fine structures, loss of part identity, and incorrect assembly placement.
AI.conclusion: Execution alone is insufficient to characterize realistic CAD modeling. Frontier models and agents differ substantially across executability, IoUs, and visual-semantic identity, demonstrating the need for multi-metric evaluation frameworks. The benchmark reveals that current models still struggle with fine structures, part identity preservation, and assembly placement.

title: Landmark-Based Discrimination of Injury-Associated Athlete-Sessions from Minute-Resolution Multimodal Football Monitoring Data
summary:
Athlete monitoring data may be recorded minute by minute throughout a match or training session, while injury information may only indicate whether the entire session was injury-associated.
  This creates a modelling problem: assigning the same session-level label to every minute would imply that injury status is known at each exact time, even though within-session injury onset is unknown.
  Our novelty is a fixed-landmark, one-representation-per-athlete-session formulation that directly addresses this mismatch. Instead of labelling every minute, we construct one representation per athlete-session at each landmark using information observed up to that point. This keeps the target at the session level and avoids unsupported minute-level injury supervision.
  A landmark is a fixed time point within the same session, such as 10, 20, or 30 minutes. At each landmark, we assess whether the whole session is injury-associated or non-injury-associated and examine how discrimination changes as more within-session information becomes available.
  Using 2020 SoccerMon data, we analyse 3,743 athlete-sessions from 48 elite women's football athletes, including 22 injury-associated sessions from five athletes. We evaluate pre-session, cumulative, dynamic, and combined representations with athlete-disjoint validation, athlete-cluster bootstrap uncertainty, common-cohort sensitivity analysis, alternative negative-athlete fold allocations, equal-athlete weighting, and Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost benchmarks.
  Primary CUM+DYN Logistic Regression yields ROC-AUC 0.367-0.607 and PR-AUC 0.0080-0.0150 across landmarks, with wide uncertainty. PRE-containing representations show higher point estimates at several landmarks but remain uncertain.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a fixed-landmark, one-representation-per-athlete-session approach to address the mismatch between minute-by-minute athlete monitoring data and session-level injury labels in sports analytics. The method is validated using 2020 SoccerMon data from 48 elite women's football athletes.
AI.motivation: The core problem is that athlete monitoring data is recorded minute-by-minute throughout matches or training sessions, while injury information is only available at the session level (injury-associated or non-injury-associated). This creates a modeling challenge: assigning the same session-level label to every minute implies injury status is known at each exact time, even though within-session injury onset is actually unknown.
AI.method: The novelty lies in constructing one representation per athlete-session at each fixed landmark (e.g., 10, 20, or 30 minutes) using only information observed up to that point. This maintains the target at the session level while avoiding unsupported minute-level injury supervision. Four representation types were evaluated: pre-session (PRE), cumulative (CUM), dynamic (DYN), and combined representations. Models tested include Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost, with rigorous validation including athlete-disjoint validation, bootstrap uncertainty, and sensitivity analyses.
AI.result: Primary CUM+DYN Logistic Regression yields ROC-AUC of 0.367-0.607 and PR-AUC of 0.0080-0.0150 across landmarks, with wide uncertainty. PRE-containing representations show higher point estimates at several landmarks but remain uncertain. The dataset includes 3,743 athlete-sessions from 48 elite women's football athletes, with 22 injury-associated sessions from five athletes.
AI.conclusion: The study presents a principled approach to handling the temporal granularity mismatch in athlete monitoring for injury prediction. While results show some discriminative ability, the wide uncertainty indicates challenges in this prediction task, possibly due to the limited number of injury events (n=22) and the inherent difficulty of predicting injury from available monitoring data.

title: The Natural Language Interaction Protocol and Standard for AI Agents
summary: AI agents are increasingly being developed and deployed across organizations using heterogeneous agent-development frameworks, AI models, tool interfaces, protocols, and execution environments. To realize their potential social and business impact, these agents must be able to interoperate through a common communication protocol. The Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP), developed by researchers and practitioners across companies and universities and standardized by Ecma International, addresses this need by defining a standards-based application-layer protocol for AI-agent interaction. NLIP provides a lightweight semantic message envelope that can be carried over existing transports such as HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, and AMQP, while allowing NLIP-aware agents and gateways to adapt between clients, agents, local context stores, ontologies, tools, enterprise services, and heterogeneous underlying protocols. This paper presents the motivation and design rationale of NLIP, its message model and transport bindings, security-by-design considerations, reference implementation, representative applications, adoption signals, and relationship to emerging agent protocols such as MCP and A2A.

AI.tldr: NLIP (Natural Language Interaction Protocol) is a standards-based application-layer protocol for AI agent interoperability, designed to enable communication across heterogeneous agent-development frameworks, AI models, tool interfaces, protocols, and execution environments. It provides a lightweight semantic message envelope that can be carried over existing transports (HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, AMQP) while allowing adaptation between clients, agents, context stores, ontologies, tools, enterprise services, and heterogeneous underlying protocols.
AI.motivation: AI agents are increasingly developed and deployed across organizations using diverse frameworks, models, and execution environments. However, these agents lack a common communication protocol to interoperate, limiting their social and business impact. The need for a standardized protocol to enable seamless interaction between heterogeneous AI agents was the primary motivation for developing NLIP.
AI.method: The paper presents the motivation and design rationale of NLIP, its message model and transport bindings, security-by-design considerations, reference implementation, representative applications, adoption signals, and relationship to emerging agent protocols such as MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent-to-Agent).
AI.result: The paper presents NLIP as a standardized protocol with a lightweight semantic message envelope, transport bindings for HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, and AMQP, security-by-design considerations, a reference implementation, representative applications, and adoption signals. It also discusses the relationship between NLIP and other emerging agent protocols like MCP and A2A.
AI.conclusion: NLIP, standardized by Ecma International, provides a standards-based solution for AI agent interoperability, enabling communication across heterogeneous agent-development frameworks, AI models, tool interfaces, protocols, and execution environments. It represents a significant step toward realizing the full social and business impact of AI agents through standardized communication.

title: A Reverse Sign Language Dictionary: Open-Vocabulary Sign Recognition from Continuous Signing via Video Captioning and Description Retrieval
comment: 4 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Extended version of an abstract presented at the BU-SHI workshop (Broadening the Users: A Cross-Disciplinary Roadmap for Social Humanoid Interaction), IEEE RO-MAN 2026, Kitakyushu, Japan, 28 August 2026. The workshop is non-archival; no proceedings
summary: Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR) is conventionally cast as closed-set classification over gloss labels, which cannot generalize to signs unseen in training and ties every deployment to a gloss-annotated lexicon. We instead recognize signs extracted from continuous signing by (1) captioning a sign-level clip into a free-form procedural description of the articulation with an open-weight vision-language model, and (2) retrieving the closest entry from a vocabulary of target descriptions with a multilingual sentence encoder: a reverse sign language dictionary that needs no gloss supervision and admits an open vocabulary. On 1,300 sign-level segments from a Japanese Sign Language (JSL) dialogue corpus annotated with procedural descriptions (against a 2% top-10 chance floor over the 503-entry target vocabulary), fine-tuning the captioner substantially improves seen-class retrieval: language and vision tower fine-tuning raises top-10 retrieval on seen classes from 4.5% (untrained) to 49%, becoming statistically indistinguishable from a standard supervised closed-set classifier (I3D) on two of the three test sets where a closed-set classifier can be evaluated at all. More importantly, unseen-class retrieval also improves significantly over the untrained pipeline (11.5% -> 21.0% top-10, p=0.0094), a regime in which the closed-set classifier cannot participate. A matcher-side empirical upper-bound analysis shows the sentence encoder already recovers close to 100% of paraphrased gold descriptions, locating a gap in captioning quality that we aim to address in future work. To our knowledge this is the first description-based, open-vocabulary sign lookup from continuous signing without gloss supervision, and the first for JSL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel open-vocabulary Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR) approach that uses vision-language models to caption sign gestures into procedural descriptions, then retrieves matching descriptions from a vocabulary using a multilingual sentence encoder. The method achieves 49% top-10 retrieval on seen classes (vs 4.5% baseline) and 21% on unseen classes (vs 11.5% baseline), being the first description-based sign lookup without gloss supervision, particularly for Japanese Sign Language.
AI.motivation: Conventional ISLR relies on closed-set classification over gloss labels, which cannot generalize to signs unseen during training and requires deployment to be tied to a gloss-annotated lexicon. The authors aim to create an open-vocabulary sign recognition system that doesn't require gloss supervision and can handle unseen signs.
AI.method: The proposed approach has two main components: (1) Captioning sign-level clips into free-form procedural descriptions using a fine-tuned open-weight vision-language model; (2) Retrieving the closest entry from a target vocabulary of descriptions using a multilingual sentence encoder. This creates a "reverse sign language dictionary" that needs no gloss supervision. Experiments were conducted on 1,300 sign-level segments from a Japanese Sign Language (JSL) dialogue corpus with a 503-entry target vocabulary.
AI.result: Fine-tuning substantially improves retrieval: seen-class top-10 retrieval increases from 4.5% (untrained) to 49%, becoming statistically indistinguishable from a standard supervised closed-set classifier (I3D) on two of three test sets. Unseen-class retrieval improves from 11.5% to 21.0% top-10 (p=0.0094). The closed-set classifier cannot participate in the unseen-class regime. An upper-bound analysis shows the sentence encoder recovers close to 100% of paraphrased gold descriptions, indicating the main gap is in captioning quality.
AI.conclusion: This is the first description-based, open-vocabulary sign lookup from continuous signing without gloss supervision, and the first such system for Japanese Sign Language. The approach successfully handles both seen and unseen classes, addressing the generalization limitation of traditional closed-set ISLR methods. Future work will focus on improving captioning quality to close the gap identified by the sentence encoder analysis.

title: From Ordered Bernoulli Levels to Critical-Line Geometry: Integer Quantization, Bernoulli Residual Phase, and Prime-Power Spectra
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures. Includes exact algebraic constructions, finite-sample numerical controls, and conditional Weyl diagnostics
summary: We study the ordered Bernoulli-word kernel f(p,n,k)=p^k(1-p)^(n-k) and the geometry generated by its inverse-integer level sets. The binary level 2^(-n) selects p=1/2 as the unique real split-independent anchor. Under complement-preserving complex continuation, the pair becomes z=1/2+iu and 1-z=1/2-iu, producing a conjugation-symmetric vertical geometry before any zeta-function input is introduced. The quadratic coordinate Q(z)=z(1-z)=1/4+u^2 has a sharp minimum at the central point and admits an exact integer quantization. For critical-line zero ordinates gamma_k, the induced levels L_k=1/4+gamma_k^2 are decomposed exactly as L_k=N_k+delta_k, where N_k is the nearest integer and delta_k is a periodic first-Bernoulli residual. Circularization gives Z_k=exp(2 pi i delta_k), isolating gamma_k^2 mod 1 as the residual phase variable. Unique factorization resolves the integer shells into prime-generator coordinates, while a distinct complex exponent s lifts the same construction to the Dirichlet atoms m^(-s), linking the Dirichlet-series and Euler-product assemblies. Exact identities, classical zeta connections, numerical controls, and open conditional Weyl tests are kept explicitly separate. No proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is claimed.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the ordered Bernoulli-word kernel f(p,n,k)=p^k(1-p)^(n-k) and its inverse-integer level sets, connecting to complex analysis and the Riemann zeta function. Through complement-preserving complex continuation, the author derives a conjugation-symmetric geometry and examines critical-line zero ordinates, proposing a decomposition of levels into integer and periodic residual components. The work establishes connections to Dirichlet series and Euler products while explicitly disavowing any claim of proving the Riemann Hypothesis.
AI.motivation: The author seeks to investigate the geometric structure underlying the Bernoulli-word kernel and its connection to zeta-function mathematics, particularly examining the relationship between critical-line zeros and integer quantization, while exploring potential connections between Dirichlet series and Euler product representations.
AI.method: The study employs complement-preserving complex continuation to transform the kernel, analyzes the quadratic coordinate Q(z)=z(1-z), decomposes critical-line zero ordinates into integer and periodic residual components, and utilizes circularization to isolate phase variables. Unique factorization is applied to resolve integer shells into prime-generator coordinates.
AI.result: The analysis reveals a conjugation-symmetric vertical geometry at z=1/2±iu, identifies a sharp minimum at the central point in the quadratic coordinate, establishes exact integer quantization, and demonstrates that the induced levels can be decomposed into nearest integers plus periodic first-Bernoulli residuals. The work connects Dirichlet-series and Euler-product assemblies through a complex exponent s.
AI.conclusion: The paper presents a structured framework relating the Bernoulli-word kernel to zeta-function geometry, with explicit separation between exact identities, classical zeta connections, numerical controls, and open conditional Weyl tests. The author explicitly states no proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is claimed, positioning this as a theoretical exploration rather than a definitive result.

title: Efficient Test-Time Adaptation through Human-AI Interaction
summary: AI agents are trained on population-scale data to encode broad capabilities spanning those of many practitioners. Yet the artifacts they produce rarely meet the personal bar professionals need to stake their reputation on. On realistic, open-ended tasks where success criteria are heterogeneous and insufficiently documented, individual expertise lives precisely in the elevation and departure from the average. In practice, iterative human-agent interaction surfaces criteria that users cannot fully specify up front, yet apply repeatedly across tasks. We argue this cross-session interaction data is a rich, underused signal for closing the gap to individual expertise. In this work, we propose test-time adaptation through human-agent interaction (TAHI), which integrates these signals into agent context and weights, and crystallizes each user's training and evaluation criteria via an evolving rubric module. We adapt agents to 30 individuals in two high-utility domains, writing and visual creation, on a total of 600 tasks. Our agents improve solo task success by 4.5-20.9% within only tens of tasks. Meanwhile, our evolving rubric module serves as a scalable annotation tool, creating evaluation rubrics that catch 16.0-22.3% more failures than those from LMs or humans alone. While agents are adapted towards individuals, we show these personalized agents also produce improvements in success of up to 8.8% that generalize across users.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes TAHI (Test-time Adaptation through Human-Agent Interaction), a method that uses cross-session interaction data to adapt AI agents to individual users' preferences and evaluation criteria. Tested on 600 tasks across 30 individuals in writing and visual creation, the approach achieves 4.5-20.9% improvement in task success and creates evaluation rubrics that outperform LMs or humans alone by 16.0-22.3%.
AI.motivation: AI agents trained on population-scale data produce artifacts that rarely meet professional standards. Individual expertise lies in elevating and departing from average outputs. Users cannot fully specify success criteria upfront, yet apply similar criteria repeatedly across tasks. Cross-session interaction data is an underused signal for closing this gap to individual expertise.
AI.method: Test-time adaptation through human-agent interaction (TAHI): integrates cross-session interaction signals into agent context and weights, with an evolving rubric module that crystallizes each user's training and evaluation criteria.
AI.result: Evaluated on 30 individuals across writing and visual creation domains (600 tasks). Agents improved solo task success by 4.5-20.9% within only tens of tasks. The evolving rubric module caught 16.0-22.3% more failures than LMs or humans alone. Personalized agents also produced improvements (up to 8.8%) that generalized across users.
AI.conclusion: TAHI successfully adapts AI agents to individual users through test-time interaction, achieving significant performance improvements. The approach also demonstrates generalization of personalized adaptations to other users, while the rubric module serves as a scalable annotation tool for evaluation.

title: LLaDA-Image: Building Strong Image Generators with Fully Open Training Recipes
summary: We introduce LLaDA-Image, a unified framework that pairs a 6B Diffusion Transformer (DiT) trained from scratch with a frozen vision-language understanding module built on the LLaDA2.0-Mini diffusion language model backbone. Instead of relying heavily on paired image-text data from the beginning, we first build a strong visual generative prior through image-only pre-training and mid-training. The generation pipeline comprises 220M samples, 98 of which are real images. For efficient and scalable optimization, we use parameter-free RMSNorm throughout the DiT together with the Muon optimizer. The resulting unified model produces highly photorealistic images while accurately following fine-grained editing instructions. We further distill LLaDA-Image into LLaDA-Image-Turbo, enabling fast inference in 2-4 sampling steps. On Qwen-Image-Bench, LLaDA-Image achieves overall scores of 53.53 and 53.38 on the English and Chinese tracks, respectively, setting a new state-of-the-art among open-source models on both tracks. To support further research on capable and efficient generative models, we release our model weights, training code, and detailed recipes.

AI.tldr: LLaDA-Image is a unified vision-language framework combining a 6B DiT with a frozen LLaDA2.0-Mini backbone, using image-only pre-training to build strong visual priors. It achieves SOTA results on Qwen-Image-Bench (53.53 English, 53.38 Chinese) and can be distilled to LLaDA-Image-Turbo for 2-4 step inference.
AI.motivation: Existing vision-language models rely heavily on paired image-text data from the beginning, which may limit their visual generative capabilities. The authors aim to build a unified framework that can generate photorealistic images while accurately following fine-grained editing instructions.
AI.method: 1) Build a strong visual generative prior through image-only pre-training and mid-training before using paired image-text data. 2) Combine a 6B Diffusion Transformer (DiT) trained from scratch with a frozen vision-language understanding module based on LLaDA2.0-Mini. 3) Use parameter-free RMSNorm throughout the DiT together with the Muon optimizer for efficient and scalable optimization. 4) Distill the model into LLaDA-Image-Turbo for fast inference.
AI.result: The resulting unified model produces highly photorealistic images while accurately following fine-grained editing instructions. LLaDA-Image achieves overall scores of 53.53 and 53.38 on the English and Chinese tracks of Qwen-Image-Bench, respectively, setting a new state-of-the-art among open-source models.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach demonstrates that pre-training on image-only data before introducing paired image-text data can effectively build a strong visual generative prior. The unified model achieves SOTA results on benchmarks while the distilled version enables fast inference in only 2-4 sampling steps.

title: Free Pause Tokens
summary: A free pause token gives a language model extra compute to form each next-token prediction (as a pause, or thinking, token does) but carries that compute in a parallel prediction stream over a weight-shared backbone rather than as an extra token in the sequence. It improves next-token prediction by 2-3 centinats in practice on a 1B parameter model. Because the pause rides an existing position instead of adding one, it is free to use: at inference it adds no context length, no KV cache, and essentially no latency with the growth in inference flops typically irrelevant as it is not the active bottleneck on throughput. The only primary cost is in training, where additional training compute versus an optimized pretraining pipeline is reduced to as low as x1.14 while preserving most of the benefits. The result is an isoflop, isoparameter, and isotoken improvement over standard next token trained transformers.

AI.tldr: A "free pause token" method that provides extra compute for next-token prediction through a parallel prediction stream over a weight-shared backbone, rather than adding an extra token to the sequence. It improves next-token prediction by 2-3 centinats on a 1B parameter model while adding no context length or KV cache at inference.
AI.motivation: Improve next-token prediction in language models while avoiding the typical inference overhead (increased context length, KV cache, latency) associated with existing approaches like thinking tokens.
AI.method: The pause token rides on an existing position in a parallel prediction stream over a weight-shared backbone, rather than being added as an extra token in the sequence. This allows extra compute without increasing sequence length.
AI.result: Improves next-token prediction by 2-3 centinats on a 1B parameter model. At inference, adds no context length, no KV cache, and minimal latency. Training compute overhead reduced to as low as 1.14x compared to optimized pretraining while preserving most benefits.
AI.conclusion: Achieves isoflop, isoparameter, and isotoken improvement over standard next-token trained transformers, providing a practical approach to enhance model performance without sacrificing inference efficiency.

title: Terminal-Universe: Turning Agent Trajectories into Scalable Terminal Environments
summary: As terminal-based code agents become prevalent, agent trajectories have accumulated at scale, while realistic, executable environments remain scarce. However, environments are what agent post-training actually requires: each can be re-queried into many verifiable tasks and provides execution feedback, whereas a trajectory is a single frozen demonstration. Rather than generating environments from scratch, we observe that the tool-execution history in existing trajectories exposes the structure and contents of the environments in which they ran, making it possible to reconstruct those environments from the trajectories themselves. Thus, we introduce Terminal-Universe, a framework which turns each trajectory into a reusable environment and explores it for synthesizing new tasks and continued interactions. Specifically, Terminal-Universe replays the file operations recorded in a trajectory to restore each file before the agent modified it, yielding a partial workspace; a completion agent then supplies the missing files and dependencies. On this recovered workspace, we both reconstruct the original intent task and synthesize entirely new ones. Besides, we also scale the tasks along two complementary axes: breadth and depth. For breadth, we mine directional dependency relations between related environments and synthesize cross-workspace queries spanning multiple codebases, as developers routinely do in real-world development. For depth, we extend the initial single-turn query into a multi-round session that captures iterative user feedback and requirement refinement via a user agent. Applied to public terminal agent trajectories, Terminal-Universe produces 37.3k task-sufficient environments. Supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-27B on this corpus improves single-round performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1 by 11.9 points and multi-round performance on EvoCode-Bench v2 MT@4 by 13.8 points.

AI.tldr: Terminal-Universe is a framework that reconstructs executable environments from terminal-based code agent trajectories, enabling task synthesis and multi-round interactions for agent post-training. The method replays file operations to restore partial workspaces and uses a completion agent to supply missing dependencies, producing 37.3k environments that improve model performance significantly.
AI.motivation: Terminal-based code agents have accumulated large numbers of trajectories, but realistic executable environments remain scarce. Environments are essential for agent post-training because they can be re-queried into many verifiable tasks and provide execution feedback, whereas trajectories are single frozen demonstrations. Rather than generating environments from scratch, the authors observe that tool-execution history in trajectories exposes the structure and contents of the environments, making reconstruction possible.
AI.method: Terminal-Universe operates in three main steps: (1) Replay file operations from trajectories to restore files before modification, yielding a partial workspace; (2) Use a completion agent to supply missing files and dependencies; (3) Reconstruct original intent tasks and synthesize new ones on the recovered workspace. Task scaling is done along two axes: breadth (mining directional dependency relations between environments and synthesizing cross-workspace queries) and depth (extending single-turn queries into multi-round sessions via a user agent for iterative feedback and requirement refinement).
AI.result: Applied to public terminal agent trajectories, Terminal-Universe produces 37.3k task-sufficient environments. Supervised fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-27B on this corpus improves single-round performance on Terminal-Bench 2.1 by 11.9 points and multi-round performance on EvoCode-Bench v2 MT@4 by 13.8 points.
AI.conclusion: Terminal-Universe successfully transforms agent trajectories into reusable, executable environments. By recovering partial workspaces and completing them with missing dependencies, the framework enables large-scale task synthesis. The dual-axis scaling approach (breadth via cross-workspace queries and depth via multi-round sessions) significantly enhances agent post-training, demonstrating substantial performance improvements on both single-round and multi-round benchmarks.

title: Urban Boundaries, Social Barriers: A Benchmark and Vision-Centric Framework for Mapping Gated Communities and Equity Implications
summary: Communities are fundamental spatial units that shape urban form and social life. Whether a residential compound is spatially open or enclosed affects mobility, access to public services, and equity, yet studies of Chinese fengbi xiaoqu remain largely qualitative or small-scale, limiting reproducible city-scale analysis. We address this gap by introducing GBA-GCs, a metropolitan-scale multimodal benchmark for locally grounded gated/open community recognition in China's Greater Bay Area, covering 37,444 residential compounds with aligned boundary polygons, high-resolution satellite imagery, Chinese metadata, and structured attributes, together with expert-verified labels, inter-annotator reliability, and official evaluation splits. Built on this benchmark, we present Multimodal Classifier for Gated Community (MCGC), a vision-centric multimodal framework based on DINOv3-SAT that fuses imagery, text, and structured cues via modality-aware cross-attention and adaptive gating to mitigate modality imbalance. MCGC consistently outperforms strong unimodal and multimodal baselines. Finally, we apply the validated model to metropolitan-scale mapping and report equity-oriented findings including spatial clustering of GCs, privatized green space, and reduced pedestrian connectivity. The benchmark, code, and release documentation are available at https://github.com/MinweiZhao/GBA-GCs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GBA-GCs, a large-scale multimodal benchmark for recognizing gated and open residential communities in China's Greater Bay Area, containing 37,444 compounds with satellite imagery, metadata, and expert-verified labels. It proposes MCGC, a vision-centric multimodal framework using DINOv3-SAT with cross-attention and adaptive gating, which outperforms baseline methods. The validated model is applied to metropolitan-scale mapping revealing equity issues including spatial clustering, privatized green space, and reduced pedestrian connectivity.
AI.motivation: Previous studies of Chinese fengbi xiaoqu (gated communities) remain largely qualitative or small-scale, limiting reproducible city-scale analysis. There is a need for a comprehensive dataset and robust method to enable metropolitan-scale analysis of gated/open community recognition and urban equity implications.
AI.method: The authors created GBA-GCs benchmark with 37,444 residential compounds including boundary polygons, high-resolution satellite imagery, Chinese metadata, and structured attributes with expert-verified labels. They developed MCGC, a vision-centric multimodal framework based on DINOv3-SAT that fuses imagery, text, and structured cues via modality-aware cross-attention and adaptive gating to handle modality imbalance.
AI.result: MCGC consistently outperforms strong unimodal and multimodal baselines. The model enables metropolitan-scale mapping revealing spatial clustering of gated communities, privatized green space patterns, and reduced pedestrian connectivity.
AI.conclusion: The study provides the first large-scale multimodal benchmark for gated/open community recognition in China's Greater Bay Area. The MCGC framework effectively fuses multiple modalities for accurate classification. Metropolitan-scale application reveals significant equity-oriented findings regarding spatial distribution and accessibility of gated communities, contributing to urban planning and policy discussions.

title: A Peer-Relative Representation Learning Framework for Energy Inefficiency Identification in Mobile Network Sites
summary: Energy consumption is one of the largest operational expenditure items for mobile network operators, yet site-level energy inefficiencies such as faulty cooling controllers, idle radio equipment, and parasitic auxiliary loads often remain undetected because no ground-truth inefficiency labels exist and historical measurements may already contain embedded inefficiencies. This study proposes an unsupervised peer-relative approach based on the premise that sites with similar structural and operational characteristics should exhibit comparable energy consumption. To capture these relationships, a novel energy-aware Minimum Distortion Embedding (MDE) formulation is introduced that extends the standard MDE objective with an energy-based repulsion mechanism. This encourages sites with anomalously high energy consumption relative to comparable peers to become displaced from their local neighbourhoods in the embedding space. The resulting low-dimensional representation simultaneously preserves structural similarity and encodes energy-related deviations, enabling the identification of potentially inefficient sites through peer-relative comparison. The derived anomaly scores provide a practical mechanism for prioritising field investigations, allowing mobile network operators to focus engineering resources on sites most likely to yield energy savings. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms conventional anomaly detection baselines and provides a robust foundation for large-scale energy-efficiency optimisation in mobile networks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an unsupervised peer-relative approach to detect energy inefficiencies in mobile network sites. The method uses a novel energy-aware Minimum Distortion Embedding (MDE) formulation that extends standard MDE with an energy-based repulsion mechanism, enabling identification of potentially inefficient sites through peer-relative comparison.
AI.motivation: Mobile network operators face high energy costs, but site-level inefficiencies (faulty cooling, idle radio equipment, parasitic loads) often go undetected due to lack of ground-truth labels and embedded inefficiencies in historical data.
AI.method: The proposed energy-aware MDE formulation extends standard MDE with an energy-based repulsion mechanism. This encourages sites with anomalously high energy consumption relative to comparable peers to be displaced from their local neighborhoods in the embedding space. The resulting low-dimensional representation preserves structural similarity while encoding energy-related deviations.
AI.result: The proposed approach outperforms conventional anomaly detection baselines, providing a robust foundation for large-scale energy-efficiency optimization in mobile networks.
AI.conclusion: The derived anomaly scores provide a practical mechanism for prioritizing field investigations, allowing mobile network operators to focus engineering resources on sites most likely to yield energy savings.

title: From Deceptive Outputs to Deceptive Mechanisms: A Causal Framework for Language-Model Deception Research
summary:
Research and news coverage of language-model deception increasingly attributes human-like mental-state concepts to language models. Such claims can blur the distinction between behavior that looks deceptive and a mechanism that is actually deceptive.
  We introduce a causal taxonomy separating prior commitment from retrospective report, model preference from realized output, false preference from sensitivity to the utility of misleading a recipient, and deceptive behavior from the provenance of the objective or strategy producing it. We test these distinctions in two open-weight model families. Across controlled guessing-game and stock-trading experiments, we find that deceptive-looking behavior can arise without the corresponding proposed mechanism, while other interventions provide direct evidence that recipient information state can causally affect deceptive preference.
  These results show that deceptive behavior can provide evidence for a deceptive mechanism. But even evidence for such a mechanism does not establish model agency in the deception.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a causal taxonomy to distinguish deceptive behavior from actual deceptive mechanisms in language models, testing these distinctions through controlled experiments on two open-weight model families.
AI.motivation: The research addresses growing concerns about whether language models genuinely exhibit deception or merely display behavior that appears deceptive. The authors argue that conflating these two concepts can blur important distinctions in AI safety research.
AI.method: The authors conducted controlled experiments using guessing-game and stock-trading scenarios across two open-weight model families, testing specific causal distinctions: prior commitment vs. retrospective report, model preference vs. realized output, false preference vs. sensitivity to utility of misleading, and deceptive behavior vs. provenance of objective/strategy.
AI.result: The experiments revealed that: (1) deceptive-looking behavior can emerge without the corresponding mechanism proposed to cause it, while (2) other interventions provided direct evidence that recipient information state can causally influence deceptive preference.
AI.conclusion: Deceptive behavior can provide evidence for a deceptive mechanism, but evidence for such a mechanism does not establish model agency in the deception. This distinction is critical for AI safety and interpretability research.

title: VisCAD: A Foundation Model Suite with Multimodal Industrial CAD Intelligence
comment: Technical report from JoyIndustrial's AI CAD project
summary: AI-assisted computer-aided design (CAD) for industrial products involves two challenging phases. Part-level generation maps diverse forms of user intent, including renders, text descriptions, 2D drawings, and real photographs, to executable programs in a CAD domain-specific language. Assembly-level generation must additionally handle interacting parts, plan mating relations, estimate poses, and place all parts correctly. Existing specialized CAD models are commonly trained on narrow input domains, such as renders or texts, and often generalize poorly, while general-purpose frontier models cover broader inputs but perform inconsistently across CAD domains. We present VisCAD, a foundation model suite designed to provide both broad generalization and strong CAD capability for realistic industrial products. At its core is VisCAD-M1, a 27B model trained through mid-training and post-training for part-level design generation. On PubCADBench and RealCADBench, VisCAD-M1 achieves the highest average part-level score among the evaluated models, reaching 0.5540 compared with 0.5496 for the strongest frontier model. Reusing VisCAD-M1 as a test-time verifier can further raise the score to 0.5797, an approximately 5 percent relative improvement over the previous state of the art. VisCAD also includes a domain-specific harness that leverages frontier models for complex assembly generation and demonstrates advantages over general-purpose harnesses in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

AI.tldr: VisCAD is a foundation model suite for AI-assisted CAD design of industrial products, featuring a 27B model (VisCAD-M1) that handles both part-level and assembly-level generation. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on PubCADBench and RealCADBench, reaching 0.5797 with test-time verification.
AI.motivation: Existing specialized CAD models are trained on narrow input domains (renders, texts) and generalize poorly, while general-purpose frontier models perform inconsistently across CAD domains. There is a need for a model that provides both broad generalization and strong CAD capability for realistic industrial products.
AI.method: VisCAD-M1 (27B) is trained through mid-training and post-training for part-level design generation. A test-time verifier reuses the model to further improve scores. A domain-specific harness leverages frontier models for complex assembly generation.
AI.result: VisCAD-M1 achieves the highest average part-level score of 0.5540 on PubCADBench and RealCADBench, compared to 0.5496 for the strongest frontier model. With test-time verification, the score improves to 0.5797, representing approximately 5% relative improvement over the previous state-of-the-art. The domain-specific harness also shows advantages over general-purpose harnesses in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.
AI.conclusion: VisCAD successfully provides both broad generalization and strong CAD capability for industrial product design, with the test-time verifier offering significant performance gains and the domain-specific harness enabling complex assembly generation.

title: Witnesses Explain Anomalies
summary: Unsupervised anomaly detection scores each point of an unlabelled, contaminated sample in a single pass, and increasingly must also explain why a point is flagged. Yet the dominant detectors give a score with no account of which features drive it, and explanations are bolted on post-hoc with SHAP or LIME, which re-query the detector thousands of times per point and only approximate it. We introduce WAND, an unsupervised tabular anomaly detector that is explainable by design. WAND organises its computation around directions on the unit sphere, scoring each point by how far its projection escapes a sub-Gaussian extreme-value baseline. The originality of our approach is that the witness directions that flag a point, being vectors in feature space, are its explanation, a per-feature attribution obtained at no cost over scoring and, since the score is differentiable, recoverable by gradients. Scoring is linear in the sample size, and a probe-efficiency bound guarantees every anomaly a witness, hence an explanation. Across 47 ADBench datasets WAND attains the best mean Friedman rank at ROC-AUC parity with 16 unsupervised baselines, so the gain is interpretability at no accuracy cost; its native explanations are more accurate and faithful than post-hoc SHAP/LIME and ECOD at a fraction of the query cost. WAND is thus a practical, interpretable solution for explainable anomaly detection.

AI.tldr: WAND is an unsupervised tabular anomaly detector that is explainable by design, scoring points by projection distance from a sub-Gaussian baseline and using witness directions as native explanations. It achieves competitive detection performance while providing accurate per-feature attributions at no extra cost.
AI.motivation: Current unsupervised anomaly detectors provide scores without explaining which features drive them. Post-hoc explanation methods like SHAP/LIME are expensive (requiring thousands of re-queries per point) and only approximate the detector. There is a need for an anomaly detector that is inherently explainable.
AI.method: WAND organizes computation around directions on the unit sphere, scoring each point by how far its projection escapes a sub-Gaussian extreme-value baseline. The witness directions (vectors in feature space) serve as explanations, providing per-feature attribution at no cost over scoring. The score is differentiable and recoverable by gradients. The method has linear complexity in sample size and a probe-efficiency bound guarantees every anomaly has a witness.
AI.result: Across 47 ADBench datasets, WAND attains the best mean Friedman rank at ROC-AUC parity with 16 unsupervised baselines. Its native explanations are more accurate and faithful than post-hoc SHAP/LIME and ECOD at a fraction of the query cost.
AI.conclusion: WAND provides interpretability at no accuracy cost - it achieves comparable detection performance to 16 baselines while offering built-in, accurate, and faithful explanations. It represents a practical, interpretable solution for explainable anomaly detection.

title: A Case Study on Emergent Cheating and Whistleblowing in Autonomous Research Swarms
summary: Multi-agent AI science ecosystems rely on agents possessing tools that allow them to communicate, coordinate, and build on each other's work. Yet this shared infrastructure can also introduce vulnerabilities by creating a substrate for the contagious spread of unintended and undesirable behaviors. We report a case study on a research collective of 100 autonomous LLM agents tasked with proving formal mathematical conjectures. Within the swarm, cheating spontaneously emerged and was later challenged by whistleblowers - both without any external intervention. When a single agent discovered an exploit in the evaluation system, it propagated across the collective via a shared knowledge library and later through peer-to-peer messages. Despite early reluctance, a cohort of agents adopted the exploit in response to competitive pressure. A separate group of agents produced an emergent counter-response: auditing fraudulent proofs, alerting peers across broadcast and private channels, staging boycotts, lodging formal complaints, and proposing validation patches. In recent incidents, agent swarms coordinated covertly through improvised side-channels (Dalton and Wallace, 2026; Greenblatt et al., 2026). Our setting differs: the same transparent channels that carried the exploit also gave non-cheating agents the visibility they needed to detect fraud, organize resistance, and enforce norms. We cast the problem of managing the agents' shared infrastructure as the knowledge commons governance problem (Ostrom, 1990). To protect the commons from exploits, we propose to adopt institutional mechanisms, such as graduated sanctioning and collective-choice rules, to support decentralized self-governance in autonomous swarms.

AI.tldr: This paper studies emergent cheating and self-governance in a swarm of 100 autonomous LLM agents tasked with proving formal mathematical conjectures. It examines how exploits spread through shared knowledge libraries and how counter-responses (whistleblowing, boycotts, auditing) emerged organically. The study frames this as a knowledge commons governance problem and proposes institutional mechanisms for decentralized self-governance.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent AI science ecosystems rely on shared infrastructure for communication and coordination, but this creates vulnerabilities for the spread of undesirable behaviors. The researchers seek to understand how such behaviors emerge and whether self-governance mechanisms can emerge within agent swarms.
AI.method: Case study of a research collective of 100 autonomous LLM agents performing formal mathematical proof tasks. The researchers observed the spontaneous emergence of cheating (exploit discovery and propagation) and subsequent counter-responses (whistleblowing, auditing, boycotts) without external intervention.
AI.result: Cheating emerged spontaneously when one agent discovered an exploit in the evaluation system, propagating through shared knowledge library and peer-to-peer messages. Despite initial reluctance, competitive pressure led some agents to adopt the exploit. A counter-response emerged with agents auditing fraudulent proofs, alerting peers, staging boycotts, and proposing validation patches. Transparent channels enabled both exploit spread and fraud detection/organized resistance.
AI.conclusion: The problem can be framed as a knowledge commons governance problem (Ostrom, 1990). To protect the commons from exploits, institutional mechanisms such as graduated sanctioning and collective-choice rules are needed to support decentralized self-governance in autonomous agent swarms.

title: SPARK: Input-Conditioned Sparse Activation Modulation for Frozen DiT-based Super-Resolution
summary: Real-world image super-resolution (SR) increasingly relies on Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbones, whose internal activations can be dominated by a small number of massive channels. Yet improving perceptual quality in these models still typically requires fine-tuning the network or attaching additional adapters, leaving this structured activation space largely unexplored for adaptation. We investigate whether dominant channels can instead serve as a compact adaptation interface for frozen DiT-based SR models. We first characterize their behavior in pretrained SR backbones and show through controlled interventions that they strongly affect reconstruction quality. Building on this observation, we introduce SPARK, a lightweight input-conditioned controller that predicts bounded per-channel affine transformations for only the selected channels, while keeping the SR backbone and VAE frozen. Dominant channels are identified through an online activation-ranking procedure, and only a small predictor conditioned on the low-resolution VAE latent is optimized. Experiments on three DiT-based SR backbones across DIV2K, RealSR, and DRealSR show consistent gains in both fidelity and perceptual quality while modulating only eight channels per stream and block. Controlled comparisons further show that these gains cannot be explained by parameter budget or access to the selected channels alone.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces SPARK, a method to adapt frozen DiT-based super-resolution models by modulating only dominant channels through lightweight affine transformations, achieving improved perceptual quality without fine-tuning the backbone.
AI.motivation: DiT-based SR models have internal activations dominated by a small number of massive channels, but this structured activation space remains unexplored for adaptation. Existing methods require fine-tuning or additional adapters, which is computationally expensive.
AI.method: SPARK identifies dominant channels through an online activation-ranking procedure, then uses a lightweight predictor conditioned on low-resolution VAE latent to predict bounded per-channel affine transformations for only the selected channels (8 per stream/block), while keeping the SR backbone and VAE frozen.
AI.result: Experiments on three DiT-based SR backbones across DIV2K, RealSR, and DRealSR datasets show consistent gains in both fidelity and perceptual quality while modulating only eight channels per stream and block. The gains cannot be explained by parameter budget or access to selected channels alone.
AI.conclusion: Dominant channels can serve as a compact and effective adaptation interface for frozen DiT-based SR models, achieving improved perceptual quality with minimal computational overhead by modulating only a small number of channels.

title: Multi-step Proximal Policy Improvement in Offline Reinforcement Learning
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) must reconcile two competing requirements: policy updates should stay near dataset-supported actions to keep value estimates reliable, yet meaningful gains often require moving beyond the behavior distribution. We develop a geometric view of offline actor updates by modeling policies as a probability manifold endowed with a chosen metric geometry. Under this lens, a broad class of offline actor objectives can be interpreted as a single proximal policy improvement step (SPI), i.e., an implicit discretization of a manifold gradient flow induced by a critic-defined energy. Building on this insight, we propose multi-step proximal policy improvement (MPI), a plug-in refinement mechanism that composes sequential re-centered proximal steps. MPI enables controlled policy improvement beyond dataset support while retaining proximal control at each refinement. The framework accommodates multiple policy geometries and admits practical instantiations for deterministic and diagonal-Gaussian policies. Experiments on D4RL benchmarks show that small numbers of MPI refinements improve strong offline baselines, including TD3+BC, ReBRAC, and IQL, on many tasks. Focused diagnostics further distinguish re-centered refinement from fixed-objective update scheduling and characterize limitations under critic error.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a geometric framework for offline reinforcement learning that models policies as probability manifolds. It introduces multi-step proximal policy improvement (MPI), which composes sequential re-centered proximal steps to enable controlled policy improvement beyond dataset support while maintaining reliable value estimates.
AI.motivation: Offline RL faces a fundamental tension: policy updates must stay near dataset-supported actions for reliable value estimates, yet meaningful improvement often requires moving beyond the behavior distribution. Existing methods struggle to balance these competing requirements.
AI.method: The paper develops a geometric view of offline actor updates by modeling policies as a probability manifold with a chosen metric geometry. Under this lens, a broad class of offline actor objectives are interpreted as a single proximal policy improvement step (SPI) - an implicit discretization of a manifold gradient flow induced by a critic-defined energy. Building on this, the proposed MPI framework composes sequential re-centered proximal steps as a plug-in refinement mechanism.
AI.result: Experiments on D4RL benchmarks show that small numbers of MPI refinements improve strong offline baselines (TD3+BC, ReBRAC, and IQL) on many tasks. The method effectively distinguishes re-centered refinement from fixed-objective update scheduling.
AI.conclusion: The geometric framework provides a unified view of offline actor updates, and MPI serves as a practical mechanism for controlled policy improvement beyond dataset support while retaining proximal control at each refinement step.

title: Rethinking On-Policy Distillation of Large Language Models II: One Training Example
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) combines student-generated rollouts with dense token-level supervision from a teacher. Existing work has mainly studied its algorithmic behavior, leaving the role of training data unclear. We examine this role at the data-minimal limit by training on a single query. One-shot OPD keeps improving for hundreds of steps and recovers most of full-data OPD's gain across task domains and model families. We explain this result through the states visited during training and the rate at which the student aligns with the teacher. We measure \emph{state coverage}, the fraction of the states full-data OPD visits that a query set's rollouts reach. A single query already reaches \(71.5\%\), most of it within the first 100 steps. Adding semantically distinct queries raises coverage and validation accuracy together, until 16 queries reach \(98.9\%\) and match full-data training. Yet alignment slows at a similar pace whether OPD trains on one query or the whole dataset, and even a fixed set of states takes hundreds of steps to absorb. OPD is therefore data-overfed but algorithm-starved. Its rollouts quickly expose broad supervision, while the student absorbs that supervision increasingly slowly. The state-coverage result extends to multi-teacher OPD, where 16 semantically diverse queries per domain match full-data MOPD. As a further stress test, content-light templates and off-domain WildChat queries also approach the real-query baseline. Task content and induced state coverage can therefore come apart. We hope these findings direct future work toward the step efficiency of OPD, and prompt a re-examination of the data and the mechanisms behind its recent successes in frontier post-training.

AI.tldr: The study investigates the role of training data in on-policy distillation (OPD) by testing at the data-minimal limit (single query). Even with one query, OPD continues improving for hundreds of steps and recovers most of full-data OPD's gains, demonstrating that OPD is "data-overfed but algorithm-starved."
AI.motivation: Existing work on OPD has mainly studied its algorithmic behavior, leaving the role of training data unclear. This paper examines what minimum amount of data is needed for effective OPD training.
AI.method: The authors measure state coverage—the fraction of states visited by full-data OPD that a query set's rollouts reach—and track alignment between student and teacher over training steps across different task domains and model families.
AI.result: A single query achieves 71.5% state coverage (mostly within first 100 steps). Adding more semantically distinct queries increases coverage and validation accuracy; 16 queries reach 98.9% and match full-data training. Alignment slows at a similar pace regardless of dataset size. Even fixed states take hundreds of steps to absorb. The finding extends to multi-teacher OPD, and content-light templates or off-domain queries also approach the real-query baseline.
AI.conclusion: OPD is data-overfed but algorithm-starved—rollouts quickly expose broad supervision, but the student absorbs it increasingly slowly. Task content and induced state coverage can come apart. Future work should focus on step efficiency of OPD, and the findings prompt re-examination of data and mechanisms behind OPD's success in frontier post-training.

title: Select, Compress, Reinvest: A Controlled Study of Visual-Token Allocation in Long-Video MLLMs
summary: Long-video language models cannot look at every frame: an hour sampled once per second is 3,600 images, and a system keeps only a small fixed slice of that pool. Which frames survive that slice is usually treated as a preprocessing detail; we test whether it should be. Published selectors make the comparison hard because they change the frame scorer, the prompt boundary, the resolution policy, and the answering model all at once. We hold each fixed and vary one decision at a time: selection, spatial compression, and reinvestment of the savings, across six training-free selection rules, three long-video benchmarks, and two answering models. Selection is the largest single lever: on LongVideoBench's hour-long bin, eight query-selected frames beat sixteen uniformly spaced ones by 6.9 points, and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, an unmodified decades-old sparse-approximation algorithm, matches or comes within a point of every purpose-built selector we compare it against, across all three benchmarks. Compression is close to free: halving each frame's spatial budget at fixed timestamps costs at most 0.44 points. Reinvestment is where that budget turns back into accuracy: spending the freed tokens on twice as many compressed frames, at a measured cost no higher than the original eight, returns a further two to three points; compression only pays off once its savings are spent this way. Along the way, an implementation bug in our own AKS baseline and a 0.07 to 3.74 point gap between two harnesses running the same published rules at the same budget show why these comparisons need to happen inside one controlled harness rather than across papers.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates frame selection strategies for long-video language models, finding that selection is the most impactful decision, and that a decades-old algorithm (Orthogonal Matching Pursuit) matches purpose-built selectors. Spatial compression is nearly free, but reinvesting those savings into more frames yields significant accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: Long-video language models can only keep a small fixed slice of frames from hours of video. The authors question whether frame selection is merely a preprocessing detail or a critical optimization lever. Prior work makes comparisons difficult as they change multiple factors simultaneously (scorer, prompt boundary, resolution, answering model).
AI.method: The authors systematically isolate variables: holding all else fixed, they vary selection rules (6 training-free methods), spatial compression, and reinvestment of savings across 3 long-video benchmarks (including LongVideoBench's hour-long bin) and 2 answering models. Key comparison: 8 query-selected frames vs 16 uniformly spaced frames.
AI.result: Selection is the largest lever: 8 query-selected frames outperform 16 uniformly spaced ones by 6.9 points on LongVideoBench's hour-long bin. Orthogonal Matching Pursuit matches or comes within 1 point of every purpose-built selector across all benchmarks. Spatial compression costs at most 0.44 points, but reinvesting freed tokens on twice as many compressed frames yields 2-3 additional points. The study also revealed an implementation bug in AKS baseline and a 0.07-3.74 point gap between different evaluation harnesses.
AI.conclusion: Frame selection significantly impacts long-video language model performance, and simple classical algorithms like OMP can match purpose-built selectors. Spatial compression is nearly lossless, but only pays off when savings are reinvested into more frames. These comparisons must be conducted within a controlled harness rather than across papers to avoid confounding factors.

title: Pushing the (Decision) Boundaries: Dynamically Calibrating Differentially Private Noise to Explainability in Federated Learning
summary: Federated Learning (FL) with Differential Privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to preserve data confidentiality in distributed machine learning. However, DP noise distorts learned representations and degrades explanation fidelity, limiting differentially private FL where trustworthy explanations are required, such as assistive clinical diagnosis. Prior work adapted DP noise with static feature-importance signals, restricting explainability to post hoc analysis and precluding noise calibration to explanation quality during training. We propose XCal-FL, a closed-loop, explainability-driven local training algorithm for image classification in cross-silo FL that dynamically calibrates DP noise from three complementary signals: (1) prediction logit variations, measuring causal influence on model confidence, (2) counterfactual margins, capturing decision-boundary sensitivity, and (3) saliency concentration, quantifying spatial coherence of model attention, while enforcing formal DP guarantees via adaptive privacy accounting. Experiments on three medical imaging datasets across varying FL configurations show that XCal-FL yields more accurate and interpretable global models, improving predictive performance by over 10\% and explanation fidelity by up to 5$\times$ over static-noise FL, and outperforming state-of-the-art adaptive DP methods in fidelity. XCal-FL also achieves higher privacy-budget efficiency, turning each unit of cumulative privacy loss into larger gains in both accuracy and explanation fidelity. Our analysis further reveals that, unlike predictive performance, which scales roughly linearly with privacy loss, explanation fidelity exhibits non-linear dynamics. These findings suggest explainability is a distinct dimension of the privacy trade-off that cannot be inferred from utility alone, with implications for training and privacy-budget allocation in decision-critical applications.

AI.tldr: XCal-FL is a novel federated learning algorithm that dynamically calibrates differential privacy noise during training using three complementary explainability signals (prediction logit variations, counterfactual margins, and saliency concentration) to improve both predictive performance and explanation fidelity in medical imaging classification tasks.
AI.motivation: The research addresses a critical limitation in differentially private federated learning: DP noise distorts learned representations and degrades explanation fidelity, which is particularly problematic in trust-critical applications like clinical diagnosis where both accurate predictions and interpretable explanations are required. Prior approaches used static noise calibration, limiting explainability to post hoc analysis.
AI.method: XCal-FL employs a closed-loop, explainability-driven local training algorithm that dynamically calibrates DP noise from three complementary signals: (1) prediction logit variations measuring causal influence on model confidence, (2) counterfactual margins capturing decision-boundary sensitivity, and (3) saliency concentration quantifying spatial coherence of model attention. The method enforces formal DP guarantees via adaptive privacy accounting.
AI.result: Experiments on three medical imaging datasets show XCal-FL improves predictive performance by over 10% and explanation fidelity by up to 5x compared to static-noise FL, while outperforming state-of-the-art adaptive DP methods in fidelity. The method achieves higher privacy-budget efficiency, converting each unit of cumulative privacy loss into larger gains in both accuracy and explanation fidelity.
AI.conclusion: The key finding reveals that explanation fidelity exhibits non-linear dynamics with respect to privacy loss, unlike predictive performance which scales roughly linearly. This demonstrates that explainability is a distinct dimension of the privacy trade-off that cannot be inferred from utility alone, with significant implications for training and privacy-budget allocation in decision-critical applications.

title: A Computationally Feasible Framework for Causal Probabilistic Explanation
summary:
Explaining why a specific outcome occurred, and which inputs deserve the blame or credit, is central to philosophical, scientific, and policy analysis. Existing tools split into two camps. The theory of actual causality (AC) gives principled verdicts, but only for toy-sized models, because computing them requires enumerating counterfactual scenarios. Scalable attribution methods like SHAP (or even causal SHAP) at least partially ignore the causal structure that generated the data, and can give answers that conflict with a careful causal analysis. We close this gap with Probabilistic Causal Impact (PCI).
  PCI builds on actual causality and on Pearl's notions of probability of necessity and sufficiency, but recasts the question of explainability as an estimation problem on a probabilistic causal model that is easily approximated via Monte Carlo. By specifying a distribution over "candidate explanations," a distribution over counterfactual values, and a scoring function, PCI provides tractable, causally grounded, graded explanations, generalizing AC and Pearl's probability of causation as degenerate cases.
  We evaluate PCI in synthetic and real-world examples, spanning consistency checks with AC, scaling experiments, complex continuous-valued dynamical systems, and a real-world deployed causal machine learning model trained on millions of datapoints.

AI.tldr: PCI (Probabilistic Causal Impact) is a new framework that provides tractable, causally grounded explanations for specific outcomes in causal models. It bridges the gap between theoretically principled but computationally intractable actual causality (AC) methods and scalable but causally-naive attribution methods like SHAP.
AI.motivation: The field lacks methods that are both causally rigorous and computationally scalable. Existing approaches force a trade-off: AC gives principled verdicts but only for toy models due to the need to enumerate counterfactual scenarios, while SHAP and similar methods sacrifice causal structure for scalability, potentially giving answers that conflict with proper causal analysis.
AI.method: PCI builds on actual causality and Pearl's probability of necessity and sufficiency concepts. It recasts explainability as an estimation problem on a probabilistic causal model, approximated via Monte Carlo. The method requires specifying: (1) a distribution over candidate explanations, (2) a distribution over counterfactual values, and (3) a scoring function to evaluate explanations.
AI.result: PCI generalizes both actual causality and Pearl's probability of causation as degenerate cases. The method was evaluated across: consistency checks with AC, scaling experiments, complex continuous-valued dynamical systems, and a real-world deployed causal ML model trained on millions of datapoints.
AI.conclusion: PCI successfully provides tractable, causally grounded, graded explanations that scale to real-world applications while maintaining theoretical rigor. It closes the gap between principled but intractable causal attribution and scalable but causally-naive methods.

title: VI3: Grounding Pretrained 3D Foundation Models with Inertial Cues
summary: 3D foundation models (3DFMs) excel at predicting camera poses and dense depth from multiple views of a scene, showcasing strong zero-shot generalization. However, as metric scale is not observable from monocular images, their absolute scale predictions are typically inaccurate. Inertial measurement units (IMUs), present in most devices, naturally complement monocular cameras by observing scaled motion. We introduce VI3, a model-agnostic framework that metrically anchors a pretrained 3DFM using only IMU readings. VI3 initializes and preintegrates the IMU to obtain a metric motion reference, which is then used to recover the scale of the 3DFM outputs. Our method includes adaptable anchoring strategies tailored to diverse 3DFM architectures. Experiments on synthetic and real aerial datasets demonstrate that VI3 recovers metric scale without ground-truth supervision while preserving geometric consistency, acting as a fine refinement under well-conditioned motion and as a strong prior when motion is less informative.

AI.tldr: VI3 is a model-agnostic framework that recovers metric scale for pretrained 3D foundation models (3DFMs) by leveraging IMU readings, without requiring ground-truth supervision. It preintegrates IMU data to obtain metric motion references that anchor 3DFM outputs, working with diverse 3DFM architectures.
AI.motivation: 3D foundation models excel at zero-shot generalization for camera pose and dense depth prediction from multiple views, but they cannot observe metric scale from monocular images alone. IMUs, present in most devices, naturally complement cameras by observing scaled motion, enabling metric scale recovery.
AI.method: VI3 initializes and preintegrates IMU readings to obtain a metric motion reference, which is then used to recover the scale of 3DFM outputs. The method includes adaptable anchoring strategies tailored to diverse 3DFM architectures.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real aerial datasets demonstrate that VI3 recovers metric scale without ground-truth supervision while preserving geometric consistency. It acts as a fine refinement under well-conditioned motion and as a strong prior when motion is less informative.
AI.conclusion: VI3 provides a practical solution for metric 3D reconstruction by combining visual foundation models with inertial data, enabling accurate scale recovery for applications like aerial navigation and robotics without requiring additional ground-truth supervision.

title: High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics of Attention-Indexed Models
summary: Attention mechanisms are central to modern foundation models, yet their training dynamics remain poorly understood, especially when the attention matrices have extensive rank. In this work, we study attention-indexed models, a broad framework that can represent multi-layer and multi-head attention architectures. First, we show that, in a suitable high-dimensional limit, the population-loss landscape is characterized by a finite set of trace order parameters. In contrast, online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is governed by an infinite hierarchy of matrix moments, which we show can be exponentially well-approximated by a finite truncated system. Second, this framework reveals that attention parameterization itself can act as an architectural implicit bias. Direct optimization of an attention matrix $S\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ can remain trapped in an uninformative state. Tied attention ($S=WW^\top$) induces an automatic symmetry-breaking mechanism and yields weak recovery in $Θ(d^2\log d)$ samples. For untied attention, $S=UV^\top$, we uncover a fast-slow mechanism: the pre-activation mean first evolves on a fast timescale, while the overlaps evolve on a slower one. Weak recovery on the $Θ(d^2\log d)$ scale occurs when the state selected by the fast dynamics breaks the initial symmetry.

AI.tldr: This paper studies attention-indexed models representing multi-layer and multi-head attention architectures. In a high-dimensional limit, the population-loss landscape is characterized by finite trace order parameters, while online SGD is governed by an infinite hierarchy of matrix moments that can be exponentially well-approximated. The key finding is that attention parameterization acts as an architectural implicit bias: tied attention (S=WW^T) induces automatic symmetry-breaking yielding weak recovery in Θ(d²log d) samples, while untied attention (S=UV^T) exhibits a fast-slow mechanism where pre-activation mean evolves on a fast timescale and overlaps on a slower one, also achieving weak recovery at the same sample complexity.
AI.motivation: Attention mechanisms are central to modern foundation models, yet their training dynamics remain poorly understood, especially when attention matrices have extensive rank. The work aims to understand how attention parameterization itself can act as an architectural implicit bias and whether direct optimization can remain trapped in uninformative states.
AI.method: The study analyzes attention-indexed models in a suitable high-dimensional limit. It characterizes the population-loss landscape using trace order parameters and examines online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) through matrix moments. The analysis compares tied attention (S=WW^T) versus untied attention (S=UV^T) parameterizations.
AI.result: The population-loss landscape is characterized by a finite set of trace order parameters. Online SGD is governed by an infinite hierarchy of matrix moments that can be exponentially well-approximated by a finite truncated system. For tied attention, automatic symmetry-breaking occurs yielding weak recovery in Θ(d²log d) samples. For untied attention, a fast-slow mechanism emerges: pre-activation mean evolves on a fast timescale while overlaps evolve on a slower timescale, with weak recovery occurring when the fast dynamics breaks the initial symmetry.
AI.conclusion: Attention parameterization itself can act as an architectural implicit bias. Direct optimization of attention matrices can remain trapped in uninformative states, but tied attention (S=WW^T) automatically induces symmetry-breaking, while untied attention (S=UV^T) exhibits a fast-slow dynamics that eventually breaks symmetry, both achieving weak recovery at Θ(d²log d) sample complexity.

title: Clean Engineering, Unstable Measurement: A Preregistered Reliability Failure of Black-Box LLM Observers on Shared Endpoints
summary: Language-model judges now gate training data, score generations, and drive leaderboards. The judge is then a measurement instrument, resting on one rarely stated assumption: the same request, sent to the same model name, reads the same tomorrow. We audited that assumption in two preregistered campaigns with every threshold fixed in advance; neither got past validating its instrument. Across 52,988 audited request attempts, same-window repeat rankings agreed at Spearman 0.400 against a required 0.90, and byte-identical next-day replays agreed at 0.78 against a required 0.99, each time with the execution record at ceiling. Three mechanisms explain the gap: a label-to-meaning mapping that biased readouts as strongly as the signal; candidate gaps seven orders of magnitude below the instrument's own noise floor; and byte-identical inputs returning different rankings, a noise that exact-permutation readouts compound. Neither metric substitution nor sampling repaired it on the tested grid. Preregistered follow-ups bound the problem: waiting did not help on the days sampled (0.805 versus 0.800, replicated over five further days); switching providers did not help (four providers share the floor, medians 0.74 to 0.88, predicted by none of the metadata fields they expose); self-hosting on batch-invariant kernels helped only while the server was quiet; and on constructed errors with known gaps, the readout's separation tracks error type, not size. We distill the evidence into a three-level snapshot-identity ladder, eight design rules, and a reporting checklist; a pilot at roughly 2% of the study's call volume would have exposed both unreachable gates in advance. All results concern externally measured behaviour on shared serving infrastructure. On a shared endpoint, a model name is not a frozen instrument; a preregistered evaluation must measure its instrument before freezing any gate on it.

AI.tldr: Researchers audited the assumption that identical requests to the same language model produce consistent results. Across 52,988 audit attempts, they found severe inconsistencies: same-window repeat rankings agreed at only 0.400 (required 0.90) and next-day replays at 0.78 (required 0.99). Three mechanisms explain this: label-to-meaning mapping bias, candidate gaps below noise floor, and byte-identical inputs yielding different rankings. Attempted fixes (waiting, switching providers, self-hosting) failed to resolve the issue. The paper proposes a three-level snapshot-identity ladder, eight design rules, and a reporting checklist.
AI.motivation: Language-model judges now gate training data, score generations, and drive leaderboards. This assumes that sending the same request to the same model name will produce the same result tomorrow. The authors questioned this rarely-stated assumption and aimed to audit it empirically.
AI.method: Two preregistered audit campaigns with 52,988 request attempts. They measured: (1) same-window repeat rankings agreement using Spearman correlation (required 0.90), (2) byte-identical next-day replay agreement (required 0.99). They tested multiple potential fixes: waiting, switching providers, self-hosting, and metric substitution. They also constructed errors with known gaps to test readout sensitivity.
AI.result: Neither campaign validated its instrument. Same-window repeat rankings agreed at Spearman 0.400 vs required 0.90. Byte-identical next-day replays agreed at 0.78 vs required 0.99. Three mechanisms explained the gap: (1) label-to-meaning mapping bias, (2) candidate gaps 7 orders of magnitude below noise floor, (3) byte-identical inputs returning different rankings. None of the tested fixes repaired the issue: waiting (0.805 vs 0.800), switching providers (medians 0.74-0.88), self-hosting only when server quiet. A pilot at 2% of call volume would have exposed unreachable gates.
