AI.conclusion: On shared serving infrastructure, a model name is not a frozen instrument. A preregistered evaluation must measure its instrument before freezing any gate on it. The authors propose a three-level snapshot-identity ladder, eight design rules, and a reporting checklist to address this issue.

title: The impact of phase information for few-shot fine-grained image classification
summary: Few-shot fine-grained image classification (FSFGIC) aims to classify similar images with limited labeled examples. This work highlights the critical yet underutilized role of phase information in capturing structural relationships within an image. This study introduces a novel plug-and-play amplitude-phase integration (API) module that effectively combines local and global frequency amplitude and phase information for obtaining more comprehensive feature descriptors. Additionally, a dedicated network, named PSF-Net, is proposed that adaptively fuses phase-based spatial and frequency information for FSFGIS. The designed PSF-Net can be easily integrated into standard episodic training architectures for end-to-end training from scratch. Extensive experiments on five public datasets demonstrate that the method outperforms existing state-of-the-art benchmarks.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses few-shot fine-grained image classification by proposing a novel amplitude-phase integration (API) module and PSF-Net that leverages underutilized phase information, along with amplitude information, to capture structural relationships in images. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on five public datasets.
AI.motivation: Few-shot fine-grained image classification (FSFGIC) aims to classify similar images with limited labeled examples. The critical yet underutilized role of phase information in capturing structural relationships within an image is highlighted, as most existing methods focus primarily on amplitude (intensity) information.
AI.method: The work introduces a plug-and-play amplitude-phase integration (API) module that combines local and global frequency amplitude and phase information to create comprehensive feature descriptors. A dedicated network called PSF-Net is proposed to adaptively fuse phase-based spatial and frequency information. The network can be integrated into standard episodic training architectures for end-to-end training from scratch.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on five public datasets demonstrate that the method outperforms existing state-of-the-art benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PSF-Net with the API module achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art methods on five public datasets for few-shot fine-grained image classification, demonstrating the effectiveness of integrating phase information with amplitude information for capturing structural relationships in images.

title: Differentiable Interval Bottlenecks for Interpretable Anomaly Detection in Numerical Data
summary: Reconstruction-based anomaly detectors are accurate but opaque: a deep autoencoder flags a sample without telling a practitioner which feature ranges made it anomalous. We propose DIFFINT, an autoencoder whose latent bottleneck is structured as a set of soft, axis-aligned interval memberships learned end-to-end directly from raw numerical data, without any discretization or binarization. Each latent unit corresponds to a human-readable hyper-rectangle in feature space; an instance is encoded by how strongly it falls inside each interval relative to the other units, and its reconstruction error is the anomaly score. This keeps the power of differentiable representation learning while exposing an inspectable internal structure. We make the inductive bias precise: a certified reconstruction-error lower bound for points that fall outside every active coordinate of the learned support (with a Lipschitz-enforced decoder), and a graded, empirically verified suppression mechanism for the usual case in which only a few features are abnormal; and we provide a closed-form, label-free importance that ranks each (unit, feature) pair from quantities the model already maintains, turning trained intervals into auditable candidate constraints without ever seeing an anomaly label. On 48 ADBench benchmarks against 22 baselines under a common [-1, 1]-normalized protocol, DIFFINT attains the best mean rank overall on both metrics (4.10 on ROC-AUC, 4.16 on AUPR); among inlier-only detectors it leads its regime clearly, and it is competitive with the strongest contaminated-data detectors (see the stratified and complete-case analyses). It is the only interpretable detector in the statistically-tied leading cluster of seven methods.

AI.tldr: DIFFINT is a novel autoencoder-based anomaly detection method that uses soft, axis-aligned interval memberships in its latent bottleneck, making it interpretable while maintaining high accuracy. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on 48 ADBench benchmarks, ranking best overall on both ROC-AUC and AUPR metrics, and is the only interpretable method in the top-performing cluster.
AI.motivation: The key problem is that reconstruction-based anomaly detectors (like deep autoencoders) are accurate but opaque - they can flag anomalies without explaining which features contributed to the anomaly. There is a need for interpretable anomaly detection that can identify which feature ranges made a sample anomalous.
AI.method: DIFFINT structures its latent bottleneck as a set of soft, axis-aligned interval memberships learned end-to-end from raw numerical data without discretization or binarization. Each latent unit corresponds to a human-readable hyper-rectangle in feature space. An instance is encoded by how strongly it falls inside each interval relative to other units, and its reconstruction error serves as the anomaly score. The method includes a certified reconstruction-error lower bound for points outside learned support (with Lipschitz-enforced decoder), and provides closed-form, label-free importance scores for ranking (unit, feature) pairs.
AI.result: On 48 ADBench benchmarks against 22 baselines under a common [-1, 1]-normalized protocol, DIFFINT achieves the best mean rank on both metrics: 4.10 on ROC-AUC and 4.16 on AUPR. It leads among inlier-only detectors and is competitive with the strongest contaminated-data detectors. It is the only interpretable detector in the statistically-tied leading cluster of seven methods.
AI.conclusion: DIFFINT successfully bridges the gap between interpretability and high accuracy in anomaly detection. It maintains the representational power of deep learning while providing inspectable internal structure through interval-based latent representations, enabling practitioners to understand which features contribute to anomaly scores.

title: ExecRetrieval: Measuring the Functional-Correctness Gap in Code-Embedding Retrieval
comment: Accepted to EMNLP 2026 (Main Conference). Camera-ready version. 17 pages, 6 figures, 8 tables
summary: Embedding-based code retrieval is a core component of coding agents and retrieval-augmented code generation, where retrieving correct code matters more than retrieving lexically similar code. Existing code-retrieval benchmarks do not plant controlled, execution-verified single-edit variants of each query's canonical implementation in the search pool, leaving the question of whether embeddings can functionally discriminate correct from near-clone-but-incorrect code unanswered in a retrieval setting. Resolving this requires a benchmark whose search pool itself contains the relevant counterfactuals -- execution-verified buggy variants near-identical to each canonical -- so that a retriever's rank ordering can be directly tested for functional discrimination rather than topical or identity overlap. We introduce ExecRetrieval, 939 Python tasks each paired with one execution-verified canonical implementation and up to four execution-verified buggy distractors, each generated by a mechanical mutation making a single targeted edit, and evaluate 23 dense embedding configurations plus BM25 under provider-native invocation with paired McNemar tests and query-level bootstrap intervals. With near-clone counterfactuals in the pool, the top hosted system reaches exec@10 = 1.00 but only exec@1 = 0.331; rank-1 misses are paired buggy variants 91.5-99.4% of the time across the four leading systems, and the canonical scores below at least one of its four paired distractors in 67-78% of queries on the leading systems. The full dataset, execution oracle, embedding matrices, environment snapshot, and pairwise statistical tests are released at the URL in Appendix D.

AI.tldr: ExecRetrieval is a benchmark for evaluating code retrieval systems, featuring 939 Python tasks with execution-verified canonical implementations and buggy distractors generated via single targeted edits. Testing 23 dense embeddings plus BM25, the study finds that while top systems achieve exec@10 = 1.00, they only achieve exec@1 = 0.331, with rank-1 misses being buggy variants 91.5-99.4% of the time.
AI.motivation: Existing code-retrieval benchmarks lack execution-verified single-edit variants of canonical implementations in their search pools, leaving unanswered whether embeddings can functionally discriminate correct from near-clone-but-incorrect code in retrieval settings.
AI.method: The authors introduce ExecRetrieval with 939 Python tasks, each paired with one execution-verified canonical implementation and up to four execution-verified buggy distractors generated by mechanical mutations making single targeted edits. They evaluate 23 dense embedding configurations plus BM25 under provider-native invocation with paired McNemar tests and query-level bootstrap intervals.
AI.result: The top hosted system achieves exec@10 = 1.00 but only exec@1 = 0.331; rank-1 misses are paired buggy variants 91.5-99.4% of the time across four leading systems, and canonical scores below at least one distractor in 67-78% of queries on leading systems.
AI.conclusion: Even state-of-the-art embedding systems struggle to functionally discriminate correct code from near-clone buggy variants at rank-1, despite achieving high recall at top-10. This reveals a critical gap in current code retrieval capabilities that requires addressing through the benchmark and released artifacts.

title: GraFT: A Training-Free Framework for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models via 3D Scene Graphs
summary: 3D spatial reasoning underpins understanding and acting in the physical world, yet it remains unreliable in current multimodal large language models (MLLMs). These models falter at precise geometric measurement, at transforming between egocentric and allocentric viewpoints, and at grounding fine-grained appearance. The most common remedies fine-tune the model on large-scale curated spatial-reasoning datasets or attach dedicated encoders for 3D geometry, which typically couples the solution to costly supervision and a specific backbone. We instead introduce GraFT, a training-free framework that supplies the missing 3D structure through a compact, easily maintained 3D scene graph (3DSG). From this 3DSG, GraFT provides three spatial reasoning capabilities: (1) deterministic geometry through symbolic tools, (2) allocentric layout through a bird's-eye-view (BEV) rendering, and (3) visual-attribute grounding through task-relevant egocentric frames. On ScanQA, GraFT improves every metric over the same-backbone baseline, raising CIDEr by 27%. On VSI-Bench, GraFT improves frozen MLLMs by up to 65%, surpassing every proprietary and general-purpose open-source baseline, and several prominent fine-tuned spatial models.

AI.tldr: GraFT is a training-free framework that enhances 3D spatial reasoning in multimodal LLMs by integrating a compact 3D scene graph (3DSG) that provides deterministic geometry, allocentric BEV rendering, and visual-attribute grounding through egocentric frames. It achieves significant improvements on ScanQA (+27% CIDEr) and VSI-Bench (+65% over frozen MLLMs) without requiring fine-tuning or costly supervision.
AI.motivation: Current MLLMs struggle with 3D spatial reasoning tasks including precise geometric measurement, viewpoint transformations (egocentric to allocentric), and fine-grained visual attribute grounding. Existing remedies require expensive fine-tuning on large datasets or dedicated 3D encoders, which couples solutions to specific backbones and requires costly supervision.
AI.method: GraFT introduces a training-free framework that supplements MLLMs with 3D structure through a compact 3D scene graph (3DSG). The framework provides three spatial reasoning capabilities: (1) deterministic geometry via symbolic tools, (2) allocentric layout through bird's-eye-view (BEV) rendering, and (3) visual-attribute grounding through task-relevant egocentric frames.
AI.result: On ScanQA, GraFT improves every metric over the same-backbone baseline, with CIDEr increasing by 27%. On VSI-Bench, GraFT improves frozen MLLMs by up to 65%, surpassing all proprietary and general-purpose open-source baselines, as well as several prominent fine-tuned spatial models.
AI.conclusion: GraFT demonstrates that training-free augmentation through 3D scene graphs can significantly enhance spatial reasoning in MLLMs without the overhead of fine-tuning or specialized encoders. The approach is easily maintainable and achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.

title: Beyond Endpoint Scores: Time- and Capacity-Conditioned Evaluation of Continual Knowledge Updating
summary:
Continual knowledge-updating methods are often declared superior from one final checkpoint and one conventional adapter rank. We show that this can be insufficient to identify the better operating point. Holding a periodic hierarchy fixed, we compare it with cumulative replay over a 24-month Wikidata stream while varying evaluation month, replay LoRA rank, and query formulation. The apparent winner changes across this region: on Qwen2.5-1.5B, the hierarchy's 5.0-point advantage over rank-8 replay becomes an 11.6-point deficit against rank-72 replay, and at high ranks a consolidation-aligned endpoint can suggest a tie while time-averaged replay leads by 9-13 points. The same rank-conditioned reversal appears on Llama-3.2-1B and held-out paraphrases.
  These results show that method ranking in continual updating can depend jointly on when performance is measured and how much replay-side adaptation capacity the baseline receives. We therefore propose reporting trajectories and capacity sweeps, and declaring a robust winner only when the ordering is stable across the evaluation region; otherwise, comparisons should report winner regions and retention-stability-cost frontiers. Under this protocol, the periodic hierarchy is a lower-update-cost operating point, not a quality winner.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the common practice of evaluating continual knowledge-updating methods using only a single final checkpoint and one adapter rank. The authors show that method rankings can completely reverse depending on when performance is measured and how much replay-side adaptation capacity is allocated. They propose a more rigorous evaluation protocol requiring trajectory reporting and capacity sweeps to identify robust winners.
AI.motivation: The standard evaluation practice in continual knowledge updating compares methods using one final checkpoint and one conventional adapter rank. This paper demonstrates this approach is insufficient because the apparent winner can change dramatically across different evaluation conditions, leading to misleading conclusions about which method is truly superior.
AI.method: The authors held a periodic hierarchy fixed and compared it against cumulative replay over a 24-month Wikidata stream. They systematically varied three factors: (1) evaluation month, (2) replay LoRA rank (8 vs 72), and (3) query formulation. They tested on Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B, and held-out paraphrases.
AI.result: The method ranking reverses across the evaluation region. On Qwen2.5-1.5B: the hierarchy shows a 5.0-point advantage over rank-8 replay, but an 11.6-point deficit against rank-72 replay. At high ranks, a consolidation-aligned endpoint suggests a tie while time-averaged replay leads by 9-13 points. The same rank-conditioned reversal appears on Llama-3.2-1B and held-out paraphrases.
AI.conclusion: Method ranking in continual updating depends jointly on evaluation timing and replay-side adaptation capacity. The authors propose reporting trajectories and capacity sweeps, and declaring a robust winner only when ordering is stable across the evaluation region. Otherwise, comparisons should report winner regions and retention-stability-cost frontiers. Under this protocol, the periodic hierarchy is a lower-update-cost operating point, not a quality winner.

title: Concept of a Sensor Test Environment for Dusty Agricultural Conditions
summary: Dust in agriculture presents a significant challenge for autonomous agricultural machinery. Dust can impair the performance of sensors and algorithms. This work, therefore, presents a concept for a proving ground consisting of an indoor and outdoor area. The indoor area comprises a laboratory test bench where dust circulates in a closed system and a test hall where life-size objects can be placed. The outdoor area features dedicated test setups that enable reproducible data to be recorded with and without dust during real-world agriculture work. The proving ground and the setups are visualized in 3D.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a proving ground concept for testing autonomous agricultural machinery under dusty conditions. The facility includes an indoor area with a laboratory test bench (closed dust circulation system) and a test hall for life-size objects, plus an outdoor area with dedicated test setups for reproducible real-world agriculture data recording. The entire facility is visualized in 3D.
AI.motivation: Dust in agricultural environments poses a significant challenge for autonomous agricultural machinery, as it can impair the performance of both sensors and algorithms, potentially compromising operational reliability and safety.
AI.method: The authors developed a comprehensive proving ground concept consisting of: 1) An indoor laboratory test bench with a closed dust circulation system, 2) An indoor test hall for testing life-size objects, and 3) An outdoor area with dedicated test setups. The facility enables reproducible data collection with and without dust during real-world agricultural operations. All test setups and the proving ground are visualized in 3D.
AI.result: A complete proving ground concept has been developed featuring both indoor and outdoor testing areas. The indoor components include a closed-loop dust circulation system for controlled laboratory testing and a test hall for full-scale object testing. The outdoor area provides reproducible real-world agricultural testing conditions. The 3D visualization enables clear representation of the facility layout and test configurations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed proving ground concept provides a systematic approach for evaluating and improving the dust resilience of autonomous agricultural machinery. By enabling controlled testing with reproducible conditions, this facility can help advance the reliability and performance of autonomous systems in dusty agricultural environments.

title: RATL: Learning from Retrieved Residuals for Robust Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) complements parametric models with retrieved external evidence. The same idea is attractive for continuous-output regression, but directly reusing retrieved target values is often not robust when samples differ in output level, numerical scale, or local dynamics. Moreover, conventional forecasting pipelines generally use residuals for model optimization and error diagnosis, but do not retain individual historical residual examples as memory that can be accessed at inference time.For multivariate time-series forecasting, we propose RATL, a plug-in residual-retrieval and feedback-correction method. RATL freezes a base forecaster to construct retrieval keys and turns its historical forecast residuals into a train-only memory specific to that base model. At inference time, RATL retrieves residual trajectories from similar historical contexts subject to causal availability constraints, then uses a set-aware router operating over forecast blocks and variables to select and combine these trajectories. Experiments show that historical residuals matched to the current context contain reusable forecasting information and that RATL improves frozen base forecasters in most experimental settings. Ablations further show that learned routing strengthens raw residual feedback, while validation-based correction-strength selection limits residual over-injection.On real-world benchmarks, we use iTransformer as the primary frozen base forecaster, compare against multiple strong forecasting baselines, and test transferability across backbones. The results show that RATL can further improve base-forecaster performance in most settings.Overall, RATL shifts the retrieved object from historical target values to base-model-specific historical forecast errors, providing a plug-in, residual-memory-based paradigm for learned feedback correction in continuous-output forecasting.

AI.tldr: RATL proposes a retrieval-augmented approach for multivariate time-series forecasting that retrieves historical forecast residuals (instead of target values) from similar contexts, using a set-aware router to select and combine residual trajectories for feedback correction. The method freezes a base forecaster and builds a residual memory specific to it.
AI.motivation: Directly reusing retrieved target values in RAG for regression is not robust when samples differ in output level, numerical scale, or local dynamics. Additionally, conventional forecasting pipelines use residuals for optimization but don't retain individual historical residual examples as accessible memory at inference time.
AI.method: RATL freezes a base forecaster to construct retrieval keys and converts its historical forecast residuals into a train-only memory. At inference, it retrieves residual trajectories from similar historical contexts subject to causal availability constraints, then uses a set-aware router over forecast blocks and variables to select and combine these trajectories.
AI.result: Historical residuals matched to the current context contain reusable forecasting information. RATL improves frozen base forecasters in most experimental settings. Ablations show learned routing strengthens raw residual feedback, while validation-based correction-strength selection limits residual over-injection.
AI.conclusion: RATL shifts the retrieved object from historical target values to base-model-specific historical forecast errors, providing a plug-in, residual-memory-based paradigm for learned feedback correction in continuous-output forecasting. The method shows transferability across different backbone forecasters.

title: OctWorld: Long-Range World-Consistent Video Generation with Octree-Based 3D Mapping
summary: We present OctWorld, a video diffusion framework with persistent 3D memory for generating explorable, world-consistent, and high-fidelity visual scenes. Given a single image, OctWorld performs stable autoregressive world generation along user-specified camera trajectories. We focus on long-range generation, characterized by extended camera paths and wide viewpoint coverage, where preserving spatial consistency is particularly challenging when previously generated regions are revisited. To address this problem, we introduce OctMap, an extensible and spatially adaptive 3D memory that progressively fuses generated visual observations and their corresponding depth maps into a global representation. OctMap employs TSDF fusion within a dynamic sparse octree whose spatial resolution adapts to image evidence. This design preserves geometric and appearance details across diverse scene scales while maintaining low memory overhead. Experiments demonstrate that OctWorld generates long-range, spatially consistent videos and outperforms prior methods on both existing benchmarks and challenging long-range generation settings. OctMap also provides clear advantages over point-based caches and fixed-resolution TSDF volumes. Project page: https://maxtirerror.github.io/octworldpage/

title: Headroom-Drift Replay: A Primitive for Principled Replay Control in GRPO
comment: 51 pages, 25 figures, 17 tables. Accepted at COLM 2026
summary: RL-based post-training for reasoning models is increasingly bottlenecked by repeated fresh rollout generation, particularly in agentic settings where environment interaction dominates wall-clock cost. Replay can reduce this burden by reusing past trajectories, but existing methods typically embed it within larger training pipelines involving exploration, experience restructuring, or mixed-policy optimization. This makes replay's own contribution difficult to isolate. We ask a focused question: how far can principled replay selection alone go? We introduce Headroom-Drift Replay, a group-level replay control primitive for GRPO that separates reuse into two decisions. Headroom ranks stored groups by remaining learning value, while Drift gates them by compatibility with the current policy. The fresh on-policy stream remains unchanged, and the method adds no auxiliary generation or training machinery. Across mathematical reasoning, multimodal reasoning, and Agentic Search benchmarks, this single intervention outperforms naive replay and matches or exceeds broader replay methods on Avg Mean@32. In Agentic Search, where environment interaction dominates cost, it delivers comparable quality at materially lower wall-clock time.

AI.tldr: Headroom-Drift Replay is a novel group-level replay control primitive for GRPO that improves efficiency of RL-based post-training for reasoning models by separately evaluating remaining learning value (Headroom) and policy compatibility (Drift) of stored trajectories. It achieves comparable or better performance than broader replay methods while significantly reducing wall-clock time, especially in agentic settings.
AI.motivation: RL-based post-training for reasoning models is increasingly bottlenecked by repeated fresh rollout generation, particularly in agentic settings where environment interaction dominates wall-clock cost. While replay can reduce this burden by reusing past trajectories, existing methods embed replay within larger training pipelines, making its contribution difficult to isolate. The authors seek to answer: how far can principled replay selection alone go?
AI.method: The authors propose Headroom-Drift Replay, a group-level replay control primitive for GRPO that separates reuse into two decisions: (1) Headroom - ranks stored groups by remaining learning value, and (2) Drift - gates them by compatibility with the current policy. The fresh on-policy stream remains unchanged, and no auxiliary generation or training machinery is added.
AI.result: Across mathematical reasoning, multimodal reasoning, and Agentic Search benchmarks, this single intervention outperforms naive replay and matches or exceeds broader replay methods on Avg Mean@32. In Agentic Search, where environment interaction dominates cost, it delivers comparable quality at materially lower wall-clock time.
AI.conclusion: Principled replay selection alone can significantly improve efficiency of RL-based post-training for reasoning models. The Headroom-Drift Replay method provides a simple yet effective approach that isolates replay's contribution, achieving strong performance across diverse reasoning tasks while reducing computational costs, particularly in agentic settings.

title: Sparse auto-regressive modeling for scene generation from multi-view images
summary: Generating complete 3D scenes from sparse, unconstrained views is a fundamental challenge in 3D vision which requires reasoning beyond observed content while remaining computationally tractable. Existing feed-forward reconstruction methods are inherently limited to content visible in the input images, while 3D generative modeling is hindered by the high computational cost of dense volumetric representations and the scarcity of large-scale 3D supervision. We introduce SPAR3S, a sparse voxel-aligned 3D latent generative model for conditional scene completion without requiring ground-truth 3D data for supervision. Our key insight is to formulate 3D scene generation in a structured, compact, voxel-aligned 3D latent space where only occupied voxels are represented. We learn this sparse latent space directly from multi-view images using photometric supervision via differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. Given a partial set of observed voxels encoded from sparse input views, scene completion reduces to predicting the missing latent tokens and their spatial support within the voxel grid. To this end, we train a masked autoregressive transformer that jointly models voxel occupancy and latent token values, enabling efficient and spatially consistent generation of unseen regions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on synthetic indoor scenes, achieving higher novel-view quality than prior work. We further validate its generalization on RealEstate10k, highlighting its applicability to real-world data.

AI.tldr: SPAR3S is a sparse voxel-aligned 3D latent generative model for conditional scene completion from sparse views, learning from multi-view images without ground-truth 3D supervision using differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of generating complete 3D scenes from sparse, unconstrained views. Existing methods are limited to observed content (feed-forward reconstruction) or are computationally expensive (dense volumetric representations in 3D generative modeling). Additionally, large-scale 3D supervision is scarce.
AI.method: 1) Formulate 3D scene generation in a structured, compact, voxel-aligned 3D latent space where only occupied voxels are represented. 2) Learn this sparse latent space directly from multi-view images using photometric supervision via differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3) Given partial observed voxels from sparse input views, train a masked autoregressive transformer to jointly model voxel occupancy and latent token values for predicting missing latent tokens and their spatial support.
AI.result: Achieved higher novel-view quality than prior work on synthetic indoor scenes, and demonstrated generalization on RealEstate10k (real-world data).
AI.conclusion: The proposed SPAR3S method effectively generates complete 3D scenes from sparse views without requiring ground-truth 3D supervision, offering a computationally tractable solution with superior novel-view synthesis quality.

title: VestigeKV: The NoPE-MLA KV Cache Carries Its Own Eviction Signal in a Vestigial Branch
summary: The problem. A long-lived KV cache must be compressed before the queries that will read it exist; selection by observed attention (H2O, SnapKV) collapses there (0.00-0.33 needle retrieval on a NoPE MLA model), because a token's importance has not yet been observed. The method. On Kimi Linear, VestigeKV evicts by a query-independent signal the cache already carries: the 64-dimensional decoupled branch, a vestige of RoPE that NoPE training repurposes into a salience channel. Reading 11% of each row, it partitions the cache: the top-m rows stay in the attended tier; every other row moves -- exactly, never deleted -- to a GPU-resident archive reachable per step by a certified trigger. No training, no quantization, no weight or kernel change. Cost. Nothing measurable: retrieval holds at 1.00 under 8x and 0.92 under 32x from 8k to 65k context, zero gap to full-row selection. The attended tier is 0.25 KB of Kimi Linear's 8.1 KB per-token cache at 32x; the archive stays bit-exact and GPU-resident, with host offload as the VRAM-reclaiming variant. The recall tier -- the standard configuration -- holds 128x at 1.00. Kimi K3 is reported to use a NoPE Gated-MLA variant; if its cache layout matches, the method plausibly extends there -- we make no claim beyond the measured model. NoPE exclusivity. The identical operator on a RoPE MLA collapses to 0.08 (plain eviction: 0.42); query-independent salience itself exists only without rotation (top-1 targets span 2.3-6.7% of tokens vs. 10.2-46.8%), and query-universal exact merging is provably impossible under RoPE. All thresholds were frozen before data; 20 archived verdicts and 8 closed routes accompany the paper.

AI.tldr: VestigeKV is a query-independent KV cache compression method for NoPE MLA models that leverages a 64-dimensional decoupled branch (vestige of RoPE) as a salience signal. It achieves 1.00 retrieval at 8x compression and 0.92 at 32x compression without training, quantization, or kernel changes, by partitioning cache into an attended tier and a GPU-resident archive.
AI.motivation: The problem is that existing KV cache compression methods (H2O, SnapKV) fail on NoPE MLA models because they rely on observed attention scores, which don't exist before queries are made. There needs to be a query-independent signal to determine token importance for eviction decisions.
AI.method: VestigeKV uses the 64-dimensional decoupled branch from NoPE training as a salience channel. It reads 11% of each row to partition the cache: top-m rows stay in the attended tier while others move to a GPU-resident archive. No training, quantization, weight or kernel changes required.
AI.result: Retrieval maintains 1.00 at 8x and 0.92 at 32x compression from 8k to 65k context. The attended tier is 0.25 KB (vs 8.1 KB total) at 32x. The recall tier achieves 128x at 1.00. On RoPE MLA, performance collapses to 0.08, demonstrating NoPE exclusivity.
AI.conclusion: VestigeKV works only on NoPE models due to the existence of query-independent salience signals. The method plausibly extends to Kimi K3 (NoPE Gated-MLA variant) but cannot work with RoPE due to the provable impossibility of query-universal exact merging under rotation.

title: WorldReward: Reward Modeling for Camera-Conditioned World Models
summary: Camera-conditioned world models generate interactive videos in which commanded actions should induce the expected scene changes while appearance, geometry, and temporal dynamics remain coherent. Existing rewards assess these requirements separately: geometry-based rewards estimate trajectory execution but cannot judge the visual quality of the executed motion, whereas image-based rewards measure frame quality without capturing action execution or temporal dynamics. We posit that a vision-language model (VLM) offers a shared reasoning space for relating actions to their visual outcomes. However, judging a complete long video against its full action sequence creates a lengthy, noisy context in which short-lived local action evidence can be missed or diluted. We present WorldReward, a VLM-based pairwise preference reward model that unifies action-consistency and visual-quality evaluation for camera-conditioned world models. WorldReward decomposes paired videos into action-aligned chunks, organizes each chunk into structured visual evidence, and aggregates chunk-level decisions by voting into separate video-level action and visual-quality preferences. To train it, we construct a large-scale reasoning-augmented preference dataset using structured judgments generated by a frontier VLM and refined through tool-based agent auditing and targeted human review. We further introduce WorldReward-Bench, a human-annotated benchmark measuring reward-model agreement with human preferences across action consistency, appearance quality, and motion quality. WorldReward achieves the highest agreement on all three dimensions, exceeding GPT-5.5 by 3.42, 1.45, and 3.56 percentage points, respectively. When used for RL post-training of HY-WorldPlay 1.5, it consistently improves both action execution and visual quality across short- to long-term horizons.

AI.tldr: WorldReward is a VLM-based reward model that evaluates camera-conditioned world models by unifying action-consistency and visual-quality assessment through chunk-level decomposition and voting aggregation. It outperforms GPT-5.5 on a human-annotated benchmark and improves RL post-training of world models.
AI.motivation: Existing rewards for world models are inadequate: geometry-based rewards can only assess trajectory execution but not visual quality, while image-based rewards can only measure frame quality without capturing action execution or temporal dynamics. A unified approach is needed.
AI.method:
1) Decompose paired videos into action-aligned chunks
2) Organize each chunk into structured visual evidence
3) Aggregate chunk-level decisions by voting into separate video-level action and visual-quality preferences
4) Train on a large-scale reasoning-augmented preference dataset constructed using frontier VLM, refined through tool-based agent auditing and targeted human review
AI.result: WorldReward achieves highest agreement on all three dimensions of WorldReward-Bench, exceeding GPT-5.5 by 3.42 (action consistency), 1.45 (appearance quality), and 3.56 (motion quality) percentage points. When used for RL post-training of HY-WorldPlay 1.5, it consistently improves both action execution and visual quality across short- to long-term horizons.
AI.conclusion: WorldReward successfully unifies action-consistency and visual-quality evaluation for camera-conditioned world models through VLM-based pairwise preference learning, providing a more effective reward signal for RL post-training of world models.

title: OSR: Output Space Redistribution for Adaptive Label Removal in Classification Models
summary: Label removal occurs frequently in classification systems with evolving taxonomies, where categories must be dynamically updated or eliminated. To accommodate such changes, classification models must adapt accordingly. Existing solutions, broadly categorized as retraining-based and feature-space-adjustment-based, share common limitations despite their variations, including reliance on access to original data, substantial computational and storage costs, inconsistent results, poor scalability, and degradation of model utility. To address this, we propose a novel approach that leverages statistical redistribution in the output space to approximate the post-removal confidence vectors of a retrained model. Applicable as a modular output filter, our method bypasses the burden of feature-space adjustments or loss-function convergence, alleviating scalability limitations. Furthermore, by requiring only existing labels and prior output confidences, the method potentially mitigates privacy concerns inherent to data-dependent solutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive performance against full retraining, with improvements in computational efficiency and privacy preservation across several classification tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel method for handling label removal in classification systems with evolving taxonomies. The approach uses statistical redistribution in the output space to approximate post-retraining confidence vectors, functioning as a modular output filter that avoids data-dependent adjustments.
AI.motivation: Label removal frequently occurs in classification systems with evolving taxonomies where categories must be dynamically updated or eliminated. Existing solutions (retraining-based and feature-space-adjustment-based) have common limitations: reliance on original data, high computational/storage costs, inconsistent results, poor scalability, and model utility degradation.
AI.method: The proposed method leverages statistical redistribution in the output space to approximate post-removal confidence vectors of a retrained model. It functions as a modular output filter, bypassing the need for feature-space adjustments or loss-function convergence. The method only requires existing labels and prior output confidences, avoiding access to original data.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive performance against full retraining, with improvements in computational efficiency and privacy preservation across several classification tasks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed statistical redistribution approach successfully addresses the limitations of existing label removal methods, offering a privacy-preserving, computationally efficient alternative that achieves performance comparable to full retraining while functioning as a modular output filter.

title: RARF: Region-Aware Rectified Flows for 3D Brain MRI Inpainting
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures. Preprint version corresponding to the initial submission prior to peer review, submitted as part of our participation in the BraTS 2026 Challenge. The final accepted version will be openly available in the official MICCAI proceedings on the conference website
summary: Medical image inpainting has the potential to improve automated brain MRI analysis by reconstructing healthy tissue within pathological regions. We introduce RARF, a task-agnostic region-aware rectified flow framework for masked data generation. We instantiate the framework for 3D brain MRI inpainting as our submission to the BraTS Inpainting Challenge 2026. RARF restricts the stochastic interpolation process to the inpainting region, while the observed voxels remain fixed and provide patient-specific anatomical context. A three-dimensional neural network receives the partially voided image, with Gaussian noise filling the missing region, together with the inpainting mask and the corresponding timestep. The model is trained using masked flow-matching and reconstruction-consistency objectives, combined with mask-aware preprocessing and data augmentation. During inference, the learned velocity field transports the initial noise toward a plausible reconstruction of the missing tissue, which is then combined with the unchanged observed anatomy. Experiments under the BraTS evaluation protocol show that the proposed approach produces competitive reconstructions while maintaining anatomical consistency. Source code is available at: https://github.com/TomasGuija/rarf.

AI.tldr: RARF is a task-agnostic region-aware rectified flow framework for 3D brain MRI inpainting, using masked flow-matching and reconstruction-consistency objectives to reconstruct healthy tissue within pathological regions while maintaining anatomical consistency.
AI.motivation: Medical image inpainting can improve automated brain MRI analysis by reconstructing healthy tissue within pathological regions, addressing the need for高质量 brain MRI reconstructions in the BraTS Inpainting Challenge 2026.
AI.method: RARF restricts stochastic interpolation to the inpainting region while keeping observed voxels fixed. A 3D neural network processes partially voided images with Gaussian noise filling missing regions, combined with inpainting mask and timestep. Training uses masked flow-matching and reconstruction-consistency objectives with mask-aware preprocessing and data augmentation. Inference uses learned velocity field to transport initial noise toward plausible reconstruction.
AI.result: Experiments under the BraTS evaluation protocol show that the proposed approach produces competitive reconstructions while maintaining anatomical consistency.
AI.conclusion: RARF demonstrates that region-aware rectified flow can effectively reconstruct missing brain MRI tissue while preserving patient-specific anatomical context, achieving competitive performance in the BraTS Inpainting Challenge 2026.

title: RobustSeiz: An Open-Source Framework for Benchmarking the Robustness of EEG Seizure Detection Models
comment: 28 pages, 13 numbered figures, 9 tables; full-page graphical abstract and supplementary material included. Submitted to the Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association (JAMIA)
summary: Despite strong performance on held-out electroencephalography (EEG) data, seizure detectors may fail under real-world acquisition variability, artifacts, and adversarial inputs. We introduce RobustSeiz, an open-source, model-agnostic framework that provides a standardized, reproducible protocol for stress-testing and comparing seizure detectors under controlled, clinically motivated distribution shifts before deployment. We standardize four public scalp-EEG corpora (CHB-MIT, TUSZ, Siena, and SeizeIT1) into BIDS-EEG trees and evaluate subject-independent detectors on held-out splits. Environment, noise, and adversarial transforms are swept over predefined hyperparameter grids. Each run reports sample- and event-level sensitivity, precision, F1, false positives per 24 h, Lead and Lag onset timing, and Monte Carlo dropout predictive agreement. RobustSeiz includes a Dockerized GPU pipeline, experiment registry, and full-evaluation and research-subset modes. We demonstrate the framework with a contemporary seizure detector on TUSZ across the complete implemented shift grid; an AWGN analysis illustrates how perturbation severity changes detection quality, onset timing, and predictive agreement. RobustSeiz provides a shared benchmarking standard for evaluating seizure-detector robustness under realistic clinical stressors, extending pre-deployment assessment beyond clean-data accuracy.

AI.tldr: RobustSeiz is an open-source, model-agnostic framework for stress-testing seizure detectors under controlled distribution shifts (environment, noise, adversarial transforms) before deployment, using standardized EEG corpora and comprehensive evaluation metrics.
AI.motivation: Despite strong performance on held-out EEG data, seizure detectors may fail under real-world acquisition variability, artifacts, and adversarial inputs. There is a need for standardized, reproducible protocols to evaluate detector robustness under clinically realistic conditions before deployment.
AI.method: 1) Standardize four public scalp-EEG corpora (CHB-MIT, TUSZ, Siena, SeizeIT1) into BIDS-EEG format; 2) Evaluate subject-independent detectors on held-out splits; 3) Sweep environment, noise, and adversarial transforms over predefined hyperparameter grids; 4) Report sample/event-level sensitivity, precision, F1, false positives per 24h, onset timing (Lead/Lag), and Monte Carlo dropout predictive agreement; 5) Dockerized GPU pipeline with experiment registry and two evaluation modes.
AI.result: Demonstrated on TUSZ dataset with a contemporary seizure detector; AWGN analysis shows how perturbation severity affects detection quality, onset timing, and predictive agreement. Framework provides comprehensive benchmarking under realistic clinical stressors.
AI.conclusion: RobustSeiz provides a shared benchmarking standard for evaluating seizure-detector robustness under realistic clinical stressors, extending pre-deployment assessment beyond clean-data accuracy.

title: Sharpening the Ensemble: An SSIM-Aligned Residual Refiner for Brain-MRI Inpainting Post-Processing
comment: Accepted at the MICCAI BraTS Local Synthesis of Brain Tissue Inpainting Challenge (Task 4), MICCAI 2026. 12 pages, 2 figures
summary: Brain-MRI inpainting replaces a masked region of a scan with synthesized, anatomically plausible healthy tissue, so that analysis tools built for healthy brains can be applied to images they would otherwise reject. On the BraTS local-synthesis benchmark, which ranks submissions on the structural similarity index (SSIM), the peak signal-to-noise ratio, and the mean squared error (MSE) jointly, the strongest recent models are accurate, but several report blurry synthesized regions and attribute this to the mean-seeking behavior of the $\ell_1$ and MSE terms in their training losses. We address this in post-processing, forming a deep ensemble of the two co-first-place 2025 models and training a lightweight residual refiner on the ensemble's own outputs under an $\ell_1$ loss augmented with a structural-similarity term whose weight $λ$ we vary. At a moderate $λ$ the refiner improves SSIM over the ensemble, from $0.8767$ to $0.8780$ on a held-out reproduction of the official scorer and from $0.8555$ to $0.8572$ on the official validation leaderboard, with essentially no change in MSE. The gain is small but consistent, improving $62.6\%$ of the held-out cases with a signed-rank $p=2.2\times10^{-7}$, whereas over-weighting the structural term reverses it. Two ablations bound the effect. Adding any third model to the two-model ensemble degrades it, and classical unsharp masking fails to improve SSIM at any strength (best $0.8765$ against $0.8767$), so the gain reflects learned rather than indiscriminate sharpening. The result is a cheap, reproducible post-processing stage that improves an already strong ensemble without any large-scale retraining.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a post-processing method to improve brain MRI inpainting quality by combining a deep ensemble of two top 2025 models with a lightweight residual refiner trained under $\ell_1$ loss augmented with a structural-similarity term. This approach achieves modest but statistically significant SSIM improvements without requiring large-scale retraining.
AI.motivation: Current state-of-the-art brain MRI inpainting models on the BraTS benchmark produce blurry synthesized regions, attributed to the mean-seeking behavior of $\ell_1$ and MSE training losses. The authors aim to address this blurriness in post-processing rather than through expensive retraining.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) forming a deep ensemble of two co-first-place 2025 models, (2) training a lightweight residual refiner on the ensemble's outputs using $\ell_1$ loss augmented with a structural-similarity term (weight $\lambda$ varied), and (3) evaluating on the BraTS local-synthesis benchmark with SSIM, PSNR, and MSE metrics.
AI.result: At moderate $\lambda$, the refiner improved SSIM from 0.8767 to 0.8780 on held-out data and from 0.8555 to 0.8572 on the official validation leaderboard, with negligible MSE change. The improvement was consistent across 62.6% of cases (signed-rank p=2.2×10⁻⁷). Over-weighting the structural term reversed gains. Ablations showed: (1) adding any third model degraded performance, and (2) classical unsharp masking failed to improve SSIM (best 0.8765 vs 0.8767).
AI.conclusion: The proposed post-processing stage is a cheap, reproducible method that improves an already strong ensemble without large-scale retraining. The gains are small but statistically significant and stem from learned rather than indiscriminate sharpening. The method demonstrates that careful post-processing can marginally enhance state-of-the-art medical image synthesis results.

title: Unlocking Lossless Speedups in LLMs via Discrete Diffusion
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) owe much of their success to next-token prediction (NTP), but their autoregressive (AR) structure requires slow, sequential token generation. To overcome this bottleneck, we introduce diffusion-augmented LLMs, a new class of models that defines an AR model distribution while using diffusion to draw multiple tokens in parallel from that distribution. We decouple the parameters of these models into two sets: AR weights, trained using the standard NTP objective, and lightweight diffusion weights, trained to generate multiple tokens simultaneously. The diffusion weights are learned through a simple Diffusion Distillation phase that adds negligible overhead to existing LLM training pipelines. We also introduce $Ψ$-Spec, a family of samplers that enables lossless acceleration and inference-time scaling at a fixed context length. Unlike speculative decoding, our method requires no separate draft model. Unlike diffusion LLMs (d-LLMs), it accelerates generation without sacrificing the quality of the underlying AR model. The resulting models, called Uno, can be trained from scratch or built by augmenting existing open-weight AR LLMs. Uno achieves higher throughput than leading speculative-decoding methods at every evaluated batch size and delivers up to $3\times$ speedups over the base AR model, including at the largest batch size supported by the device. Notably, our 8B Uno model outperforms the leading open d-LLM, the 26B DiffusionGemma, and the proprietary Mercury 2 across all evaluated benchmarks in agentic tool use, coding, and long-context reasoning. We release code and checkpoints at: https://s-sahoo.github.io/uno/

AI.tldr: Uno introduces diffusion-augmented LLMs that combine autoregressive next-token prediction with parallel token generation via diffusion, achieving up to 3x speedup over base AR models while maintaining quality and outperforming leading diffusion LLMs and proprietary models.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive LLMs suffer from slow sequential token generation due to their next-token prediction structure, creating a bottleneck in inference speed despite their success.
AI.method: Decouples model parameters into AR weights (trained with standard NTP) and lightweight diffusion weights (trained via Diffusion Distillation to generate multiple tokens in parallel). Introduces Ψ-Spec samplers for lossless acceleration and inference-time scaling at fixed context length.
AI.result: Uno achieves higher throughput than leading speculative-decoding methods at every batch size, delivers up to 3x speedups over base AR models (including at largest batch sizes), and the 8B model outperforms the 26B DiffusionGemma and proprietary Mercury 2 across agentic tool use, coding, and long-context reasoning benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-augmented LLMs (Uno) successfully accelerate generation without sacrificing AR model quality, offering a practical solution that can be trained from scratch or built by augmenting existing AR LLMs, with code and checkpoints released.

title: IchthyoNoma: Nomenclature and Context Sensitivity of Zero-Shot Biological Vision--Language Models for Bangladeshi Freshwater Fish Recognition
summary: Zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as training-free species recognizers, but reported accuracy can reflect more than visual species knowledge. We audit CLIP, BioCLIP, BioCLIP2, and a multilingual Jina CLIP v2 control on seven freshwater-fish categories from two Bangladeshi sources (10,321 images). BioCLIP2 reaches 72.36% on BFF-15 with English common names and 68.91% on SylFishBD with scientific names, versus 25.15% and 14.40% for generic CLIP. BioCLIP2 Bengali prompts are near chance in balanced accuracy (14.22-14.29%); Jina partially recovers Bengali discrimination to 21.89% and 16.36%, but bare Bengali names return to 14.29% on both sources. Paired SylFishBD interventions show no significant weak-blur effect, modest losses from stronger blur/gray masking, a larger white-mask artifact, and strong species dependence. Zero-shot biological VLM scores therefore jointly reflect biological specialization, multilingual alignment, nomenclature, prompt formulation, and context.

AI.tldr: This paper audits four zero-shot vision-language models (CLIP, BioCLIP, BioCLIP2, and multilingual Jina CLIP v2) for freshwater fish species recognition in Bangladesh. The study reveals that performance depends not just on visual knowledge but also on multilingual alignment, nomenclature, and prompt formulation. BioCLIP2 achieves 72.36% accuracy on BFF-15 with English prompts but drops to near chance (14.22-14.29%) with Bengali prompts, while Jina partially recovers Bengali performance to 21.89%.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot VLMs are increasingly used as training-free species recognizers, but reported accuracy may reflect factors beyond visual species knowledge—including multilingual alignment, nomenclature, and prompt formulation. This study audits whether VLM scores truly reflect biological specialization or confounded by other factors.
AI.method: The authors evaluated four models (CLIP, BioCLIP, BioCLIP2, and Jina CLIP v2) on 7 freshwater fish categories from two Bangladeshi datasets (BFF-15 and SylFishBD) totaling 10,321 images. They tested prompts in English common names, scientific names, and Bengali. Paired interventions tested blur/gray masking effects and white-mask artifacts.
AI.result: BioCLIP2 achieved 72.36% on BFF-15 with English common names and 68.91% on SylFishBD with scientific names, versus only 25.15% and 14.40% for generic CLIP. Bengali prompts showed near-chance performance (14.22-14.29%) for BioCLIP2, while Jina partially recovered Bengali discrimination to 21.89% and 16.36%. Weak blur showed no significant effect, but stronger blur/gray masking caused modest losses, with larger white-mask artifacts and strong species dependence observed.
AI.conclusion: Zero-shot biological VLM scores jointly reflect biological specialization, multilingual alignment, nomenclature, prompt formulation, and context—not just visual species knowledge. This audit reveals significant performance gaps when models encounter non-English nomenclature, highlighting the need to consider multilingual alignment and prompt design when deploying VLMs for biodiversity monitoring.

title: A location-invariant estimator of extremal quantile treatment effects for heavy-tailed distributions
summary: Quantile treatment effects (QTEs) measure the effect of a treatment on the distribution of an outcome, and their estimation at extreme quantile levels is of central interest in applications where the target quantiles lie far beyond the range of the data. For heavy-tailed potential outcomes, existing extremal QTE estimators rely on extrapolation combined with a causal extreme value index (EVI) estimator, but the resulting estimator is not invariant under a common location shift of the potential outcome distributions, even though the population QTE is. We address this issue in two steps. First, we adapt the location-invariant Fraga estimator of the EVI to the causal setting using inverse propensity score weighting. Second, we replace the original extrapolation formula with a difference-based scheme, under which the location parameter cancels when quantile differences are taken. The resulting QTE estimator is therefore location invariant. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed extremal QTE estimators, and provide a consistent variance estimator, leading to asymptotically valid inference. A simulation study confirms the location invariance, the stability with respect to the threshold, and the coverage of the proposed methods.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the location invariance problem in extreme quantile treatment effect estimation for heavy-tailed outcomes by adapting the Fraga EVI estimator with inverse propensity weighting and using a difference-based extrapolation scheme, establishing asymptotic properties and valid inference procedures.
AI.motivation: Estimate quantile treatment effects (QTEs) at extreme quantile levels for heavy-tailed potential outcomes, where existing extremal QTE estimators lack location invariance under location shifts of potential outcome distributions.
AI.method: Two-step solution: (1) Adapt the location-invariant Fraga estimator of extreme value index (EVI) to causal settings using inverse propensity score weighting; (2) Replace original extrapolation with a difference-based scheme that cancels the location parameter when computing quantile differences.
AI.result: Proposed estimator achieves location invariance; consistency and asymptotic normality established; consistent variance estimator developed for asymptotically valid inference.
AI.conclusion: The simulation study confirms location invariance, threshold stability, and proper coverage of the proposed methods, providing a theoretically sound and practically reliable approach for estimating extremal QTEs.

title: Catalogue Photography as a Cold Start: Toward Deployable Carbide Burr Recognition
comment: Extended abstract not yet published to a conference or journal
summary: Verifying that manufactured batches of milling tools or carbide rotary burrs conform to production order sheets remains a largely manual and error-prone quality assurance task. Automating this process with computer vision faces a critical cold-start constraint since no labelled imagery is available, leaving manufacturer catalogue photography as the sole source of supervision. We investigate how far catalogue supervision can support an industrial recognition pipeline under domain shift, explicitly measuring the gap between catalogue separability and performance on held-out field photographs. Our findings reveal three key insights. First, off-the-shelf frozen feature extractors do not reliably separate the two task attributes, head shape and tooth profile, motivating targeted representation learning. Second, metric learning produces near-perfect unsupervised cluster discovery on catalogue images (adjusted Rand index 0.94--0.97), but less than half of this gain transfers to field photographs. Third, the largest transfer gains do not come from model scale or representation complexity, but from simple changes that reduce domain sensitivity: converting images to grayscale (+0.22) and constraining retrieval using the known order sheet via Hungarian assignment (+0.11). We therefore treat catalogue photography as a useful cold start rather than a deployment-ready training domain, and provide empirical baselines and an evaluation protocol for catalogue-to-field transfer in precision tool manufacturing.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses automated quality assurance for milling tools and carbide rotary burrs using computer vision under a cold-start constraint—only unlabelled catalogue photos are available. The authors investigate catalogue-to-field transfer learning, finding that metric learning achieves near-perfect clustering on catalogue images but transfers poorly to field photographs. Simple domain-reduction techniques (grayscale conversion and Hungarian assignment) provide the largest transfer gains, challenging the assumption that model scale or complexity drives transfer success.
AI.motivation: Manual verification of manufactured milling tools/burrs against production order sheets is error-prone and inefficient. Automation via computer vision faces a critical cold-start problem: no labelled imagery exists, leaving only manufacturer catalogue photography as supervision. The authors seek to quantify how far catalogue supervision can bridge this gap under domain shift.
AI.method: The authors employ metric learning with frozen feature extractors to discover clusters on catalogue images, measuring unsupervised cluster quality via adjusted Rand index (ARI). They evaluate transfer performance on held-out field photographs and systematically test domain-reduction strategies: converting images to grayscale and using Hungarian assignment for constrained retrieval based on known order sheets.
AI.result: Three key insights emerge: (1) Off-the-shelf frozen feature extractors fail to reliably separate head shape and tooth profile attributes; (2) Metric learning achieves near-perfect unsupervised cluster discovery on catalogue images (ARI 0.94–0.97), but less than 50% of this gain transfers to field photographs; (3) The largest transfer gains come from simple domain-reduction techniques—grayscale conversion (+0.22 ARI) and Hungarian assignment (+0.11 ARI)—rather than model scale or representation complexity.
AI.conclusion: Catalogue photography serves as a useful cold-start mechanism but is not deployment-ready for direct transfer to field settings. The authors provide empirical baselines and an evaluation protocol for catalogue-to-field transfer in precision tool manufacturing, challenging the intuition that larger or more complex models improve domain transfer.

title: Subspace Inference Enables Efficient Active Reward Learning from Preferences
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a powerful yet sample-inefficient approach for learning reward models from human preferences, making active learning a critical component in synthesizing informative preference queries. However, effective uncertainty quantification required for active learning remains a key challenge for large neural network reward models. In this paper, we introduce PreferenceEKF, a sample-efficient approach that tracks reward model uncertainty by framing active preference learning as a sequential Bayesian filtering problem. Instead of relying on computationally prohibitive posterior inference over the full neural network parameter space, our method performs sequential inference via an extended Kalman filter within a low-dimensional parameter subspace, continuously updating the reward model posterior as new preference queries arrive. Our approach enables scalable sampling of neural network parameters to efficiently compute acquisition functions for active reward learning. Experiments on the D4RL and V-D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves better sample efficiency, runtime, scalability, and calibration compared to other Bayesian deep learning approaches, and the learned reward models lead to competitive offline reinforcement learning policy performance. This highlights the potential of scalable Bayesian methods for preference-based reward modeling in RLHF. Our code is available at https://github.com/yutaizhou/bnn_pref.

AI.tldr: PreferenceEKF is a sample-efficient method for active preference learning in RLHF that uses sequential Bayesian filtering via an extended Kalman filter within a low-dimensional parameter subspace to track reward model uncertainty, enabling scalable acquisition function computation for active reward learning.
AI.motivation: RLHF has emerged as a powerful approach for learning reward models from human preferences, but it suffers from sample inefficiency. Active learning could address this by synthesizing informative preference queries, but effective uncertainty quantification required for active learning remains a key challenge for large neural network reward models.
AI.method: The paper frames active preference learning as a sequential Bayesian filtering problem. Instead of performing computationally prohibitive posterior inference over the full neural network parameter space, the method performs sequential inference via an extended Kalman filter (EKF) within a low-dimensional parameter subspace. This approach enables scalable sampling of neural network parameters to efficiently compute acquisition functions for active reward learning.
AI.result: Experiments on D4RL and V-D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that PreferenceEKF achieves better sample efficiency, runtime, scalability, and calibration compared to other Bayesian deep learning approaches. The learned reward models lead to competitive offline reinforcement learning policy performance.
AI.conclusion: The results highlight the potential of scalable Bayesian methods for preference-based reward modeling in RLHF. The approach successfully balances computational feasibility with accurate uncertainty estimation, making it practical for large neural network reward models.

title: The Blind Spot in 2D Infants' Pose Estimation:Robust Learning from Noisy Annotations
summary: Noisy annotations pose a significant challenge for supervised deep learning, as neural networks rely on large-scale, high-quality labeled data whose corruption can severely impair model performance. Although robustness to label noise has been extensively studied for classification tasks, it remains relatively underexplored in Pose Estimation (PE). This limitation becomes critical in clinical contexts, including neonatology, where PE of preterm infants is used to support the assessment of spontaneous motility, a key indicator of neurodevelopmental trajectories. In such settings, infants' images labeling is further hindered by visual challenges (e.g., keypoint self-occlusions, caregiver interference), making the annotation process inherently susceptible to errors. To tackle noisy annotations in PE, we introduce REliable keypoint selection via Memory of traINing Dynamics (REMIND), a clustering-based keypoint-selection strategy that exploits keypoint-wise training dynamics to identify noisy labels without assuming any prior knowledge of the noise distribution, thus enabling noise-free model training. When evaluated on the proprietary NeoPose dataset, comprising 46 videos of 46 preterm infants recorded in real clinical settings, REMIND correctly identifies noisy annotations across multiple corruption scenarios, achieving up to 93\% Area Under the Curve (AUC) with three different PE architectures used in the relevant literature. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explicitly address label noise in preterm infants' PE, paving the way for the design of trustworthy learning-based algorithms for infants'monitoring support when data quality cannot be guaranteed.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses label noise in pose estimation for preterm infants by introducing REMIND, a clustering-based method that uses training dynamics to identify noisy keypoint annotations without prior noise distribution knowledge. The method achieves 93% AUC on a proprietary clinical dataset.
AI.motivation: Noisy annotations pose a challenge for supervised deep learning in Pose Estimation (PE), particularly in clinical contexts like neonatology where PE of preterm infants supports neurodevelopmental assessment. The annotation process is susceptible to errors due to visual challenges (keypoint self-occlusions, caregiver interference), yet this problem remains underexplored.
AI.method: REMIND (REliable keypoint selection via Memory of traINing Dynamics) - a clustering-based keypoint-selection strategy that exploits keypoint-wise training dynamics to identify noisy labels without assuming any prior knowledge of the noise distribution.
AI.result: Evaluated on NeoPose dataset (46 videos of 46 preterm infants in real clinical settings), REMIND achieves up to 93% AUC with three different PE architectures, correctly identifying noisy annotations across multiple corruption scenarios.
AI.conclusion: First study to explicitly address label noise in preterm infants' PE, paving the way for trustworthy learning-based algorithms for infant monitoring when data quality cannot be guaranteed.

title: Conditioning Degenerate Diffusion Models
summary: Current conditioned generative models heavily rely on score functions for guidance during training. When the generative model is a diffusion process with a singular diffusion coefficient and the underlying (conditional) densities either do not exist or are not smooth, we use causal optimal transport to define \emph{approximate} loss functions that identify a minimum-entropy control for guidance under minimal assumptions. Our approach relies on causal optimal transport and its characterization through the predictable representation property of (conditioned) diffusion processes whose associated martingale problem is well posed, à la Üstünel.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses limitations in conditioned generative models that rely on score functions, particularly when dealing with diffusion processes with singular diffusion coefficients or non-smooth conditional densities. The authors propose using causal optimal transport to define approximate loss functions for guidance under minimal assumptions.
AI.motivation: Current conditioned generative models heavily depend on score functions for guidance during training. However, when the generative model is a diffusion process with a singular diffusion coefficient and the underlying (conditional) densities either do not exist or are not smooth, traditional score-based approaches fail. This motivates the need for an alternative framework that works under minimal assumptions.
AI.method: The approach relies on causal optimal transport and its characterization through the predictable representation property of (conditioned) diffusion processes. The method uses the well-posed martingale problem formulation à la Üstünel to define approximate loss functions that can handle singular diffusion coefficients and non-smooth densities.
AI.result: The method defines approximate loss functions that can identify a minimum-entropy control for guidance, functioning effectively even when traditional score-based methods are inapplicable due to the absence or non-smoothness of conditional densities.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework provides a theoretically grounded approach for guidance in conditioned generative models that works under minimal assumptions, extending the applicability of diffusion-based generative models to cases with singular diffusion coefficients and non-smooth conditional distributions.

title: Stable and Scalable Bundle Adjustment of Holistic 3D Structures
comment: To appear at ECCV 2026. Code available as part of the LIMAP toolbox at https://github.com/cvg/limap/
summary: Bundle Adjustment (BA) is a cornerstone of 3D computer vision and has benefited from decades of advances in sparse optimization and numerical methods. It was originally developed for jointly optimizing camera intrinsics, poses and sparse 3D points. While extensions incorporate lines and other primitives, integrating richer geometric structures such as parallelism, coplanarity, or wireframes often introduces significantly increased computational cost and reduced numerical stability. In this paper, we propose a unified framework that extends bundle adjustment to jointly optimize geometric features and higher-order relations. We first introduce a taxonomy that distinguishes scalable geometric features with direct 2D measurements (e.g., points and lines), from groups encoding higher-order relations (e.g., coplanarity, parallelism, etc.), where we show that groups can be modeled as camera-like entities within the bundle adjustment framework. Building on this formulation, we propose that both group constraints and cross-feature relations (i.e., point-line associations) can be expressed through 2D reprojection measurements. By formulating group-induced and cross-feature reprojection errors, we preserve the sparsity structure of classical point-based BA under Schur elimination, while avoiding direct 3D regularization that degrades the conditioning and stability. Experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate runtime performance comparable to classical point-only bundle adjustment, while producing significantly richer 3D structures and improved geometric accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a unified framework that extends traditional Bundle Adjustment (BA) to jointly optimize geometric features (points, lines) and higher-order relations (coplanarity, parallelism, wireframes). The key innovation is modeling groups as camera-like entities and expressing group constraints through 2D reprojection measurements, preserving the sparsity structure of classical point-based BA while avoiding direct 3D regularization.
AI.motivation: Traditional BA optimizes camera intrinsics, poses, and sparse 3D points. While extensions incorporate lines and other primitives, integrating richer geometric structures like parallelism, coplanarity, or wireframes introduces significantly increased computational cost and reduced numerical stability. There was a need for a unified framework that can handle both geometric features and higher-order relations efficiently.
AI.method: The authors introduce a taxonomy distinguishing scalable geometric features with direct 2D measurements (points, lines) from groups encoding higher-order relations (coplanarity, parallelism). They model groups as camera-like entities within the BA framework. Both group constraints and cross-feature relations (point-line associations) are expressed through 2D reprojection measurements, preserving sparsity under Schur elimination while avoiding direct 3D regularization.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate runtime performance comparable to classical point-only bundle adjustment, while producing significantly richer 3D structures and improved geometric accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The proposed unified framework successfully extends BA to handle higher-order geometric relations without compromising computational efficiency or numerical stability. It achieves comparable runtime to classical point-only BA while delivering richer 3D structures and better geometric accuracy.

title: Hardware-Aware FP4 FlashAttention-4
summary: Blackwell's 4-bit floating-point (FP4) tensor cores do not automatically make attention faster because softmax conversion and on-chip dependencies dominate once its matrix products shrink. We address this with \emph{Direct-P} for noncausal inference and a causal path that passes the forward quantization directly into backward. Direct-P maps scores directly to FP4 probabilities and reaches up to 2.13$\times$ the bfloat16 (BF16) forward throughput on an NVIDIA GB200. The causal path reconstructs probabilities from saved quantized queries and keys and uses 8-bit floating-point (FP8) gradient operands, accelerating a complete single-GPU 8-billion-parameter update by up to 1.14$\times$. Matched distributed training retains FP8 probabilities and values; every tested MXFP4 probability/value training trajectory diverges.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses performance bottlenecks in using NVIDIA Blackwell's 4-bit floating-point (FP4) tensor cores for attention mechanisms. The authors propose Direct-P for noncausal inference and a causal path with FP8 gradient operands to overcome softmax conversion and on-chip dependency issues, achieving up to 2.13× throughput improvement over BF16 and 1.14× speedup in training.
AI.motivation: FP4 tensor cores on Blackwell GPUs do not automatically accelerate attention because softmax conversion and on-chip dependencies become bottlenecks when matrix products shrink. This limits the的实际 benefits of low-precision computation.
AI.method: The authors propose two solutions: (1) Direct-P maps attention scores directly to FP4 probabilities for noncausal inference, bypassing softmax conversion overhead; (2) A causal path that reconstructs probabilities from saved quantized queries/keys during backward pass, using FP8 gradient operands to maintain efficiency.
AI.result: Direct-P achieves up to 2.13× the bfloat16 (BF16) forward throughput on NVIDIA GB200. The causal path accelerates a complete single-GPU 8-billion-parameter update by up to 1.14×. However, matched distributed training with MXFP4 probability/value trajectories diverges in all tested cases.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that FP4 acceleration for attention requires careful design to avoid softmax and dependency bottlenecks. Direct-P and the causal path provide effective solutions for inference and training, though distributed training with FP4 probabilities/values remains unstable.

title: DSAQuant: Denoising-Stage-Aligned Quantization-Aware Training for Video Generation
summary: Video diffusion models (VDMs) have achieved impressive progress in text-to-video generation, but their high memory and computational costs hinder practical deployment. Quantization-aware training (QAT) is an effective solution for compressing and accelerating advanced generative models without runtime overhead at inference.
